AI.conclusion: Biologically inspired modular controllers with tunable inter-module communication offer a practical approach for robust movement under noise and energy constraints in robotics, enabling trade-off control between precision, stability, and actuation cost.

title: Robust Dual-Model Collaborative Random Vector Functional Link Network
summary: Random vector functional link (RVFL) networks are lightweight and fast neural models that offer efficient training and strong generalization through randomized hidden-layer weights and direct input-output connections. However, conventional RVFL models are sensitive to noisy labels, outliers, and imbalanced data, which limits their performance in real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose the kernel risk-sensitive mean p-power based RVFL (KRPRVFL) model, which integrates the computational efficiency of RVFL with the robustness of the kernel risk-sensitive mean p-power (KRP) criterion. By replacing the standard least-squares objective with a KRP-based loss, KRPRVFL adaptively reduces the influence of corrupted or unreliable samples during training, resulting in improved stability and generalization. Additionally, a collaborative learning mechanism is introduced to enable adaptive interaction among model components, further enhancing robustness in complex and noisy environments. The proposed framework also leverages kernel-induced feature mapping to capture nonlinear relationships without requiring explicit hidden-layer selection, maintaining both efficiency and scalability. Extensive experiments on UCI and KEEL benchmark datasets demonstrate that KRPRVFL consistently outperforms baseline models in terms of accuracy, robustness, and statistical significance, highlighting its effectiveness as a fast, scalable, and reliable solution for challenging classification tasks.

AI.tldr: KRPRVFL: a robust, kernelized mean-p-power risk-sensitive RVFL that improves robustness to noisy labels, outliers, and imbalance while maintaining efficiency, via kernel mapping and collaborative learning; shows superior accuracy and robustness on UCI/KEEL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional RVFLs are lightweight and fast but fragile to noisy labels, outliers, and imbalanced data, limiting real-world performance; need a robust, scalable learning framework that preserves RVFL efficiency.
AI.method: Replace the standard least-squares objective in RVFL with a kernel risk-sensitive mean p-power (KRP) loss. Employ kernel-induced feature mapping to capture nonlinearities without explicit hidden-layer tuning. Introduce a collaborative learning mechanism to enable adaptive interaction among model components, enhancing robustness in noisy environments.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on UCI and KEEL datasets shows KRPRVFL achieves higher accuracy, improved robustness, and statistically significant gains over baselines, while maintaining efficiency and scalability.
AI.conclusion: KRPRVFL provides a fast, scalable, and reliable solution for challenging classification tasks, combining RVFL efficiency with kernelized, risk-sensitive robustness and collaborative learning.

title: Face Re-morphing: Differential Morphing Attack Detection via Feature-Space Similarity Changes
summary: Face morphing attacks pose a serious threat to face recognition systems because a single morphed document image can be matched to multiple contributors. Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) addresses this threat by comparing a document image with a trusted live image, but existing methods often rely on static feature differences, constituent-face reconstruction, or multi-cue fusion. This paper proposes Face Re-morphing, a D-MAD method that uses the feature-space response to an additional morphing operation as a detection cue. Given a document image and a trusted live image, the proposed method generates a re-morphed image and uses the change between the document--live and live--re-morphed cosine similarities as the detection score. Experiments on FRLL-Morphs and FEI Morph show that the proposed cue is effective across different morphing conditions, re-morphing methods, and face recognition models. Comparisons with existing methods show favorable results on AMSL and indicate that the proposed method performs well under the Criminal condition on FEI Morph Version~1, particularly when using MorDIFF. These results indicate that re-morphing-induced similarity change provides a complementary cue for D-MAD.

AI.tldr: A re-morphing cue is used for differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD). By generating a re-morphed image from the trusted live image and document image, the method measures the change in cosine similarity (document-live vs. live-re-morphed) as the detection score, providing a complementary cue to existing D-MAD techniques.
AI.motivation: Face morphing attacks enable a single morphed document to match multiple individuals, compromising FR systems. Current D-MAD methods rely on static feature differences, constituent-face reconstruction, or multi-cue fusion, which can be vulnerable or limited. A dynamic cue derived from re-morphing may capture non-linear feature-space behavior not exposed by static cues.
AI.method: Given a document image and a trusted live image, generate a re-morphed image. Compute cosine similarities for two pairs: document–live and live–re-morphed. Use the change between these similarities as the D-MAD detection score. Evaluate across FRLL-Morphs and FEI Morph datasets, under various morphing conditions, re-morphing methods, and face recognition models. Compare with existing methods and assess performance under AMSL and FEI Morph Version 1 Criminal condition, especially with MorDIFF.
AI.result: The re-morphing-induced similarity change provides an effective and complementary detection cue for D-MAD. It yields favorable results on AMSL and robust performance under the Criminal condition on FEI Morph Version 1 when using MorDIFF, indicating robustness across morphing conditions and FR models.
AI.conclusion: Re-morphing-induced similarity change is a valuable addition to D-MAD, offering a complementary cue that generalizes across datasets, morphing conditions, and recognition models, and enhances detection performance when integrated with existing methods.

title: Stable Miscalibration in Large Language Models: A Practical View of High-Confidence Errors
comment: Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning (EIML)@ICML 2026. 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: High-confidence errors in large language models are often treated as evidence of fragile internal inference. We study a different possibility: stable miscalibration, where a confident wrong answer remains locally stable under small perturbations. We combine two diagnostics: a label-aware output-level audit score that ranks domains by confidence variation and overconfident mistakes under a forced-answer baseline, and an internal sensitivity probe that measures hidden-state movement. On a multi-domain binary factual audit set, this audit score tracks where abstention-aware self-critique reduces decision loss, although direct labeled baselines rank the same gain more strongly. Internally, self-critical prompting consistently reduces hidden-state sensitivity across layers in three open-weight models. This supports prompt-induced local stabilization rather than a purely output-level abstention pattern, but it does not imply calibration: audit-defined overconfident errors are not clearly more locally sensitive than confidently correct answers, so some high-confidence errors may be stable and miscalibrated rather than simply fragile.

AI.tldr: High-confidence errors in LLMs can reflect stable miscalibration rather than fragile inference. The study uses an audit score and internal sensitivity probes to show self-critical prompting induces local stabilization, while calibration is not guaranteed by these findings.
AI.motivation: To distinguish between fragile inference and stable miscalibration as sources of high-confidence errors and to evaluate whether self-critique prompts cause genuine internal stabilization of representations.
AI.method: Combine a label-aware output-level audit score (confidence variation across domains and forced-answer baseline) with an internal hidden-state sensitivity probe; evaluate on a multi-domain binary factual audit set; analyze the effect of self-critical prompting across three open-weight models.
AI.result: The audit score correlates with where abstention-aware self-critique reduces decision loss; internally, self-critical prompting reduces hidden-state sensitivity across layers; this suggests prompt-induced local stabilization rather than purely output-level abstention; however, high-confidence errors are not clearly more locally sensitive than correct answers, so calibration is not implied.
AI.conclusion: Self-critical prompting can induce local stabilization of representations resulting in reduced sensitivity, but high-confidence errors can remain stable and miscalibrated, indicating that calibration cannot be inferred from these diagnostics.

title: BICPO-VLA: Behavior-Identified Continuation Preference Optimization for Smooth Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control
summary: The request-to-handoff gap has three coupled sources: ambiguity about the behavior intended at request time, physical-state drift accumulated during action generation, and residual incompatibility when the new action finally assumes control. BICPO-VLA addresses them in sequence. First, an instruction-aware causal history encoder identifies the behavior supported by the command and current task progress. Second, sequential Haar subspace generation decomposes each action chunk into complementary pairwise scaffold and residual coefficients, enabling two specialized generation stages followed by exact reconstruction. By reducing iterative refinement in the original action space, it shortens the interval over which the robot continues moving before the new chunk becomes available. Finally, BICPO rolls the known outgoing actions to the actual handoff state and applies reference-relative Flow-DPO among behaviorally matched candidates, adapting the generated chunk to the remaining request-to-handoff mismatch without changing its intended behavior.

AI.tldr: BICPO-VLA proposes a three-stage, instruction-aware handoff framework to close the request-to-handoff gap in robot control: (1) history-aware behavior identification, (2) Haar-subspace chunking for two-stage generation and exact reconstruction, and (3) alignment with handoff state via Flow-DPO among matched candidates to adapt remaining mismatch without changing intent.
AI.motivation: To address the three coupled sources of the request-to-handoff gap: ambiguity about the intended behavior at request time, physical-state drift during action generation, and residual incompatibility when the new action assumes control.
AI.method: Three-part approach: (1) instruction-aware causal history encoder to infer behavior supported by the command and current progress; (2) sequential Haar subspace generation to decompose each action chunk into complementary scaffold and residual coefficients, enabling two specialized generation stages and exact reconstruction; (3) roll known outgoing actions to the handoff state and apply reference-relative Flow-DPO among behaviorally matched candidates to adapt the generated chunk to remaining request-to-handoff mismatch without altering its intended behavior.
AI.result: Shortens the interval before a new action chunk is available by reducing iterative refinement in the original action space; adapts the generated chunk to residual request-to-handoff mismatch while preserving intended behavior; improves responsiveness and handoff robustness.
AI.conclusion: The architecture resolves the request-to-handoff gap in a staged, behavior-aware manner, combining history-conditioned behavior identification, efficient chunk-based generation, and post-handoff adaptation to achieve seamless control transfer.

title: Contrastive Learning for Interpretable Anomaly Detection at Collider Experiments
summary: Generic event-level anomaly detection for collider physics has two recurring problems: anomaly scores are hard to interpret, and they correlate strongly with energy scale and object multiplicity. We present Organized Representation via Contrastive learning for Anomaly detection (ORCA), a two-stage framework that first learns an embedding space via supervised contrastive learning across a diverse set of physics processes, then runs a standard autoencoder in that space to generate event-level anomaly scores. On a simulated dataset consistent with conditions at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, ORCA delivers significant gains in both breadth and depth of sensitivity to new physics signals with respect to a baseline autoencoder architecture. Beyond improved sensitivity, the contrastive embedding makes the anomalous sample interpretable: because known processes occupy distinct regions of the space, a maximum-likelihood template fit to the embedding distributions can attribute events in an anomalous sample to template physics processes with quantified uncertainties. We demonstrate that the fit accurately recovers injected signal yields, including for signals excluded from the training of the embedding, and characterizes signals absent from the template library through the known processes they most resemble. These results establish ORCA as a route to interpretable anomaly detection-based searches at colliders, where the embedding geometry carries higher dimensional physics information compared to standard one-dimensional output fits, enhancing downstream statistical analysis.

AI.tldr: ORCA combines supervised contrastive embedding learning across physics processes with a subsequent autoencoder in that space to produce interpretable, event-level anomaly scores. On HL-LHC-like simulated data, it improves sensitivity to new physics over a baseline autoencoder and enables template-fit-based attribution of anomalies to known processes, including signals outside the embedding’s training set.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection in collider experiments often yields hard-to-interpret scores that correlate with energy scale and object multiplicity, hindering physical interpretation and robust statistics. A representation that is both discriminative across standard processes and interpretable could improve discovery potential and enable physics-informed interpretation of anomalies.
AI.method: Stage 1: Train a supervised contrastive learner to map events from a diverse set of standard-model and physics processes into a discriminative embedding space. Stage 2: Train a conventional autoencoder in the embedding space to produce anomaly scores for events. Use a maximum-likelihood fit to the embedding distributions (templates built from known processes) to attribute anomalous events to specific processes with uncertainties. Evaluate on HL-LHC-like simulated data, comparing to a baseline autoencoder.
AI.result: Significant gains in both breadth and depth of sensitivity to new physics signals relative to a baseline autoencoder. The embedding makes anomalies interpretable: known processes occupy distinct regions, enabling template fits that recover injected signal yields and characterize signals not in the template library. The geometry of the embedding enhances downstream statistical analysis beyond traditional one-dimensional outputs.
AI.conclusion: ORCA provides a practical, interpretable anomaly-detection framework for collider searches. The two-stage approach yields stronger sensitivity to new physics and a physics-informed interpretation of anomalies through embedding geometry, enabling robust template-based attribution and uncertainty quantification.

title: XSA-MAD: Cross-modal Semantic Alignment for Morphing Attack Detection
summary: Morphing attacks pose a serious threat to face recognition systems. However, existing image-based morphing attack detection (MAD) methods often generalize poorly to unseen generation techniques because they rely solely on visual cues. We propose XSA-MAD, a CLIP-based multimodal framework that explicitly models semantic inconsistencies between bona-fide and morphed faces. Morphing concepts are decomposed into four interpretable attributes, including identity, facial geometry, texture, and consistency, and are encoded as structured and attribute-aware textual representations. The image encoder is progressively aligned with this discriminative textual space, resulting in a unified semantic representation that captures generation-invariant and concept-level discrepancies between bona-fide and morph images. Experiments on MAD22 and MorDIFF, following training on SMDD, demonstrate strong generalization across diverse morphing principles. In particular, XSA-MAD achieves an equal error rate of 2.92% on GAN-based morphs and consistently outperforms existing methods under high-fidelity generative attacks.

AI.tldr: A CLIP-based multimodal MAD (XSA-MAD) decomposes morphing into four attributes (identity, geometry, texture, consistency) encoded as textual representations; aligns the image encoder to this space to achieve generation-invariant detection; strong generalization with EER 2.92% on GAN-based morphs.
AI.motivation: Generalization gap in image-based MAD across unseen morphing techniques due to reliance on visual cues; need generation-invariant, concept-level detection.
AI.method: Decompose morphing into four interpretable attributes; encode as structured textual representations; progressively align image encoder with discriminative textual space; multimodal fusion via CLIP; train on SMDD and evaluate on MAD22, MorDIFF.
AI.result: Improved generalization to diverse morphing techniques; EER 2.92% on GAN-based morphs; outperforms existing methods under high-fidelity attacks.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-aligned, attribute-aware, CLIP-based MAD yields robust cross-domain morphing detection and better generalization to unseen generation methods.

title: Measuring Cross-Task Behavioral Consistency in Language Model Agents
summary: Agent evaluation relies almost entirely on outcome metrics such as success rate, which capture whether an agent succeeds but not how consistently it behaves. We argue that behavioral consistency across tasks is a distinct and measurable property, and we introduce the Behavioral Consistency Metric (BCM) to quantify it. BCM trains a model to predict task success from behavioral features of agent execution traces, derives a per-trajectory feature-attribution vector, and measures the mean pairwise similarity of these vectors within an agent system. Across roughly 9,000 trajectories from six language model agents on software engineering tasks, our central finding is that cross-task and within-task consistency are distinct axes that can diverge: some systems are locally reproducible, behaving similarly on repeated attempts at one task, yet globally fragmented, with no stable strategy across different tasks, while others are consistent at both scales. Prior work measures only same-task reproducibility and so cannot observe this separation. We further find that consistency is not reducible to success rate, since systems with comparable success can differ sharply in consistency, and that the frontier-versus-open-source consistency gap persists under a within-task control that holds task difficulty constant. We position BCM as a process-level reliability signal that complements outcome metrics, and we are explicit about the conditions under which it is meaningful.

AI.tldr: BCM is a new process-level reliability metric for AI agents that captures behavioral consistency across tasks, complementing outcome-based metrics like success rate.
AI.motivation: Outcome metrics alone miss how consistently agents behave; cross-task and within-task behavioral consistency are distinct and measurable and can diverge, affecting reliability and trust.
AI.method: Train a model to predict task success from behavioral features of agent execution traces, derive a per-trajectory feature-attribution vector, and compute the mean pairwise similarity of these vectors within an agent system. Evaluate on ~9,000 trajectories from six language-model agents solving software engineering tasks.
AI.result: Cross-task and within-task consistency are distinct axes that can diverge; some agents are locally reproducible but globally fragmented; consistency is not reducible to success rate; frontier vs open-source consistency gap persists even when controlling task difficulty; BCM serves as a complementary process-level signal to outcomes.
AI.conclusion: BCM provides a meaningful, complementary reliability signal to outcome metrics, revealing dimensions of agent behavior unexplained by success rates and clarifying conditions under which such a signal is informative.

title: AdvDex: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Human Demonstrations via Joint-Aligned Actions and Adversarial Learning
summary: Dexterous manipulation is a fundamental capability for embodied intelligence, but scaling it remains difficult because robot demonstrations are expensive to collect and action spaces vary across embodiments. Policies trained on heterogeneous data can also entangle task-relevant visual cues with embodiment-specific appearance, limiting cross-embodiment generalization. We present AdvDex, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework for learning dexterous manipulation from human and robot demonstrations. First, we introduce OmniShare, a large-scale multimodal dataset of human manipulation demonstrations that provides high-quality kinematic supervision and tactile measurements while reducing reliance on robot teleoperation. Second, we propose the Joint-Aligned Action Space (JAAS), a canonical action representation comprising an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ wrist pose and 15 finger joints, thereby functionally aligning human hands, dexterous robot hands, and parallel grippers. Finally, we use domain-adversarial learning to reduce embodiment-specific information in the learned visual representation. Experiments on hand-action prediction and real-world dexterous manipulation show consistent improvements over baselines, effective zero-shot human-to-robot skill transfer, generalization to unseen objects and environments, and data-efficient few-shot adaptation.

AI.tldr: AdvDex presents a unified Vision-Language-Action framework for dexterous manipulation, introducing OmniShare (multimodal human manipulation data with kinematic/tactile supervision), JAAS (a canonical SE(3) wrist pose + 15 finger joints action space), and domain-adversarial learning to reduce embodiment-specific cues, achieving improved hand-action prediction, zero-shot human-to-robot transfer, generalization to unseen objects/environments, and data-efficient adaptation.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation scales poorly due to costly data collection and wide variation across embodiments. Cross-embodiment generalization is hindered when policies mix task cues with embodiment-specific appearance. A unified dataset and canonical action representation could facilitate transfer and generalization.
AI.method: 1) OmniShare: large-scale multimodal human manipulation dataset with high-quality kinematic supervision and tactile measurements. 2) JAAS: a canonical action space combining SE(3) wrist pose and 15 finger joints to align human hands, dexterous robot hands, and parallel grippers. 3) Domain-adversarial learning to suppress embodiment-specific information in visual representations. 4) Vision-Language-Action framework integrating these components for training.
AI.result: Improved hand-action prediction and real-world dexterous manipulation; effective zero-shot human-to-robot skill transfer; generalization to unseen objects and environments; data-efficient few-shot adaptation.
AI.conclusion: AdvDex offers a unified framework to improve cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation by integrating a large multimodal human manipulation dataset, a canonical action representation, and domain-adversarial learning to reduce embodiment-specific cues, yielding better generalization and transfer.

title: The Query Knows What to Forget: A Second Erase Direction for Linear Attention
summary: Linear attention keeps a state of fixed size. At long context, many stored items share this state, and interference between them degrades retrieval. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2), like every delta-rule model before it, derives its erase vector from the key of the current token. However, the interference in its reads is measured through the query, and the erase step cannot reach it. We introduce the Query-derived Erase Direction (QED). QED adds a second erase direction derived from the query and orthogonal to the key. In the fast-weight view, a key-directed delta edit cannot change the key-orthogonal part of a read. It uses the editable part to cancel old-state content measured along the query. It also improves retrieval at every length past the training window, and it about doubles the usable context length on S-NIAH-1.

AI.tldr: Introduces Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) for delta-rule models with linear attention. It adds a query-orthogonal erase direction to complement the key-directed erase, mitigating interference in fixed-size state reads and substantially extending usable context length (doubling on S-NIAH-1).
AI.motivation: Linear attention with a fixed-size state suffers from interference as long-context items compete for the same state. In GDN-2, the erase is derived from the current token's key, but the read is influenced by the query; this mismatch impairs retrieval when many items are stored.
AI.method: Propose QED: a second erase direction derived from the query and orthogonal to the key. In the fast-weight view, a key-directed delta edit cannot alter the key-orthogonal part of a read; QED uses the editable part to cancel old-state content measured along the query.
AI.result: QED improves retrieval at every length beyond the training window and approximately doubles the usable context length on the S-NIAH-1 benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Query-derived Erase Direction effectively mitigates interference in delta-rule / linear-attention models, enabling longer effective context and improved retrieval beyond the training window.

title: Attention Capture Is Not Detection: A Two-Stage Account of How Humans Miss Localized AI Image Edits
summary: As AI-generated image edits proliferate, the platforms meant to curb the resulting disinformation treat detectability as a single, undifferentiated property: an edit either gets a warning or it does not. We show this is the wrong model. Across a controlled eye-tracking study ($N=59$, Latin-square design, four conditions crossing edit area and semantic plausibility), a mixed-effects analysis reveals that whether an edit is noticed and whether it is correctly judged as fake are dissociable stages, governed by different factors: edit area drives attention capture ($p<0.001$) while semantic plausibility drives judgment accuracy and look-but-fail-to-see (LBFS) error rates ($p<0.001$). This dissociation survives correction for multiple comparisons; a secondary interaction between the two factors does not. This two-stage account extends a long-standing distinction in visual attention research (between pre-attentive capture and effortful recognition) into the new domain of AI-edit detectability. We then test whether a generative eye-movement model can computationally operationalize the attention-capture stage: a Transformer trained to generate scanpaths tracks per-image attention with strong discriminative power (Pearson $r=0.77$--$0.82$ across held-out stimuli) and, on the harder task of predicting LBFS incidence, modestly outperforms a two-parameter linear baseline even without access to the plausibility label ($r=0.52$ vs. $r=0.48$). We report this comparison, our ablations, and our method's limitations (a single fixed train/validation split, not leave-one-subject-out) without inflation, consistent with responsibly communicating what a machine learning system can and cannot do to help curb AI-driven disinformation.

AI.tldr: Two-stage model of AI-edit detectability: attention capture depends on edit area, while judgment accuracy depends on semantic plausibility; supports dissociation via eye-tracking and mixed-effects analysis; a Transformer can simulate scanpaths and predict LBFS with modest accuracy; results include strong attention correlation (r ~ .77–.82) and LBFS prediction (r ~ .52) with caveats.
AI.motivation: Current moderation often treats detectability as a single binary property. The authors propose a two-stage account distinguishing attention capture from later judgment, aligning with pre-attentive vs. effortful recognition, to better understand and potentially improve AI-edit detection.
AI.method: Controlled eye-tracking study (N=59, Latin-square design), four conditions crossing edit area and semantic plausibility; mixed-effects analysis to identify drivers of attention vs judgment; testing a generative eye-movement model (Transformer) to produce scanpaths; evaluation via Pearson correlations and ablations; limitations acknowledged (single train/validation split; not leave-one-subject-out).
AI.result: Edit area drives attention capture (p<0.001); semantic plausibility drives judgment accuracy and LBFS error rates (p<0.001). Interaction between factors not significant after correction. Transformer-generated scanpaths show strong attention prediction (r=0.77–0.82) and modest LBFS incidence prediction (r=0.52 vs baseline 0.48). Analyses include ablations and transparent reporting of limitations.
AI.conclusion: Supports extending the pre-attentive vs. effortful recognition distinction to AI-edit detectability; provides a computational model for attention capture; highlights the need for differentiated moderation strategies and careful communication about ML capabilities and limitations.

title: Cross-Disciplinary Taxonomy and Modeling of Misunderstanding Generation, Amplification, and Detection, from Pragmatics to AI Agents
comment: 49 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables, 94 references. Cross-disciplinary conceptual synthesis across multiple fields. Includes a source-by-source evidence matrix in Appendix A and a coding manual in Appendix B for independent application of the taxonomy
summary: Detection of misunderstanding is an urgent problem to solve because communication has moved away from real-time, in-person interaction and is increasingly handled by AI-mediated channels. This shift cuts communicators off from the resources repair depends on faster than new means of detection are being built. In this paper we analyse misunderstanding as a layered process in which a divergence is generated, may then be amplified, and is either detected and repaired or left to persist unnoticed. Consolidating accounts from nine fields of research that do not ordinarily cite one another, we identify eleven exact failure modes and show that each operates at a specific point in a communicative process rather than anywhere within it. Those points give eight analytical layers, derived from the literature rather than adopted from an existing model. Eight of the mechanisms primarily generate a divergence, two primarily amplify one already present, and one governs whether a divergence is detected and repaired. We model the eight layers formally, extending information and communication theory from the transmission of signals to the reconstruction of meaning, and we supply a source-by-source evidence matrix that makes every rating auditable, a coding manual, and nine analysed dialogue cases. No prior classification of misunderstanding both locates mechanisms at points in the process and types them by function.

AI.tldr: A multi-layer, cross-disciplinary framework for misunderstanding detection that locates divergence-generating and -amplifying mechanisms at discrete points in communication; eight analytical layers, eleven failure modes, auditable evidence, and nine dialogue case studies.
AI.motivation: Misunderstanding is an urgent problem in AI-mediated communication, where repair resources are scarce; existing work lacks a unified, point-specific taxonomy linking mechanisms to stages of meaning reconstruction.
AI.method: Synthesize nine fields of research to identify eleven exact failure modes, assign them to eight analytical layers, classify functions (eight divergences, two amplifications, one repair/detection); formal modeling extending information/communication theory to meaning reconstruction; provide a source-by-source evidence matrix, a coding manual, and nine analyzed dialogue cases.
AI.result: Eight layers with eight divergence-generating mechanisms, two amplification mechanisms, and one repair/detection mechanism; a formal, auditable model mapping mechanisms to process points; nine dialogue cases and supporting materials for replication.
AI.conclusion: First comprehensive classification locating misunderstanding mechanisms at specific process stages, enabling targeted detection and repair; extends theory and provides auditable materials (evidence matrix, coding manual, case studies) for transparent validation.

title: Demonstration of Space Robot Teleoperation over a Lossy and Delayed Network using ATMOS
comment: (c) 2026 the authors. This work has been accepted to IFAC for publication under a Creative Commons License CC-BY-NC-ND. 6 pages, 8 figures. Inkyu Jang and Gregorio Marchesini contributed equally to this work
summary: We present a demonstration showcasing the Autonomy Testbed for Multi-purpose Orbiting Systems (ATMOS), a planar spacecraft-analog robot designed for hardware-in-the-loop evaluation of guidance and control strategies in microgravity-like conditions. Using ATMOS as the physical test platform, we investigate the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of control architectures for remotely operated spacecraft under round-trip communication delays. In this work, we develop and experimentally validate a control strategy that combines state prediction and trajectory tracking control to perform a docking maneuver, accounting for time-varying random communication latency between ground operators and the ATMOS system. The demonstration includes a long-distance remote control experiment between Seoul and Stockholm, introducing realistic intercontinental delays and variability. The results highlight the capability of ATMOS to support rapid, reliable, and cost-effective testing of spacecraft teleoperation concepts, establishing a first step toward robust validation of on-orbit operations in microgravity-like environments.

AI.tldr: Hardware-in-the-loop planar spacecraft testbed ATMOS demonstrates latency-tolerant docking control via state prediction and trajectory tracking, validated with cross-continental remote experiment.
AI.motivation: Address need for realistic, repeatable testing of teleoperation and guidance/control under round-trip communication delays in microgravity-like conditions; enable rapid, cost-effective validation of on-orbit operations.
AI.method: Develop ATMOS; implement control strategy combining state prediction and trajectory tracking; handle time-varying random latency; perform docking maneuver; long-distance remote experiment Seoul-Stockholm; hardware-in-the-loop.
AI.result: Experimental validation of docking under latency; intercontinental delays mimic real-world; demonstrates ATMOS capability for rapid, reliable testing; supports cost-effective testing of teleoperation concepts.
AI.conclusion: ATMOS provides a practical platform for validating onboard and ground-based teleoperation in microgravity-like environments; a first step toward robust on-orbit operations validation.

title: From BERT to Frontier Agents: Eight Years of Language-Model Progress, the Collapse of the Capability-Cost Curve, and the Rise of Task-Targeted Models
summary: Between October 2018 and July 2026 AI models progressed from simple systems like BERT to massive agents that solve complex math and write software. The ability to resolve real coding issues improved by nearly six times per year since late 2024. During this time costs dropped sharply with OpenAIs budget model GPT 5 point 6 Luna matching flagship capabilities for just one to six dollars per million tokens beating older versions at a fraction of the price. Top performance is now split across specialized models as Claude Opus 5 leads in frontend coding Claude Fable 5 excels at repository level coding and GPT 5 point 6 Sol dominates terminal tasks. In a grade school math test using the Qwen 2 point 5 model basic methods solved 58 of 100 problems while advanced sampling solved up to 79. A confidence ranking tool correctly identified 47 right answers in its top 50 choices proving highly useful for sorting tasks with all research materials made fully public.

AI.tldr: AI progress is accelerating with specialization across domains, cost declines, and improved problem-solving across coding and math tasks.
AI.motivation: To summarize recent developments in AI models (2018–2026) and highlight performance, cost, and sorting tools.
AI.method: Narrative synthesis of reported results across models and benchmarks; cross-task comparison of coding, math, and ranking tools.
AI.result: Coding issues solved at ~6x/year growth since late 2024; GPT 5.6 Luna costs $1–$6 per million tokens; performance split across Claude Opus 5 (frontend coding), Claude Fable 5 (repository-level coding), GPT 5.6 Sol (terminal tasks); grade-school math with Qwen 2.5 achieves 58/100 basic, 79/100 advanced sampling; confidence ranking tool correctly picks 47 of the top 50 answers; all materials publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The AI landscape is moving toward specialization and cost-efficiency, with diversified strengths across domains and enhanced reliability via confidence tools; public data sharing and benchmarks appear prevalent and ongoing.

title: Consensus-gated Multi-Agent Neural Architecture Search for Seismic Fault Segmentation
summary: Neural networks for seismic fault segmentation are often borrowed from computer vision and medical imaging domains where they train under relatively much larger labeled data resources. Optimizing their architecture under tight labeled data budgets as are common in geophysical applications is not a trivial problem. Manually designing data-optimal architectures is time-consuming while classical neural architecture search (NAS) is restricted to hand-crafted search spaces and large compute budgets. We present an agentic NAS system in which a panel of three large language models (Claude, GPT-5.1, and Gemini~2.5~Pro) debates each candidate architecture to unanimous consensus, authors the complete PyTorch implementation, cross-reviews it, and submits it to an automated validate-train-score loop with a hard 450K parameter budget, keep-or-revert lineage, and a memory of failed mechanisms. Operating on source code rather than a predefined operation menu, the search ran on a single consumer GPU and trained only eight candidates. It discovered \ours{}: a 425K-parameter encoder-decoder with a strip-pooling bottleneck, squeeze-and-excitation gating, an asymmetric one-conv decoder, and a feature-pyramid fusion neck. Trained under a protocol identical to all baselines on sections derived from the Thebe fault dataset, it attains the highest F1 (0.578) and IoU of all models tested while being the smallest, outperforming a published-capacity U-Net (31M parameters, F1 0.484), DeepLabV3-ResNet50 (39.6M, 0.516), an Attention U-Net(1.83M, 0.502). The search cost 101 LLM calls ($\sim$1.15M input / 0.39M output tokens) and roughly one GPU-day, making consensus-gated LLM panels a practical, low-cost route to domain-specific architecture discovery.

AI.tldr: Consensus-guided neural architecture search (agentic NAS) uses three LLMs to debate and select architectures under a tight compute budget, yielding a 425k-parameter encoder-decoder that outperforms larger baselines on seismic fault segmentation (F1 0.578, IoU highest) while remaining smallest.
AI.motivation: Seismic fault segmentation faces limited labeled data and high NAS costs; the study aims for data-efficient, low-cost architecture discovery tailored to geophysical tasks.
AI.method: A panel of three LLMs (Claude, GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro) debates each candidate architecture to unanimous consensus, authors a complete PyTorch implementation, cross-reviews it, and runs an automated validate–train–score loop with a 450k parameter budget, keep-or-revert lineage, and memory of failed mechanisms. The search operates on source code (not a fixed operation menu), runs on a consumer GPU, and evaluated eight candidates. The resulting architecture (ours) is a 425k-parameter encoder–decoder with a strip-pooling bottleneck, squeeze-and-excitation gating, an asymmetric one-conv decoder, and a feature-pyramid fusion neck, trained on Thebe fault dataset with the same protocol as baselines.
AI.result: The discovered model achieves the highest F1 (0.578) and IoU among models tested while being the smallest, outperforming a 31M-parameter U‑Net (F1 0.484), DeepLabV3-ResNet50 (39.6M, 0.516), and Attention U‑Net (1.83M, 0.502). The search cost was ~101 LLM calls (~1.15M input tokens, ~0.39M output tokens) and roughly one GPU-day.
AI.conclusion: Consensus-gated panels of language models enable practical, low-cost domain-specific architecture discovery in data-constrained geophysics, demonstrating the viability of agentic NAS for seismic fault segmentation.

title: Active Perception for Embodied Disambiguation
summary: Natural language provides robots with a flexible task interface, but target ambiguity in embodied environments arises not only from user intent; it can also result from missing taskrelevant physical evidence in the current observation. Existing interactive disambiguation methods primarily obtain additional information by asking the user, whereas occlusion, restricted viewpoints, unreadable text, and unobserved targets require the robot to actively change its observation. We propose an active-perception framework for embodied target disambiguation that uses active observation as the backbone for information acquisition and uses a vision-language model to decide, on the basis of accumulated visual evidence and interaction information, whether to continue observing, request clarification, or complete target selection. Active observation can both directly recover missing discriminative evidence and reveal object names, labels, and semantic attributes, thereby improving user clarification when it remains necessary. Real-robot experiments show that the framework combines physical information acquisition and userintent clarification within a unified embodied disambiguation process.

AI.tldr: An active-perception framework for embodied target disambiguation that uses active observation and a vision-language model to decide whether to keep observing, ask for clarification, or select a target, validated on real robots.
AI.motivation: Target ambiguity in embodied environments arises from missing task-relevant physical evidence and observation gaps; existing disambiguation methods rely on user questions and passive perception, which may fail under occlusion or unseen targets.
AI.method: Develops an active observation backbone for information acquisition and uses a vision-language model to fuse accumulated visual evidence and interaction data to decide to continue observing, request clarification, or complete target selection; active observation also reveals object names, labels, and semantic attributes to aid clarification.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments demonstrate the end-to-end feasibility and effectiveness of integrating physical information acquisition with user-intent clarification in a unified embodied disambiguation loop.
AI.conclusion: Active observation effectively recovers missing discriminative evidence and reveals attributes, improving opportunities for user clarification when needed and enabling a unified, embodied disambiguation process.

title: Evolve Vision-Language-Action Model into an Agent with On-the-fly Tool-use
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern (CVPR) Findings
summary: This paper integrates end-to-end Visual-Language-Action (VLA) models with agentic tool-use to propose Agentic Robot with Tool-use (ART). ART is a tool-injection framework that tunes any VLA model to leverage off-the-shelf tool modules for low-level vision, high-level affordance, and embodiment enhancement. Compared to vanilla VLA models with a whole continuous action solution space, ART reduces the complexity of the action solution space through tool-use, which not only improves generalizability across different tasks but also reduces data dependency. To demonstrate the advantages (high generalizability and low data dependency) of this framework, we first built a dataset of 30K tool-use trajectories and action demonstrations, which is much smaller than those used by baseline methods. We then designed a training regimen for long-trajectory tool-use reasoning in challenging environments. Experiments show that ART achieves a 20% higher success rate than mainstream baselines on simulation and real-world tasks, such as pick-and-place in the dark at novel viewpoints. Empirical results highlight the benefits of an agent-based approach: modular tool utilization enables more efficient training, lightweight deployment, and scalable integration of new tools. This design fosters robustness, adaptability, and extensibility, paving the way for the practical deployment of VLA systems in complex real-world scenarios.

AI.tldr: ART injects modular tool-use into end-to-end Visual-Language-Action models, reducing action-space complexity and improving generalization and data efficiency; reports ~20% better success on simulation/real-world tasks like dark-object manipulation.
AI.motivation: Address the data-hungry and poorly generalizing nature of vanilla end-to-end VLA models with continuous action spaces by introducing a modular tool-use framework that can leverage off-the-shelf tools for perception, affordance reasoning, and embodiment, enabling robust, scalable deployment.
AI.method: A tool-injection framework that tunes VLA models to use off-the-shelf tool modules for low-level vision, high-level affordance, and embodiment enhancement. Built a 30k trajectory/tool-use dataset; designed a training regimen for long-trajectory tool-use reasoning in challenging environments; evaluated in simulation and real-world tasks such as pick-and-place in the dark across novel viewpoints.
AI.result: ART achieves a 20% higher success rate than mainstream baselines on both simulated and real-world tasks, demonstrating improved generalizability and data efficiency. The modular tool approach enables more efficient training, lightweight deployment, and scalable integration of new tools.
AI.conclusion: Agent-based tool-use with modular tool integration enhances robustness, adaptability, and extensibility of VLA systems, paving the way for practical deployment in complex real-world scenarios.

title: EEG-PRISM: Physiologically-Grounded Interpretability of Predictions by EEG Foundation Models
summary: Objective: Foundation models represent the next advancement in AI for EEG analysis; however current explainable AI techniques provide attribution scores in the time-channel input space, which is mismatched to clinical intuition about EEG. Thus, there is a critical need for a universal method that can extend the interpretability of any foundation model to alternative and physiologically relevant domains without modifying or retraining the underlying model. Methods: EEG-PRISM leverages linear transformations and established backpropagation rules to map time-channel attribution scores into alternative domains. We derive mappings to the frequency domain via an invertible DFT and to the source domain via an approximately invertible EEG generative model. We evaluate EEG-PRISM in simulated and real data, assessing recovery of ground-truth phenomena across domains with five foundation models and four AI explainers. Results: In simulation, EEG-PRISM achieves near-perfect spectral recovery and 69.2% spatial accuracy. In epilepsy, EEG-PRISM correctly determines that delta-theta activity is most salient and correctly localizes the seizure onset region with 50% accuracy. In autism, EEG-PRISM localizes the predictive delta-alpha biomarkers to frontal and temporal regions, consistent with prior work. Conclusion: EEG-PRISM is a theoretically-grounded post-hoc attribution method with accurate mapping into the spectral and spatial domains. It supports window-level analysis of transient events (e.g., seizures) and group-level identification of clinically relevant biomarkers (e.g., autism), thus advancing interpretable EEG foundation models. Significance: This work enables physiologically-grounded interpretation of EEG foundation models and supports clinically relevant insights such as event localization and biomarker identification.

AI.tldr: EEG-PRISM maps time-channel attribution from foundation models into spectral and source domains using an invertible DFT and an approximate EEG generator, enabling physiologically meaningful interpretation without retraining.
AI.motivation: Current AI explanations for EEG are in time-channel space, which poorly matches clinical EEG intuition. A universal, post-hoc method is needed to translate attributions into clinically relevant domains without modifying models.
AI.method: Apply linear transformations and backpropagation rules to convert time-channel attribution scores to frequency and source domains. Use an invertible DFT for spectral mapping and an approximately invertible EEG generative model for source localization. Validate on simulated and real EEG data across multiple foundation models and explainers.
AI.result: Simulation shows near-perfect spectral recovery and 69.2% spatial accuracy. In epilepsy, delta-theta salience is correctly identified and seizure onset localization is 50% accurate. In autism, predictive biomarkers localize to frontal and temporal regions, aligning with prior findings.
AI.conclusion: EEG-PRISM provides a theoretically grounded, effective post-hoc attribution method with accurate cross-domain mappings, enabling window-level analysis of transient events and group-level biomarker identification in EEG foundation models.

title: Beyond Control Points: Arcsecond Relative-Motion Estimation of Vision Measurement Platforms With Incomplete or Absent Control Fields
comment: 13 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Image Processing
summary: Long-range vision-based deformation monitoring is highly sensitive to motion of the camera platform. Absolute-pose differencing typically relies on dedicated control data and propagates two independent pose errors into the relative-motion estimate. We develop a control-adaptive differential framework that estimates inter-frame platform motion directly from image displacements and known 3D points. With no dedicated control point, the framework recovers platform rotation from measurement-point observations. One surveyed control point enables prior-constrained translation recovery, while two nonparallel control rays recover full 3D translation. The framework requires neither nonlinear optimization nor an initial pose estimate. Excluding control data from the rotation stage makes the rotation estimate exactly immune to contamination confined to the control field. The inherited differential formulation also cancels translational extrinsic errors exactly. We derive the rotation observability condition, a leakage bound for unmodeled translation and nonrigid point motion, and the single-point axial-prior bias law. Under 0.5-pixel image noise, attitude changes of up to 30~arcmin, and 3D point perturbations of up to 2~mm, the multi-camera estimator achieves a rotation RMSE of 2.97~arcsec and an average runtime of 0.46~ms. With one surveyed control point, its prior-constrained translation RMSE is 1.19~mm. In a bridge experiment without a stable control field, the median coordinate-wise displacement RMSE relative to total-station measurements is 0.85~mm. The estimator also maintains zero divergence under the tested 3D coordinate perturbations on public RGB-D and stereo sequences. These results establish state-of-the-art accuracy, calibration robustness, and computational efficiency among the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: A control-adaptive differential framework estimates inter-frame motion using image displacements and known 3D points, enabling rotation without dedicated control data and translating with minimal control points; claims state-of-the-art accuracy and real-time performance for long-range deformation monitoring.
AI.motivation: Long-range deformation monitoring is highly sensitive to camera motion; traditional absolute-pose differencing relies on dedicated control data that propagate pose errors. The goal is to estimate motion directly from imagery and sparse 3D information without extra control infrastructure, achieving robust rotation and translation estimation.
AI.method: A differential formulation that uses image-point displacements and known 3D points to estimate inter-frame platform motion. Rotation is recovered from measurement-point observations; translation is inferred with one surveyed control point (prior-constrained) or two nonparallel control rays for full 3D translation. The approach avoids nonlinear optimization and does not require an initial pose. It decouples rotation from control-field contamination, cancels translational extrinsic errors, and provides an observability condition, leakage bounds for unmodeled effects, and a single-point axial-prior bias law.
AI.result: With 0.5-pixel image noise and small 3D perturbations, multi-camera rotation RMSE is 2.97 arcsec; runtime 0.46 ms. Prior-constrained translation RMSE with one control point is 1.19 mm. In a bridge test without stable control, median coordinate-wise displacement RMSE is 0.85 mm relative to total-station references. The method maintains zero divergence for tested 3D perturbations on public RGB-D and stereo data; claimed state-of-the-art accuracy, calibration robustness, and computational efficiency among evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed estimator delivers high-precision rotation and translation estimates without heavy dependence on control data, enabling robust, real-time long-range deformation monitoring with strong calibration resilience across varied datasets; supports deployment in scenarios with limited or no dedicated control infrastructure.

title: MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences
summary: The next generation of AI agents is increasingly moving beyond systems that answer isolated questions toward persistent personal assistants that can understand, remember, and continuously learn from users' experiences. Such assistants require long-term memory to accumulate and leverage user-specific experiences over time, yet existing benchmarks remain inadequate for realistic mobile settings, where experiences are heterogeneous, multimodal, evolving, and deeply personal. We introduce MobileMem, a benchmark and framework for studying on-device long-term memory, grounded in a year-scale collection of mobile experiences. MobileMem employs a knowledge-grounded synthesis pipeline to construct coherent and temporally consistent long-horizon trajectories from user-app sessions. It provides complementary text and multimodal settings covering multi-hop and temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, and implicit preference inference. Specifically, MobileMem enables agents to remember the past, understand the present, and adapt to the future. By modeling experiences rather than isolated facts, MobileMem moves memory beyond information retrieval toward experiential intelligence for continuous personal learning.

AI.tldr: MobileMem introduces a year-scale on-device memory benchmark and framework for persistent personal AI assistants, using a knowledge-grounded synthesis pipeline to create coherent long-horizon trajectories from mobile experiences, with multimodal tasks for memory, reasoning, updating and inference.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks fail to capture realistic, on-device long-term memory across heterogeneous, multimodal user experiences; there is a need to model experiences over time to support continuous personal learning in mobile agents.
AI.method: Proposes MobileMem benchmark and framework; a knowledge-grounded synthesis pipeline to construct coherent long-horizon trajectories from user-app sessions; provides text and multimodal tasks covering multi-hop and temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, and implicit preference inference.
AI.result: Provides a comprehensive benchmark and framework enabling memory-from-experiences rather than fact retrieval; supports memory retention, understanding of present context, and adaptation to future interactions; enables experiments on on-device lifelong learning.
AI.conclusion: Modeling experiences rather than isolated facts is essential for experiential intelligence; MobileMem lays the groundwork for continuous personal learning and on-device long-term memory in AI assistants.

title: FlatLab: A Unified Methodology Framework and Simulation-Based Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation of Flat Objects
comment: This paper is accepted to ICML 2026
summary: Robotic manipulation of flat objects is challenging due to the ungraspable configurations and strong variations in object geometry and material. Existing methods rely on heuristic pre-manipulation and are often evaluated in closed settings with limited generalization. We propose a unified framework that decouples the manipulation into a strategy generator and an action execution module. The strategy generator predicts appropriate manipulation strategies from object point clouds by learning strategy-centric, object-invariant representations via simulated data transformation and contrastive learning. Conditioned on the predicted strategy, the execution module decomposes long-horizon manipulation into reusable action primitives and dynamically composes them to generate stable trajectories. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce FlatLab, a comprehensive simulation benchmark for robotic flat object manipulation. FlatLab provides high-fidelity physical simulation of diverse rigid and deformable flat objects, automated multi-modal data collection, and standardized task definitions and evaluation protocols. Experiments conducted in FlatLab demonstrate that our approach generalizes effectively to unseen objects and categories, outperforming existing baselines. The project page and the code are provided at https://flatlab-web.github.io/.

AI.tldr: A two-module framework for robotic flat-object manipulation: a strategy generator that predicts manipulation strategies from point clouds using contrastive learning over simulated data transformations, and an action execution module that decomposes long-horizon tasks into reusable primitives to form stable trajectories; accompanied by FlatLab, a high-fidelity simulation benchmark for evaluation showing strong generalization and superior performance.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation of flat objects is difficult due to ungraspable configurations and large variations in geometry and material; existing methods rely on heuristic pre-manipulation and lack generalization in real-world, diverse settings.
AI.method: The approach decouples manipulation into two modules: (1) a strategy generator that learns strategy-centric, object-invariant representations from object point clouds via simulated data transformation and contrastive learning; (2) an execution module that decomposes long-horizon tasks into reusable action primitives and dynamically composes them to generate stable trajectories. It introduces FlatLab for systematic evaluation with high-fidelity physics, automated multi-modal data collection, and standardized task definitions and evaluation protocols.
AI.result: Experiments in FlatLab show that the proposed method generalizes to unseen objects and categories and outperforms existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: A decoupled, strategy-driven framework together with a standardized FlatLab benchmark provides a robust, generalizable solution for robotic manipulation of flat objects and enables reproducible evaluation for future work.

title: SAGE: Surrogate-gradient Adaptation via Attention-Guided Entropy for Spiking Transformers
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer an energy-efficient alternative to conventional deep neural networks by exploiting sparse event-driven computation, but their training remains challenging because the non-differentiable spike function requires surrogate gradients whose fixed shape may be suboptimal across layers and training stages. In this work, we introduce SAGE, an uncertainty-modulated surrogate-gradient mechanism for Transformer-based SNNs. SAGE estimates block-level uncertainty from normalized self-attention entropy and uses this signal to adapt the surrogate-gradient slope during training while leaving the inference model unchanged. By modulating only the training-time surrogate parameter, the proposed method preserves the original architecture and deployment cost while improving optimization flexibility. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100 demonstrate that SAGE achieves improved accuracy over fixed-surrogate baselines, with results up to 1-2\% consistent gains across multiple simulation time steps. These results highlight the potential of attention-derived uncertainty as a lightweight training signal for adaptive surrogate-gradient learning in transformer-based SNNs.

AI.tldr: SAGE uses uncertainty-modulated surrogate gradients based on transformer self-attention entropy to adapt training-time gradient slopes in SNNs, improving CIFAR-10/100 accuracy with no architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Surrogate-gradient design is a key bottleneck in SNN training; fixed gradient slopes may be suboptimal across layers and training stages, limiting optimization and performance.
AI.method: Compute block-level uncertainty from normalized self-attention entropy; adapt the surrogate-gradient slope during training while preserving the inference architecture by modifying only the training-time surrogate parameter.
AI.result: Achieves improved accuracy versus fixed-surrogate baselines on CIFAR-10/100, with consistent 1–2% gains across multiple simulation time steps.
AI.conclusion: Attention-derived uncertainty can serve as a lightweight, effective training signal for adaptive surrogate-gradient learning in transformer-based SNNs, preserving deployment cost and architecture.

title: OpenBelief-Nav: Evidence-Preserving Object Memory for Open-Vocabulary Language-Guided Navigation
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs provide compact semantic memory for language-guided navigation, but mapped objects are often exposed through a single fused feature or committed semantic label. Such commitment can remove minority yet task-relevant hypotheses from the task-time interface. We present OpenBelief-Nav, an evidence-preserving object memory that retains observation-level phrases, reliability cues, and frame-mask provenance while maintaining separate aggregate geometric and visual representations. Semantically related phrases are consolidated into a vocabulary-independent object belief from which task-specific readouts perform fixed-vocabulary projection or free-form retrieval. On five ScanNet200 and eight Replica scenes, full-belief projection achieves mIoU scores of 0.2742 and 0.2912, compared with 0.2393 and 0.2701 for a matched early-commit readout. Across 78 HM3D-YCB navigation trials, consensus and early-commit retrieval each achieve 60/78 successes, compared with 58/78 for belief-weighted retrieval and 55/78 for DualMap. Across 20 Unitree G1 runs organized as 10 matched evaluation cases, a correction policy permitting at most two verified candidate attempts improves target-confirmation success from 6/10 to 8/10 relative to top-1-only execution. Code will be released upon acceptance at https://openbelief-nav.github.io/.

AI.tldr: OpenBelief-Nav preserves evidence-rich memory for open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs, retaining observation-level phrases, reliability cues, and provenance, while maintaining separate geometric/visual representations and vocabulary-independent beliefs for fixed-vocabulary or free-form readouts.
AI.motivation: Current open-vocabulary scene graphs risk discarding minority yet task-relevant hypotheses by collapsing observations into a single fused feature or label. OpenBelief-Nav aims to preserve diverse evidence and support robust decision-making in navigation tasks.
AI.method: Maintain observation-level phrases and frame provenance; separate aggregate geometric and visual representations; consolidate related phrases into a vocabulary-independent object belief; provide task-specific readouts via fixed-vocabulary projection or free-form retrieval; include a correction policy enabling multiple candidate verifications; report results across multiple datasets (ScanNet200, Replica, HM3D-YCB, Unitree G1).
AI.result: Full-belief projection improves mIoU on ScanNet200/Replica (0.2742/0.2912) over early-commit (0.2393/0.2701); HM3D-YCB: consensus and early-commit retrieval reach 60/78 successes, higher than belief-weighted (58/78) and DualMap (55/78); Unitree G1: a correction policy increasing candidate verifications raises target-confirmation success from 6/10 to 8/10 compared with top-1-only.
AI.conclusion: Preserving evidence and maintaining separate, flexible representations yields tangible gains in perception and navigation across diverse scenes and tasks, validating the utility of an evidence-preserving object memory for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding; code release planned.

title: No Universal Signal Predicts Sample-Level LLM Regression under Version Updates
summary: Frontier LLMs are updated frequently and typically outperform their predecessors in aggregate. But aggregate gains say little about individual samples: an update can still cause sample-level regression, where a response correct under the old model becomes incorrect under the new one. This paper studies how to predict such regressions from signals available at inference time. We compare single-model signals (confidence, logit margin, attention entropy) against cross-version signals (output KL divergence, likelihood drift, token-level KL, representation drift) under a unified added-value test that isolates each signal's gain over a confidence baseline. Across six benchmarks in three task families (multiple-choice question answering, or MCQ; math reasoning; code generation) and six model update pairs, we find that (1) signal effectiveness is task-dependent: confidence is strongest on MCQ and simpler math, while likelihood/KL signals give the most frequent gains on harder math and code; (2) no signal is universally best across model updates either; and (3) some cross-version signals stay informative even when confidence fails, including without labels, which supports a proof-of-concept selective fallback that routes high-risk samples back to the old model. Practitioners can use these task-level patterns to choose which regression signal to trust for a given update. Code is available at https://github.com/jiashengsally/llm-regression-signals.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes inference-time regression signals to predict when updated LLMs regress on individual samples, showing task-dependent signal usefulness, no one-size-fits-all signal, and potential for selective fallback to the old model.
AI.motivation: Aggregate gains from model updates can conceal sample-level regressions; need signals at inference time to identify high-risk samples and potentially route them away from the updated model.
AI.method: Compare single-model signals (confidence, logit margin, attention entropy) and cross-version signals (output KL divergence, likelihood drift, token-level KL, representation drift) under an added-value test against a confidence baseline, across six benchmarks (MCQ, math reasoning, code generation), three task families, and six model update pairs.
AI.result: Signal effectiveness depends on task; confidence dominates MCQ and simpler math, while likelihood/KL signals are more predictive on harder math and code; no single signal outperforms others across all updates; some cross-version signals remain informative without labels, enabling a proof-of-concept selective fallback to the old model.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners can leverage task-level patterns to choose regression signals for a given update; the work supports building robust, per-update inference-time strategies and provides code for replication.

title: PILOT: Privileged Imitation Learning for End-to-End Motion Planning of Autonomous UAVs under Partial Observability
summary: Autonomous navigation in cluttered environments is hampered by partial observability and dynamic constraints. This paper presents PILOT, a constraint-aware privileged imitation learning framework for vision-based end-to-end UAV motion planning under partial observability. The framework distills planning strategies from a computationally intensive optimal control expert into a student policy regularized toward safety and dynamic requirements via a dual-objective loss function. To mitigate partial observability, a spatiotemporal perception fusion module using a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) is developed to integrate historical depth images and odometry. This module infers task-relevant latent context from historical observations, enhancing spatial awareness beyond the instantaneous FOV without maintaining persistent map memory. A trajectory parameterization layer mapping network outputs to a structured trajectory, while enabling explicit continuity, dynamic-consistency, and obstacle soft penalties during training, encouraging constraint satisfaction for unseen observations without formal guarantees. Simulations on quadrotor and fixed-wing aircraft demonstrate that PILOT achieves performance comparable to the privileged expert while reducing computational overhead by over 80\%. Successful indoor and outdoor zero-shot deployment confirms the practical feasibility and cross-domain generalization of the planner.

AI.tldr: PILOT is a constraint-aware privileged imitation learning framework for vision-based UAV motion planning under partial observability, combining privileged expert imitation, spatiotemporal perception fusion with a Temporal CNN, and a trajectory-parameterization layer to deliver efficient, safe end-to-end planning with strong generalization; achieves near-expert performance with >80% computational savings and zero-shot cross-domain deployment.
AI.motivation: Autonomous navigation under partial observability and dynamic constraints is hampered by limited sensing, occlusions, and high computational cost of optimal control. A method that imitates strong planners while maintaining safety and real-time feasibility is needed, especially for vision-based UAVs.
AI.method: Distill planning strategies from a computationally intensive optimal-control expert into a student policy using a dual-objective loss that regularizes safety and dynamic constraints. Mitigate partial observability with a spatiotemporal perception fusion module based on a Temporal Convolutional Network to fuse historical depth images and odometry, inferring a task-relevant latent context. Use a trajectory parameterization layer to map network outputs to structured trajectories with explicit continuity, dynamic-consistency, and obstacle soft penalties during training.
AI.result: In simulations with quadrotor and fixed-wing aircraft, PILOT achieves performance comparable to the privileged expert while reducing computational overhead by over 80%. The planner succeeds in indoor and outdoor zero-shot deployments, demonstrating cross-domain generalization and practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: PILOT provides an efficient, generalizable end-to-end UAV planner under partial observability by combining privileged imitation learning, spatiotemporal perception fusion, and constrained trajectory generation. It shows strong cross-domain generalization and practical viability, though formal guarantees under all conditions are not reported.

title: Capacity-Dependent Effects of Data Selection for Reasoning
summary: In reasoning supervised fine-tuning, candidate responses for the same instruction can differ substantially in how well they match the student's current distribution. Recent likelihood-based response selection methods suggest that responses closer to the student distribution provide more effective supervision, motivating the hypothesis that high-likelihood responses may generally be preferable for fine-tuning. In this paper, we revisit this intuition and show that the value of likelihood-based data selection depends critically on model capacity and training duration. Through controlled experiments on mathematical reasoning, using students ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters and supervision generated by stronger teacher models, we observe a clear \emph{capacity-dependent} ``{\color{SMALLCOLOR}\textbf{Fast-Fit}} / {\color{LARGECOLOR}\textbf{Slow-Gain}}'' pattern. High-likelihood data provides faster and more stable early improvements, especially for smaller models, but low-likelihood data becomes increasingly beneficial for larger models when training is allowed to continue longer. To explain this phenomenon, we analyze learning dynamics, showing that small models often fail to absorb low-likelihood supervision and instead fall into shallow or repetitive behaviors, while larger models are better able to move toward the teacher distribution under such data. We further provide a capacity-constrained theoretical view of distillation that clarifies how data difficulty, data span, and student capacity jointly govern transfer. Overall, our findings show that effective data selection for reasoning should be aware of model capacity and computing budget rather than based on a single universal preference for high-likelihood supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper disputes the universal benefit of high-likelihood supervision for reasoning fine-tuning, showing a capacity- and compute-dependent tradeoff: small models benefit from high-likelihood data early, while larger models gain from low-likelihood data when training longer; it offers a capacity-constrained distillation view and a Fast-Fit/Slow-Gain paradigm to guide data selection.
AI.motivation: To understand when likelihood-based data selection helps supervised fine-tuning for reasoning, given varying model capacities and training budgets, and to resolve conflicting intuitions about preferring high-likelihood data.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on mathematical reasoning with student models from 1.5B to 8B parameters, supervised by stronger teacher models. Systematic variation of data likelihood for supervision, analysis of learning dynamics, and a capacity-constrained distillation theory.
AI.result: Identification of a capacity-dependent Fast-Fit / Slow-Gain pattern: high-likelihood data accelerates early gains for smaller models; low-likelihood data becomes beneficial for larger models with extended training. Small models struggle to absorb low-likelihood supervision and may converge to shallow behaviors, while larger models align toward the teacher distribution under such data. A theoretical perspective links data difficulty, span, and student capacity to transfer.
AI.conclusion: Data selection for reasoning should adapt to model capacity and compute budget rather than universally favor high-likelihood supervision; guidance should calibrate data difficulty and quantity to model size and training duration.

title: RGBX-Next: Towards Realistic Generative Rendering from G-Buffers
summary: Diffusion models have achieved impressive results in image, video, and streaming generation. However, compared to traditional 3D rendering, they still lack precise control over the generated output. We believe a viable path forward is to use generative models as learned renderers conditioned on traditionally rendered G-buffers. We introduce RGBX-Next, a unified generative framework for forward and inverse rendering, which allows estimating G-buffers from images, videos, and streams, and rendering realistic images, videos, and streams from G-buffers. Our key contribution is a general recipe for finetuning diffusion transformer (DiT) models into generative forward and inverse renderers. We show that the resulting models achieve high quality in both realistic generative rendering and intrinsic decomposition. We will make all our models publicly available. We believe that the design principles presented in this paper will benefit future research on controllable generative forward and inverse rendering.

AI.tldr: RGBX-Next: a unified diffusion-based framework that uses G-buffers to drive forward and inverse rendering via finetuned diffusion transformers (DiT), enabling estimation of G-buffers from media and rendering from G-buffers; claims high-quality rendering and intrinsic decomposition; aims for controllable generative rendering with public release.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models excel in generation but lack fine-grained control compared to traditional 3D rendering. Conditioning generative models on traditional G-buffers offers a path toward controllable forward and inverse rendering.
AI.method: Introduce RGBX-Next and a general recipe for finetuning diffusion transformer (DiT) models into forward and inverse renderers. The framework can estimate G-buffers from images, videos, and streams and render images, videos, and streams from G-buffers.
AI.result: Models achieve high quality in realistic generative rendering and intrinsic decomposition.
AI.conclusion: The design principles should benefit future research on controllable generative forward and inverse rendering, and the authors plan to release all models publicly.

title: Evaluating Agentic Learning Harness Capabilities Without Labels via the Scaling Hypothesis
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at CAMLIS 2025 (Conference on Applied Machine Learning for Information Security)
summary:
Agentic "Continual Learning Harnesses", systems that pair an LLM with retrieval or memory to improve from feedback without retraining, have shown growing value in cybersecurity. But their value is conventionally measured by gains against labeled benchmarks, an approach that often fails in operational security settings. Benchmark labels are scarce, stale, and unrepresentative, so a practitioner often cannot tell whether a given harness helps at all or which of two is better for their task. Traditional LLM-as-a-judge offers little signal because it is no stronger than the agent it evaluates, and distillation is unreliable on scarce, sporadic, and biased labels.
  We propose a framework for evaluating learning harnesses end-to-end without a labeled benchmark, grounded in the scaling hypothesis. A stronger teacher model provides sparsely sampled corrections to a smaller student with a continual learning harness. We score a harness by how much its student converges toward the teacher over time.
