Across security tasks, model families, and harness designs, we show that improvement relative to the teacher correlates with improvement relative to a held-out gold standard, validating teacher-relative lift as a proxy for true harness uplift when labels are absent. We further show that LLM-as-a-judge between similarly powered models yields no usable signal. These results suggest that a teacher-sized model can be improved through the same harness when humans provide the same kind of sparse, high-precision corrections.

AI.tldr: Proposes a teacher-relative evaluation framework for continual learning harnesses that pair LLMs with retrieval/memory. Without labeled benchmarks, a stronger teacher model provides sparse corrections to a smaller student; harness effectiveness is measured by how the student converges toward the teacher. Additional findings show that improvement relative to the teacher aligns with gold-standard gains, and LLMs acting as judges offer little signal.
AI.motivation: Operational security settings have scarce, stale, and unrepresentative labels, making traditional benchmark-based evaluation unreliable for LLM-based learning harnesses.
AI.method: Use a stronger teacher model to supply sparse, high-precision corrections to a student with a continual learning harness. Score a harness by the degree of convergence of the student toward the teacher over time, across tasks, model families, and harness designs.
AI.result: Teacher-relative lift correlates with improvement on a held-out gold standard, validating the proxy. LLM-as-a-judge between similarly powered models yields no usable signal.
AI.conclusion: A teacher-sized model can be effectively improved via the same harness with sparse human corrections, enabling end-to-end evaluation without labeled benchmarks.

title: AgilePE: Autonomous UAV Pursuit-Evasion via Self-Play Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous pursuit-evasion is a fundamental challenge for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), requiring rapid decision-making under tightly coupled dynamics and continuously changing opponent behaviors. Traditional rule-based or differential-game approaches often struggle with high-dimensional aerial interactions and agile maneuvering. We present AgilePE, a complete system for autonomous UAV pursuit-evasion via self-play reinforcement learning. AgilePE integrates agile low-level control, competitive policy optimization, and sim-to-real deployment in a unified framework. The policy directly maps onboard state observations to Collective Thrust and Body Rates (CTBR) commands, enabling end-to-end agile maneuvering without intermediate trajectory planners or waypoint controllers. For training, we use competitive self-play with Prioritized Fictitious Self-Play (PFSP) and a diversified opponent pool, enabling agents to improve against historical policies while stabilizing optimization and reducing policy oscillation. This process leads to the emergence of sophisticated pursuit and evasion strategies. For real-world deployment, we develop a hardware-aligned simulation pipeline that models actuator-response dynamics, communication latency, and domain randomization. The learned policies transfer zero-shot to real quadrotors without task-specific tuning. Real-world experiments reproduce pursuit-evasion tactics observed in simulation, including rapid dodging and flanking, and demonstrate interactive two-agent zero-shot deployment.

AI.tldr: A self-play reinforcement learning framework (AgilePE) for autonomous UAV pursuit-evasion learns end-to-end CTBR control via competitive self-play with diverse opponents, along with a hardware-aligned sim-to-real pipeline that enables zero-shot transfer to real quadrotors; real-world tests demonstrate rapid dodging and flanking behaviors and interactive two-agent deployment.
AI.motivation: Pursuit-evasion with aerial vehicles involves high-dimensional, tightly coupled dynamics and adaptive opponent behavior; traditional rule-based or differential-game methods struggle to scale and adapt, necessitating end-to-end learning with robust sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: End-to-end policy mapping from onboard state observations to Collective Thrust and Body Rates (CTBR); competitive self-play using Prioritized Fictitious Self-Play (PFSP) and a diversified opponent pool; hardware-aligned simulation with actuator dynamics, latency modeling, and domain randomization; zero-shot sim-to-real deployment without task-specific tuning.
AI.result: Policies transfer to real quadrotors without task-specific tuning; observed tactics include rapid dodging and flanking; two-agent interactive zero-shot deployment demonstrated in real world.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates end-to-end RL for UAV pursuit-evasion with robust sim-to-real transfer; PFSP stabilizes training and enables emergence of sophisticated strategies; integration of hardware-aligned sim and diverse opponents yields practical zero-shot deployment for real-world UAVs.

title: The Integer Alibi: Localizing Cross-Kernel Divergence in INT8-Quantized LLM Inference
comment: 10 pages (IEEEtran two-column), 4 figures, 4 tables. Pre-registered protocol with append-only amendments; measurement artifacts and per-run manifests with kernel-selection evidence are described in the artifact statement. Companion to arXiv:2608.11693
summary: Two GPU kernels implementing the same scaled INT8 GEMM interface are usually treated as interchangeable. We test that assumption: holding the checkpoint, prompts, hardware, inference engine, decoding, and quantization configuration fixed, we swap only the INT8 linear kernel (CUTLASS versus Triton) inside vLLM. At 1.7B each arm reproduces itself bit-for-bit across cold restarts, yet the arms agree on no sequence in any end-to-end comparison we ran (0/8, 0/16, and 0/64). What makes this more than a benchmark discrepancy is an integer alibi: for shared INT8 operands under a verified no-overflow bound, the INT32 dot product is exact and order-independent, so the accumulator cannot be the source of any difference. Feeding both kernels identical operands from every linear layer of Qwen3-1.7B and 8B (196 and 252 layers), we find bit-identical outputs under power-of-two scales, confirming a pinned prediction list 196/196 and 252/252 (pre-registered at 1.7B, pinned but not blind at 8B), and observed differences of at most one bfloat16 spacing under the checkpoints' real scales. This localizes the divergence to scale application and output rounding after the exact accumulator. Applied as a probe checkpoint, the same intervention restores end-to-end bitwise agreement (8/8 and 16/16 sequences). Cross-implementation FP8 GEMM shows a different signature: both the prevalence and the magnitude of differences grow with reduction depth, while the INT8 fraction stays at parts per million and within one spacing over a 64x range of K. Teacher-forced replay ties layers to tokens: flips concentrate at small logit margins, which predict flip risk with ROC-AUC 0.94 on 16,384 positions. We will release the pre-registration, per-layer predictions, manifests with kernel-selection evidence, and a conformance procedure that turns these controls into a concrete check for kernel interchangeability.

AI.tldr: Two GPU INT8 GEMM kernels (CUTLASS vs Triton) are not interchangeable in end-to-end inference; bit-for-bit equality can occur locally, but differences arise from scale application and output rounding rather than accumulators; FP8 GEMM shows different patterns; a conformance procedure and preregistrations are proposed to certify interchangeability.
AI.motivation: Assess whether two ostensibly equivalent quantized GEMM kernels can be swapped without affecting end-to-end model outputs, under fixed model, hardware, and quantization settings.
AI.method: Swap only the INT8 linear kernel inside a fixed inference pipeline (vLLM), across multiple model sizes (Qwen3-1.7B and 8B). Evaluate bitwise agreement end-to-end, per-layer behavior, and scales. Use probe checkpoints to test whether scale/rounding causes divergence. Extend to FP8 GEMM and analyze logit-based flip risks with teacher-forced replay and ROC-AUC metrics. Pre-register per-layer predictions and conformance procedures.
AI.result: At 1.7B, each kernel arm is bit-for-bit identical under cold restarts but fails end-to-end comparisons (0/8, 0/16, 0/64). With shared INT8 operands under a no-overflow bound, the INT32 dot product is exact; divergence localizes to scale application and post-accumulator rounding. Feeding identical layer operands yields bit-identical outputs for Qwen3-1.7B across 196 layers and 8B across 252 layers when using power-of-two scales; observed end-to-end differences are limited to at most one bf16 spacing. A probe checkpoint intervention restores end-to-end bitwise agreement (8/8 and 16/16). FP8 GEMM shows broader differences that grow with depth, while INT8 fraction remains at ppm and within one spacing over a 64x range of K. Teacher-forced replay links flips to small logit margins, achieving ROC-AUC 0.94 on 16,384 positions. Plans to release preregistration, per-layer predictions, kernel-selection evidence, and a conformance procedure for practical interchangeability checks.
AI.conclusion: Kernel interchangeability for INT8 GEMM is nuanced: exact accumulators do not explain end-to-end differences; scale handling and post-accumulator rounding drive divergence. A concrete conformance framework can certify interchangeability, but it requires per-layer, per-scale validation and may differ across precision regimes (INT8 vs FP8).

title: CoANeRV: Coordinate-Aware Token-Space Neural Video Representation
comment: 27 pages, 13 figures. Code is available at https://github.com/jialong2023/CoANeRV
summary: Neural representations for videos (NeRV) have shown strong reconstruction fidelity by storing video-specific information in network weights. However, existing formulations typically require either costly per-video optimization or video-specific weight generation, making it difficult to scale to efficient amortized video representation. We propose CoANeRV, a coordinate-aware token-space framework that adapts the broader token-conditioned neural-field paradigm to amortized video representation. CoANeRV forms compact video tokens in one feed-forward pass and uses a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder to reconstruct continuous spatio-temporal queries, avoiding per-video decoder optimization or generation while retaining coordinate-level reconstruction flexibility. To make token-space reconstruction effective, CoANeRV introduces a coordinate-aware decoding architecture that aligns spatio-temporal queries with video tokens through axis-adaptive positional encoding and temperature-modulated cross-attention. Block-wise coordinate querying further reduces peak attention memory, making high-resolution reconstruction practical. Experiments on diverse video datasets show that CoANeRV consistently improves reconstruction quality over prior feed-forward NeRV and INR baselines, reduces peak memory compared with attention-based coordinate decoders, and provides efficient amortized encoding without per-video optimization. These results support the proposed video-specific combination of feed-forward token formation, spatio-temporal coordinate retrieval, and memory-bounded dense querying. The code is available at https://github.com/jialong2023/CoANeRV.

AI.tldr: CoANeRV introduces an amortized, token-based video representation with a coordinate-conditioned decoding pipeline, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction without per-video optimization and with lower peak memory than attention-based decoders.
AI.motivation: Overcome the scalability limits of NeRV and INR that rely on per-video optimization or video-specific weight generation, enabling efficient, scalable video representations.
AI.method: Form compact video tokens in a single pass; use a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder to reconstruct spatiotemporal queries; employ axis-adaptive positional encoding and temperature-modulated cross-attention; apply block-wise coordinate querying to reduce peak attention memory.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse video datasets show improved reconstruction quality over prior feed-forward NeRV and INR baselines, reduced peak memory compared to attention-based coordinate decoders, and efficient amortized encoding without per-video optimization.
AI.conclusion: A video-specific combination of feed-forward token formation, coordinate retrieval, and memory-bounded querying enables effective amortized video representation, with practical reconstruction fidelity and memory efficiency; code is available.

title: SemPlan: Benchmarking Structured Semantic Planning for LLM-Based Queries over Enterprise Data
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Natural-language interfaces to enterprise data must translate underspecified requests into governed, executable behavior while controlling invalid queries, policy failures, cost, and nondeterminism. SemPlan Benchmark evaluates this architectural design space with a deterministic synthetic bilingual benchmark containing 1,800 cases in English and Brazilian Portuguese; 1,200 cases form the frozen scientific evaluation subset. Four architectures are compared under the same model configuration: direct SQL generation (A1), a bounded tool-agent baseline (A2), structured semantic-request generation followed by deterministic planning and execution (A3), and a clarification/stateful semantic-plan variant (A4). Across 4,800 primary records, answer correctness was low in absolute terms: 22.25% for A1, 22.58% for A2, 25.67% for A3, and 24.25% for A4. A3 had the highest observed correctness and significantly exceeded A1, A2, and A4 in the pre-specified paired correctness analysis, while A1 retained the highest policy-correct rate and the lowest unsafe-or-invalid rate. A4 had the lowest mean API cost and lowest false-refusal rate. On a preselected 150-case stability subset, answer-correct repeatability ranged from 92.00% to 98.67%. The results support a trade-off interpretation rather than a universal ranking: additional structural constraints changed failure modes and efficiency, but did not monotonically improve correctness or solve ambiguity and multi-turn state consistency.

AI.tldr: Cross-architecture benchmark shows no universal winner; A3 achieves highest answer correctness but policy/invalid-rate trade-offs persist, with A1/A2 lower correctness but safer policy, and A4 lowest API cost.
AI.motivation: Evaluate how architectural design choices affect translating underspecified natural-language requests into governed, executable actions in enterprise data settings, focusing on correctness, safety, cost, and determinism.
AI.method: Four architectures (A1: direct SQL generation; A2: bounded tool-agent baseline; A3: structured semantic-request generation with deterministic planning/execution; A4: clarification/stateful semantic-plan variant) are evaluated on a deterministic bilingual benchmark of 1,800 English/Portuguese cases (1,200 in frozen scientific subset) across 4,800 primary records; performance metrics include answer correctness, policy-correct rate, unsafe/invalid rate, API cost, plus stability on a 150-case subset with 92.00%–98.67% repeatability.
AI.result: Answer correctness: A1 22.25%, A2 22.58%, A3 25.67%, A4 24.25%. A3 highest correctness and significantly better than A1/A2/A4 in paired analyses; A1 highest policy-correct rate and lowest unsafe/invalid rate. A4 lowest API cost and lowest false-refusal rate. Stability subset (150 cases): repeatability 92.00%–98.67%.
AI.conclusion: The results support a trade-off interpretation: adding structural constraints changes failure modes and efficiency but does not monotonically improve correctness or resolve ambiguity/multi-turn state consistency; no architecture dominates across all metrics.

title: OccPlanner: Goal-Aware Occupancy-Conditioned Diffusion Planner for Pixel-Goal Navigation
comment: Technical report. 11 pages, 6 figures, and 2 tables
summary: Pixel-goal navigation specifies targets directly in the agent's camera view, but a target pixel provides neither metric depth nor traversability, making 3D goal grounding and collision-free continuous planning challenging. We present OccPlanner, a goal-aware occupancy-conditioned diffusion planner that grounds pixel goals in egocentric metric space and sequentially conditions the goal representation on temporal visual context and learned local 3D occupancy features. To provide occupancy supervision at scale, we introduce L3ROcc, which converts monocular RGB navigation videos into robot-centric local 3D occupancy annotations through geometric reconstruction and ray-based visibility reasoning. We train OccPlanner on InternData-N1 and evaluate it in closed-loop simulation across four unseen scene categories from InternScenes and two goal-distance ranges. In the 5-8 m setting, OccPlanner increases the average success rate (SR) over NavDP from 20.81% to 71.55% across the four categories, reaching 86.20% and 84.92% in cluttered-easy and cluttered-hard scenes, respectively. Real-world open-loop experiments on a Unitree Go2 further provide initial evidence of sim-to-real transfer and adaptation with L3ROcc-generated supervision.

AI.tldr: OccPlanner is a diffusion-based planner that grounds pixel goals in egocentric metric space using learned local 3D occupancy, supervised by L3ROcc; it outperforms NavDP in simulation and shows initial sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Pixel-goal navigation lacks depth and traversability signals, making 3D grounding and continuous planning difficult. The work seeks to enable metric-space grounding of pixel goals with occupancy-aware planning and scalable supervision.
AI.method: OccPlanner is a goal-aware occupancy-conditioned diffusion planner that grounds pixel goals in egocentric metric space and progressively conditions the goal representation on temporal visual context and learned local 3D occupancy features. L3ROcc converts monocular RGB navigation videos into robot-centric local 3D occupancy annotations via geometric reconstruction and ray-based visibility reasoning. Training uses InternData-N1; evaluation uses InternScenes, two goal-distance ranges, 5-8 m setting; real-world tests on Unitree Go2.
AI.result: In 5-8 m, OccPlanner raises average SR over NavDP from 20.81% to 71.55 across four categories; achieves 86.20% (cluttered-easy) and 84.92% (cluttered-hard). Real-world open-loop tests on Unitree Go2 indicate initial sim-to-real transfer with L3ROcc supervision.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully grounds pixel goals in metric space with occupancy supervision, yielding substantial gains in success rate and demonstrating promising sim-to-real transfer; L3ROcc offers scalable supervisory signals for monocular navigation data.

title: CutClean: Neural Network Pruning for Privacy-Preserving Inference
summary: Neural networks are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications with growing privacy leakage concerns. We show that this privacy leakage can occur even in the absence of representation imbalances that lead to traditional dataset biases. This poses significant privacy risks when deploying models that process sensitive attributes. In this context, we propose CutClean, a privacy-aware pruning method that allows to reduce privacy information flow through the network, while increasing its sparsity. Our approach employs auxiliary linear privacy heads placed at each network's block to quantify information leakage, and further applies increasing levels of sparsity to remove the private attribute leakage, measured in terms of the accuracy of the privacy head attached to the last block. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively minimizes private information flow while achieving high sparsity rates and preserving classification target accuracy.

AI.tldr: CutClean is a privacy-aware pruning method that uses auxiliary privacy heads to measure leakage and prune for higher sparsity, reducing privacy information flow without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.motivation: Privacy leakage in neural networks can occur even without representation imbalances or traditional dataset biases, creating risks when models handle sensitive attributes.
AI.method: Attach linear privacy heads at each network block to quantify information leakage, then progressively increase sparsity to remove leakage—evaluated by the privacy head accuracy at the last block.
AI.result: The method effectively minimizes private information flow, achieves high sparsity, and preserves the target classification accuracy on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: CutClean provides a practical approach to privacy-preserving model pruning by directly targeting information leakage through structured privacy heads while maintaining performance.

title: CMCNet: Aligning Ultrasound Image Embeddings with Textual TI-RADS Representations for Fine-Grained Thyroid Classification
summary: Ultrasound is the primary imaging modality for assessing thyroid nodules, and the ACR TI-RADS framework standardizes diagnosis through five ultrasound feature categories that are aggregated into five risk levels (TR1-TR5). Although widely adopted in clinical practice, most deep learning approaches focus on binary malignancy classification, while multi-class prediction and explicit utilization of feature-level supervision remain underexplored, largely due to limited annotated data. In this study, we introduce the STN dataset of 600 thyroid nodules with paired transverse and longitudinal ultrasound images, bounding box annotations, and complete labels for all five TI-RADS feature categories. Following the clinical decision process, we investigate how structured feature information can guide representation learning during training while requiring only images at inference. We demonstrate that text embeddings derived from standardized feature descriptions form a stable surrogate representation for TI-RADS risk levels. Based on this observation, we propose CMCNet, which aligns image embeddings to fixed textual embeddings via a Center-Margin Contrastive Loss that simultaneously promotes intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. Experimental results show that this embedding alignment strategy is more data-efficient and robust than direct multitask learning, and consistently outperforms InfoNCE, center loss, a strong multitask baseline, and a VQA-style multimodal model, particularly in imbalanced settings. The dataset is freely available at doi: 10.5281/zenodo.19125693 and the source code is available at: https://www.healthinformaticslab.org/supp/.

AI.tldr: A dataset and method for TI-RADS thyroid nodule risk classification using image-text embedding alignment; introduces STN data with five TI-RADS feature annotations and utilizes fixed text descriptions to guide representation learning via Center-Margin Contrastive Loss (CMCNet).
AI.motivation: To move beyond binary malignancy classification in TI-RADS by exploiting multi-class, feature-level supervision under limited labeled data, and to leverage standardized textual feature descriptions as stable guidance for learning robust image embeddings.
AI.method: Propose CMCNet, which aligns image embeddings to fixed textual embeddings derived from TI-RADS feature descriptions using a Center-Margin Contrastive Loss that promotes intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. Training uses the STN dataset (600 nodules with transverse and longitudinal images, bounding boxes, and complete TI-RADS feature labels); at inference, only images are required. Comparative evaluation against InfoNCE, center loss, a multitask baseline, and a VQA-style multimodal model.
AI.result: Embedding alignment to text descriptions yields more data-efficient and robust representations than direct multitask learning, with consistent performance gains over baselines, particularly under class-imbalanced conditions.
AI.conclusion: Text-driven surrogate representations for TI-RADS risk levels are effective; the STN dataset and code are publicly available, enabling further exploration of feature-level supervision and label-efficient learning in ultrasound-based TI-RADS assessment.

title: How Compliant is Sepsis Treatment? An Expert-Guided Neuro-symbolic Pipeline for Generating Clinical Compliance Insights
comment: This has been submitted and accepted in NeSy 2026 (https://2026.nesyconf.org/)
summary: Verifying whether clinical care follows evidence-based protocols is a natural neuro-symbolic problem, yet the safety-critical setting defeats either paradigm alone. We present an expert-guided pipeline that constrains a large language model strictly to semantic normalization, mapping messy drug and microbiology strings onto a fixed clinical vocabulary, while a Sugeno fuzzy inference system reasons over the normalized events. The fuzzy layer encodes eight Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle rules and replaces binary judgments with graded scores in [0,1]. Applied to 2,438 MIMIC-IV v3.1 sepsis episodes, it surfaces antibiotic timing as the most critical breakdown (mean 0.24, 13% within one hour), Hour-1 underperformance (mean 36.7%), a 51% elevated-lactate drop-off, and descriptive differences in ICU stay across compliance groups (3.8 versus 5.1 days).

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic pipeline combines expert-guided semantic normalization with a Sugeno fuzzy inference to verify adherence to Surviving Sepsis Campaign rules on 2,438 MIMIC-IV sepsis episodes, highlighting antibiotic timing as critical and Hour-1 underperformance.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical clinical verification challenges where pure NLP or symbolic systems fall short; need robust mapping of messy biomedical strings to a fixed clinical vocabulary and reasoning with graded, non-binary judgments to assess adherence to guidelines.
AI.method: An expert-guided pipeline constrains a language model to semantically normalize drugs and microbiology strings into a fixed clinical vocabulary, then applies a Sugeno fuzzy inference system over the normalized events encoding eight Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle rules; binary judgments are replaced with graded scores in [0,1].
AI.result: Applied to 2,438 MIMIC-IV v3.1 sepsis episodes, the approach surfaces antibiotic timing as the most critical breakdown (mean 0.24, 13% within one hour), Hour-1 underperformance (mean 36.7%), a 51% elevated-lactate drop-off, and descriptive differences in ICU stay across compliance groups (3.8 vs 5.1 days).
AI.conclusion: The integrated neuro-symbolic approach yields actionable compliance signals through graded scores, identifying specific care gaps (notably antibiotic timing) and their association with differing ICU lengths of stay.

title: MMUSV-Sim: A Perception-Oriented Simulation and Data-Generation Platform for Multi-USV Cooperative Perception
summary: Cooperative perception among multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) combines complementary observations to extend maritime target sensing beyond the view range and field of a single platform. Developing such systems at scale calls for a unified workflow for configurable multi-USV scenarios, multimodal acquisition, and shared annotations. We present MMUSV-Sim, a perception-oriented maritime simulation and data-generation platform built on Unreal Engine 5 and Project AirSim. It provides island, open-sea, and port environments; configurable weather, time of day, and wave conditions; a diverse vessel asset library; and spline-based multi-vessel motion. MMUSV-Sim acquires RGB, depth, semantic, LiDAR, and radar observations across multiple USVs and captures a common world state for per-agent annotation export. Experiments verify that the configured wave settings produce the intended changes in vessel heave, roll, and pitch, and evaluate the geometric consistency between projected annotations and semantic renderings. In LiDAR-based cooperative BEV vessel detection experiments on the generated multi-USV dataset, Early Fusion achieves an AP@0.5 of 72.74, compared with 45.54 using a single USV.

AI.tldr: MMUSV-Sim is a unified maritime-simulation and data-generation platform for cooperative perception with multiple USVs, enabling configurable environments, multimodal sensing, and shared annotations; demonstrates improved LiDAR-based BEV vessel detection with Early Fusion versus a single USV.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable, configurable, and shareable multi-USV perception research by unifying simulation, data generation, and annotation export across diverse maritime scenarios and sensor modalities.
AI.method: Builds MMUSV-Sim on Unreal Engine 5 and Project AirSim with island/open-sea/port environments, configurable weather/time/wave, diverse vessel assets, and spline-based multi-vehicle motion. Sim captures RGB, depth, semantic, LiDAR, and radar across multiple USVs and exports per-agent annotations from a common world state. Validates wave-settings influence on vessel heave/roll/pitch and the geometric consistency between projected annotations and semantic renderings. Evaluates LiDAR-based cooperative BEV vessel detection with Early Fusion (AP@0.5 = 72.74) vs single-USV (AP@0.5 = 45.54).
AI.result: Demonstrates that cooperative perception via data-generation and fusion on a multi-USV platform yields substantial improvements in BEV vessel detection accuracy compared to single-USV setups; confirms physical plausibility of simulated dynamics and annotation projections; provides a scalable workflow and dataset for multi-USV maritime perception.
AI.conclusion: MMUSV-Sim offers a scalable, configurable framework for multi-USV cooperative perception research, enabling shared annotations and multimodal data generation; empirical results endorse the advantage of coordination (Early Fusion) over isolated sensing for BEV vessel detection, and the platform supports standardized evaluation and experimentation in maritime perception.

title: PPAPlace: Differentiable Cross-Stage Objectives for Chip Placement Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables, accepted at ICCAD 2026
summary: Macro placement significantly affects a chip's post-route performance, power, and area (PPA). Most placement methods optimize half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) as the primary objective. However, recent benchmarking shows a near-zero correlation between HPWL and post-route timing metrics such as the worst negative slack (WNS) and total negative slack (TNS). As a result, all six evaluated artificial intelligence (AI) placers degraded PPA relative to the hierarchical baseline. Recent efforts have tried to train cross-stage predictors to close this gap. However, existing methods focus on macro-only representations and use pre-route metrics as training labels. A label fidelity study of ten circuits at four design flow stages reveals that HPWL and pre-route timing poorly reflect final post-route timing rankings. In contrast, post-global-routing achieves the best balance between final timing fidelity and label generation cost-effectiveness. Based on this finding, PPAPlace is a timing-driven differentiable surrogate predicting post-route PPA from macro and standard-cell placements. The surrogate is a dual-stream predictor that combines graph attention over the chip netlist with spatial convolution over the placement grid. It is trained on post-global-routing labels. The predicted WNS and TNS gradients flow end-to-end back to cell coordinates. PPAPlace exploits these gradients in two ways: as a co-objective injected into an analytical placer's optimization loop (PPAPlace-CoOpt), and as a post-placement refinement step that adjusts macro positions via projected gradient descent (PPAPlace-Refine). On five ChiPBench test circuits excluded from training, PPAPlace improves average WNS and TNS by 22\% and 51\% over the hierarchical baseline while preserving power and routability, using the same predictor without test-circuit retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/ValleyC/PPAPlace.

AI.tldr: PPAPlace is a differentiable, timing-driven surrogate for post-route PPA that predicts WNS/TNS from macro and standard-cell placements using a dual-stream graph attention + spatial convolution model trained on post-global-routing labels; it enables co-optimization and refinement, achieving ~22% WNS and ~51% TNS improvements on unseen ChiPBench circuits.
AI.motivation: HPWL-based placement poorly predicts post-route timing; existing AI placers degrade PPA; label fidelity favors post-global-routing data; a differentiable surrogate with end-to-end gradients can guide placement toward better PPA.
AI.method: Dual-stream predictor combining graph attention over the chip netlist with spatial convolution over the placement grid; trained on post-global-routing labels (WNS/TNS). Gradients flow back to cell coordinates. Two deployment modes: PPAPlace-CoOpt (co-optimization within an analytical placer) and PPAPlace-Refine (gradient-based post-placement refinement).
AI.result: On five ChiPBench test circuits excluded from training, PPAPlace improves average WNS by 22% and TNS by 51% over the hierarchical baseline while preserving power and routability; achieves this using the same predictor without retraining on test circuits.
AI.conclusion: Timing-driven differentiable surrogates can provide robust, cross-circuit improvements to post-route PPA, enabling co-optimization and refinement without per-circuit retraining; open-source code is available.

title: Fast Implicit Neural Light Field Representation via Geometric Decomposition and Multi-Resolution Low-Rank Features
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, submitted to IEEE CYBER 2026
summary: Implicit neural representations provide a compact and continuous way to reconstruct dense light fields from sampled ray coordinates. However, fast light field reconstruction remains challenging because a light field is a high-dimensional signal with strong spatial-angular redundancy and structured disparity variations. Directly fitting 4D ray coordinates with a neural network often requires considerable optimization time to recover both view appearance and cross-view consistency. To address this issue, this paper proposes a fast implicit light field representation based on geometric decomposition and multi-resolution low-rank features. The proposed method decomposes a 4D light field into a horizontal disparity plane, a spatial texture plane, and a vertical disparity plane. Each plane is represented by a low-rank structure that combines a low-resolution 2D grid with the element-wise product of two high-resolution 1D line features at multiple resolution levels. The fused features are decoded by a lightweight multilayer perceptron to predict RGB values. Experiments on public light field datasets show that the proposed method achieves competitive reconstruction quality while providing a better trade-off among model parameters, training time, and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Fast implicit light field reconstruction via geometric decomposition into horizontal/vertical disparity planes and a spatial texture plane, each with a low-rank, multi-resolution 2D grid plus 1D line features; decoded by a lightweight MLP to predict RGB.
AI.motivation: Light fields are high-dimensional with strong spatial-angular redundancy and structured disparity; direct 4D coordinate fitting is slow. A fast, efficient representation is needed to recover view consistency and appearance.
AI.method: Decompose a 4D light field into three planes: horizontal disparity, spatial texture, vertical disparity. Each plane is modeled with a low-rank structure combining a low-resolution 2D grid with the element-wise product of two high-resolution 1D line features, at multiple resolution levels. The fused features are decoded by a lightweight MLP to estimate RGB values.
AI.result: Experiments on public light field datasets show competitive reconstruction quality with favorable trade-offs between model size, training time, and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Geometric decomposition plus multi-resolution low-rank features enables fast implicit LF reconstruction with good quality and efficiency, offering a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost.

title: Algorithm Design and Physician Liability
comment: 65 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables; includes online appendix (pp. 51-65)
summary: A single clinical algorithm can deliver unequal accuracy across patient groups, and concern about such disparity has grown as artificial intelligence (AI) spreads through clinical decision-making. In response, a liability rule introduced in the United States holds healthcare providers responsible when their reliance on disparate algorithms contributes to erroneous clinical decisions. We examine how such liability considerations reshape (i) an AI firm's algorithm design decisions that drive group-specific accuracy and (ii) a physician's decisions to use AI in healthcare delivery. The AI firm designs an algorithm for two patient groups, and improving accuracy for the disadvantaged group is more costly. The physician (who remains the accountable decision-maker) then decides whether to consult AI, weighing the reduction in clinical uncertainty against expected liability exposure when AI errors disproportionately affect the disadvantaged group. We find the liability rule can induce disparate use of AI: the physician may reduce AI use overall and, over an intermediate range of liability, rely on AI less for disadvantaged patients. The effect is non-monotone. As liability increases, the physician's use of AI for disadvantaged patients first declines, then rises as the firm reallocates investment toward reducing disparity or switches to an equal-accuracy design. Mandating equal algorithmic accuracy across patient groups can then inadvertently harm both groups, because a uniform accuracy requirement distorts the firm's investment incentives and the physician's equilibrium AI-use decisions.

AI.tldr: Liability for AI errors can reshape both AI firms' investment in group-specific accuracy and physicians' AI use, yielding non-monotone, potentially disparate effects; mandating equal accuracy can backfire by distorting incentives.
AI.motivation: Clinically deployed AI often exhibits unequal accuracy across patient groups. A liability rule in the U.S. makes providers responsible when reliance on such algorithms contributes to errors, prompting investigation into how liability affects (i) AI design decisions targeting group-specific accuracy and (ii) physicians' decisions to use AI.
AI.method: The paper uses a theoretical, game-theoretic model with two players: an AI firm choosing an algorithm that affects two patient groups’ accuracy and a physician deciding whether to consult AI, weighing uncertainty reduction against liability exposure from AI errors disproportionately affecting the disadvantaged group. The model analyzes how costs to improve disadvantaged-group accuracy and liability levels shape equilibria.
AI.result: Liability can induce disparate AI use: physicians may reduce overall AI use and, for mid-range liability, rely less on AI for disadvantaged patients. As liability rises further, firms reallocate investment toward reducing disparity or switch to equal-accuracy designs, causing disadvantaged-use to rise. A uniform accuracy mandate can distort investment incentives and harm both groups by misaligning firm designs with physician usage choices.
AI.conclusion: Liability regimes interact with algorithm design incentives in nontrivial ways. Policy makers should anticipate non-monotone and redistribution effects and that equal-accuracy mandates may backfire; nuanced approaches are needed to avoid harming both patient groups.

title: Vibration Suppression in Collaborative Flexible Payload Manipulation Using Passive Force Control
comment: Published in the proceedings of the 2026 European Control Conference (ECC)
summary: In large and heavy structures, vibrations arise during motion, posing significant challenges for precise manipulation. To accomplish the desired motion, control algorithms must effectively suppress these structural vibrations. In cutting edge projects, such as remote maintenance of future fusion energy reactors (tokamaks), the manipulation of this type of structure is defined as a crucial task. This paper presents a control strategy to suppress transverse vibrations in flexible payloads during motion using a collaborative payload manipulation approach. Two different industrial robot arms are arranged in a leader follower configuration for the manipulation strategy. The leader robot guides the motion with shaped velocity commands, while the follower robot ensures compliance with the estimated external forces applied by the leader on the payload through an admittance controller. Unlike existing methods, the proposed approach enables collaborative manipulation of heavier and larger flexible objects, addressing additional challenges such as vibration suppression and heterogeneous robot specifications. The dynamics of the leader follower payload system are modeled using an equivalent mass spring damper model, and it is shown that, with appropriate admittance parameters, the total energy of the system is passively dissipated. A stability proof is also provided. Numerical simulations validate the proposed method, and experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Collaborative leader-follower manipulation with admittance control suppresses vibrations in large flexible payloads; stability via passive energy dissipation is demonstrated with simulations and experiments.
AI.motivation: Vibration suppression in motion of large/heavy structures; relevant to remote maintenance of tokamaks; enabling manipulation of heavy flexible payloads during motion.
AI.method: Two industrial robots in leader-follower; leader shapes velocity; follower uses admittance control to comply with leader's applied forces on payload; dynamics modeled as mass-spring-damper; energy dissipation and stability proven; validated numerically and experimentally.
AI.result: Admittance-based follower with proper parameters ensures passive energy dissipation; system stability proven; simulations and experiments confirm vibration suppression and effective collaboration for heavy payloads.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative manipulation extends capabilities to heavier, larger flexible objects while achieving vibration suppression; the approach provides stability guarantees and practical validation.

title: Recent Advances in Deep Learning-Based Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
summary: Computational approaches to drug discovery involve multiple sub-problems, and among them, drug-target binding affinity prediction plays an important role. Despite recent advances, accurately predicting binding affinity remains an open research area. The major objective of our paper is to perform a comprehensive review and comparative analysis of recent machine learning methods for drug-target binding affinity prediction, with a focus on identifying strengths, limitations, and research gaps. We review representative recent deep learning approaches that use common benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, covering a range of neural network architectures and representation strategies. In addition, we analyze seven widely used benchmark datasets and commonly adopted evaluation metrics for drug-target binding affinity prediction. Our analysis indicates that although many methods report strong performance on standard benchmarks, their effectiveness is often influenced by dataset bias and limited evaluation settings. Furthermore, most methods exhibit reduced performance in cold-start scenarios, highlighting challenges in generalization. We identify several limitations of current approaches, including dataset imbalance, the lack of standardized evaluation, limited real-world applicability, and challenges in cold-start scenarios. We also discuss future research directions, including better dataset design, more robust evaluation methods, improved handling of cold-start problems, and the integration of multimodal representations.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey and benchmark-driven critique of ML-based drug–target binding affinity prediction, revealing dataset biases, cold-start weaknesses, and the need for standardized evaluation and multimodal data.
AI.motivation: DTA prediction is essential but current methods underperform in generalization; there is heterogeneity in datasets and evaluation, necessitating systematic review and benchmarking.
AI.method: Systematic review of representative deep learning approaches, datasets, and metrics; comparative analysis across seven benchmark datasets; synthesis of strengths/limitations and gaps; discussion of future directions.
AI.result: Although many methods achieve high scores on standard benchmarks, performance is sensitive to dataset bias and evaluation setup; cold-start scenarios show degraded performance; major limitations include dataset imbalance, inconsistent evaluation, limited real-world applicability, and poor generalization; identified research gaps and potential improvements.
AI.conclusion: Call for better dataset design, standardized evaluation protocols, robust handling of cold-start, and integration of multimodal representations to improve generalization and real-world applicability.

title: SAFE: Scene-Aware Feature Modulation for Color Constancy with Learned Color Space in Pure-Color Scenes
summary: Color constancy on pure-color scenes is challenging: when most pixels share a narrow band of hues, every chromaticity-based cue collapses to a single point and standard estimators become ambiguous. We propose a compact framework that couples two innovations: (i) SAFE, a Scene-Aware FeaturE modulation network that organizes illumination cues into a structured four-token representation, which is then selectively reweighted based on scene complexity features; (ii) the Learned Color Space (LCS), a scene-dependent chromaticity normalization that directly addresses the chromaticity collapse problem for pure-color scenes. Experiment results show that SAFE consistently improves performance in pure-color scenes. Compared to the best-performing baseline in each metric, it reduces the mean angular error by 10%, the best-25% error by 20%, and the worst-25% error by 5.8%.

AI.tldr: A compact color-constancy framework for pure-color scenes combining SAFE (Scene-Aware FeaturE modulation) and LCS (Learned Color Space). It addresses chromaticity collapse by structured cue representation and scene-dependent chromaticity normalization, yielding robust gains across angular-error metrics.
AI.motivation: Color constancy on pure-color scenes suffers from chromaticity collapse: most pixels share a narrow hue range, causing chromaticity-based cues to collapse to a point and standard estimators to become ambiguous. A need exists for scene-aware cue organization and normalization to improve robustness.
AI.method: (i) SAFE: a Scene-Aware FeaturE modulation network that represents illumination cues as a structured four-token representation, selectively reweighted by scene complexity features. (ii) LCS: a Learned Color Space that performs scene-dependent chromaticity normalization to mitigate chromaticity collapse in pure-color scenes.
AI.result: Experiment results show consistent improvements in pure-color scenes. Relative to the best baseline in every metric, mean angular error is reduced by 10%, best-25% error by 20%, and worst-25% error by 5.8%.
AI.conclusion: The SAFE + LCS framework provides robust color constancy in challenging pure-color scenes by combining structured illumination cues with adaptive chromaticity normalization, delivering across-the-board gains in key angular-error metrics.

title: Your Probabilistic JEPA Is Secretly a Hidden Markov Model: A State-Space Interpretation of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
summary: A hidden Markov model (HMM) combines three roles: inference of a hidden-state belief from observations, propagation through a Markov transition, and emission back to observation space. We show that full, time-indexed Predictive Information Bottleneck VJEPA (PIB-VJEPA) exposes the same computational structure: a stochastic context encoder plays the role of an amortized filtering distribution, a probabilistic predictor defines latent-state dynamics, and a decoder, inverse target encoder, or induced implicit conditional supplies the emission direction. We distinguish 4 progressively stronger levels of correspondence and give sufficient conditions for exact sequence-level HMM equivalence. To make the connection concrete, we introduce Markov-Chain JEPA (MCJEPA), which replaces the latent predictor by a learned transition matrix; in the finite time-homogeneous case, matrix powers guarantee exact multi-horizon Chapman--Kolmogorov consistency. Conditioned discrete-state transitions, continuous-state Markov kernels, and continuous-time dynamics extend this construction, while deterministic temporal JEPA appears as a degenerate Dirac-kernel special case. We further interpret predictive information-bottleneck learning as seeking a compact predictive state: compression promotes minimality, while residual predictability tests sufficiency. Controlled experiments support transition composition, the filtering interpretation, predictive Markovization in a known synthetic process, and the distinction between JEPA latent prediction and HMM-style sequence learning. Together, these results give temporal JEPA a principled state-space interpretation.

AI.tldr: PIB-VJEPA recasts HMMs as a predictive-information bottleneck pipeline, mapping a stochastic encoder to filtering, a predictor to latent dynamics, and a decoder to emissions. The work delineates four levels of correspondence, gives exact HMM-equivalence conditions, introduces MCJEPA with a learned transition matrix, extends to discrete/continuous/time settings (including Dirac/degenerate cases), and interprets compression as seeking a compact predictive state. Empirical results support transition composition, filtering interpretation, and a distinction between JEPA latent prediction and HMM-style learning, offering a principled state-space view of temporal JEPA.
AI.motivation: To unify temporal JEPA approaches with traditional sequence models (HMMs) by showing they share the same computational structure, thereby providing a principled state-space interpretation and extending JEPA to exact/HMM-like behavior across settings.
AI.method: Map HMM components to PIB-VJEPA elements: stochastic context encoder as amortized filtering distribution, probabilistic predictor for latent-state dynamics, and decoder/inverse target encoder as the emission mechanism. Define four levels of correspondence with sufficiency conditions for exact sequence-level HMM equivalence. Introduce MCJEPA by replacing latent predictor with a learnable transition matrix; in finite time-homogeneous cases, use matrix powers to ensure Chapman–Kolmogorov consistency. Extend to conditioned discrete states, continuous-state Markov kernels, and continuous-time dynamics; show deterministic JEPA as a Dirac-kernel degenerate case. Interpret predictive information-bottleneck learning as constructing a compact predictive state (compression for minimality, residual predictability for sufficiency).
AI.result: Derived four-tier correspondence between PIB-VJEPA and HMM structure; established exact/approximate equivalence conditions and Chapman–Kolmogorov consistency through MCJEPA; extended the framework to discrete/continuous/time settings, including degenerate deterministic JEPA as a Dirac kernel; provided experimental validation showing transition composition, filtering interpretation, and the distinction between JEPA latent prediction and HMM-style sequence learning.
AI.conclusion: Temporal JEPA can be given a principled state-space interpretation by aligning it with HMM structure through PIB-VJEPA and MCJEPA, with predictive compression yielding a compact predictive state and enabling exact or exact-like HMM behavior across discrete/continuous/time regimes.

title: Accelerating Large-scale Bundle Adjustment for LiDAR Mapping via Parallel Computing
comment: Accepted by IEEE International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE), 2026
summary: LiDAR bundle adjustment is widely utilized in mapping to construct globally consistent point cloud maps. In this paper, we propose the first fully parallel computing framework to accelerate LiDAR bundle adjustment for large-scale mapping, incorporating three key techniques. First, we design an adaptive, asynchronous data loading strategy to efficiently process large-scale point cloud datasets on memory-constrained GPUs. Secondly, we present a novel bottom-up voxelization method for extracting planar features, enabling fully parallelized pre-processing. Thirdly, we build upon a majorization-minimization formulation to accelerate compute-intensive tasks in the optimization via parallel computation, including the computation of residuals, Jacobian and Hessian matrices, and a parallel increment solver. To support our design, we provide both theoretical and experimental analysis of the time complexity of our approach. Extensive benchmarking on large-scale public datasets across various computational platforms validates the robustness and adaptability of our approach, achieving up to a tenfold improvement in computational efficiency while preserving mapping accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods. To benefit future research, the implementation code is available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: A fully parallel LiDAR bundle adjustment framework with adaptive data loading, parallel planar feature extraction via bottom-up voxelization, and majorization-minimization optimization, achieving up to 10x speedups with comparable accuracy.
AI.motivation: To address memory constraints and computational demands in large-scale LiDAR BA, enabling scalable, robust mapping across diverse hardware.
AI.method: Three key techniques: (1) adaptive asynchronous data loading for memory-constrained GPUs; (2) bottom-up voxelization for planar feature extraction enabling fully parallel pre-processing; (3) majorization-minimization optimization to parallelize computation of residuals, Jacobians, Hessians, and an incremental solver; theoretical and empirical time complexity analysis; benchmarking on large-scale public datasets across multiple platforms; open-source on GitHub.
AI.result: Demonstrates robustness and adaptability; up to 10x speedup; mapping accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods; code released on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for large-scale LiDAR mapping with parallel acceleration, offering theoretical and empirical validation, and enabling future extensions and broader adoption.

title: Dynamic Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing with Online Requests: Event-Driven Transformer--DRL and Rolling-Horizon Benchmarking
summary: This paper presents an event-driven learning and benchmarking framework for the Dynamic Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing Problem with progressively revealed requests and evolving vehicle states. Masked MLP and Transformer policies are trained through behavior cloning and proximal policy optimization. Deterministic feasibility masking prevents invalid vehicle--request assignments, while fixed-prefix/flexible-suffix route commitments protect completed, active, and near-term decisions and separately measure vehicle reassignment and resequencing. The learned policies are compared with dynamic insertion heuristics and time-limited rolling-horizon optimization. In a 20-scenario policy benchmark, all methods completed every request without invalid actions, but nearest feasible achieved the lowest mean objective and outperformed the learned policies in routing quality, waiting time, stability, makespan, and runtime. Across five independent training runs, PPO had little average effect on the MLP and improved the Transformer on average, although with greater seed variability. Under the common protocol, nearest feasible achieved the lowest combined objective and route disruption, whereas rolling horizon achieved the lowest waiting times and makespan at substantially higher computational cost. The learned policies retained millisecond-level decisions and transferred to instances with up to 80 requests without retraining, but did not outperform the strongest heuristic. No single method was best across routing efficiency, service responsiveness, stability, and online computation.

AI.tldr: Event-driven learning framework for Dynamic Multi-Depot VRP with progressively revealed requests; trains Masked MLP and Transformer via behavior cloning and proximal policy optimization; compares with heuristics and rolling-horizon; learned policies offer millisecond-level decisions and transfer to larger instances but often underperform the best heuristic in routing quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Study ML-based decision policies for dynamic VRP under progressive information reveal and evolving vehicle states; benchmark across routing quality, responsiveness, stability, and online computation with a reproducible protocol.
AI.method: Event-driven framework with deterministic feasibility masking; fixed-prefix/flexible-suffix route commitments to protect decisions and measure reassignment/resequencing; policies (Masked MLP and Transformer) trained with behavior cloning and PPO; comparisons against dynamic insertion heuristics and time-limited rolling-horizon optimization; 20-scenario policy benchmark with multiple training seeds.
AI.result: All methods completed requests without invalid actions; nearest feasible achieved lowest mean objective but learned policies did not outperform the strongest heuristic in routing quality, waiting time, stability, makespan, or runtime; PPO had little average effect on MLP and improved Transformer with greater seed variability; rolling horizon yielded lowest waiting times and makespan at higher computational cost; learned policies transferred to instances with up to 80 requests without retraining; no single method dominated across routing efficiency, service responsiveness, stability, and online computation.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates viable learning-based policies with millisecond decisions and transferability, but strong heuristics still outperformed learned policies on key routing metrics. Tradeoffs exist between solution quality and computation; further improvements or hybrid approaches may be needed for consistent supremacy across all objectives.

title: PPOM: Marginalizing Patch-Grid Phase for CLIP-Based Generalizable Vision-Language Prompt Tuning
summary: Prompt tuning adapts CLIP-based vision-language models with few trainable parameters, yet its predictions remain sensitive to the spatial sampling imposed by a frozen vision transformer. In particular, non-overlapping patch tokenization makes predictions depend on the alignment (phase) between image and the patch lattice. To reduce prediction sensitivity to patch-grid alignment, we introduce Patch-Phase Orbit Marginalization (PPOM), a training-free inference operator that treats phase shift as a nuisance variable. Given a patch stride, PPOM evaluates the identity view and reflection-padded translations, pairs opposite shifts into horizontal, vertical, and diagonal antithetic families, and assigns equal mass to these families and the identity prediction to avoid view-count bias during phase integration. In summary, PPOM provides a deterministic interface between prompt adaptation and patch-grid sensitivity. Across multiple prompt-learning hosts, PPOM improves host performance without re-training.

AI.tldr: PPOM is a training-free operator that marginalizes patch-phase shifts in prompt-tuned CLIP models to reduce sensitivity to patch-grid alignment, improving performance across hosts without retraining.
AI.motivation: Non-overlapping patch tokenization makes predictions depend on the alignment (phase) between image and patch lattice. Reducing this sensitivity is essential for robust prompt-tuning with vision-language models.
AI.method: Introduce Patch-Phase Orbit Marginalization (PPOM): at inference, given a patch stride, evaluate the identity view and reflection-padded translations; group opposite shifts into horizontal, vertical, and diagonal antithetic families; assign equal mass to these families and to the identity prediction to avoid view-count bias during phase integration; provides a deterministic interface between prompt adaptation and patch-grid sensitivity.
AI.result: Across multiple prompt-learning hosts, PPOM improves host performance without retraining, demonstrating reduced sensitivity to patch-grid phase and more stable predictions.
AI.conclusion: PPOM offers a training-free, deterministic mechanism to marginalize patch-phase variation, enabling prompt adaptation to work more robustly with fixed patch grids across diverse hosts.

title: ARC: Fair Relative Advantage Comparison in Open-Ended Real-World Interaction
summary: Open-ended real-world interaction admits multiple valid behaviors: an agent may answer directly, ask for clarification, provide progress updates, or confirm before acting. This flexibility breaks a core assumption behind group-based RL: rollouts compared within a group are no longer guaranteed to be behaviorally comparable. As a result, reward-model preferences over interaction style can distort relative advantages and steer optimization toward reward-preferred behaviors rather than context-appropriate ones. We formalize this as a \textit{reward fairness problem} and propose \textbf{ARC} (Advantage Regularization via Conditioning), a training recipe that restores fairer relative comparison through strategy-conditioned rollout grouping, together with hybrid rewards and entropy regularization. We study ARC in our proposed \inter, a novel paradigm for responsive, steerable, and execution-aware user-agent interaction that decouples user-visible communication from latent reasoning and tool use. \inter\ also provides the annotation and distillation pipeline for constructing \inter-86K, our strategy-annotated training corpus for supervised and RL training. Empirically, ARC substantially strengthens the core $τ/τ^2$ tool-use benchmarks, while \inter\ reduces time-to-first-token from 4.91s to 1.27s relative to a think-style baseline. Together, these results suggest that a central bottleneck in open-ended interactive learning is not only how agents are rewarded, but whether their behaviors are compared fairly in the first place. The ARC implementation and \inter-86K training data will be released.

AI.tldr: ARC tackles reward fairness in open-ended interactive learning by conditioning rollouts on strategy, using hybrid rewards and entropy regularization, paired with a responsive interface (Inter) and a large annotated corpus; empirically improves tool-use benchmarks and reduces time-to-first-token; release planned.
AI.motivation: Reward-model preferences can bias optimization when agents display diverse interaction styles. Group-based RL can make behaviorally non-comparable rollouts. This leads to distorted relative advantage and context- inappropriate optimization.
AI.method: Introduce ARC (Advantage Regularization via Conditioning) with strategy-conditioned rollout grouping, hybrid rewards, and entropy regularization. Apply ARC within Inter, a responsive, execution-aware user-agent interaction paradigm that separates visible communication from latent reasoning/tool use. Provide annotation/distillation pipeline and Inter-86K corpus for supervised/RL training.
AI.result: ARC substantially improves core τ/τ^2 tool-use benchmarks. Inter reduces time-to-first-token from 4.91s to 1.27s relative to a think-style baseline.
AI.conclusion: Fairness in behavior comparisons is a central bottleneck in open-ended interactive learning. ARC and Inter together offer a fairness-aware framework and data/resources, with plans to release implementations and the Inter-86K corpus.

title: PRM-as-a-Judge 1.5: A Toolkit for Robot Process Assessment
summary: Fine-grained robotic evaluation matters for understanding embodied models, going beyond binary success rates and rule-based process scores. We present PRM-as-a-Judge 1.5, a toolkit for robot process assessment that turns rollout videos into dense progress curves and derives multiple fine metrics. PRM-as-a-Judge 1.5 introduces three metrics, building on version 1.0, that characterize failure-side progress, post-drawdown recovery, and success-side execution quality, helping users understand embodied model capability. Based on the rollout videos from benchmarks, we perform a comprehensive assessment of the embodied models, providing some fine-grained metric results and key findings. We further introduce RoboPulse++ to evaluate the reliability of process reward models (PRM), providing evaluators with a more accurate testing platform. Moreover, we release a user-friendly assessment suite, including the benchmark, metric implementation, and visualization tools, to support reproducible manipulation process evaluation. We call on the community to rethink how robots are evaluated and establish transparent, procedural, and reproducible assessment as a foundation for the next generation of embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: PRM-as-a-Judge 1.5 introduces dense, fine-grained metrics for robotic process evaluation from rollout videos, adds metrics for failure-side progress, post-drawdown recovery, and success-side execution quality, and introduces RoboPulse++ to assess process reward model reliability, plus a reproducible assessment suite.
AI.motivation: Move beyond binary success rates and rule-based scores to richly characterize embodied model capability and failure modes, enabling transparent, reproducible evaluation of robotic processes.
AI.method: Convert rollout videos from benchmarks into dense progress curves; derive three new metrics (failure-side progress, post-drawdown recovery, success-side execution quality) building on PRM-v1.0; perform comprehensive assessments on benchmarks; introduce RoboPulse++ to evaluate the reliability of process reward models; release a user-friendly assessment suite including benchmark, metric implementations, and visualization tools.
AI.result: Present a comprehensive, fine-grained evaluation of embodied models with new metrics and reliability tooling; provide several metric results and key findings, demonstrating the utility of dense process evaluation and reproducible tooling.
AI.conclusion: Advocate for the community to adopt transparent, procedural, and reproducible assessment as a foundation for the next generation of embodied intelligence.

title: Stochastic Control Policies for Robust Molecular Transition Path Sampling
summary: Transition path sampling (TPS) aims to efficiently generate rare molecular transition trajectories between metastable states and is essential for understanding biomolecular mechanisms. Beyond traditional molecular dynamics (MD)-based sampling, machine learning has become central to state-of-the-art TPS. One major class of methods learns control forces during explicit MD rollouts. By preserving the underlying molecular dynamics, these methods tend to produce more physically plausible trajectories than endpoint-conditioned generators that construct paths directly. However, rollout-based control methods have been reported to exhibit unstable and strongly seed-dependent performance. We recast rollout-based control as learning a path-space proposal distribution and investigate stochasticity placement as a design choice for improving exploration and optimization robustness. We develop two stochastic policies: FS-TPS, which directly parameterizes a state-dependent Gaussian distribution over the control policy output, and LaS-TPS, which samples a compact latent control variable and decodes it into structured, cross-atom-correlated force variation. We conduct extensive multi-seed experiments on three biomolecular systems of increasing size: alanine dipeptide, chignolin, and BBL, a fast-folding protein. Stochastic policies consistently improve transition success and path quality over deterministic-policy baselines while substantially reducing sensitivity to random initialization.

AI.tldr: Reframes rollout-based transition path sampling (TPS) as learning a stochastic path-space proposal distribution, introducing FS-TPS and LaS-TPS to improve exploration and robustness; experiments on alanine dipeptide, chignolin, and BBL show improved transition success and path quality with reduced seed sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Rollout-based control in TPS tends to be unstable and highly seed-dependent; preserving MD dynamics while enabling robust exploration is essential for reliable sampling of rare biomolecular transitions.
AI.method: Two stochastic policies are proposed: FS-TPS, which parameterizes a state-dependent Gaussian over the control policy output, and LaS-TPS, which samples a compact latent control variable decoded into structured, cross-atom-correlated force variations. Rollout-based control is reframed as learning a path-space proposal distribution. The approach is validated via extensive multi-seed experiments on three biomolecules of increasing size: alanine dipeptide, chignolin, and BBL (a fast-folding protein).
AI.result: Across all systems, stochastic policies yield higher transition success and better path quality than deterministic baselines, and substantially reduce sensitivity to random initializations.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic path-space policies provide more robust exploration for TPS while preserving the underlying MD dynamics, offering a promising direction to stabilize rollout-based TPS and enhance sampling efficiency; future work could explore additional stochastic architectures, larger systems, and integration with other TPS strategies.

title: Rethinking Auxiliary Modalities in Multimodal Zero-shot Anomaly Detection: From Semantic Fusion to Conditional Modulation
summary: Recent foundation model-based methods have endowed RGB images with strong zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) through vision-language pretraining. However, RGB observations alone remain limited in perceiving anomalies dominated by geometric deformation, depth variation, or subtle surface changes. Auxiliary modalities can provide complementary structural information, but existing multimodal methods typically fuse them directly into a shared semantic space, which may disturb the text-aligned anomaly semantics established by RGB foundation models and often requires modality-specific architectures. To address this issue, we propose a plug-and-play auxiliary-conditioned enhancement framework for zero-shot anomaly detection. Instead of reconstructing a joint multimodal anomaly semantic space, our framework preserves the original RGB image-text anomaly matching pathway and uses auxiliary observations as conditional signals for RGB feature refinement, allowing auxiliary modalities to seamlessly enhance existing RGB-based zero-shot anomaly detectors. Specifically, a lightweight meta-learning module takes global RGB and auxiliary representations as input and generates sample-adaptive low-rank residual updates to determine how RGB features should be refined. We further construct uncertainty-aware spatial modulation from the initial RGB anomaly response and auxiliary reliability, which determines where local residual updates are strengthened or suppressed. This global-to-local conditional modulation enables selective multimodal enhancement while preserving the original RGB anomaly semantics. Extensive experiments on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies demonstrate that our framework consistently improves multiple popular RGB-based zero-shot anomaly detectors, achieving state-of-the-art performance for multimodal zero-shot anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play auxiliary-conditioned enhancement for zero-shot anomaly detection that preserves RGB-text alignment while using auxiliary modalities to condition RGB feature refinement via a meta-learning residual module and spatial modulation, achieving state-of-the-art multimodal ZSAD on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies.
AI.motivation: RGB-based ZSAD struggles with anomalies driven by geometry, depth, or subtle surface changes; auxiliary modalities offer structural cues but direct fusion can disrupt RGB-derived text-aligned anomaly semantics. A modular, non-disruptive multimodal improvement is needed.
AI.method: Introduce a lightweight meta-learning module that takes global RGB and auxiliary representations to generate sample-adaptive low-rank residual updates for RGB feature refinement. Build uncertainty-aware spatial modulation from the initial RGB anomaly response and auxiliary reliability to gate residual updates, enabling global-to-local, selective multimodal enhancement while preserving RGB anomaly semantics.
AI.result: Empirically boosts existing RGB-based ZSAD detectors and achieves state-of-the-art performance for multimodal ZSAD on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a versatile, plug-and-play approach that enhances RGB-based ZSAD with auxiliary information without altering core RGB text-aligned anomaly semantics, demonstrating strong cross-dataset effectiveness.

title: Reward Machines for Signal Temporal Logic
summary: Signal temporal logic (STL) provides a formal language for specifying real-time properties of real-valued observations, along with a quantitative robustness score for monitoring satisfaction. Control synthesis from STL specifications is of interest since manual controller design becomes infeasible as real-world systems grow in complexity. Moreover, many modern autonomous and AI-enabled systems lack accurate and complete system models, which makes optimization-based synthesis approaches unsuitable and motivates learning-based control. Prior work uses STL robustness scores as rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) to obtain control policies satisfying given specifications; however, robustness depends on execution history, leading to intractable state space expansion for general long-horizon specifications with arbitrarily nested temporal operators. This work introduces a novel automata-based approach that provides an efficient memory mechanism and associated Markovian rewards suitable for RL frameworks. Our approach constructs a timed alternating automaton from the given STL specifications, augments the state space with automaton locations and clock valuations, and derives rewards from the automaton acceptance condition. We empirically demonstrate that our approach learns policies that achieve higher robustness scores and satisfaction rates than those learned by existing approaches using robustness-based rewards.

AI.tldr: An automata-based RL framework for STL: uses a timed alternating automaton to provide memory-efficient, Markovian rewards, enabling robust RL satisfaction of STL specs; outperforms robustness-based reward baselines.
AI.motivation: STL enables real-time specifications with robustness scores, but RL with long-horizon, history-dependent robustness is intractable. A memory-efficient, model-free approach is needed to synthesize controllers that satisfy STL in uncertain systems.
AI.method: Build a timed alternating automaton from STL specifications, augment the agent state with automaton locations and clock valuations, derive rewards from the automaton acceptance condition, and integrate these rewards into reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Empirically, the approach yields policies with higher STL robustness scores and satisfaction rates than existing RL methods using robustness-based rewards.
AI.conclusion: An automata-based memory mechanism and Markovian reward structure improves learning of STL-satisfying policies in RL, facilitating effective control synthesis under incomplete models.

title: CORAL: Curriculum-Optimized Reward Adaptation for LiDAR-Based Goal-Directed Urban Driving
summary: Reinforcement learning is promising for autonomous urban driving, but long-horizon goal-directed navigation asks a policy to acquire several competing behaviors at once--reaching a distant goal, tracking a route, avoiding obstacles, obeying signals--and a fixed objective gives no order in which to learn them. This paper presents CORAL, which advances two schedules together: a five-stage curriculum that progressively lengthens routes and tightens behavioral constraints, and a stage-aware reward whose component weights shift emphasis from mission progress toward route following, safety, smoothness, and rule compliance as the task hardens. The policy is a multi-stream actor-critic network trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in CARLA on a compact 99-dimensional state pairing a polar LiDAR histogram with vehicle telemetry, ego-frame route geometry, and traffic-rule indicators--no point-cloud encoder, no bird's-eye-view rasterization. Against two PPO baselines under an identical protocol, CORAL reaches the goal in all twenty evaluation episodes on the longest routes under the full set of behavioral constraints, where the baselines reach 5% and 10%; a factorial ablation shows that neither schedule alone matches their combination: removing either lowers both success and route completion, and disabling both drops success to 55%. Trained in one town, the policy transfers zero-shot to seven unseen towns, succeeding in 68-98% of episodes on routes of the same 100-150 m length, with mean lateral deviation below 0.35 m.

AI.tldr: CORAL introduces a dual-schedule training regime for long-horizon urban driving: a five-stage curriculum that lengthens routes and tightens constraints, and a stage-aware reward that shifts emphasis from progress to route-following, safety, smoothness, and rule compliance as tasks become harder.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon, goal-directed navigation requires balancing multiple concurrent behaviors (route following, obstacle avoidance, signals, safety) without a natural learning order; naive training often underperforms due to conflicting objectives and curriculum design.
AI.method: Train a PPO-based actor-critic in CARLA using a multi-stream network (no BEV or point-cloud encoder) with a compact 99-dimensional state: LiDAR histogram, vehicle telemetry, ego-route geometry, and traffic-rule indicators. Employ a five-stage curriculum that increases route length and tightens behavioral constraints, coupled with a stage-aware reward whose weights progressively emphasize route following, safety, smoothness, and rule compliance.
AI.result: CORAL outperforms two PPO baselines under identical protocol, achieving success on all 20 evaluation episodes for the longest routes with full constraints (baselines reach 5% and 10%). Ablation shows that removing either the curriculum or the stage-aware reward degrades performance, and disabling both yields 55% success. Zero-shot transfer to seven unseen towns achieves 68–98% success on similar-length routes with lateral error <0.35 m.
AI.conclusion: Jointly employing a staged curriculum and stage-aware reward is crucial for mastering long-horizon, multi-objective driving. The approach enables robust transfer outside the training town and demonstrates the practical viability of curriculum-guided, multi-objective RL in autonomous driving without complex perception encoders.
