title: HI-MeshGraphNets: Efficient and Accurate Mesh-based Physics Learning with Hierarchical Multi-scale Graph Neural Networks
summary:
Machine-learned physical surrogate models have become promising alternatives to mesh-based numerical solvers. Among them, graph neural networks (GNNs) are well suited for representing simulation meshes and learning nodal state evolution through message passing. However, conventional flat message passing becomes inefficient on large, high-fidelity meshes because information propagates only one hop per layer, requiring deep processors for long-range interactions and increasing computational cost, memory usage, and the risk of over-smoothing.
  To address this limitation, we propose Hierarchical Interpolating MeshGraphNets (HI-MGN), a multiscale extension of MeshGraphNets for efficient long-range communication on unstructured meshes. HI-MGN replaces the flat processor with a hierarchical multiscale processor that coarsens graphs using farthest-point sampling and Voronoi partitioning while preserving the original mesh topology. Message passing on coarse graphs enables information to travel over larger geometric distances with fewer layers, and a learned graph interpolation network reconstructs fine-resolution features.
  Across three structural and fluid benchmarks, HI-MGN achieves improved accuracy compared with MeshGraphNets and the Bi-Stride Multi-Scale GNN while reducing training time and peak memory usage. The results show that topology-aware hierarchical message passing and learned coarse-to-fine interpolation provide an effective and practical framework for scalable mesh-based physics surrogate modeling.

AI.tldr: HI-MGN is a hierarchical, multiscale GNN extension of MeshGraphNets for efficient long-range communication on unstructured meshes, using farthest-point sampling and Voronoi partitioning to coarsen graphs, plus a learned interpolation network to reconstruct fine features.
AI.motivation: Flat message passing in GNNs propagates information one hop per layer, causing inefficiency on large, high-fidelity meshes due to high compute/memory demands and over-smoothing.
AI.method: Introduce a hierarchical multiscale processor that coarsens graphs via farthest-point sampling and Voronoi partitioning while preserving mesh topology. Perform message passing on coarse graphs to allow longer-range information flow with fewer layers, and employ a learned graph interpolation network to map coarse features back to the original fine mesh.
AI.result: Across three structural and fluid benchmarks, HI-MGN achieves higher accuracy than MeshGraphNets and Bi-Stride Multi-Scale GNN while reducing training time and peak memory usage.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware hierarchical message passing with learned coarse-to-fine interpolation provides an effective and practical framework for scalable mesh-based physics surrogate modeling.

title: ProFocus: Interpreting Affective Experience in Artistic Images with Progressive Visual Focusing
summary: Interpreting the emotional responses triggered by images is central to achieving emotional intelligence. Compared with natural images, visual art is intentionally created to elicit emotional responses from its viewers through abstract concepts and visual metaphors, making affective interpretation particularly challenging. However, most existing methods rely on general-purpose visual embeddings (e.g., CLIP), failing to capture the nuanced cues underlying artistic emotion. To address this gap, we propose \textbf{ProFocus}, a novel framework that models affective experience in artistic images via progressive visual focusing. The key idea is to model visual representation learning inspired by a hierarchical cognitive theory of human aesthetic appreciation. Technically, ProFocus contains two core components: a Hierarchical Art Critic (HAC) and a Progressive Hint Fusion (PHF) module. HAC leverages multimodal large language models to generate structured linguistic priors at three cognitive levels--atmospheric style, narrative subjects, and concrete details--thereby translating artistic perception into coherent semantic guidance. Building upon these priors, PHF departs from conventional cross-modal fusion by sequentially injecting the hierarchical hints into visual features, enabling a progressive focusing process that mirrors human perception. This design allows the model to capture subtle affective cues and produce more faithful explanations. Extensive experiments on the ArtEmis v1.0 and v2.0 datasets demonstrate that ProFocus consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both emotion recognition and affective explanation. Project page: https://github.com/Zhang-Zhiyan/ProFocus.

AI.tldr: ProFocus presents HAC and PHF for affective interpretation of artistic images, using hierarchical linguistic priors and progressive visual fusion, achieving state-of-the-art results on ArtEmis datasets for emotion recognition and explanations.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches rely on general-purpose visual embeddings and often fail to capture nuanced cues underlying artistic emotion; there is a need for structured multimodal priors and a progressive focusing mechanism aligned with human aesthetic appraisal.
AI.method: Hierarchical Art Critic (HAC) uses multimodal LLMs to generate linguistic priors at three cognitive levels—atmospheric style, narrative subjects, and concrete details—providing semantic guidance. Progressive Hint Fusion (PHF) sequentially injects these hierarchical hints into visual features to realize progressive focusing during representation learning. Evaluation on ArtEmis v1.0/v2.0 with analysis of emotion recognition and affective explanations; project page provided.
AI.result: ProFocus consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on ArtEmis 1.0/2.0 for both emotion recognition and affective explanation, demonstrating more faithful and interpretable affective reasoning in artistic images.
AI.conclusion: The combination of hierarchical, language-guided priors and progressive visual fusion enables more accurate and interpretable affective understanding of art, highlighting the value of progressive focusing in visual aesthetics tasks.

title: A Calibrated Test of Internal Action Maps: State Signals Without Global Affine Closure
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; includes supplementary results and ancillary reproducibility files
summary: A hidden state signal can be decodable or causally usable without supporting a reusable action map. We test whether action maps fitted without a source reach its natural post-action activation and compose. We organize the tests as an evidence lattice and validate the geometric branch on a known affine S_5 carrier: all held-source folds pass one-step, composition, inverse, decoding, and commutativity gates. Structured curvature and held-domain conjugacy raise error monotonically, but only 23/30 strongest cells flip a closure gate, bounding rather than universalizing calibration. In post-trained Qwen/Qwen3-4B, frozen final-token h28 affine maps have mean held-entity error .519, versus .398 for within-test-domain cross-fit. Seven randomized entity splits and map geometry do not support a purely entity-specific account. Earlier h4/h16 layers fit one-step transitions better, but h4 conflict-state decoding is weak and lexical controls remain unresolved. Three matched intervention datasets regenerated from one frozen checkpoint show causal effects only at h28/h36. Outcome-aware refitting improves h28 one-step error to .474 (.469 with weighting), yet no refit passes composition. Learned finite worlds likewise preserve relative algebraic signals or shared charts without held-source affine closure. Within the tested carriers, state availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure are separable. The result is limited to one pretrained model, sampled final-token layers, two finite worlds, and the tested affine or diagnostic function classes.

AI.tldr: Hidden-state signals can be decodable or causally usable without a reusable action map, but universal affine closure is not demonstrated; findings are limited to a single pretrained model, two finite worlds, and tested affine/diagnostic function classes.
AI.motivation: To determine whether decodability and causal influence of hidden-state signals require an explicit, reusable action map, and how geometry, held-source/held-domain constraints, and interventions affect closure and calibration.
AI.method: Tests organized as an evidence lattice; evaluated one-step, composition, inverse, decoding, and commutativity gates on an affine S5 carrier with held-source folds; analyzed curvature and held-domain conjugacy; tested frozen final-token affine maps in Qwen/Qwen3-4B; cross-fit across tests and multiple randomized entity splits; three matched intervention datasets from a single frozen checkpoint; analyzed state availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure.
AI.result: Across tests, some gates pass (e.g., many one-step and some inverse/decoding checks); 23/30 strongest cells flip a closure gate; curvature raises error monotonically; mean held-entity error around .469–.519 depending on setup; seven randomized splits and map geometry do not support a purely entity-specific account; h4/h16 fit one-step transitions better, but decoding in h4 is weak; causal effects observed only at h28/h36 in matched interventions; outcome-aware refitting improves h28 one-step error but does not yield a passing composition; learned finite worlds preserve algebraic signals and shared charts without held-source affine closure; conclusions remain bounded to the tested model, layers, finite worlds, and function classes.
AI.conclusion: State availability, causal use, local geometry, and reusable closure appear separable within the tested carriers; there is no evidence of universal affine closure under the tested conditions; generalization beyond the single pretrained model and specified settings remains limited.

title: Reflex: Enabling Fast and Predictive Vision-Language-Action Models for Reaction-Critical Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently achieved promising performance in robotic manipulation. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate generalization on static manipulation tasks and largely overlook dynamic interaction scenarios. To address this gap, we present ReflexBench, a benchmark for reaction-critical manipulation. ReflexBench contains six dynamic tasks and introduces an evaluation framework that decouples simulator stepping from robot control while supporting configurable latency under synchronous and asynchronous inference. Building upon ReflexBench, we propose ReflexVLA, an efficient VLA model designed for reaction-critical manipulation without large-scale robot-data pretraining. ReflexVLA enhances temporal reasoning through latent future prediction and multi-frame temporal fusion within the vision backbone, while reducing deployment latency through batched visual encoding and CUDA Graph replay. Experiments show that ReflexVLA consistently improves dynamic manipulation performance while maintaining competitive accuracy on standard static manipulation benchmarks, and real-world experiments further demonstrate its effectiveness under practical deployment conditions. Project website: https://reflexvla.github.io

AI.tldr: Dynamic manipulation benchmark ReflexBench and an efficient VLA model ReflexVLA for reaction-critical tasks; they address latency, asynchronous inference, and temporal reasoning, achieving improved dynamic performance while preserving static-task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on static tasks; need evaluation for reaction-critical, dynamic manipulation with real-time constraints and latency considerations.
AI.method: Introduce ReflexBench that decouples simulator stepping from control and supports configurable latency under synchronous/asynchronous inference; propose ReflexVLA with latent future prediction, multi-frame temporal fusion in vision backbone, and latency optimizations via batched encoding and CUDA Graphs.
AI.result: ReflexVLA improves dynamic manipulation performance across tasks, maintains competitive static-task accuracy, and shows real-world deployment viability.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables robust evaluation and deployment of reaction-critical VLA models; ReflexVLA offers efficient temporal reasoning for dynamic manipulation with low latency.

title: Federated Prompt Learning: A Unified Framework, Empirical Analysis, and Future Directions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become core components of cloud-based intelligent services in academia and industry, yet their training and deployment are hindered by high computational costs, data centralization, and privacy concerns. Federated learning (FL) offers a decentralized training paradigm that enables clients to collaboratively train a learning model without sharing raw data, making it a promising solution for privacy-preserving LLM training and reasoning. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of federated prompt learning (FPL) to review recent advances in integrating the federated learning paradigm and large language models, answering the following research questions: RQ1: The fundamental motivations, characteristics, and enabling technologies of FPL, and how it differs from conventional FL and full-model federated fine-tuning; RQ2: The trade-offs FPL approaches exhibit in performance, communication efficiency, computational overhead, scalability, personalization, and heterogeneity handling; RQ3: The remaining security, privacy, robustness, and system challenges, along with key future research directions. To this end, we systematically examine existing FPL methods across the full model lifecycle: pre-training, fine-tuning, and practical applications, while discussing security, privacy, and robustness issues and summarizing existing defense mechanisms. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future directions, aiming to help readers understand how the insights drive research in FPL.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey on Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) for LLMs, outlining motivations, techniques, trade-offs, security/privacy/robustness considerations, and future directions across pre-training, fine-tuning, and practical applications.
AI.motivation: Address the high computational costs, data centralization, and privacy concerns in LLM training/deployment by leveraging federated learning to enable decentralized training and privacy-preserving reasoning.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of FPL methods, comparing them with conventional FL and full-model federated fine-tuning; analysis across the full model lifecycle (pre-training, fine-tuning, applications); assessment of performance, communication, computation, scalability, personalization, heterogeneity, security, privacy, and robustness; synthesis of defense mechanisms and future research directions.
AI.result: Summaries of existing FPL approaches across pre-training, fine-tuning, and applications; identification of enabling technologies, architectural patterns, and trade-offs; documentation of security/privacy/robustness challenges and corresponding defenses; consolidation of open challenges and potential research directions.
AI.conclusion: FPL is a promising privacy-preserving paradigm for LLMs, yet significant challenges remain in performance, efficiency, personalization, heterogeneity handling, and defense against threats; the survey outlines directions needed to advance research and practical deployment.

title: FIRM: Fine-Grained Intra-Token Representation of Masks for Remote Sensing Reasoning Segmentation
summary: Reasoning segmentation requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate implicit instructions into precise pixel-level masks. MLLMs encode an image as visual tokens, each of which merges a group of image patches. In remote sensing images, small targets, thin structures, and adjacent instances can occupy different parts of the same visual token. Assigning a single binary mask label to such a token loses its internal spatial structure, causing nearby targets to merge and object boundaries to become coarse. To bridge this representational gap, we introduce FIRM, a Fine-grained Intra-token Representation of Masks. For each visual token, FIRM predicts a mask code that specifies an $r\times r$ binary sub-cell pattern rather than a single foreground/background label. Given a target identified by the MLLM, the complete grid of mask codes is predicted in one mask pass. Fixed lookup converts the predicted codes into a discrete sub-cell mask, while marginalizing the code distribution yields a soft structural field. To further recover fine-grained boundaries within each sub-cell, we introduce a lightweight continuous renderer that refines this field using pre-merge visual features and image details. Across five reasoning and referring segmentation benchmarks on satellite and UAV images, FIRM achieves leading results, including $70.5/80.5$ gIoU/cIoU on LaSeRS and a $3.0$-point average gain on EarthReason. These results demonstrate the value of explicitly representing intra-token mask patterns for fine-grained MLLM segmentation.

AI.tldr: Proposes FIRM: a fine-grained intra-token mask representation for MLLMs to preserve within-token spatial structure in remote-sensing segmentation by predicting r×r sub-cell mask codes per token, converting to discrete masks via lookup and refining with a lightweight renderer; achieves leading results on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In remote sensing, visual tokens may contain multiple nearby or touching targets, so a single binary label per token loses spatial structure, causing target merging and coarse boundaries. A finer intra-token representation could preserve boundaries and improve pixel-level masks.
AI.method: For each visual token, predict an r×r binary sub-cell mask code set representing intra-token structure. Inference yields a complete grid of codes for a target in one pass. Use a fixed lookup to convert codes to a discrete sub-cell mask, and marginalize the code distribution to obtain a soft structural field. Apply a lightweight continuous renderer that refines this field using pre-merge visual features and image details.
AI.result: Five reasoning and referring segmentation benchmarks on satellite/UAV data; reported state-of-the-art gains: e.g., 70.5/80.5 gIoU/cIoU on LaSeRS; ~3.0-point average gain on EarthReason; overall strong evidence that intra-token patterns improve fine-grained MLLM segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling intra-token mask patterns with FIRM improves pixel-level segmentation in MLLMs for remote sensing, yielding finer boundaries and reducing instance merging; the approach is effective across multiple benchmarks and suggests a new direction for token-level mask representations.

title: Exploring ESC Winners with Nested Diagrams
comment: Accepted for CONCEPTS 2026 Data Analysis Showcase (CDAS)
summary:
We present ConceptFlow, a scikit-learn-compatible Python library for Formal Concept Analysis that constructs and renders nested line diagrams from many-valued formal contexts. Given a many-valued context and a partition of its attributes into conceptual scales, ConceptFlow performs conceptual scaling, computes the factor lattices, identifies filled nodes of the corresponding subdirect product, and produces an interactive visualization.
  We apply ConceptFlow to the winners of the Eurovision Song Contest from 1975 to 2025, exploring relationships between voting patterns and musical characteristics. Voting support is captured by an outer scale spanning regional, cultural, historical, and political dimensions, while an inner scale captures musical characteristics via tempo and key. The resulting nested line diagram reveals implications across both scales, exposing dependencies between how winning entries were voted for and the musical properties they share.

AI.tldr: ConceptFlow is a scikit-learn-compatible Python library for Formal Concept Analysis that builds and renders nested line diagrams from many-valued contexts, and, applied to Eurovision winners 1975–2025, reveals cross-scale dependencies between voting patterns and musical characteristics.
AI.motivation: To analyze complex, cross-domain relationships in datasets where attributes have multiple values and are grouped into conceptual scales; to provide scalable, interpretable visualizations via FCA aligned with scikit-learn.
AI.method: Perform conceptual scaling of a many-valued context into an outer voting scale and an inner musical scale; compute factor lattices and the subdirect product; identify filled nodes; render interactive nested line diagrams; provide a scikit-learn-compatible library.
AI.result: The nested line diagrams expose implications across the two scales and reveal dependencies between how winning entries were voted for and their musical properties.
AI.conclusion: ConceptFlow offers a practical FCA-based tool for analyzing multi-valued data, enabling cross-scale insights and interactive visualization within a SciKit-Learn-compatible framework.

title: Effect of Twisted-Yarn Architecture on Pressure and Proximity Sensing Characteristics of Textile Capacitive Sensors for Robotic Skin
comment: 10 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
summary: Textile-integrated capacitive sensors offer flexible and conformable tactile sensing for wearable electronics and human-robot interaction; however, the influence of yarn-level architecture on capacitive transduction characteristics remains insufficiently quantified. This work presents a textile capacitive sensing platform based on silver-coated yarns coated with polydimethylsiloxane and assembled into one-, two-, and four-layer twisted configurations. The influence of effective electrode overlap area and inter-fiber separation on the capacitive response is systematically investigated, enabling architecture-dependent tuning of pressure and proximity sensing characteristics. Pressure was calculated using the localized single-fiber contact area, corresponding to stresses of 0.4-3.9 MPa. Increasing the layer number improved mechanical strength and sensing performance: elongation at break increased from 37.5% to 62.5% and 85.0%, while the maximum load increased from 23.3 to 42.7 and 89.7 N. Sensitivity increased with layer number and frequency, reaching 0.1331 MPa$^{-1}$ for the four-layer sensor at 100 kHz. The four-layer configuration also exhibited low hysteresis, minimal thermal drift from 25 to 90 $^\circ$C, and stable operation over 15,000 cycles. Proximity detection ranges of 60, 50, and 40 mm were obtained for the one-, two-, and four-layer sensors, respectively, revealing an architecture-dependent sensitivity-range trade-off. A 4$\times$4 textile sensing array enabled spatial contact mapping, while robotic-arm integration demonstrated real-time touch and proximity detection with an end-to-end robotic system latency (from detection to robot reaction) of 403 ms. The results establish yarn architecture as a tunable design parameter governing the measurement characteristics of textile-integrated capacitive sensing systems.

AI.tldr: Textile capacitive sensor platform using silver-coated yarns coated with PDMS, arranged in 1-, 2-, and 4-layer twisted configurations; layer number tunes capacitive transduction, mechanical robustness, and sensing ranges; architecture-dependent trade-offs for pressure and proximity sensing; demonstrated 4x4 array and robot integration with 403 ms latency.
AI.motivation: Quantify how yarn-scale architecture affects capacitive transduction and how layer count impacts sensitivity, range, hysteresis, thermal stability, and durability to enable design guidelines for textile tactile sensors.
AI.method: Fabricate silver-coated PDMS-coated yarn electrodes assembled into 1-, 2-, and 4-layer twisted stacks. Systematically vary effective electrode overlap and inter-fiber spacing. Calibrate pressure via localized single-fiber contact area. Characterize mechanical properties (elongation at break, maximum load). Measure capacitive response as a function of layer number and frequency. Assess hysteresis, thermal drift (25-90 C), and cycle stability (15k cycles). Evaluate proximity sensing ranges (60, 50, 40 mm). Build a 4x4 textile array for spatial mapping. Integrate with a robotic arm to assess real-time touch/proximity and end-to-end latency (403 ms).
AI.result: Layering increases sensitivity and range with higher layer counts; four-layer sensor achieves 0.1331 MPa^-1 at 100 kHz; proximity ranges decrease with more layers (60 mm, 50 mm, 40 mm). Mechanical properties improve: elongation at break from 37.5% to 62.5% to 85.0%; max load from 23.3 N to 42.7 N to 89.7 N. Low hysteresis, minimal thermal drift, stable over 15k cycles. A 4x4 array enables spatial contact mapping; robotic integration yields real-time sensing with 403 ms latency.
AI.conclusion: Yarn architecture is a tunable parameter controlling capacitive sensing characteristics; multilayer arrangements offer enhanced mechanical robustness and sensing performance; trade-offs exist between sensitivity and sensing range; supports scalable textile tactile sensing for wearables and HRI.

title: Geometric Filtering of LLM-Generated Samples for Few-Shot Text Classification
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, to be published in IEEE LACCI 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate synthetic training data for text classification, but the quality of generated samples is heterogeneous: some fall in correct class regions of the embedding space while others land in peripheral or cross-class zones. We propose a geometric filtering framework that evaluates each LLM-generated sample by its Euclidean distance to real class examples in a sentence embedding space, selecting only geometrically consistent candidates. A soft weighting mechanism transforms filter scores into sample weights for classifier training. Evaluated across 13 datasets, 5 classifiers, 10 augmentation methods, and over 6,700 configurations, our method achieves +2.61 percentage points (pp) over SMOTE ($p<0.0001$, Cohen's $d=0.95$, 88.9% win rate). The approach generalizes to named entity recognition (+9.26pp, 100% win rate) without filter modification, and is robust across 5 LLMs from 4 providers. A key finding is that the simplest distance-based filter consistently outperforms complex multi-criteria alternatives.

AI.tldr: A simple, geometry-based filter for LLM-generated synthetic data in text classification and NER, using distance to real class exemplars in embedding space to select and weight samples; outperforms SMOTE and more complex filters across many experiments; generalizes to NER and shows robustness across LLMs.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous quality of LLM-generated samples; need an objective criterion to filter and weight synthetic data to improve classifier performance.
AI.method: For each candidate sample, compute Euclidean distance to real class exemplars in a sentence embedding space; select based on distance; convert filter score to soft weights for training; evaluated across 13 datasets, 5 classifiers, 10 augmentation methods, and 6,700 configurations; also tested on NER without filter modification and across 5 LLMs from 4 providers.
AI.result: +2.61 percentage points over SMOTE (p<0.0001, Cohen's d=0.95, 88.9% win rate); NER gains +9.26pp with 100% win rate; robustness across 5 LLMs from 4 providers; 13 datasets, 5 classifiers, 10 augmentation methods, 6,700 configurations.
AI.conclusion: A simple distance-based filter suffices and outperforms complex multi-criteria filters; geometry-based filtering is effective for synthetic data augmentation and generalizes to NER without modification.

title: MedClaw: Heuristic Agent Harness for Long-Horizon Surgical Video Reasoning
summary: Understanding tens-of-minutes surgical videos requires long-horizon temporal reasoning, answering what happens before, after, or across stages of a procedure by grounding the question in visual evidence spread across time. Existing approaches handle this poorly: a one-shot vision-language model (VLM) compresses the whole procedure to fit its context window and loses the detail a "before" or "after" question depends on, while video agents that train the model where to look are data-hungry and transfer poorly to out-of-domain surgery. We build an agent harness that separates reasoning from perception and improves by evolving context rather than optimizing weights. A text-only orchestrator plans which evidence to gather and issues an auditable sequence of tool calls, while frozen vision-language sub-agents execute each call over the pixels, viewing, cropping, inspecting frames, and retrieving external knowledge. We further propose a gradient-free, reward-gated Heuristic Skill Distillation loop that mines the agent's own low-scoring traces and keeps a candidate skill only when it raises a validation reward, yielding reusable retrieval skills, notably directed re-look. Growing an external skill library rather than tuning weights, the loop adapts from only about 100 labeled examples, far fewer than supervised or reinforcement fine-tuning requires. To evaluate this agent, we introduce MedClawBench, a de-leaked, doctor-grounded benchmark of 1,123 questions over self-built long neurosurgery recordings and a held-out public lecture-video test split. Across both datasets and all four evaluation dimensions, our agent consistently outperforms one-shot VLMs and general video-agent frameworks, with the largest gains on the long, out-of-domain neurosurgery videos. Project page: https://fyycs.github.io/medclaw/.

AI.tldr: Planning-based agent harness for long-horizon surgical video QA. Uses a text-only orchestrator with frozen vision-language sub-agents, plus a gradient-free Skill Distillation loop to build an external skill library from ~100 labeled examples. Introduces MedClawBench benchmark and shows state-of-the-art performance on long, out-of-domain neurosurgery videos.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon understanding of surgical procedures is difficult with current one-shot VLMs that compress context and data-hungry video agents that overfit to training data. There is a need to separate reasoning from perception and to reuse retrieved evidence through reusable skills, enabling better transfer to out-of-domain surgeries.
AI.method: A text-only orchestrator plans which evidence to gather and issues auditable sequences of tool calls; frozen vision-language sub-agents execute calls over the pixels (view, crop, inspect, retrieve external knowledge). Introduces Gradient-free, reward-gated Heuristic Skill Distillation that mines low-scoring traces and retains skills only if they raise validation reward, forming a reusable external skill library (e.g., directed re-look). Data-efficient, leveraging ~100 labeled examples.
AI.result: Agent outperforms one-shot VLMs and general video-agent frameworks across MedClawBench and held-out lecture-video split on four evaluation dimensions; largest gains on long, out-of-domain neurosurgery videos.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective long-horizon reasoning with a modular perception-perception separation, data-efficient skill reuse, and a new benchmark for long surgical videos, supporting transfer to out-of-domain scenarios.

title: Ontology-Grounded Project Memory for Coding Agents
comment: 5 pages. Accepted at NeSy 2026 (Industry Track); to appear in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research vol. 284. Benchmark artifact: https://github.com/Trivyn/moosedev
summary: Coding agents have become the primary means of generating new code in many software projects, and the resulting velocity of changes makes keeping track of the reasons behind those changes challenging. This paper introduces MOOSEDev, a system designed to give coding agents structured, ontology-grounded project memory. The system captures architectural decisions, lessons, constraints, and rationales in a knowledge graph exposed to agents via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Records carry lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession links, queryable via MOOSE, a proprietary neurosymbolic engine that treats the symbolic layer as the primary reasoning substrate. We compared MOOSEDev against a production vector-memory tool on a neutral public corpus of 835 typed records. MOOSEDev returned the expected answer set essentially in full (0.98-1.00) on supersession, set-completeness, and negation questions, whereas the baseline's top-k retrieval surfaced between 6% and 27%. Conversely, relevance recall and token cost were largely equivalent between the two systems. We also describe a temporal commit-history bootstrap of our own codebase, a pre-registered live trial, and lessons learned.

AI.tldr: MOOSEDev is an ontology-grounded, memory-augmented coding-agent system using a knowledge graph and a neurosymbolic engine; it outperforms a production vector-memory baseline on key retrieval metrics (supersession, set-completeness, negation) while matching recall and token cost.
AI.motivation: As coding agents generate rapid changes, there is a need for structured, provenance-rich project memory that captures architectural decisions, constraints, lessons, and rationales to support traceability, governance, and reasoning.
AI.method: Develop MOOSEDev with a knowledge-graph–based project memory, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface for agents, lifecycle status, provenance, and supersession links; expose via MOOSE, a neurosymbolic engine where the symbolic layer is the primary reasoning substrate; evaluate against a production vector-memory tool on a neutral public corpus of 835 typed records; include a temporal commit-history bootstrap and a pre-registered live trial.
AI.result: MOOSEDev retrieved the expected answer set essentially in full (0.98–1.00) for supersession, set-completeness, and negation questions; the baseline top-k retrieval yielded 6%–27%; relevance recall and token cost were largely equivalent between systems.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-grounded, memory-augmented coding agents can achieve higher precision on targeted semantic queries (supersession, set-completeness, negation) without sacrificing recall or efficiency; the approach is viable and yields actionable deployment learnings.

title: Control-Informed Constraint Adaptation in Minimum-Time Trajectory Planning for Autonomous Racing
summary: Autonomous racecars operate at the limits of vehicle dynamics, where small control errors translate into safety-critical behavior and lost performance. Trajectory planners assume perfect tracking and remain blind to execution errors. To guarantee safety, trajectory planners therefore restrict themselves to conservative spatial margins, leaving usable track space untapped. To overcome these issues, we introduce a control-informed online trajectory planning framework that learns from its own execution errors. By measuring systematic tracking deviations during runtime, we dynamically adapt spatial track constraints and iteratively expand the free-space planning area. The planner remains time-optimal while compensating for accumulated execution errors. This method was analyzed in a high-fidelity closed-loop simulation environment with autonomous racecars. The results demonstrate that our approach reduces lap time by 1.8\,s without increasing computational burden, maintaining a median runtime of 25 ms. Our finding indicates that feeding control-induced deviations back into the planning layer unlocks performance previously inaccessible to modular architectures and enables autonomous vehicles to exploit track limits systematically.

AI.tldr: Control-informed online trajectory planning learns from execution errors to adapt spatial constraints, enabling time-optimal planning and improved lap times without extra computation.
AI.motivation: Autonomous racing exposes a gap between planning models (assumed perfect tracking) and real execution (systematic tracking errors); purely conservative planners waste track space and limit performance.
AI.method: Online measurement of systematic tracking deviations during runtime, dynamic adaptation of spatial track constraints, and iterative expansion of the planning free-space; evaluated in a high-fidelity closed-loop simulation with autonomous racecars; maintains time-optimality.
AI.result: Lap time reduced by 1.8 seconds; median planning runtime ~25 ms; no increase in computational burden; demonstrates that closing the loop between control errors and planning unlocks previously inaccessible performance.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating control-induced deviations into the planner enables exploiting track limits within modular architectures, enabling safer, faster autonomous racing and potentially broader dynamic-vehicle applications.

title: Variation Brownian Kernel Ladders
summary: Claims about the benefit of depth depend on the complexity assigned to a representation. We introduce the \emph{Variation Brownian Kernel Ladder} (VBKL), a path-atomic function-space framework that separates nonlinear recursive dictionary construction from linear variation superposition. Starting from linear projections, each atom recursively composes unit-ball profiles from the Brownian reproducing kernel Hilbert space; the full VBKL space is then the signed-measure variation hull of the completed dictionary. We identify each recursive dictionary as a union of Brownian pullback RKHS balls and establish variation-controlled Hölder regularity, compactness and attainment, and strict growth with depth under a local non-degeneracy condition whose trace lies in the support of the input measure. For associated finite lower-support architectures, we derive Rademacher and generalization bounds through Brownian quadratic chaos, signed threshold traces, and VC entropy. We also construct two-stage approximants by discretizing the outer measure and the selected outer Brownian profiles, obtaining an $M^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2}$ error bound, a sharp interpolation constant $\sqrt{A/2}$, and at most $2M$ active outer-profile basis contributions per evaluation. Controlled experiments illustrate the approximation mechanisms and indicate a favorable limited-data accuracy--complexity trade-off.

AI.tldr: Introducing the Variation Brownian Kernel Ladder (VBKL), a path-atomic function-space framework that separates nonlinear dictionary construction from linear variation, yielding regularity, compactness, and depth-growth guarantees; provides generalization bounds for finite architectures and two-stage discretized approximants with provable error bounds and favorable data-efficiency.
AI.motivation: To explain depth benefits in representation learning by controlling the complexity of the representation and separating dictionary construction from variation, enabling rigorous regularity, approximation, and generalization guarantees in a Brownian RKHS setting.
AI.method: Define VBKL as a union of Brownian pullback RKHS balls; recursively build a dictionary from unit-ball Brownian RKHS profiles; compute variation hull; derive Hölder regularity, compactness, attainment; derive bounds via Brownian quadratic chaos; design discretized two-stage approximants with M and m parameters; derive error bounds and constants; provide experiments.
AI.result: Proved variation-controlled Hölder regularity, compactness and attainment; strict growth with depth under non-degeneracy; Rademacher and generalization bounds for finite architectures; two-stage approximants with error O(M^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2}) and interpolation constant sqrt(A/2); runtime bound on active outer-profile basis; experimental validation showing favorable trade-off.
AI.conclusion: VBKL offers a principled, scalable framework linking depth to representation complexity, with finite-sample guarantees and practical discretization schemes.

title: Content Based Video Narration of Gameplay with Vision Language Models
summary: Live game commentary is scarce: it exists for professional esports broadcasts and almost nowhere else. We present a content-based video narration system that produces spoken, esports-style commentary for arbitrary gameplay recordings using a general-purpose vision-language model (VLM) and a text-to-speech back end, with no game-specific instrumentation, no engine telemetry, and no task-specific training. Three mechanisms carry the system. Temporal mosaic packing arranges nine uniformly sampled frames into a single 3x3 image, letting an image-native VLM reason about motion while consuming one image payload per segment instead of nine. Context-conditioned prompting replays the K most recent narrations as assistant-role history, suppressing the repetition that dominates per-segment captioning of static scenes. Duration-conditioned generation and elastic alignment constrain narration length in the prompt, then time-scale or symmetrically pad the synthesized audio so each utterance fills its segment slot exactly, giving frame-accurate muxing without a forced aligner. The implementation supports either cloud TTS or a 6-bit quantized 4B-parameter on-device TTS model on Apple silicon, making the speech stage fully local. We report a qualitative case study on real-time strategy footage, a cost model showing the mosaic reduces per-minute image payloads by 9x, and a candid account of observed failure modes - hallucinated game state, resolution loss from mosaicking, and prosody artifacts from time-scaling. We release the system as a reproducible baseline, with an evaluation protocol for the quantitative study a full version will report.

AI.tldr: A general-purpose vision-language model-based system can generate esports-style narration for arbitrary gameplay video using mosaic frames, context recall, and duration-controlled TTS, achieving local processing and 9x image payload reduction, with identified failure modes and a reproducible baseline.
AI.motivation: Scarcity of live game commentary beyond professional broadcasts and the need to auto-narrate arbitrary gameplay without game-specific instrumentation or training.
AI.method: Three mechanisms: (1) temporal mosaic packing: encode 9 frames as a single 3x3 image to reduce payload and enable motion reasoning; (2) context-conditioned prompting: replay the K most recent narrations as assistant history to reduce repetition in static scenes; (3) duration-conditioned generation with elastic alignment: constrain narration length to the segment and adjust audio timing to fill slots; plus a local text-to-speech backend (cloud or on-device) and no task-specific training.
AI.result: Qualitative RTS case study; a cost model shows mosaic reduces per-minute image payload by 9x; identified failure modes include hallucinated game state, mosaic-induced resolution loss, and prosody artifacts from time-scaling; released as a reproducible baseline with a protocol for quantitative evaluation to be reported in full version.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of end-to-end, local, content-based esports narration for arbitrary gameplay without instrumentation; provides a scalable baseline and highlights key failure modes and directions for future improvements and evaluation.

title: Second Thought: Reasoning in Parallel as LLM Agents Act and Observe
summary: LLM agents in the ReAct paradigm alternate between reasoning, acting, and observing, but deliberate reasoning is confined to the Thought phase: while the agent serializes an action and waits for the environment, its reasoning is frozen. We identify this recurring interval for Action and Observation as a reasoning idle window and ask whether it can host additional reasoning in parallel that serves future turns. Therefore, we propose Second Thought, a training-free inference framework that forks four auxiliary branches the instant each Thought phase concludes, decodes them concurrently with the main loop, and merges the generated thoughts back when the environment observation arrives. In this way, Second Thought relocates the added reasoning off the main thread's sequential decoding path. Across three agentic benchmarks and three reasoning LLMs, Second Thought lowers the average turn count in all nine (model,benchmark) pairs and reduces main thread decoding in six of them by up to 43% (roughly 20% on average among those settings), while leaving it essentially unchanged in a seventh; Pass@1 shows no significant change in seven of nine pairs and the two significant differences are +12.4 and +10.2 points. Against a compute-matched control that forces an equivalent budget onto the main thread's own reasoning, it attains strictly higher Pass@1 with 1.3 to 3.2 less sequential decoding in all four settings where the control applies.

AI.tldr: Second Thought is a training-free inference framework for LLM agents in the ReAct paradigm. It forks auxiliary reasoning branches at the end of each Thought phase, decodes them in parallel with the main loop, and merges results when the observation arrives, reducing sequential decoding and turn count while preserving or improving Pass@1 under compute budgets.
AI.motivation: Mitigate the main sequential bottleneck in ReAct-style agents where reasoning is confined to the Thought phase and the Action-Observation cycle enforces idle waiting. Explore whether parallel offline reasoning can improve efficiency and performance without retraining.
AI.method: Introduce a training-free inference technique: at each Thought completion, fork four auxiliary branches that decode in parallel with the main loop; merge the generated thoughts when the environment observation arrives. Evaluate across three agentic benchmarks and three reasoning LLMs, comparing against a baseline and a compute-matched control.
AI.result: Across nine model-benchmark pairs, Second Thought reduces average turn count in all; main-thread decoding decreases in six pairs by up to 43% (avg ~20%). Pass@1 largely unchanged in seven of nine pairs; two notable gains (+12.4, +10.2). A compute-matched control achieves higher Pass@1 with 1.3–3.2x less sequential decoding in settings where applied.
AI.conclusion: Second Thought demonstrates a practical, training-free method to relocate added reasoning off the main decoding thread, yielding efficiency gains with minimal or no penalties to accuracy under comparable compute. It suggests parallel reasoning can complement sequential LLM reasoning in agentic workflows.

title: THRIVE: Therapeutic Humanoid Robot In Virtual Environment
summary: This paper presents THRIVE (Therapeutic Humanoid Robot In Virtual Environment), an at-home rehabilitation platform that integrates a suite of virtual-reality upper-body rehabilitation games, a real-time camera-based motion-tracking system, and a socially interactive robot therapist. The system is designed for therapy and intervention in children with upper-limb motor impairments, which can be improved through consistent, task-specific practice. THRIVE features a set of newly designed, engaging games that target functional reaching, grasping, and object-manipulation movements through customizable popping, hitting, catching, and grabbing tasks, while the camera-based tracking system captures the child's kinematic performance during play. A robot therapist - deployable either as a physical robotic coach or as a remote-presence virtual agent - delivers adaptive, dynamic feedback to motivate the child and guide their movements toward therapeutic goals. THRIVE decouples the therapeutic games from the robot embodiment, extending the platform to support various embodiments and different robots within one modular system. This robot-agnostic design makes THRIVE affordable, scalable, and readily adaptable for sustained use in the home, offering a practical pathway to more consistent and engaging upper-limb therapy for children with motor function impairments.

AI.tldr: Modular robot-augmented at-home rehabilitation platform (THRIVE) for children with upper-limb impairments using VR games, real-time camera tracking, and a robot therapist; robot-agnostic and home-ready.
AI.motivation: Address the need for frequent, task-specific, engaging therapy outside clinics to improve adherence and outcomes in pediatric upper-limb rehabilitation via home-based, adaptive assistance.
AI.method: Develop THRIVE: a suite of engaging upper-limb rehab VR games, a camera-based motion-tracking system, and a robot therapist; decoupled game logic from robot embodiment to enable multiple robots; can function as a physical coach or remote agent; modular, scalable design.
AI.result: Proposes a functional platform with targeted motor tasks (reaching, grasping, object manipulation) and real-time performance capture; adaptive feedback; robot-agnostic architecture enabling affordability and home deployment.
AI.conclusion: THRIVE offers a practical, scalable pathway to more consistent, engaging pediatric upper-limb therapy and can be adapted to different robots and home contexts.

title: Fashion Outfit Generation via Unified Sequential Composition Models
summary: The task of synthesizing stylistically coherent fashion outfits from massive item libraries, known as fashion outfit generation, remains a non-trivial challenge, primarily due to the non-monotonic and implicit nature of aesthetic compatibility, coupled with the exponentially large combinatorial search space. In this paper, we formalize this task as Constrained Ensemble Generation (CEG) and model it as a finite-horizon deterministic Markov Decision Process. To address CEG in fashion, we propose the Unified Sequential Composition Model (USCM), which jointly models set-level compatibility and latent composition intents. Guided by USCM's learned priors, a Latent Expansion Monte Carlo Tree Search (LE-MCTS) mechanism is proposed to handle item retrieval during composition, balancing local aesthetic synergy with global structural balance. Extensive experiments on the Polyvore Outfits dataset, along with zero-shot evaluations on the iFashion and PolyvoreU datasets, demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance across independent human preference evaluations, automated aesthetic proxies, and structural validity metrics for constrained fashion outfit generation.

AI.tldr: Formalizes fashion outfit generation as Constrained Ensemble Generation (CEG) and solves it with USCM and LE-MCTS, achieving state-of-the-art results on Polyvore Outfits and zero-shot benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Aesthetic compatibility in fashion is non-monotonic and implicit, and the combinatorial search space is exponentially large; there is a need for principled, scalable methods that jointly model compatibility and composition intent.
AI.method: Introduce Unified Sequential Composition Model (USCM) that jointly models set-level compatibility and latent composition intents, and a Latent Expansion Monte Carlo Tree Search (LE-MCTS) to retrieve items during composition guided by USCM priors within a finite-horizon deterministic MDP framework for Constrained Ensemble Generation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Polyvore Outfits and zero-shot on iFashion/PolyvoreU shows state-of-the-art performance across human preference judgments, automated aesthetic metrics, and structural validity for constrained outfit generation.
AI.conclusion: USCM with LE-MCTS effectively balances local aesthetic synergy and global structure, enabling scalable, constrained fashion outfit generation with strong empirical performance.

title: ForgeWM: Progressive Causal Training for Few-Step Action-Conditioned Video World Models
summary: Action-conditioned video world models require low-latency causal generation and reliable responses to game-native controls. Although causal distillation enables one- or few-step video synthesis, extending it to interactive world models remains challenging, as discrete keyboard states and continuous mouse motion must remain aligned with temporally compressed latent chunks during causal training and autoregressive rollout. We introduce ForgeWM, a progressive framework that transforms a bidirectional action-conditioned video generator into efficient few-step world models through domain adaptation, teacher-forced causal training, causal consistency distillation, and on-policy distribution matching with a bidirectional teacher. The resulting budget-specialized students operate at steady-state denoising budgets of 1, 2, and 4 steps. ForgeWM further supports a dual-path deployment protocol combining latency-critical interaction with optional replay-time refinement, where the one-step student re-noises and refines its saved draft. On paired Minecraft trajectories, ForgeWM leads the evaluated systems in Imaging Quality, reference-aligned motion-profile agreement, action-sign accuracy, and mouse-control accuracy, while achieving the lowest reference LPIPS; the same four-stage recipe transfers to gamepad-controlled FPS gameplay. Replay-time refinement matches four-step reference quality while remaining roughly three times closer to the experienced trajectory than regeneration from noise. These results demonstrate ForgeWM's effectiveness for controllable few-step video generation.

AI.tldr: ForgeWM converts a bidirectional action-conditioned video generator into few-step, budget-specialized world-models (1, 2, 4 steps) using domain adaptation, teacher-forced causal training, causal consistency distillation, and on-policy distribution matching with a bidirectional teacher; supports latency-critical interaction with replay-time refinement via dual-path deployment; achieves state-leading quality and control accuracy on Minecraft trajectories and FPS gameplay; replay-time refinement matches multi-step references with improved trajectory fidelity.
AI.motivation: Enable low-latency, controllable, interactive video world models that stay aligned with discrete controls and continuous cursor/mouse motion while operating on temporally compressed latent chunks.
AI.method: ForgeWM comprises a four-stage recipe: (1) domain adaptation to tailor a bidirectional action-conditioned video generator to world-model tasks; (2) teacher-forced causal training to align training-time causal steps with rollout; (3) causal consistency distillation to produce budget-specialized 1-, 2-, and 4-step students; (4) on-policy distribution matching using a bidirectional teacher; plus a dual-path deployment protocol where a one-step student can re-noise/refine a saved draft during replay-time.
AI.result: On paired Minecraft trajectories, ForgeWM achieves leading Imaging Quality, reference-aligned motion-profile agreement, action-sign accuracy, and mouse-control accuracy, while attaining the lowest reference LPIPS. The same four-stage recipe transfers to gamepad-controlled FPS gameplay. Replay-time refinement matches four-step reference quality and remains ~3x closer to the experienced trajectory than regeneration from noise.
AI.conclusion: ForgeWM is an effective framework for controllable few-step video generation, enabling efficient, responsive world-models with tunable latency via budget-specific students and optional replay-time refinement.

title: Learning to Assemble Novel Structures with Unfamiliar Parts under Semantic Constraints
comment: Accepted to, and to appear in the 20th Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning (NeSy 2026)
summary: This paper describes a neurosymbolic architecture for learning to assemble novel structures using evidence from embodied conversations and task demonstrations. We focus on scenarios where an agent encounters, after deployment, semantic constraints on structures--in other words, constraints as to which part types and features make valid structures--that were not available during training, and where it is initially unaware of the relevant structure and component part concepts. The agent must acquire and exploit such knowledge through user interactions while attempting assembly. We study this setting in a simulated toy truck assembly domain, learning from symbolic evidence encoded in natural language and from dense visual observations. Our experiments show that communicating semantic constraints through natural language (e.g., "dump trucks have a dumper") yields more data-efficient online adaptation than relying only on task demonstrations and/or only naming the parts through natural language.

AI.tldr: Neurosymbolic learning uses natural-language constraints and visual evidence to quickly acquire unseen structural rules for assembling novel parts post-deployment.
AI.motivation: Agents face unseen semantic constraints after deployment and must learn from user interactions and demonstrations in a data-efficient way.
AI.method: A neurosymbolic architecture integrating symbolic linguistic constraints with dense visual observations in a toy truck assembly domain; leverages natural-language cues (e.g., 'dump trucks have a dumper') to guide online adaptation.
AI.result: Language-based semantic constraints yield more data-efficient online adaptation than using only task demonstrations or only naming parts.
AI.conclusion: Language-grounded semantic constraints enhance rapid acquisition of unseen structural knowledge in neurosymbolic assembly tasks during deployment.

title: Expected Free Energy-based Informative Path Planning for Robotic Mars Exploration
summary: An autonomous robot efficiently exploring an unknown environment, such as looking for water sources on Mars, faces two simultaneous demands: building an accurate information map while quickly finding the regions of greatest value, and paying for every meter of travel and the cost of every measurement it takes. Classical information-seeking and reward-seeking criteria address only one of these objectives at a time. Here, we propose Expected Free Energy (EFE), the principled action-selection objective from active inference, as a unifying criterion for budgeted robotic informative path planning. Maintaining a Gaussian-process belief over the information field, our agent plans continuous trajectories that minimize expected free energy under hard path-length constraints. The results from multiple realizations show that EFE-based planning yields accurate posterior maps and locates the highest-value regions simultaneously, outperforming information-theoretic baselines under the same settings. In robotic exploration, these unified, easy-to-tune principled information-gathering strategies facilitate autonomous deployment while enforcing efficiency and resource constraints.

AI.tldr: EFE unifies information-seeking and reward-seeking under budgeted planning via Active Inference; Gaussian-process map; continuous trajectories; outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Address the dual objective in robotic exploration: build accurate information maps while efficiently exploring under resource constraints; existing criteria optimize only one objective.
AI.method: Maintain a Gaussian-process belief over the information field and plan continuous trajectories that minimize expected free energy, under hard path-length constraints; use EFE as the action-selection objective.
AI.result: EFE-based planning yields accurate posterior maps and identifies high-value regions simultaneously, outperforming information-theoretic baselines under the same settings.
AI.conclusion: Unified, principled information-gathering strategies based on EFE enable efficient, resource-constrained autonomous robotic exploration.

title: MedMix: Specialization-Consistent Federated Sparse MoEs under Modality Heterogeneity
summary: Federated multimodal medical AI faces modality heterogeneity at both the client and sample levels: clients may systematically lack access to specific modality types, while individual records within the same client may contain different partial modality subsets. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are a promising remedy for modality-adaptive computation, but their use in federated learning is fragile under cross-client modality heterogeneity, where locally learned routing policies can diverge across clients and drive experts toward incompatible specializations. Different clients may assign the same observed modality configuration to different experts, or train similarly indexed experts on different missing-modality configurations, causing standard aggregation to misalign or overwrite the expert specialization that sparse MoEs are intended to learn. To address this challenge, we propose MedMix, a semantic-alignment framework for federated multimodal sparse MoEs that coordinates cross-client routing and expert specialization using modality context. At the client side, MedMix uses modality-context-aware routing to guide expert selection using each token's modality identity, position, and incompleteness context. Across clients, it uses consensus-guided routing alignment to construct server-side consensus anchors for shared modality patterns and align local routing distributions across clients. Complementing these routing mechanisms, client-adaptive expert aggregation leverages client-specific modality-pattern prototypes to match and aggregate functionally similar experts across clients. Experiments on real-world multimodal medical datasets show that MedMix achieves the best average F1 across diverse modality heterogeneity and modality incompleteness settings, with especially clear gains under severe heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: MedMix aligns cross-client routing and expert specialization in federated sparse MoEs for multimodal medical data, using modality-context routing, consensus anchors, and client-adaptive aggregation to handle modality heterogeneity and incompleteness, improving F1 scores.
AI.motivation: Federated multimodal medical AI faces modality heterogeneity across clients (and within samples). Sparse MoEs offer modality-adaptive computation but are fragile when clients diverge in routing, leading to misaligned expert specialization. A robust federated approach is needed to harmonize routing and specialization across clients.
AI.method: MedMix uses: (1) client-side modality-context-aware routing to select experts based on token modality, position, and incompleteness; (2) server-side consensus-guided routing alignment to create anchors for shared modality patterns and align local routing distributions; (3) client-adaptive expert aggregation using client-specific modality-pattern prototypes to match/aggregate functionally similar experts across clients.
AI.result: In experiments on real-world multimodal medical datasets, MedMix achieves the best average F1 across diverse modality heterogeneity and incompleteness settings, with clear gains under severe heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: MedMix mitigates cross-client misalignment in federated sparse MoEs for multimodal medical data, enhancing robustness to modality heterogeneity through semantic alignment and adaptive aggregation.

title: SSP: An Event-Matched Syn2Sim2Phy Cross-Domain Evaluation Framework for Autonomous Driving VLA Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving jointly produce scene interpretation, language-based reasoning, and driving trajectories. Existing evaluations often use independently selected synthetic, simulated, and physical data, so measured performance gaps can be confounded by changes in scenario content rather than genuine domain sensitivity. We propose SSP (Synthetic-Simulation-Physical), an event-matched Syn2Sim2Phy evaluation framework that anchors cross-domain comparison to the same safety-critical interaction. Starting from a synthetic long-tail video, SSP builds a validated event specification that preserves road topology, participant roles, relative motion, conflict evolution, passing order, response constraints, and event phases. Platform-specific realizations are then constructed in CARLA and on a closed proving ground and are evaluated only after transfer audits confirm preservation of mandatory event properties. SSP maps heterogeneous outputs from OpenEMMA, LLaViDA, and Alpamayo-R1 into common semantic slots and a 1 s trajectory window to assess output validity, semantic accuracy, critical-interaction recognition, trajectory quality, and risk response. Across Cut-in and vulnerable-road-user crossing cases, the macro-averaged Integrated VLA Capability Scores are 0.259, 0.291, and 0.325 in the Synthetic, Simulation, and Physical domains, respectively, while the best domain varies by scenario. Alpamayo-R1, OpenEMMA, and LLaViDA obtain scores of 0.405, 0.338, and 0.131. SSP provides a reproducible scene-transfer chain and an evidence-qualified evaluation of VLA behavior without assuming that the Physical domain is universally superior.

AI.tldr: SSP provides a Syn2Sim2Phy evaluation framework for VLA models in autonomous driving that anchors cross-domain comparisons to identical safety-critical events, maps outputs to common semantics, and evaluates across synthetic, simulation, and physical domains.
AI.motivation: Address confounding between scenario content and domain sensitivity in VLA evaluations by enforcing event-level equivalence across data sources.
AI.method: Construct an event-validated specification from a synthetic long-tail video preserving topology, participant roles, relative motion, conflict evolution, passing order, response constraints, and event phases; build platform-specific realizations in CARLA and a closed proving ground; perform transfer audits to verify property preservation; map heterogeneous outputs from OpenEMMA, LLaViDA, and Alpamayo-R1 into shared semantic slots and a 1 s trajectory window; compute macro-averaged Integrated VLA Capability Scores across domains and scenarios.
AI.result: Integrated VLA Capability Scores: Synthetic 0.259, Simulation 0.291, Physical 0.325; best domain varies by scenario. Model-wise: Alpamayo-R1 0.405, OpenEMMA 0.338, LLaViDA 0.131. SSP yields a reproducible scene-transfer chain and evidence-qualified evaluation without assuming Physical superiority.
AI.conclusion: SSP enables fair, cross-domain VLA evaluation rooted in matched events, revealing domain-specific strengths and limitations and avoiding bias toward the Physical domain.

title: Coverage Aware Active Evaluation for Failure Discovery with Paired Systems
comment: 9 main pages followed by Appendix, total 21 pages, 12 figures
summary: Autonomous systems can fail in rare and heterogeneous ways, making real-world failure discovery difficult under limited testing budgets. Although cheaper proxies such as simulators, lower-fidelity systems, or related policies can be sampled extensively to find failures, proxy failures often do not transfer to the real world due to sim-to-real and system-to-system gaps. The key challenge is therefore to effectively leverage proxy system information for accurate prediction of severe target system failures. We propose an adaptive failure discovery method that combines proxy evaluations with limited target system results to guide scenario selection for target system testing. Our method learns a local predictor of target risk by correcting proxy failure signals using control-variate-inspired residual modeling. To find failures that are both likely and diverse, we combine this predictor with a support-aware mutual-information objective that favors realistic, well-supported regions while expanding coverage across failure modes. Across autonomous driving, manipulation, and quadruped velocity-tracking tasks, our method discovers up to 2$\times$ as many failures as random sampling and active-learning baselines, including severe and diverse failures missed by competing methods.

AI.tldr: An adaptive failure discovery framework that uses control-variate residuals to calibrate proxy signals with scarce target data, plus a mutual-information objective for diverse, realistic failure coverage; achieves up to 2x more failures than baselines.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems exhibit rare, heterogeneous failures; testing budgets limit real-world evaluation. Proxy proxies (simulators, lower-fidelity systems) are cheaper but do not transfer perfectly due to sim-to-real and system-to-system gaps. The challenge is to leverage proxy information to predict and discover severe target-system failures efficiently.
AI.method: An adaptive failure discovery method that (1) learns a local predictor of target risk by correcting proxy failure signals using control-variate-inspired residual modeling, and (2) selects scenarios via a support-aware mutual-information objective that emphasizes realistic, well-supported regions while expanding coverage across failure modes.
AI.result: On autonomous driving, manipulation, and quadruped velocity-tracking tasks, the method discovers up to 2× as many failures as random sampling and active-learning baselines, including severe and diverse failures missed by competing methods.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively leverages proxy information to predict target-system risk and guide efficient, diverse failure discovery under limited testing budgets.

title: Ensuring Safe Physical AI in Urban Mobility via Hazard-Informed Synthesized Envelopes
comment: The 2026 International Conference on Control, Robotics Engineering and Technology (CRET 2026), https://www.cret.net/
summary: As heterogeneous robotic systems deploy across diverse urban zones, maintaining safety amid complex human-robot interactions remains a critical challenge. We present a unified framework that bridges systematic hazard analysis and runtime enforcement using hazard-informed safety envelopes. Rather than treating safety as a static constraint isolated within individual software modules, we introduce a cross-layer safety transformation process spanning symbolic, spatial, and dynamic world models. We show how this representation naturally interfaces with physical AI runtime harnesses to guarantee safe urban mobility.

AI.tldr: Unified cross-layer safety framework for heterogeneous urban robotics that links hazard analysis with runtime enforcement via hazard-informed safety envelopes across symbolic, spatial, and dynamic world models to ensure safe urban mobility.
AI.motivation: Safety in heterogeneous robotic systems operating in urban environments is challenged by fragmented hazard analysis and siloed safety constraints across software/hardware layers. A unified, cross-layer approach promises robust, real-time safety guarantees.
AI.method: Introduces a cross-layer safety transformation process that translates hazard information into safety envelopes. Integrates with physical AI runtime harnesses and aligns symbolic, spatial, and dynamic world models to enable runtime enforcement of safety constraints across layers.
AI.result: Conceptual framework that demonstrates how hazard-informed safety envelopes can be propagated through world representations and enforced at runtime, enabling consistent safety guarantees for urban mobility.
AI.conclusion: Cross-layer hazard-informed safety envelopes reduce fragmentation of safety constraints, enabling coherent, enforceable guarantees across perception, planning, and control in heterogeneous urban robotic systems.

title: Hybrid Quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Privacy-Aware Federated Biosignal Learning
summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings are sensitive biomedical data, limiting the ability of hospitals and wearable devices to share raw signals for centralized model training. Federated learning addresses this practical privacy constraint by enabling collaborative model training while keeping raw biosignal data at their respective sources. However, federated ECG classification remains challenging due to limited client-side samples, imbalanced arrhythmia labels, and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across clients. These constraints require classifiers that are both communication-efficient and robust to cross-client distribution shifts. In this work, we evaluate a hybrid quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network (HQKAN) against a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for five-class arrhythmia classification on the MIT-BIH dataset and three-class classification on the INCART dataset under federated averaging (FedAvg). Across multiple client configurations, HQKAN improves most aggregate and minority-class metrics while using 37.35% fewer trainable parameters and reducing communication cost by 24.89% on MIT-BIH; on INCART, it achieves corresponding reductions of 44.81% and 36.41%. These results indicate that HQKAN offers a compact, communication-efficient and robust alternative to the MLP baseline for privacy-aware federated learning on biosignal data.

AI.tldr: HQKAN is a compact, communication-efficient, and robust alternative to MLP for privacy-preserving federated ECG classification, achieving similar or better minority-class performance with substantial parameter and communication savings on MIT-BIH and INCART datasets.
AI.motivation: Federated ECG learning is hampered by limited client data, label imbalance, and non-IID distributions; there is a need for lightweight, robust models that reduce communication.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of a hybrid quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network (HQKAN) versus a multilayer perceptron (MLP) under FedAvg across two datasets (MIT-BIH five-class, INCART three-class) with multiple client configurations; metrics include aggregate and minority-class performance and resource usage (trainable parameters, communication cost).
AI.result: HQKAN reduces trainable parameters by 37.35% (MIT-BIH) and 44.81% (INCART) and lowers communication cost by 24.89% (MIT-BIH) and 36.41% (INCART); it also improves most aggregate and minority-class metrics across configurations.
AI.conclusion: HQKAN is a compact, communication-efficient, and robust alternative to MLP for privacy-aware federated learning on biosignal data.

title: E-S2Feat:Semantic-Guided Spiking Local Feature Detection and Description for Event Cameras
summary: Benefiting from high temporal resolution and dynamic range, event-based local feature methods have attracted increasing attention. However, event sparsity, noise, and limited texture still hinder robust local feature learning. Deploying such methods on resource-constrained platforms such as unmanned aerial vehicles also requires balancing accuracy and energy efficiency. To address these challenges, this paper proposes \textbf{E-S2Feat}, a spiking neural network framework for event-based local feature detection and description. The framework jointly optimizes local feature learning from the perspectives of feature representation and selection. First, a module-specific spiking activation mechanism preserves fine-grained structural cues and discriminative information under low-bit, energy-efficient inference, thereby improving overall representation fidelity. Furthermore, a semantic-guided feature modulation mechanism leverages semantic priors to refine keypoint response distributions and enhance local descriptor discriminability, thereby guiding the model to extract local features with greater geometric stability and stronger discriminative capability. Experiments on the ECD and EDS datasets show that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline methods such as SuperEvent in pose estimation accuracy. It also achieves accuracy comparable to its artificial neural network counterpart while delivering an approximately 4.8-fold improvement in theoretical computational energy efficiency. Visual-inertial odometry experiments on the TUM-VIE dataset further verify the effectiveness and practical application potential of the proposed method in complete SLAM systems.

AI.tldr: E-S2Feat, an SNN-based framework for event-based local feature detection/description, achieves strong pose estimation and competitive ANN performance with ~4.8x energy efficiency, validated on ECD/EDS and TUM-VIE for SLAM.
AI.motivation: Event-based cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range but suffer from sparsity, noise, limited texture, and strict energy constraints on platforms like UAVs; robust, energy-efficient local features are needed for real-time SLAM.
AI.method: Propose E-S2Feat with joint optimization of feature representation and selection. Introduces module-specific spiking activation to preserve fine-grained cues under low-bit inference, and semantic-guided feature modulation using semantic priors to refine keypoint responses and enhance descriptor discriminability, improving geometric stability and discriminability.
AI.result: Significantly outperforms baseline SuperEvent in pose estimation on ECD/EDS; comparable to artificial neural networks in accuracy; about 4.8× reduction in theoretical computational energy; VIO experiments on TUM-VIE validate practical SLAM applicability.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of energy-efficient event-based local features via spiking nets; combining representation fidelity and semantic modulation yields robust, discriminative features suitable for SLAM in resource-constrained platforms.

title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Pre-registered analysis plan; code and results available
summary:
The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to file technical documentation describing how the system reaches its decisions. Mechanistic interpretability is the obvious source of such evidence, and circuit discovery is its most developed instrument. We ask whether that evidence survives the condition under which it would be relied upon: two competent analysts, the same system, the same tool, different defensible settings.
  We pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes, every level taken from a published implementation, and mapped each discovered circuit through a deterministic claim map to a structured Annex IV statement. Across 15,840 pre-registered specifications on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task, of which 7,561 produced a claim, the derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs (95% CI 0.725 to 0.738) and the modal claim commands 41.1% of the space. The evidence fails a filability criterion at every tolerance a conformity assessment body would plausibly accept.
  Standardising the single most influential choice, the evaluation metric, leaves the flip rate at 59.4%. Removing circuit size from the claim entirely and holding it fixed leaves 27.1% (95% CI 0.255 to 0.286), still above the pre-registered threshold. The circuits underlying these claims are structurally near-disjoint, median pairwise Jaccard overlap 4%, and functionally uncorrelated at Cohen's kappa 0.015, so the instability is not one mechanism described in different words.
  We give the filability criterion as a standalone protocol, and we report that one of the seven documented discovery objectives does not execute at all on the library's own canonical task. The study covers one model and one task, and whether the conclusion holds at scale is untested.

AI.tldr: Cross-validated, preregistered test of mechanistic interpretability evidence reliability using circuit discovery on GPT-2 small across a regulatory-like framework. Finds high instability: large flip rate in derived statements across analytic choices, low overlap between circuits, near-zero agreement, and a failed filability protocol. Scaling remains untested; limited to one model/task.
AI.motivation: Question whether mechanistic interpretability provides robust, regulatory-grade evidence of system behavior under the EU AI Act.
