Specifically, whether two competent analysts using the same system and tool but different defensible settings converge on stable, legally usable claims about decision processes.
AI.method: Pre-registered a crossed grid of seven analytic axes (from published implementations). Map each discovered circuit to a structured Annex IV claim. Evaluate 15,840 specifications on GPT-2 small and the indirect object identification task; 7,561 produced a claim. Two analysts with the same system/tool but varying settings test reproducibility. Assess flip rate across specification pairs, use a claim map, compute Jaccard overlap and Cohen's kappa, and evaluate a standalone filability protocol. Also test a sensitivity: standardize the evaluation metric and remove circuit size as a feature from the claim.
AI.result: Found a 73.2% flip rate across specification pairs (95% CI 0.725–0.738); modal claim covers 41.1% of the space. Filability criterion fails across plausible tolerances. Standardizing the evaluation metric reduces flips to 59.4%; removing circuit size further reduces to 27.1% (95% CI 0.255–0.286). Circuits underlying claims are structurally near-disjoint (median Jaccard overlap 4%) and functionally uncorrelated (Cohen’s kappa 0.015). At least one discovery objective does not execute on the canonical task. Study covers a single model and task; scalability untested.
AI.conclusion: Circuit-based mechanistic interpretability provides unstable, potentially non-reproducible evidence under defensible analytic variation. This challenges using such evidence for regulatory documentation without standardized, scalable evaluation protocols. More comprehensive, multi-model, multi-task validation is needed before relying on these claims in high-stakes conformity assessments.

title: Spatiotemporal Tube-Based Safety-Certificate for Autonomous Navigation of Articulated Vehicles
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC 2026)
summary: Articulated vehicles are the workhorses of freight transportation, and their autonomous navigation is challenging. Their physical characteristics and motion constraints pose significant challenges in manoeuvring these vehicles on narrow routes. This paper presents a spatiotemporal tube-based approach to plan autonomous navigation of vehicles like tractor semi-trailers, truck/ tractor trailers, towing Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs), and road trains. This planning approach provides a certified path plan for the truck or tractor, ensuring that the towed series of trailers always remains within the road corridor, limited by permissible corrections. The planning leverages the kinematics of the linked elements along with sway constraints to arrive at a safe tube for the actuated prime mover. We modify the spatiotemporal tube using permissible corrections to provide a route safety certificate to the vehicle for the given route. The proposed planning method is verified on a truck-trailer navigation simulation for a complex route.

AI.tldr: Proposes a spatiotemporal tube-based path planning method for articulated vehicles to generate certified, corridor-constrained feasible trajectories, accounting for kinematics and sway with permissible corrections.
AI.motivation: To enable safe autonomous navigation of tractor-trailer configurations on narrow routes by providing safety-certified trajectories that respect vehicle linkage constraints and road boundaries.
AI.method: Develop a spatiotemporal tube around the actuated prime mover, incorporate kinematic constraints and sway limits of linked trailers, and modify the tube using permissible corrections to produce a route safety certificate; verify via truck-trailer simulation on a complex route.
AI.result: The method yields a safety-certified tube along a given route and is validated in a simulation with a truck-trailer configuration on a complex route.
AI.conclusion: A tube-based planning framework can provide certified paths for articulated vehicles with sway constraints; future work may involve dynamic obstacles, uncertainty, and real-world experiments.

title: High-dimensional nonparametric changepoint detection via low-rank degree-two density projection
summary: Detecting distributional changes in high dimension is difficult when neither the pre-change nor post-change density is parametrically specified. We introduce a representation-based approach that retains all degree-at-most-two density information while replacing density estimation by matrix mean estimation. For observations in $[-1,1]^d$, a symmetric feature matrix $H_2(X)\in\R^{(d+1)\times(d+1)}$ is constructed so that $M(f)=\E_f H_2(X)$ is an isometric encoding of the degree-two orthogonal projection of the density. We scan matrix CUSUMs after rank-$r$ truncation, exploiting the low rank of the projected jump rather than sparsity of individual coordinates. The resulting \LRD{} estimator has a tent-shaped population objective and a nonasymptotic operator-norm analysis whose leading stochastic term scales as $\sqrt{rd\log(nd)}$. For multiple changes, we give a seeded narrowest-over-threshold procedure and prove exact recovery by an induction that preserves an isolating interval for every undetected change. A cross-fitted scalar refinement learns the changing low-rank direction on one fold and localizes on the other, attaining $\widetilde O_{\Pp}(κ^{-2})$ error; a matching Le Cam lower bound shows optimality up to logarithms. A geometrically $β$-mixing extension follows from a dependent matrix Bernstein inequality. Experiments with ambient dimension up to $200$, a three-change $d=100$ sequence, and a $128$-feature human-activity benchmark show that the method remains computationally practical and accurately detects pure dependence changes that are invisible to mean CUSUMs.

AI.tldr: A representation-based, nonparametric change-point detector for high-dimensional distributions using degree-2 density information encoded in a symmetric matrix H2(X) and matrix CUSUM with low-rank projections; provides nonasymptotic guarantees, exact recovery for multiple changes, and cross-fitted refinement, with beta-mixing extension and practical performance up to dimension 200.
AI.motivation: To detect distributional changes in high-dimensional data without assuming parametric forms for pre- and post-change densities, by preserving second-order (degree-2) density information and avoiding direct density estimation.
AI.method: Construct a symmetric feature matrix H2(X) on [-1,1]^d so that M(f)=E_f[H2(X)] encodes the degree-2 projection of the density. Apply matrix CUSUM after rank-r truncation to detect low-rank changes in the projected density. Define the LR D estimator with a tent-shaped population objective and establish nonasymptotic operator-norm bounds. For multiple changes, use a seeded narrowest-over-threshold procedure with an inductive exact-recovery argument. Introduce a cross-fitted scalar refinement to learn the changing low-rank direction on one fold and localize on another, achieving ~kappa^{-2} error up to logs. Prove a matching Le Cam lower bound, and extend to geometrically beta-mixing via a dependent matrix Bernstein inequality. Empirically validate up to ambient dimension 200, with a 3-change sequence at d=100 and a 128-feature human-activity benchmark, showing detection of pure dependence changes invisible to mean CUSUMs.
AI.result: Leading stochastic term scales as sqrt(r d log(nd)). Exact recovery for multiple changes via seeded NOT with an isolating interval. Cross-fitted refinement attains ~O_P(kappa^{-2}) error (up to logs); optimality via Le Cam lower bound (up to logs). Beta-mixing extension established. Practical on large d with competitive detection of changes undetectable by mean-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed representation-based matrix-CUSUM approach provides a theoretically sound, computationally practical framework for detecting distributional changes in high dimensions by leveraging degree-2 density information, with strong guarantees and empirical validation.

title: Beyond Text Conditioning: A Systematic Study of MLLM-DiT Fusion for Video Generation
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity video generation, yet their ability to perform high-level semantic planning remains limited. While hybrid architectures integrating MLLMs with diffusion backbones have shown strong advantages in image synthesis, such designs remain underexplored in video generation, where existing approaches often treat MLLMs primarily as frozen feature encoders rather than semantic generators. To fill this gap, we systematically study how an MLLM should be integrated with a DiT for video generation by answering three questions: what intermediate representation should bridge the MLLM and DiT, how the MLLM should generate it, and how the DiT should incorporate it during diffusion rendering. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) discrete semantic visual tokens produced by an EMA-based tokenizer provide a stable and expressive interface, (2) autoregressive causal modeling is effective for generating these tokens, and (3) explicit visual-token conditioning is more effective than prompt refinement or latent bridging. Based on these findings, we propose BiVidGen, a hybrid framework where an MLLM first generates semantic visual tokens and a DiT renders videos conditioned on both text and these tokens via multi-layer cross-attention. Extensive experiments show that BiVidGen improves semantic alignment and temporal coherence over a fine-tuned DiT baseline, achieving stronger performance on VBench-Long. These results demonstrate that explicit MLLM-based visual planning provides an effective intermediate interface for text-to-video generation beyond text-only conditioning.

AI.tldr: A hybrid BiVidGen framework integrates an MLLM with a diffusion-based video generator by producing discrete visual tokens via an EMA tokenizer and guiding video diffusion through autoregressive token generation and cross-attention conditioning on text and tokens.
AI.motivation: To overcome limited high-level semantic planning in diffusion video models by providing an explicit, learnable intermediate interface between language models and diffusion renderers, rather than treating MLLMs as frozen feature extractors.
AI.method: BiVidGen: (1) an EMA-based tokenizer yields discrete visual tokens; (2) an MLLM generates tokens autoregressively; (3) a DiT renders video conditioned on text and tokens via multi-layer cross-attention.
AI.result: BiVidGen improves semantic alignment and temporal coherence over a fine-tuned DiT baseline, achieving stronger performance on VBench-Long.
AI.conclusion: Explicit MLLM-based visual planning with discrete tokens is an effective intermediate interface for text-to-video generation beyond text-only conditioning.

title: Simulation-Aware In-Context Policy Improvement for LLM-Aided Analog Layout Refinement
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD 2026)
summary: Analog IC layout design remains a labor-intensive iterative process dominated by simulation-driven refinement. Although end-to-end layout generators accelerate initial placement and routing, they still require experts to manually tune layout optimization parameters with repeated post-layout simulations for stringent design specifications. While Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely adopted for parameter tuning in analog IC design, at the layout level it typically requires hundreds to thousands of evaluations, each involving costly parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation, which makes it impractical. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in improving the sample efficiency of such simulation-driven tuning. However, their restricted access to geometric layout context and design-specific heuristics limits their ability to manipulate the layout optimization process. In this paper, we propose a simulation-aware LLM multi-agent framework that performs in-context policy improvement (ICPI) by iteratively updating layout optimization parameters exposed by an analog layout generator through an act-observe-reflect loop on compact structured layout representations. Experiments on real-world analog circuits show that, with only tens of post-layout simulations, our approach improves post-layout performance over the generator's built-in heuristics and BO-based tuning method.

AI.tldr: Simulation-aware LLM multi-agent framework with in-context policy improvement (ICPI) for analog layout tuning, achieving better post-layout performance with only tens of post-layout simulations, outperforming built-in heuristics and Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Analog IC layout remains labor-intensive; Bayesian optimization (BO) is sample-inefficient at the layout level due to costly parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation; LLMs can help but lack geometry context and design-specific heuristics; need a method that fuses simulation feedback with structured layout context to improve parameter tuning.
AI.method: Proposes a simulation-aware, multi-agent LLM framework that applies in-context policy improvement (ICPI) through an act-observe-reflect loop, updating layout optimization parameters exposed by an analog layout generator. Operates on compact structured layout representations to bridge shallow LLM reasoning with geometry-aware decisions.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world analog circuits show that with only tens of post-layout simulations, the approach improves post-layout performance over the generator's built-in heuristics and BO-based tuning.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates favorable sample efficiency and potential to reduce design cycle time by integrating LLM-based policy refinement with simulation feedback, highlighting the importance of structured representations and multi-agent collaboration; future directions include scalability, generalization to diverse layout flows, and robustness of ICPI.

title: CForce: Boosting Parallel Decoding for dLLMs via Consistency Forcing
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) accelerate language generation by predicting multiple masks in a single forward pass. However, existing dLLMs can suffer from unreliable predictions in early denoising stages under aggressive parallelism strategies, leading to errors that can propagate to later stages. To tackle this issue, we present Consistency Forcing (CForce) for dLLMs, a distillation method to force the mask predictions of early stages to align with those of later stages. CForce trains the model on pre-collected self-rollout trajectories, thereby improving training-inference alignment. We introduce Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence as a distillation objective to conjoin the merits of forward and reverse KL. We further provide a theoretical analysis for the consistency objective to explain why CForce can approximately minimize the prediction error of early stages. Critically, the same formulation applies to both mask-to-token decoding and edit-capable decoding; in the edit-capable case, later token-to-token refinements provide additional supervision for earlier masked-state predictions. Experiments on non-edit and edit-capable LLaDA models show improved speed-quality trade-offs, especially under high-parallelism decoding budgets. Code is available at: https://github.com/inclusionAI/dFactory.

AI.tldr: Presents Consistency Forcing (CForce), a distillation-based approach for diffusion LLMs to align early-stage mask predictions with later-stage refinements, using Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence, improving speed-quality at high parallelism; supports both mask-to-token and edit-capable decoding; code released.
AI.motivation: In aggressive parallel decoding, early denoising mask predictions are unreliable and propagate errors; a training-time alignment objective is needed to improve inference quality and speed.
AI.method: Train on pre-collected self-rollouts; use Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence as the distillation objective to align early-stage predictions with later-stage refinements by combining forward and reverse KL. The framework applies to both mask-to-token decoding and edit-capable decoding; theoretical analysis explains why consistency reduces early-stage prediction errors; in the edit-capable case, later token-to-token refinements provide extra supervision for the earlier masked-state predictions.
AI.result: Empirical results on non-edit and edit-capable LLaDA models show improved speed-quality trade-offs, particularly under high parallelism decoding budgets; code is available at the cited repository.
AI.conclusion: CForce improves training-inference alignment and robustness of diffusion LLMs under aggressive parallelism, with theoretical justification and applicability to multiple decoding modes; demonstrates practical gains and a publicly available implementation.

title: Source-Agnostic Image Translation Based on Latent Aware Adaptive Masking
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication at the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2026
summary: In this work, we propose a source-agnostic framework that dynamically refines a binary mask throughout the reverse diffusion process by computing the discrepancies of a pretrained diffusion model's prediction for each latent time step. Rather than relying on a fixed threshold, our method introduces a time-dependent statistical thresholding scheme derived from the empirical mean and standard deviation of prediction discrepancies across the latent noisy images from the target distribution. This allows the mask to adapt to the model's varying predictive confidence at different noise levels, effectively isolating domain-specific regions while preserving global structural coherence. Experimental results on the AFHQ and Celeba-HQ datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised Image-to-Image methods in both realism (FID, KID) and faithfulness (SSIM, LPIPS). By requiring only a pretrained model of the target domain, our approach enables precise, automated localization and seamless translation across diverse source distributions without any specialized training. The project source code is available at: https://github.com/dtoma95/PM-Edit

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based, source-agnostic mask refinement method for unsupervised image-to-image translation that dynamically thresholds prediction discrepancies during reverse diffusion to localize domain-specific regions while preserving global structure.
AI.motivation: Enable precise, automated cross-domain image translation using only a pretrained target-domain diffusion model, avoiding fixed thresholds or task-specific training on diverse source distributions.
AI.method: During reverse diffusion, compute per-time-step discrepancies between the pretrained target-model's predictions and the current latent. Build a time-dependent threshold from the empirical mean and standard deviation of these discrepancies across latent noisy images from the target distribution. Apply this adaptive mask to isolate domain-specific regions while maintaining global structure, enabling dynamic refinement of the binary mask throughout denoising.
AI.result: On AFHQ and CelebA-HQ, the method outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised image-to-image methods in realism (FID, KID) and faithfulness (SSIM, LPIPS). It requires only a pretrained target-domain model and no specialized training; code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, time-adaptive masking during reverse diffusion yields precise localization and robust translation across diverse source distributions with a pretrained model, demonstrating strong performance and generality without additional training.

title: FLARE MCMC: Fidelity-based Layer-Adaptive REcursive proposals for MCMC
comment: This is the author's accepted manuscript of an article published in SIAM Journal on Uncertainty Quantification. The final version is available at \url{https://doi.org/10.1137/25M1795194
summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) requires only the ability to evaluate the likelihood, making it a common technique for inference in complex models. However, it can have a slow mixing rate, requiring the generation of many samples to obtain good estimates and an overall high computational cost. FLARE MCMC is a multi-fidelity layered MCMC method that exploits lower-fidelity approximations of the true likelihood calculation to improve mixing and leads to overall faster performance. Such lower-fidelity likelihoods are commonly available in scientific and engineering applications where the model involves a simulation whose resolution or accuracy can be tuned. Our technique uses recursive, layered chains with simple layer tuning; it does not require the likelihood to take any form or have any particular internal mathematical structure. We demonstrate experimentally that FLARE MCMC achieves larger effective sample sizes for the same computational time across different scientific domains including hydrology and cosmology.

AI.tldr: FLARE MCMC uses multi-fidelity, layered MCMC with cheaper, lower-fidelity likelihoods to improve mixing and reduce wall-clock time, achieving higher effective sample sizes without requiring likelihood-specific structure.
AI.motivation: MCMC mixing can be slow and costly; many scientific models involve tunable simulations that yield cheaper approximations of the likelihood. Exploiting these approximations can accelerate sampling while targeting the true posterior.
AI.method: Recursive, layered MCMC chains that use simple, tunable lower-fidelity likelihoods at multiple layers. The approach does not require the likelihood to have a particular form or structure and relies on layering to improve mixing.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows FLARE MCMC achieves larger effective sample sizes for the same computational time across domains such as hydrology and cosmology.
AI.conclusion: FLARE MCMC offers a general, structure-agnostic multi-fidelity sampling strategy that can speed up Bayesian inference by leveraging cheap surrogate evaluations without imposing strict likelihood forms.

title: Post-training Quantization for Hybrid Iterative Generative Models
summary: Iterative Generative Models (IGMs) span autoregressive and diffusion paradigms, and hybrid variants that couple them can achieve remarkable image-generation fidelity. However, their iterative inference incurs substantial computational overhead, making Post-training Quantization (PTQ) appealing for acceleration, while directly applying vanilla PTQ to hybrid IGMs can trigger model collapse. By analyzing these failures, we identify two critical challenges: Excessive Outliers (EOs) in the activations create an irreconcilable trade-off between preserving normal precision and covering EOs, resulting in severe degradation in generation quality; Amplified Anomalies (AAs) arising unpredictably from minor quantization errors, create a mismatch between calibration and inference, thus iteratively triggering model collapse. To address these challenges, we introduce HyGenQ, a PTQ framework for hybrid IGMs. HyGenQ comprises Hierarchical Cluster Decoupling (HCD) and Scaling Recalibration (SR). HCD identifies and decouples outlier channels via a multi-stage clustering process, effectively isolating EOs while maintaining normal value precision, thereby alleviating performance degradation. SR scales AAs beyond Gaussian Bound, thereby avoiding model collapse caused by aggressive truncation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HyGenQ successfully quantizes representative hybrid IGMs to 8-bit precision (W8A8), significantly outperforming existing baselines and validating its robustness across different model families.

AI.tldr: HyGenQ enables robust 8-bit post-training quantization (W8A8) of hybrid iterative generative models by decoupling outlier channels (HCD) and recalibrating scaling to bound amplified anomalies (SR).
AI.motivation: IGMs (autoregressive, diffusion, and hybrids) yield high fidelity but are expensive. Direct PTQ on hybrids causes model collapse due to extreme outliers and amplified anomalies in activations. A robust PTQ method is needed to reduce computation without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: HyGenQ consists of two components: (1) Hierarchical Cluster Decoupling (HCD): a multi-stage clustering process to identify and decouple outlier channels (EOs) to isolate them from normal precision paths; (2) Scaling Recalibration (SR): recalibrates scaling factors to bound amplified anomalies (AAs) beyond Gaussian assumptions, preventing instability during inference.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show HyGenQ quantizes representative hybrid IGMs to 8-bit weights and activations (W8A8) with significant performance gains over baselines, maintaining generation quality and robustness across different model families.
AI.conclusion: HyGenQ provides a practically effective, calibration-based PTQ framework for hybrid IGMs by decouplingExtreme Outliers and stabilizing anomaly-induced instabilities, enabling reliable 8-bit quantization with broad applicability.

title: Discovery and Spatial Characterisation of Multiple Shortcut Groups for Auditing Vision Model Bias
summary: Deep learning models trained on datasets with spurious correlations can achieve high average accuracy whilst relying on shortcut features that do not generalise out of distribution. Whilst out-of-distribution testing highlights subgroup performance disparities arising from shortcut learning, it does not localise the regions within images that are associated with it. Existing research mostly uses attribution maps from interpretability methods to understand the spatial nature of spurious correlations. For example, conditional alignment methods separate task-relevant evidence from evidence tied to spurious correlations by comparing attribution maps from a task model, a sensitive attribute model, and a bias-reduced reference model. This yields shortcut-aligned and task-aligned contribution maps for each image. However, existing methods aggregate these maps across the dataset, potentially masking recurring spatial shortcut patterns that occur only in subsets of images. We address this limitation by grouping per-image shortcut and task contribution maps into recurring spatial patterns using K-means and non-negative matrix factorisation, and visualising the resulting shortcut groups through contribution maps and representative examples. Across CelebA, CheXpert, Waterbirds, Camelyon17, and ISIC2019, and across ResNet and ViT models, the discovered shortcut groups reveal both shared and distinct spatial patterns of shortcut and task contribution, with varying subgroup composition and error rates, enabling targeted inspection of image subsets with higher error rates. We perform input occlusion and internal test-time interventions to show that masking or suppressing task contribution regions substantially degrades the model classification performance and propose a combined shortcut suppression and task amplification feature intervention approach which generally reduces performance disparities.

AI.tldr: Group-wise analysis of spurious shortcuts via clustering attribution maps to reveal recurring spatial patterns and inform interventions.
AI.motivation: To localize and understand spurious correlations (shortcuts) in deep models beyond average accuracy, capturing recurring spatial cues within image subsets that standard OOD tests miss.
AI.method: Compute per-image contribution maps (shortcut/task) using conditional alignment. Cluster these maps with K-means and non-negative matrix factorization to obtain recurring spatial patterns. Visualize shortcut groups via contribution maps and representative images. Validate across CelebA, CheXpert, Waterbirds, Camelyon17, ISIC2019 with ResNet and ViT. Evaluate via input occlusion and test-time interventions; propose a combined shortcut suppression and task amplification approach.
AI.result: Discovered recurring shortcut groups that reveal shared and dataset/model-specific spatial patterns, with varying subgroup compositions and error rates. Enables targeted inspection of image subsets with higher errors. Interventions like masking task regions degrade performance and the proposed combined suppression/amplification strategy reduces observed disparities.
AI.conclusion: Spatially grouped attribution maps uncover structured shortcuts; targeted interventions informed by these groups can mitigate performance disparities across subgroups.

title: From Passive Delegates to Strategic Negotiators: Reinforcing Social Reasoning in Small Language Models with SocialRL
summary: AI agents increasingly act on their users' behalf, handling tasks such as scheduling meetings, comparing offers, and haggling over prices. These principal-driven tasks routinely place the agent across from a counterpart (another user's agent, a seller, a recruiter) whose goals may conflict with its principal's. Yet the dispositions that make an assistant pleasant can make it a poor delegate: a friendly, helpful frontier model may disclose its principal's private information unprompted and concede at the first sign of resistance. We present SocialRL, a general recipe that trains social reasoning directly, and apply it to a 4B model across six domains: Deal-or-No-Deal, CaSiNo, Craigslist, Job Interview, Calendar, and Marketplace. Every domain is trained in-domain under the same recipe, and every policy is evaluated on all six. We find that (1) in-domain training reaches the frontier: on held-out scenarios the 4B matches or exceeds the GPT-5 family per domain, closing 73-122% of the baseline-to-frontier gap on the negotiation games, with 78% of buyer openings anchoring below target versus 3% untrained; (2) cross-domain transfer follows game structure: structurally paired games lift each other, a broad multi-issue donor lifts nearly all domains, and structurally isolated games transfer nothing; (3) guided by this transfer structure, two strategies, cascade RL and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD), consolidate the per-domain specialists into a single unified 4B that reaches 0.627 average utility across all six environments, matching or exceeding GPT-4.1 (0.625), GPT-5.1 (0.619), and GPT-5.2 (0.613); (4) an explicit theory-of-mind scaffold helps only through training: distilling the ToM trace, rather than actions alone, lifts utility on every environment and generalizes better across them, and of the two ToM skills, only next-action prediction predicts negotiation outcomes.

AI.tldr: SocialRL trains a general social-reasoning recipe for 4B models across six negotiation-centric domains, achieving strong in-domain performance, systematic cross-domain transfer, and a unified model that rivals GPT-4/5. Theory-of-Mind scaffolding helps via distillation of ToM traces, with next-action prediction being the key predictor.
AI.motivation: As agents increasingly act on behalf of users in negotiations, they must balance being pleasant with protecting principal interests. The work investigates whether a single training recipe can imbue agents with robust social reasoning capable of negotiating across diverse domains.
AI.method: Train a 4B model with the SocialRL recipe across six domains (Deal-or-No-Deal, CaSiNo, Craigslist, Job Interview, Calendar, Marketplace) in-domain. Evaluate on all six to test cross-domain transfer. Develop two consolidation strategies: cascade RL and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) to create a unified 4B. Analyze a theory-of-mind scaffold by distilling ToM traces (actions+mental state) and compare to using actions alone.
AI.result: In-domain training reaches frontier performance: the 4B model matches or exceeds GPT-5 per domain, closing 73-122% of the frontier gap on negotiation games; buyer opening bias improves (78% anchored below target vs 3% untrained). Cross-domain transfer follows game structure: structurally paired games help; a related donor lifts most domains; structurally isolated games transfer nothing. Cascade RL and OPD effectively merge per-domain specialists into a single 4B achieving 0.627 average utility across six domains, rivaling GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, and GPT-5.2. An explicit ToM scaffold helps mainly through distilling ToM traces, improving generalization; next-action prediction is the key ToM skill for predicting outcomes.
AI.conclusion: SocialRL provides a general, transfer-aware training recipe for social agents. Transfer patterns align with game structure, and a ToM-informed distillation strategy improves cross-domain performance. The resulting unified 4B model attains competitive utility across six environments, suggesting practical viability for principal-driven negotiation tasks.

title: Probabilistic indirect models for undrained shear strength: addressing significant data missing and variability with advanced imputation and machine learning techniques
summary: Accurate prediction of undrained shear strength (su) is crucial for geotechnical design, but is often hampered by substantial uncertainty in traditional empirical methods. This study uses the CLAY/10/7490 global database to develop probabilistic indirect models to predict su based on Atterberg limits and piezocone cone penetration (CPTU) measurements. Firstly, the dataset has a high missing data rate and variability. We test three imputation methods - multivariate normal (MN), multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), and miss forest (MF) - to fill the missing values. To validate their effectiveness, a Probabilistic Extreme Gradient Boosting (PXGB) model is developed, and the imputation methods are evaluated by comparing the PXGB's performance when trained on the imputed datasets against that on the original incomplete data. Secondly, the indirect model is built by integrating a multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism into an artificial neural network (ANN) to enhance information extraction from limited data, which leads to the MHA-based probabilistic neural networks (MHA-PNN) model. The models' performance, alongside a conventional MN-based prediction model, was evaluated using root mean square error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), conditional interval width (wCI), and coverage rate (CR). Results demonstrate that the proposed MN-enhanced MHA-PNN model substantially outperforms other models in both prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. These findings highlight the potential of this integrated strategy for building robust probabilistic indirect models in geotechnical applications, particularly when confronted with sparse and incomplete datasets.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic indirect model framework for predicting undrained shear strength (su) using Atterberg limits and CPTU, addressing missing data via MN, MICE, MF imputation and using an MHA-enhanced ANN (MHA-PNN) with PXGB validation; MN-enhanced MHA-PNN delivers superior prediction and uncertainty quantification on sparse data.
AI.motivation: Need for robust su prediction under uncertainty due to data sparsity and high missingness; conventional empirical methods have high uncertainty; integrating probabilistic imputation and advanced neural architectures can improve accuracy and quantify uncertainty.
AI.method: 1) Use CLAY/10/7490 database; 2) compare three imputation methods (MN, MICE, MF); 3) validate imputation by training PXGB on imputed vs original data; 4) develop MHA-PNN by embedding multi-head attention into ANN for indirect Si model; 5) compare with MN-based model; 6) assess with RMSE, R2, MAPE, wCI, CR.
AI.result: MN-enhanced MHA-PNN outperforms other models in accuracy and uncertainty quantification; indicates effective handling of sparse incomplete data and improved information extraction; demonstrates potential for robust probabilistic indirect modeling in geotechnical applications.
AI.conclusion: Integrated strategy combining probabilistic imputation and MHA-augmented ANN yields robust predictive models for su with incomplete datasets; applicable to geotechnical design and similar domains where data sparsity and missingness hinder traditional methods.

title: Voxel-based 3D Facies Segmentation from Seismic Data: A Comparative Study
summary: Seismic facies segmentation has emerged as a significant challenge in geophysics, requiring robust methods and systems to effectively identify geologically analogous facies with limited labeled data. Although existing studies have shown promising results in 2D facies segmentation, they often preprocess the original 3D seismic volumes into sets of 2D slices, typically the inline and crossline directions, and treat this problem as a purely 2D segmentation task. This simplification introduces discontinuities across slices and fails to preserve the spatial and structural continuity in 3D seismic data, thus limiting the model's ability to learn coherent geological patterns. In this work, we present a comparative and reproducible benchmark for voxel-based 3D seismic facies segmentation, built upon publicly available seismic volumes including the Netherlands F3 and the Parihaka datasets, with standardized data splits and evaluation metrics. By evaluating the three representative families of modern 3D segmentation architectures, we establish strong baseline results that highlight the potential and remaining challenges for future research in this domain.

AI.tldr: Proposes a voxel-based 3D seismic facies segmentation benchmark using public volumes to compare 3D segmentation architectures.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of 2D slice-based seismic facies segmentation which disrupts 3D spatial continuity and learning of coherent geological patterns, especially with limited labeled data.
AI.method: Build a reproducible benchmark on public 3D seismic volumes (Netherlands F3, Parihaka) with standardized data splits and evaluation metrics; evaluate three representative families of modern 3D segmentation architectures.
AI.result: Establishes strong baseline results for 3D seismic facies segmentation and highlights the remaining challenges and potential directions for future research in this domain.
AI.conclusion: Voxel-based 3D segmentation is feasible and advantageous for seismic facies delineation; standardized benchmarks enable fair comparisons and drive advances, though further improvements are needed to handle data limitations and architectural diversity.

title: SDO: Subspace Deconflicting Operator for Multi-Adapter Composition
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted by ACM MM 2026 Main Track
summary: Composing independently trained adapters within a shared diffusion backbone provides a modular approach to multi-character generation, but naive joint deployment often causes identity mixing, cross-character attribute leakage, and unstable scene composition. We study this interference from a parameter-space perspective and hypothesize that it arises partly from conflicts between overlapping dominant subspaces in shared layers. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SDO}, a \textbf{S}ubspace \textbf{D}econflicting \textbf{O}perator for multi-adapter composition. SDO reconstructs layer-wise low-rank updates from the selected adapters, extracts compact subspace signatures, measures pairwise conflict through output-subspace overlap, and applies a permutation-equivariant transformation that suppresses harmful shared directions while retaining identity-specific characteristics. The resulting representations are mapped back to standard adapter updates and can be directly incorporated into existing diffusion inference pipelines. Experiments demonstrate that SDO consistently improves identity fidelity and compositional stability, with particularly clear gains as the number of jointly composed adapters increases.

AI.tldr: SDO mitigates interference when composing multiple adapters on a shared diffusion backbone by reconstructing layer-wise low-rank updates, extracting subspace signatures, and applying a permutation-equivariant transform to suppress harmful shared directions, yielding improved identity fidelity and compositional stability as adapters scale.
AI.motivation: Interference during multi-adapter composition arises from overlapping dominant subspaces in shared layers, causing identity mixing and attribute leakage in diffusion models.
AI.method: For each adapter: compute layer-wise low-rank updates; derive compact subspace signatures; quantify pairwise conflict via output-subspace overlap; apply a permutation-equivariant transformation to suppress shared directions while preserving identity-specific traits; map the resulting representations back to standard adapter updates for use in diffusion inference pipelines.
AI.result: Empirical experiments show consistent improvements in identity fidelity and compositional stability, with larger gains as more adapters are jointly composed.
AI.conclusion: SDO offers a practical, plug-in solution for disentangling subspaces in multi-adapter diffusion systems, enabling scalable and stable multi-character generation without sacrificing identity fidelity.

title: Polar Code Based Federated Learning: Convergence Analysis and Resource Allocation
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed devices without sharing raw data; however, it faces significant communication bottlenecks and channel impairments in practice. Conventional network layer treatments either idealize the channel as error free or apply equal error protection (EEP) to transmitted model updates, failing to account for the inherently unequal importance of quantization bits within a single local model. To address this limitation, we propose a cross layer polar code based FL scheme that leverages the unequal error protection (UEP) property of polar codes under finite block lengths. Specifically, the proposed design selectively protects more significant quantization bits, thereby mitigating the detrimental effects of channel noise. We further provide a rigorous convergence analysis of the proposed scheme, deriving an upper bound on the convergence gap, which we then jointly optimize over the number of quantization bits and the polar code block length across all training iterations. Experimental results demonstrate that both constant and variable block length configurations of our polar code based scheme consistently achieve substantial performance gains over uncoded and LDPC-based EEP benchmarks, with the advantage becoming increasingly pronounced as the channel quality deteriorating. These findings confirm the efficacy of our cross-layer design in enhancing FL robustness and efficiency under realistic channel conditions.

AI.tldr: Cross-layer FL with UEP polar codes; protect significant quantization bits; convergence bound; joint optimization; gains over uncoded and LDPC-EEP, especially on poor channels.
AI.motivation: FL is hampered by communication bottlenecks and channel impairments. Existing treatments assume error-free channels or equal error protection, ignoring that quantized updates have uneven bit importance. A cross-layer design aligning coding with quantization can mitigate noise impact.
AI.method: Introduce polar codes that exploit unequal error protection (UEP) under finite blocklength. Dynamically protect more significant quantization bits; derive an upper bound on the convergence gap; jointly optimize the number of quantization bits and the polar code block length across training iterations; explore both constant and variable blocklength configurations.
AI.result: Empirical results show substantial performance gains over uncoded transmission and LDPC-based EEP benchmarks, with larger gains as channel quality degrades.
AI.conclusion: A cross-layer polar-code FL scheme with UEP effectively mitigates channel noise, improving robustness and efficiency in realistic networks; the approach offers a promising direction for robust FL under practical communication constraints.

title: InstructVVT: Instruction-Driven Video Virtual Try-On without Auxiliary Spatial Priors
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures. Dingbao Shao and Song Wu contributed equally. Zili Yi is the corresponding author
summary: Video virtual try-on is a highly constrained editing task requiring the precise replacement of a target person's clothing while strictly preserving the original video's spatial structure and temporal dynamics. Existing methods heavily rely on auxiliary handcrafted spatial priors (e.g., masks, poses) for editing control. However, these priors are prone to failure in unconstrained real-world videos and often compress rich visual context into incomplete structural signals. Furthermore, standard reconstruction objectives fail to fully capture try-on-specific human preferences. To address these challenges, we propose InstructVVT, an instruction-driven and reference-guided video virtual try-on framework based on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that operates without inference-time spatial priors. Our core insight is to recover fine-grained control directly from the input triplet (source video, reference garment, and instruction) via a dual-level reference conditioning scheme. Specifically, an MLLM infers semantic edit tokens for target disambiguation and structural preservation, while a lightweight conditioning pathway explicitly injects fine-grained visual garment details. Finally, we design a try-on-specific reward and utilize the DiffusionNFT algorithm to align the model with human preferences. Extensive experiments on ViViD-S and TripVVT-Bench demonstrate that InstructVVT outperforms state-of-the-art open-source methods in garment fidelity, structural preservation, and temporal consistency, despite requiring fewer inference-time controls.

AI.tldr: Proposes InstructVVT, an instruction-driven, reference-guided video virtual try-on framework using a Diffusion Transformer that removes the need for inference-time spatial priors, featuring dual-level conditioning (MLLM-based semantic edit tokens and a fine-grained garment detail pathway) and a DiffusionNFT-based reward, achieving superior garment fidelity, structural preservation, and temporal consistency with fewer controls.
AI.motivation: Existing video VTO methods rely on handcrafted spatial priors (masks, poses) that fail in unconstrained real-world videos and often compress context; standard reconstruction objectives miss try-on-specific preferences. There is a need to recover fine-grained control directly from the input triplet (source video, reference garment, instruction) without inference-time priors.
AI.method: Diffusion Transformer-based architecture with dual-level reference conditioning: (1) an MLLM that infers semantic edit tokens for target disambiguation and structural preservation, (2) a lightweight conditioning pathway that injects fine-grained garment details. The framework is instruction-driven and reference-guided, uses a try-on-specific reward, and applies the DiffusionNFT algorithm to align with human preferences. Evaluation on ViViD-S and TripVVT-Bench.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art open-source methods in garment fidelity, structural preservation, and temporal consistency, while requiring fewer inference-time controls.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that instruction-driven, reference-guided video VTO without spatial priors is viable, with dual-level conditioning and human-preference alignment yielding superior editing fidelity and temporal coherence.

title: Joint Optimization of Memory and Computing Frequency for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference
summary: Deep neural network (DNN) inference on mobile devices often incurs high latency and energy consumption due to limited computing and memory resources. To enable energy-efficient DNN inference, most existing studies focus on dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) for adjusting the computing frequency, while the impact of memory frequency on the inference performance has been greatly overlooked. In this paper, we consider the impact of memory frequency and computing frequency on DNN inference time, and jointly optimize these two frequencies together with communication resources for energy-efficient DNN inference. Based on a realistic inference time model, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the energy consumption of all mobile devices under the deadline constraint. For local inference, we derive a near-optimal closed-form solution via convex optimization, while an optimal closed-form solution for transmission power is obtained for edge inference with the given bandwidth. Furthermore, we propose a low-complexity heuristic algorithm to effectively solve the overall problem with polynomial time complexity. Simulation results based on measured data show that the proposed near-optimal solution for local inference can achieve optimal performance under strict deadline constraints, with a performance gap of up to 2.5% compared with the optimal solution. Meanwhile, our proposed algorithm significantly reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 10.4% compared to other methods.

AI.tldr: Joint optimization of memory and computing frequencies with communication resources for energy-efficient mobile/edge DNN inference; yields near-optimal local solutions and closed-form transmission power, with practical energy savings.
AI.motivation: DNN inference on mobile devices is latency- and energy-constrained; memory frequency effects on inference time are underexplored, yet memory bandwidth can be a bottleneck. A joint optimization of memory frequency, computing frequency, and communication resources could substantially reduce energy under deadlines.
AI.method: Formulates an energy-minimization problem under a deadline constraint that jointly optimizes memory frequency, computing frequency, and communication resources. For local inference, derives a near-optimal closed-form solution via convex optimization. For edge inference with given bandwidth, obtains an optimal closed-form transmission-power solution. Proposes a low-complexity heuristic to solve the overall problem with polynomial time. Validates using measured data.
AI.result: The proposed near-optimal local-inference solution achieves performance within 2.5% of the optimal under strict deadlines. The algorithm reduces device energy consumption by up to 10.4% compared with competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Memory-frequency-aware joint optimization is effective for energy-efficient DNN inference under deadlines. The combination of convex-optimization-based closed-form solutions and a low-complexity heuristic provides a practical, scalable approach with quantifiable energy gains.

title: QUASAR: Lowering the Loss Floor of Quantization-Aware Training with Loss-Aware Reconstruction
summary: As large language model inference shifts toward lower precision, post-training quantization (PTQ) becomes increasingly brittle, making quantization-aware training (QAT) essential for preserving model quality. However, QAT computes the loss and surrogate gradients using a lossy reconstruction of latent full-precision weights, while applying updates to the latent weights themselves. This mismatch can lead to suboptimal training trajectories and a higher loss floor. Second-order PTQ methods mitigate a similar gap by minimizing loss-aware reconstruction error, but doing it once for a frozen model can take hours; repeating this process throughout QAT as the weights evolve is impractical. We introduce QUASAR, a QAT method that continuously performs lightweight, loss-aware reconstruction in the training loop to lower the loss floor and improve the resulting low-bit model. At each training step, QUASAR uses the exponential moving average of squared gradients as online saliency estimates, searches over a small set of clipping ranges, and fits affine dequantizers via saliency-weighted least squares. Our analysis shows that the loss-aware reconstruction error is the only reconstruction-dependent term in the QAT convergence bound and controls the loss of the final quantized model, establishing QUASAR's objective as a principled optimization target. QUASAR modifies only the training procedure and supports standard deployment formats, including integer quantization and NVFP4, with no inference-time changes or overhead. Across Qwen3 and Llama-3.1, QUASAR achieves the lowest held-out KL divergence among competitive QAT methods at 2, 3, and 4 bits, reducing KL by at least 10% at 3 and 4 bits and by 29% at 2 bits. At 2 bits, it improves average accuracy across eight tasks by 3.5-4.3 percentage points over strong QAT and PTQ baselines.

AI.tldr: QUASAR is a QAT method that continuously performs loss-aware reconstruction during training using online saliency estimates (EMA of squared gradients), small search over clipping ranges, and saliency-weighted least squares to fit affine dequantizers. It reduces the loss floor and improves quantized model quality at 2–4 bits across Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 without inference-time overhead.
AI.motivation: QAT at low-bit precision suffers from a mismatch between the lossy latent weight reconstruction used for loss/gradient computation and the actual weight updates, leading to a degraded loss floor. Second-order PTQ can reduce this gap but is impractical to apply repeatedly during training.
AI.method: At each training step, QUASAR uses the exponential moving average of squared gradients as online saliency estimates, searches over a small set of clipping ranges, and fits affine dequantizers via saliency-weighted least squares; this loss-aware reconstruction is integrated into the training loop. The method only changes the training procedure and supports standard deployment formats (integer quantization, NVFP4) with no inference-time overhead.
AI.result: QUASAR achieves the lowest held-out KL divergence among competitive QAT methods at 2–4 bits on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1, reducing KL by at least 10% at 3/4 bits and 29% at 2 bits. At 2 bits, average accuracy across eight tasks improves by 3.5–4.3 percentage points over strong QAT and PTQ baselines.
AI.conclusion: Loss-aware reconstruction error is the sole reconstruction-dependent term in the QAT convergence bound and governs the final loss of the quantized model; QUASAR provides a principled optimization target that improves quantized model quality without extra inference-time cost, while remaining deployment-compatible.

title: Owner3D: Ownership-Guided Style Writing for Training-Free Localized 3D Stylization
summary: Localized 3D stylization aims to modify the appearance of a specified object part while preserving the remaining surfaces. In large reconstruction models (LRMs), this task is challenging because style is injected into intermediate appearance representations before rendering, while compact triplane features are shared across target and non-target surfaces, causing style leakage and boundary ambiguity. We propose Owner3D, a training-free framework for localized 3D stylization that integrates localized appearance control directly into the LRM reconstruction process. Specifically, Owner3D introduces ownership-guided style writing to restrict reference-style injection to target regions, producing a single localized stylized triplane without additional training while avoiding separate global style and appearance representations. To resolve appearance ambiguity near semantic boundaries, we further introduce boundary dual slots that maintain separate local feature sources for target and non-target regions. Finally, a surface-first texture readout hierarchically combines surface, 3D, and triplane ownership evidence to robustly recover appearance under incomplete visibility. Experiments on a benchmark constructed from Google Scanned Objects and PartNet demonstrate that Owner3D consistently outperforms existing 3D stylization methods in target-region style fidelity and non-target appearance preservation, reducing appearance leakage by 86.4% and 89.9% compared with StyleSplat and LAENeRF, respectively.

AI.tldr: Owner3D delivers training-free localized 3D stylization for large reconstruction models by integrating ownership-guided style writing, boundary dual slots, and a surface-first readout to confine style to target regions; it reduces leakage and preserves non-target appearance, achieving state-of-the-art results on Google Scanned Objects/PartNet benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In LRMs, style injection occurs at intermediate representations; shared triplane features cause style leakage and boundary ambiguity when stylizing only parts. Existing methods either need explicit local representations or require retraining; there is a need for a training-free, localized approach.
AI.method: Introduce ownership-guided style writing to confine style injection to target regions; use boundary dual slots to maintain separate local feature sources for target vs non-target areas; a surface-first texture readout hierarchically fuses surface, 3D, and triplane ownership cues for robust appearance recovery under partial visibility.
AI.result: Benchmark on Google Scanned Objects/PartNet shows consistent improvements in target-region style fidelity and non-target preservation, with appearance leakage reduced by 86.4% vs StyleSplat and 89.9% vs LAENeRF.
AI.conclusion: Owner3D provides a training-free, localized stylization framework for LRMs that improves target fidelity and non-target preservation while avoiding extra global/style representations; it may rely on accurate ownership estimation and boundary handling, with potential generalization considerations.

title: MemoryLake on MemoryArena: A Matched Study of Agent Memory Backends
summary: Most agent-memory benchmarks test post-hoc recall, whereas MemoryArena evaluates whether memory supports interdependent, multi-session task completion. We compare MemoryLake, a structured multi-track memory backend, with Mem0, text-embedding-3-small vector RAG, and a long-context control across all five MemoryArena domains. The systems share the same agent framework, requested gpt-5-mini model alias, task samples, and scoring code; the memory integration is the intentionally changed component. Because each backend bundles write, retrieval, consolidation, budgeting, and prompt-assembly choices, the study is a matched system-level comparison, not a representation-only ablation or a cost-matched experiment. On the shared evaluation sets, MemoryLake has the highest observed success rate (SR) in mathematics (9/40), physics (12/20), and progressive retrieval (4/20). Every system has zero SR in travel planning, and web shopping yields a single bundle-level success (long context, 1/150); MemoryLake ranks third on both the travel soft process score and shopping step match. Following MemoryArena's suite-level convention, a post-hoc equal-weight average over the five SRs is 20.5% for MemoryLake versus 13.6% for the best comparator. These are point estimates: sample sizes are modest, confidence intervals overlap, and we do not report paired significance tests. A separate MemoryLake-only run over all 221 progressive queries yields a failure-counted SR of 26.7% (59/221) and is not a baseline comparison. The results support a workload-dependent view of memory backends and an observed lead among the four evaluated systems on the shared sets; they do not establish benchmark-wide state of the art or a causal advantage of representation structure.

AI.tldr: A matched-system evaluation shows MemoryLake generally outperforming Mem0 and long-context baselines on several MemoryArena tasks, but results are workload-dependent with modest sample sizes; no claim of universal state-of-the-art or causal advantage for representation structure.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the impact of memory backends (structured, multi-track memories) on interdependent, multi-session tasks in a realistic agent pipeline, extending beyond post-hoc recall benchmarks.
AI.method: Five MemoryArena domains; compare MemoryLake vs Mem0 vs long-context control using a shared agent framework, prompt alias, task samples, and scoring code. Each backend handles write, retrieval, consolidation, budgeting, and prompt assembly; compute per-domain success rates and a suite-level average (post-hoc equal-weight) across five domains; also include a MemoryLake-only progression run (221 queries).
AI.result: MemoryLake achieves the highest observed SR in mathematics (9/40), physics (12/20), and progressive retrieval (4/20); all systems fail on travel planning (0 SR) and long-context/shopping perform poorly (shopping 1/150 for long-context); MemoryLake ranks third on travel soft process score and shopping step match. The post-hoc average SR is 20.5% for MemoryLake vs 13.6% for the best comparator. The 221-query MemoryLake run yields 59/221 (26.7%) SR but is not a baseline comparison. Confidence intervals overlap due to modest sample sizes; no paired significance tests reported.
AI.conclusion: Findings support a workload-dependent view of memory backends; MemoryLake shows a relative advantage on shared tasks but does not establish benchmark-wide state-of-the-art or a causal benefit from representation structure. Results are exploratory with limited power.

title: Identifiability and Order-Dimension Limits of In-Context Learning on Partial Orders
summary: In-context learning is commonly formalized as inference from examples of a function. Partial orders instead combine transitivity, antisymmetry, and incomparability, so a finite prompt may not determine a queried comparison. We develop a theory of in-context learning on partial orders that separates logical identifiability, prompt teaching cost, structural complexity, and the exact capacity of a formal coordinate-decoder class. A version-space semantics makes background knowledge and open- versus closed-world assumptions explicit. For finite open-world prompts with positive and negative comparisons, we prove an exact completion trichotomy: after taking the reflexive transitive closure of the positive demonstrations, a query is forced true, forced false because every true completion creates a cycle or violates a negative demonstration, or remains genuinely ambiguous. For a known $n$-element universe, we characterize the open-world teaching number as the number of covers plus a blocker-set hitting number, prove that its maximum over all $n$-element posets is $n(n-1)$ and is uniquely attained by the antichain, and identify the blocker term as the exact cost of open-world rather than complete-Hasse semantics. We formalize prompt-dependent $s$-coordinate decoders and use the classical coordinate-order equivalence to obtain an exact representation boundary: dimension at most $s$ is necessary and sufficient, while width at most $s$ is a convenient sufficient condition.

AI.tldr: Develops a formal theory of in-context learning on partial orders, introducing version-space semantics, an exact completion trichotomy for open-world prompts, a combinatorial characterization of open-world teaching number (max n(n-1) achieved by the antichain), and a representation-bound via prompt-dependent s-coordinate decoders.
AI.motivation: To understand how partial-order relations constrain in-context learning with finite prompts and different world assumptions, and to separate identifiability, teaching cost, structural complexity, and decoder capacity.
AI.method: Version-space semantics; reflexive transitive closure of positive demonstrations; combinatorial poset analysis (covers and blocker-set); open-world vs complete-world framing; finite n-element universe; coordinate-order equivalence to derive representation bounds; define prompt-dependent s-coordinate decoders.
AI.result: Exact completion trichotomy: after closure, a query is forced true, forced false (due to cycles or negative demos), or genuinely ambiguous. Open-world teaching number equals number of covers plus blocker-set hitting number; maximum over posets on n elements is n(n-1), uniquely attained by the antichain. Blocker term captures open-world cost distinct from complete-Hasse semantics. Dimension bound: dim ≤ s is necessary and sufficient; width ≤ s is a convenient sufficient condition.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for in-context learning with partial orders, clarifying learnability under open/closed-world assumptions, offering precise combinatorial characterizations, and establishing exact representation limits via coordinates decoders.

title: CoDS: Robust Collaborative Perception via Expert-driven Detection and BEV Segmentation
summary: Collaborative perception breaks through single-view limitations via multi-agent information exchange. However, multi-source noise such as pose errors and communication delays degrades fusion feature quality, constraining perception performance. Joint training of detection and BEV segmentation provides a natural remedy, where segmented road regions help constrain target distributions and detection bounding boxes help recover ambiguous segmentation boundaries. To this end, we propose a robust Collaborative perception framework with expert-driven Detection and bev Segmentation (CoDS). To address spatial inconsistency in fusion quality, we first introduce the Collaborative Reliability Map (CoRM) to explicitly quantify feature quality distribution. Based on CoRM, we design the Semantic Mixture-of-Experts (S-MoE) module to extract differentiated features for inconsistent feature demands. Finally, to further mitigate feature noise degradation, the Bidirectional Task Complementary Interaction (BTCI) refines task-aware features through bidirectional injection. Extensive experiments on OPV2V and V2V4Real datasets show that our CoDS surpasses existing baselines on both tasks and maintains stable robustness under multi-source noise. Code: https://github.com/JinlongW128/CoDS and https://openi.pcl.ac.cn/OpenAIDriving/CoDS.

AI.tldr: A robust multi-agent perception framework (CoDS) that uses a reliability-aware fusion pipeline with a Collaborative Reliability Map, a Semantic Mixture-of-Experts, and Bidirectional Task Complementary Interaction to enhance detection and BEV segmentation under multi-source noise.
AI.motivation: Collaborative perception across vehicles suffers from pose errors and communication delays that degrade fusion features. Jointly training detection and BEV segmentation can constrain target distributions and sharpen boundaries, but existing methods lack reliable feature-quality assessment and cross-task synergy under multi-source noise.
AI.method: Propose CoDS with three components: (1) Collaborative Reliability Map (CoRM) to quantify spatial feature quality; (2) Semantic Mixture-of-Experts (S-MoE) to extract differentiated features aligned to local quality demands; (3) Bidirectional Task Complementary Interaction (BTCI) to refine task-specific features via bidirectional injection. The framework jointly trains detection and BEV segmentation for robustness, evaluated on OPV2V and V2V4Real with code released.
AI.result: CoDS surpasses baselines on both detection and BEV segmentation tasks and maintains robust performance under multi-source noise across OPV2V and V2V4Real datasets, with publicly available implementation.
AI.conclusion: CoDS offers a reliable, cross-task collaborative perception solution that leverages feature-quality quantification, specialized feature fusion, and bidirectional task interactions to improve robustness and accuracy in multi-agent settings.

title: When Personal Memory Has No Single Answer: Evaluating LLM Agents under Irreducible Conflict
summary: LLM agents increasingly maintain personal memory across sessions, but it can conflict. Preferences depend on context, behavior evolves, and sources can conflict. When a query lacks context, time, or source authority to interpret conflict, treating one memory as definitive converts unresolved conflict into an unjustified, overconfident action. Existing benchmarks recover one answer from conflicting evidence, overlooking whether agents recognize underdetermination, preserve alternatives, seek missing information, and choose appropriate actions. We introduce \underline{T}esting \underline{A}gents' \underline{N}avigation of \underline{G}enuine, \underline{L}atent, and \underline{E}ntangled Memory Conflicts (\textsc{TANGLE}), a benchmark for genuinely unresolvable memory conflicts. It comprises 541 instances across 40 personas and three types: Context-Partitioned Conflict (CPC), Behavior-Oscillation Conflict (BOC), and Source-Contradiction Conflict (SCC). We evaluate two tracks---an oracle track with curated memory and a pipeline track that extracts memory from multi-session dialogues---on five dimensions: conflict perception, causal reasoning, confidence calibration, clarification seeking, and memory faithfulness. Experiments reveal pipeline challenges. With curated memory, models recognize conflicts more reliably than they calibrate actions or seek targeted clarification. With end-to-end pipeline memory, extraction fails to preserve conflict-bearing relations needed for downstream reasoning. Policy comparisons show fixed rules are insufficient when actions must reflect conflict. These findings motivate Conflict-Aware Action Policy (CAAP), which adapts actions to each conflict using available evidence. \textsc{TANGLE} frames conflict handling as recognizing underdetermination, retaining conflicting evidence, and acting without forcing a definitive answer.

AI.tldr: Introduces TANGLE, a benchmark for genuinely unresolvable memory conflicts in LLM agents, revealing underdetermination in memory, extraction failures in pipelines, and the need for memory-aware action policies (CAAP).
AI.motivation: Addresses the failure modes where memory conflicts across sessions can lead to unjustified, overconfident actions. Existing benchmarks pick a single answer from conflicting evidence and miss whether agents recognize underdetermination, retain alternatives, seek missing information, or choose appropriate actions.
AI.method: Constructs 541 instances across 40 personas and three conflict types—Context-Partitioned Conflict (CPC), Behavior-Oscillation Conflict (BOC), and Source-Contradiction Conflict (SCC). Evaluates two tracks (oracle with curated memory and pipeline extraction from multi-session dialogues) on five dimensions: conflict perception, causal reasoning, confidence calibration, clarification seeking, and memory faithfulness.
AI.result: Finds pipeline extraction struggles to preserve conflict-bearing relations; curated memory improves conflict recognition but not action calibration or clarification; fixed-rule policies are inadequate for actions reflecting conflict. CAAP (Conflict-Aware Action Policy) proposed to adapt actions to each conflict using available evidence.
AI.conclusion: TANGLE frames conflict handling as recognizing underdetermination, retaining conflicting evidence, and acting without forcing a definitive answer, guiding memory-aware decision policies in LLM agents.

title: When Does More Correct Data Hurt? Insertion-Stability and the Limits of Dimension-Based Theory
summary:
Adding data known to be correct ought to be safe. Not always. Larsen, Pabbaraju and Shetty model the failure with a monotone adversary, which reads an i.i.d. training sample and may append as many further examples as it likes, provided the target hypothesis labels them all. Mehrotra has since settled the cost, showing that for classes of VC dimension d >= 2 no learner can guarantee expected error better than Theta((d/n)log(en/d)), a logarithmic factor above the clean PAC rate.
  Because that rate is a worst case over all classes, it says nothing about which classes actually suffer the penalty, and the answer turns on the learner. We call a learner insertion-stable if feeding it more correctly labeled examples can only shrink the region where it errs. Such learners are immune to the adversary, since on any given sample the risk after insertions never exceeds the risk on the clean part alone, however much is added and however cleverly it is chosen. High- probability guarantees carry over unchanged, and because Closure is insertion-stable every intersection-closed class keeps its clean rate of E[Err] <= (21d+34)/n.
  Immunity is not something the classical dimensions can predict. Two classes can agree on VCdim = Ldim = 2 and still split, one at Theta(1/n) and the other at Theta(log(en)/n), while intervals have unbounded Littlestone dimension and are immune anyway. On Mehrotra's hard class we prove more than the failure of a single algorithm, showing that no monotone permutation-invariant compression scheme of any finite size attains the clean rate.
  The question is therefore not whether a class is hard, nor whether a learner is good, but whether the two suit each other. Given an insertion-stable learner that is optimal on clean data, correct additions are free, and without one the cost belongs to the class, so changing the learner will not avoid it.

AI.tldr: Insertion-stable learners avoid degradation from adversarial additions of correctly labeled data; for intersection-closed (Closure) classes, the clean O(d/n) error bound is preserved despite insertions. This immunity is not captured by classical dimensions: classes with equal VC and Littlestone dimensions can behave very differently. Moreover, on Mehrotra’s hard class, no finite monotone compression can achieve the clean rate. The takeaway: robustness depends on the compatibility between the learner and the class, and with an insertion-stable learner optimal on clean data, correct additions are effectively free.
AI.motivation: To understand robustness of learning algorithms when additional data known to be correctly labeled can be added by an adversary. The goal is to identify properties of learners and hypothesis classes that preserve the clean learning rate under such insertions.
AI.method: 1) Define insertion-stable learners as those where adding correct labeled examples cannot increase the error region. 2) Show that Closure (intersection-closed) classes are insertion-stable and derive high-probability error bounds that keep the clean rate: E[Err] ≤ (21d+34)/n. 3) Demonstrate immunity is not predicted by VC-dimension or Littlestone dimension: there exist classes with d = Ldim = 2 that differ in rates, while intervals (unbounded Littlestone dimension) are immune. 4) Prove that for Mehrotra’s hard class, no monotone permutation-invariant finite compression attains the clean rate. 5) Argue that success depends on the matching of the learner with the class, i.e., an insertion-stable learner optimal on clean data renders correct additions effectively free.
AI.result: Key findings: (i) Insertion-stable learners preserve the clean O(d/n) learning rate for intersection-closed/Closure classes, with high-probability bound E[Err] ≤ (21d+34)/n. (ii) Immunity to data insertions is not determined by classical dimension measures; identical VC-dimension and Littlestone dimension do not guarantee similar robustness. (iii) Some classes (e.g., Mehrotra’s hard class) resist any finite monotone compression achieving the clean rate, illustrating limits of compression-based immunity. (iv) The main message is that robustness to data additions hinges on the compatibility between the learner and the class; with a correctly-behaved learner, correct additions are effectively free, while other combinations incur the class-dependent cost.
AI.conclusion: Robustness to insertions is a property of the learner-class pair, not a universal feature of a class. Choose an insertion-stable learner when working with intersection-closed classes to maintain the clean learning rate; otherwise, even with the same classical dimensions, the unavoidable cost may persist.

title: Fixed-Budget Gaussian Volume Encoding with Structure-Aware Allocation
summary: Scientific simulations often produce scalar volumes faster than they can be stored, transferred, and loaded, while in situ reduction must use only a limited share of simulation resources. This work encodes scalar fields as anisotropic Gaussian primitives under a fixed budget. The complete primitive set is allocated analytically from local field structure, including position, orientation, and shape, then refined directly against the scalar field without densification, pruning, or count changes. The selected budget determines encoded storage before refinement and, together with the iteration schedule, provides a controllable refinement-time budget. In a controlled benchmark, truncation-aware field evaluation reduces encoding time by up to 51x; 1.4 million Gaussians encode a billion-voxel volume in at most four minutes on one desktop GPU, with reduced-iteration refinement completing in under one minute. Across five datasets spanning 2.1 million to 1.1 billion evaluated voxels, compression-useful configurations achieve 15.0-38.7 dB PSNR at compression ratios from 2.2x to over 40,000x. Pre-encoding structure statistics characterize fields for which one-shot allocation yields limited gains from additional capacity. Because primitives retain scalar attributes rather than baked appearance, a single compact model serves every subsequent visualization state - supporting post-hoc transfer-function, colormap, lighting, and viewpoint changes without re-encoding.

AI.tldr: Anisotropic Gaussian primitives encode scalar fields under a fixed budget for in-situ compression, enabling fast encoding and post-hoc visualization with high compression and PSNR.
AI.motivation: Reduce data movement/storage bottlenecks in scientific simulations by performing in-situ compression that preserves visualization flexibility for later analysis.
AI.method: Allocate a complete set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives analytically from local field structure (position, orientation, shape) under a fixed budget; refine directly against the scalar field without densification, pruning, or count changes; budget and iteration schedule control refinement-time cost; use truncation-aware evaluation and pre-encoding statistics to guide allocation; single compact model supports post-hoc transfer-function, colormap, lighting, and viewpoint changes.
AI.result: Encoding time can be reduced up to 51x; 1.4 million Gaussians encode a 1B-voxel volume in ≤4 minutes on a desktop GPU; reduced-iteration refinement completes in under 1 minute; across datasets, PSNR 15.0–38.7 dB at compression ratios from 2.2x to >40,000x; pre-encoding statistics identify fields where one-shot allocation suffices; primitives retain scalar attributes enabling future visualizations without re-encoding.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic Gaussian primitive encoding offers fast, tunable, in-situ compression with strong data reduction while preserving visualization flexibility, enabling post-hoc adjustments without re-encoding.

title: Never the Number: Structural Abstention for AI Systems Whose Answers Are Consumed as Fact
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Technical report. Describes architecture and design principles only; contains no code, schemas, datasets, or performance metrics
summary:
Large language models have made natural language interfaces to databases (NLIDB) newly credible, but LLM text-to-SQL systems fail in a way that matters for deployment: a hallucinated column or a mis-aggregated total yields a fluent wrong answer, indistinguishable at the point of use from a right one.
