Where the consumer cannot inspect the generated query, as in enterprise AI deployments and operational dashboards, and increasingly where the consumer is a tool-using agent rather than a person, accuracy alone is insufficient: nothing marks which answers to distrust. This is a reliability problem before it is an accuracy problem.
  We propose an architectural pattern for such systems, a trusted kernel with a generative shell, resting on one invariant: a component that can fabricate may influence which question the system answers, never which value it returns. A generative shell interprets underspecified input and phrases replies; a deterministic kernel matches fully specified questions against a bounded set of answerable question shapes and compiles them to queries by deterministic execution. The two meet at a confirmation the user reads before any value is computed, and requests the kernel cannot express are declined rather than approximated. We call this structural abstention, and distinguish it from the statistical abstention of selective prediction and calibrated confidence: refusal here needs no confidence estimate, because unanswerable requests are unrepresentable.
  We specify the pattern implementation-independently, give a five-decision recipe and work it across three domains, extend the invariant from returned values to the actions of agentic systems, and report a two-year production case study alongside two generative alternatives, a fine-tuned parser and a tool-retrieval agent. We close against enterprise and reliability benchmarks published since.

AI.tldr: A reliability-focused NLIDB architecture combining a deterministic kernel with a generative shell, using structural abstention to prevent unanswerable or misrepresented queries; validated via a five-decision recipe, cross-domain deployment, and a two-year production case study.
AI.motivation: In deployed NLIDB systems, hallucinated columns and mis-aggregations can produce fluent but incorrect results that are indistinguishable from correct ones. When users cannot inspect or control the generated queries, accuracy alone fails as a reliability measure; a design pattern is needed to prevent the system from influencing questions or values in unsafe ways.
AI.method: Propose architectural pattern: a trusted kernel (deterministic) paired with a generative shell. The shell can handle underspecified input and craft responses, while the kernel matches fully specified questions to a bounded set of answerable shapes and compiles them into queries through deterministic execution. A structural abstention mechanism ensures the system refuses to answer when no representable, answerable form exists, and a five-decision recipe guides implementation. The pattern is demonstrated across three domains, extended to agentic actions, and evaluated against enterprise reliability benchmarks, including comparisons to a fine-tuned parser and a tool-retrieval agent, with a two-year production case study.
AI.result: A specification of the pattern and an operational recipe (five decisions), validated across multiple domains, with a production case study and comparative analyses of two alternative generative approaches, benchmarking against enterprise reliability criteria.
AI.conclusion: Structural abstention offers a practical reliability guarantee for NLIDB in enterprise contexts by separating value computation from question shaping, enabling safe refusals when unrepresentable and supporting robust, auditable deployments across domains and agentic systems.

title: Adversarial Learning of Classifier-Free Guidance Schedules
summary: Modern text-to-image diffusion models rely on classifier-free guidance (CFG) to achieve high image fidelity and text alignment. However, CFG typically applies a static, global scale across all timesteps, samples, and conditions -- a choice that is generally suboptimal and can introduce artifacts, as different states may benefit from different levels of guidance. While time-varying schedules are known to improve quality, designing them by hand is non-trivial and application-dependent. In this paper, we learn the guidance schedule as a function of diffusion time, conditioning and the current noisy sample, in order to better align sampled images with the text prompt. We frame this as a density ratio estimation problem: a discriminator is trained to estimate the time-dependent log-density ratio between the true and guided marginal distributions, while a lightweight generator network predicts the optimal, state-dependent guidance scale. Empirically, our approach outperforms both heuristic CFG schedules and prior methods for learning dynamic guidance on text-to-image generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Learnable, time- and state-dependent guidance for classifier-free diffusion in text-to-image generation, using a density-ratio discriminator and a lightweight generator to predict optimal scales; outperforms static CFG and prior dynamic methods on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Static, global CFG scales across all timesteps, samples, and prompts often misalign fidelity and text guidance, causing artifacts. Hand-tuned, time-varying schedules are challenging and data/application-specific; a learnable, adaptive schedule is desirable.
AI.method: Formulate CFG schedule as a density-ratio estimation problem. Train a discriminator to estimate the time-dependent log-density ratio between true and guided marginals conditioned on diffusion time t, conditioning c, and current noisy sample x_t. Train a lightweight generator to predict the optimal state-dependent guidance scale s(t, c, x_t). Use the predicted scale to modulate CFG during diffusion sampling, enabling a time-, condition-, and state-aware guidance.
AI.result: Empirically surpasses heuristic CFG schedules and prior dynamic guidance methods on text-to-image generation benchmarks, achieving better fidelity and alignment with prompts.
AI.conclusion: A principled, learnable framework for dynamic CFG yields improved image quality and prompt adherence over static or manually designed schedules, with potential applicability to broader diffusion-based tasks.

title: HiCo-GS: Hierarchical Context Aggregation and Geometric Consistency for Octree Gaussian Splatting
comment: 21 pages, including supplementary material. To appear in the Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26)
summary: Octree-based anchor Gaussian Splatting has emerged as a scalable representation for city-scale novel view synthesis, where multi-level anchors adaptively capture scene content from coarse building structures to fine architectural details. However, we identify a fundamental limitation in existing methods: cross-level feature isolation, where each level's anchor features are optimized independently with no inter-level communication, causing color drift on building facades and over-smoothing in textured regions. We present HiCo-GS, a high-fidelity reconstruction framework with two complementary modules. Cross-Level Context Aggregation (CLCA) enables bidirectional hierarchical prior injection by leveraging the octree's spatial containment structure to aggregate per-level context vectors into parent-self-child triplets, fused via a lightweight MLP with residual connection. Coarse-level structural priors flow down to inform fine-level anchors, while fine-level detail statistics feed back to prevent over-smoothing, at negligible computational overhead. Depth-Normal Geometric Consistency (DNGC) regularization enforces agreement between rendered normals and depth-derived normals through an alpha-weighted consistency loss, complemented by edge-aware smoothness losses with progressive warmup that exploit the strong planar priors ubiquitous in urban geometry to suppress floating artifacts. We further introduce the China-Pagoda dataset comprising 8 ancient Chinese pagodas with over 1,200 images each, featuring dense ornamental carvings, curved multi-layer eaves, and repetitive fine-grained textures. Extensive experiments on Mill19, UrbanScene3D, MatrixCity, and China-Pagoda demonstrate that HiCo-GS achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality and substantially cleaner geometry across real-world and synthetic urban benchmarks.Code: https://github.com/WZ-CS/HiCo-GS.

AI.tldr: HiCo-GS introduces Cross-Level Context Aggregation and Depth-Normal Geometric Consistency to fix cross-level feature isolation in octree-based anchor Gaussian Splatting, achieving higher fidelity city-scale view synthesis and cleaner geometry; it also introduces the China-Pagoda dataset and reports state-of-the-art results on Mill19, UrbanScene3D, MatrixCity, and China-Pagoda; code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.motivation: Cross-level feature isolation in octree-based anchor Gaussian Splatting causes color drift on façades and over-smoothing in textured regions; there is a need for inter-level communication to propagate coarse priors downward and fine-level cues upward to preserve detail and color consistency in urban scenes.
AI.method: HiCo-GS comprises two modules: (1) Cross-Level Context Aggregation (CLCA): uses the octree containment relations to create parent-self-child triplets of per-level context vectors, fused via a lightweight MLP with a residual connection; enables bidirectional context transfer so coarse-level structure informs finer anchors and fine-level detail statistics feedback to prevent over-smoothing; (2) Depth-Normal Geometric Consistency (DNGC): an alpha-weighted loss enforcing agreement between rendered normals and depth-derived normals, complemented by edge-aware smoothness losses with progressive warmup that leverage planar urban priors to suppress floating artifacts; computational overhead is negligible.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Mill19, UrbanScene3D, MatrixCity, and China-Pagoda show HiCo-GS achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality and significantly cleaner geometry across real-world and synthetic urban benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The combination of CLCA for robust cross-level feature fusion and DNGC for geometry-consistent shading yields high-fidelity city-scale novel view synthesis with reduced color drift and over-smoothing, and the China-Pagoda dataset provides a challenging resource for evaluating fine-grained architectural detail. Code is released at the linked GitHub repository.

title: AI Research Preference Models
summary: AI research agents (AIRA) can now propose, implement, and evaluate their own machine learning experiments, but progress on frontier tasks is throttled by cost: a candidate solution can be written in minutes, whereas evaluating it can take hours to days of GPU time. An agent can therefore propose far more candidates than it can afford to run, and its progress depends on its research preference: how it allocates a fixed execution budget across many candidates. We introduce AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) that predict which of multiple candidate solutions are most worth executing, without paying the cost of executing them all. We build RPMs from frozen pretrained language models (with no task-specific training), in two forms: an inference-only model that reasons over candidate plans, code, and prior executed solutions, and an agentic model that additionally runs small-scale pilot experiments before deciding. We integrate both into the AIRA-dojo search agent and evaluate on AIRS-Bench, a recent benchmark of machine learning research tasks for AI research agents. The two variants raise the average normalized score from 0.684 to 0.711 and 0.729 respectively, and reach the unguided agent's 24-hour performance in roughly 15 hours, using less than two-thirds of its execution budget. Our best RPMs also yield new state-of-the-art results on two AIRS-Bench tasks.

AI.tldr: Frozen-language-model–based RPMs (inference-only and agentic) guide AIRA's budget for evaluating candidate ML experiments, delivering faster, high-quality progress and state-of-the-art results on AIRS-Bench.
AI.motivation: To overcome evaluation cost bottlenecks in autonomous ML research agents by predicting which candidate solutions are worth evaluating without full execution.
AI.method: Construct RPMs from frozen pretrained LMs; design two forms: inference-only (reason over candidate plans, code, prior results) and agentic (adds small pilot experiments); integrate into AIRA-dojo; evaluate on AIRS-Bench.
AI.result: RPMs improve average normalized scores (0.684→0.711 and 0.729); reach 24-hour performance in ~15 hours and use <2/3 budget; achieve state-of-the-art on two AIRS-Bench tasks.
AI.conclusion: RPMs demonstrate effective, resource-efficient guidance for AI research agents, enabling faster exploration and higher-quality outcomes without task-specific training.

title: Model-agnostic Retrieval-Augmented Extended Forecasting for time series
summary: Time series forecasting with pretrained foundation models has demonstrated strong zero-shot capabilities. However, achieving optimal performance on time series with short or negligible historical data in domain-specific applications typically requires adaptation via either fine-tuning or RAG. While fine-tuning is effective, it incurs substantial computational costs. This work explores RAG within univariate time series (Retrieval Augmented Generation) as a more efficient alternative, in particular RAF (Retrieval Augmented Forecasting), and introduces RAEF (Retrieval-Augmented Extended Forecasting), a model-agnostic method built upon RAF. RAEF incorporates key refinements to the retrieval and aggregation mechanisms: (1) direct retrieval in input-space rather than embedding-space, reducing inference overhead, and (2) concatenation-based aggregation that preserves temporal structure instead of averaging. Empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrates that RAEF outperforms RAF in both accuracy and inference overhead. Furthermore, comprehensive comparisons with zero-shot and fine-tuned foundation models show that RAEF achieves competitive or superior performance to fine-tuning while avoiding its computational burden, establishing it as a practical and scalable approach for domain adaptation in time series forecasting.

AI.tldr: RAEF is a model-agnostic retrieval-augmented forecasting method for univariate time series that uses input-space retrieval and concatenation-based aggregation to preserve temporal structure, achieving accuracy and efficiency improvements over RAF and competitive results relative to fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To enable effective domain adaptation for time-series forecasting when historical data are scarce, leveraging Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning while maintaining high accuracy.
AI.method: RAEF builds on RAF and introduces two refinements: (i) direct retrieval in input-space (instead of embedding-space) to lower inference overhead, and (ii) concatenation-based aggregation that preserves temporal order rather than simple averaging; the approach is model-agnostic and evaluated against zero-shot, RAF, and fine-tuned baselines on benchmark datasets.
AI.result: Empirical results show RAEF outperforms RAF in both accuracy and inference overhead, and provides competitive or superior performance compared to fine-tuning, offering a practical and scalable solution for domain adaptation in time-series forecasting.
AI.conclusion: RAEF provides a scalable, efficient alternative to fine-tuning for adapting foundation models to new time-series domains, combining principled retrieval with structure-preserving aggregation to achieve strong performance with reduced computational cost.

title: SPARGen: Unifying Spatial Perception and Reasoning through Native Multimodal Generation
summary: Spatial perception and reasoning from visual observations require recovering geometric structure, establishing correspondences, and understanding spatial relations. Existing approaches typically address these capabilities separately using task-specific architectures or external geometric modules, limiting knowledge transfer among complementary representations of the same physical scene. We introduce SPARGen, a unified multimodal framework that casts 3D reconstruction, dense correspondence, and spatial reasoning as instruction-conditioned generation tasks. SPARGen serializes compact structured and linguistic outputs as token sequences while generating dense geometric fields in image-aligned forms, enabling spatial supervision to jointly shape shared representations within a native multimodal generative model. Experiments across benchmarks for 3D reconstruction, correspondence, and spatial reasoning show that SPARGen achieves competitive performance across heterogeneous spatial tasks within a single native multimodal generative framework.

AI.tldr: SPARGen unifies 3D reconstruction, dense correspondence, and spatial reasoning in a single multimodal generative framework by instruction-conditioned generation and tokenized outputs, with image-aligned dense geometric fields, achieving competitive results on heterogeneous spatial benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current spatial perception methods tackle reconstruction, correspondences, and reasoning with separate task-specific architectures or external geometry modules, hindering knowledge transfer and shared representation learning across modalities. A unified framework should enable cross-task benefits by learning joint representations.
AI.method: SPARGen casts 3D reconstruction, dense correspondence, and spatial reasoning as instruction-conditioned generation tasks. It serializes compact structured and linguistic outputs as token sequences and generates dense geometric fields in image-aligned forms within a native multimodal generative model, enabling joint spatial supervision to shape shared representations.
AI.result: Experiments on benchmarks for 3D reconstruction, correspondence, and spatial reasoning show SPARGen achieves competitive performance across heterogeneous spatial tasks within a single native multimodal generative framework.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of a unified multimodal generative approach for spatial understanding, enabling cross-task knowledge transfer and shared representations among disparate spatial tasks, and suggests a path toward more integrated spatial reasoning systems.

title: HELIX: Model-Harness Co-evolution for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Scaling agent capability has largely focused on improving the model, yet an interactive agent acts through a runtime harness that mediates context, tools, control flow, and stopping. The harness shapes both what a model can accomplish and the trajectories from which it learns. This coupling motivates model-harness co-evolution for recursive self-improvement: build harnesses for a fixed model, update the model from verified sibling trajectories, and rebuild the harnesses as model capabilities change. Realizing this loop requires a controlled way to evolve harnesses while preserving intervention identity and effect. We present HELIX, a source-traceable substrate for harness evolution. HELIX decomposes agent systems into typed ports, reusable atoms, recipes, product shells, and runtime policies. It makes interventions explicit and auditable while retaining trajectories, test outcomes, and provenance. Harness evolution thus serves two linked roles: improving fixed-model execution and producing matched successes, regressions, near misses, and alternative solutions as data for subsequent model improvement. We evaluate HELIX in one evolution round on code repair. A 65-candidate portfolio discovers a fixed harness that improves task coverage by 4.0% over Pi, while the full portfolio exposes up to 58.0% more verified coverage through complementary sibling behavior. Selected candidates are assessed with repeated runs and the SWE-bench evaluator. A 200-slot sibling slice yields 438 verified SFT, critic, filter, and preference records. These results show how harness, model, and data form a feedback system: harness evolution expands current capability and creates learning signal for the next model; model updates motivate the next round of harness evolution. HELIX provides an auditable interface for studying this recursive process. Code is available at https://github.com/HKUDS/HELIX.

AI.tldr: HELIX introduces a source-traceable substrate for harness evolution to enable co-evolution of agents and their runtime harnesses, yielding auditable interventions and a feedback loop for recursive self-improvement; preliminary evaluation on code repair shows improved coverage and rich learning signals, with code available.
AI.motivation: To address uncontrolled evolution of agent capabilities and loss of traceability when models are updated via harness-mediated interactions; to enable repeatable, auditable harness changes that preserve intervention identity while collecting learning signals.
AI.method: Decompose agent systems into typed ports, reusable atoms, recipes, product shells, and runtime policies; implement HELIX as an auditable substrate; evaluate through a one-round evolution on code repair with a 65-candidate portfolio and 200-slot sibling slice, measuring test coverage and verified data using SWE-bench.
AI.result: Harness discovery yields a fixed harness increasing task coverage by 4.0% over Pi; full portfolio yields up to 58.0% more verified coverage via complementary sibling behavior; 438 verified SFT/critic/filter/preference records; results demonstrate a closed-loop harness-model-data feedback.
AI.conclusion: Harness evolution expands capability and provides data for subsequent model improvement; HELIX offers an auditable interface to study recursive harness-model co-evolution; code is publicly available.

title: When Denoising Hurts: Rethinking the Terminal Step of Diffusion Time Series Forecasters -- Extended Version
summary: Diffusion models offer a natural way to model uncertainty in time series forecasting, yet their iterative sampling process is often treated as a uniformly beneficial refinement procedure. Our study challenges this view by examining how forecast quality evolves throughout reverse diffusion. We find that general temporal structure is often recovered at relatively high noise levels, whereas continued low-noise refinement can introduce statistical drift and degrade the final forecast. Our analysis further suggests that this behavior explains why prior methods often favor relatively narrow diffusion architecture and schedule design. Building on this observation, we propose a label-free global stopping criterion that detects the optimal termination point, eventually speeding up inference and improving predictive accuracy. Additionally, since early stopping terminates inference in high-noise regions, we propose a Bernoulli timestep sampler that concentrates training on this region while preserving coverage of the full diffusion process. Extensive experiments conducted across eight real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Diffusion-based time-series forecasting shows non-monotonic forecast quality across reverse-diffusion steps: early high-noise steps recover structure, while late low-noise refinement can drift and harm accuracy. The paper introduces a label-free global stopping criterion to terminate diffusion at the optimal point, and a Bernoulli timestep sampler to focus training on high-noise regions while preserving full diffusion coverage. Empirical evaluation on eight real-world datasets demonstrates faster inference and improved predictive performance compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: To understand how forecast quality evolves during reverse diffusion in time-series forecasting, explain why aggressive refinement at low noise may degrade results, and improve practical efficiency and accuracy by adaptive termination and targeted training.
AI.method: 1) analyze forecast quality across diffusion steps; 2) design a label-free global stopping criterion to detect optimal termination; 3) propose a Bernoulli timestep sampler to emphasize high-noise regions during training while maintaining coverage of the diffusion process; 4) validate via extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets comparing to existing diffusion-based approaches.
AI.result: The study finds that high-noise steps generally recover general temporal structure, but continued low-noise refinement introduces statistical drift and degrades the final forecast. The global stopping criterion speeds inference and improves accuracy; the Bernoulli timestep sampler concentrates training on high-noise regions while preserving full diffusion coverage. Across eight real-world datasets, the proposed method demonstrates superior predictive performance relative to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive termination and targeted training in diffusion-based time-series forecasting can mitigate drift introduced by low-noise refinement, leading to faster inference and higher accuracy. The approach also sheds light on why diffusion architectures and schedules are often narrowly designed.

title: PISA: A Pseudo-Individual Source-Domain Feature Adaptation Framework for Test-Time Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection test-time adaptation (OVOD-TTA) aims to address the performance degradation that pre-trained base models suffer when encountering image-domain shifts. Existing source-free OVOD-TTA methods rely either on refined test-time information for re-scoring or on pseudo-labels for self-training, leading to significant accuracy degradation when initial predictions are poor. Meanwhile, most conventional source-domain estimation methods recover abstract, sparse representations suitable for the classification task, but fail to capture the dense, concrete features required for detection. To address these issues, we propose PISA, a novel source-free OVOD-TTA method that can be seamlessly integrated into open-vocabulary visual backbones. The core components of our method are the Corruption-Invariant Feature Extractor (CIFE), the Feature Alignment Module (FAM), and a multi-scale alignment framework (BAA). To capture detection-suitable features, we develop CIFE to exploit the invariance of CLIP's visual features across corrupted images, ensuring robustness against various corruptions. We further develop FAM and BAA for the pre-training and adaptation to transform the corruption-invariant features into pseudo-individual source-domain features that are close to the original source-domain features. In this way, dense and concrete pseudo-individual source-domain features are used for supervision instead of unreliable pseudo-label signals. Experiments on the corrupted VOC-C, COCO-C, and LVIS-C benchmarks across three base models demonstrate that PISA substantially improves both the localization precision and the category recognition accuracy of the original models. Notably, PISA achieves state-of-the-art performance without requiring access to source-domain data, surpassing existing methods by 3.92% in AP@50% on COCO-C.

AI.tldr: A source-free OVOD-TTA method (PISA) that uses corruption-invariant features and alignment modules to generate dense pseudo-source-domain representations, improving detection under domain shifts without source data.
AI.motivation: OVOD-TTA models degrade under image-domain shifts and rely on unreliable test-time scoring or pseudo-labels; conventional source-domain estimates are sparse and insufficient for dense detection. A method is needed to produce dense, concrete features that resemble source-domain representations without accessing source data.
AI.method: PISA introduces three components: Corruption-Invariant Feature Extractor (CIFE) to leverage CLIP feature invariance across corrupted images, a Feature Alignment Module (FAM), and a multi-scale alignment framework (BAA). These components pre-train and adapt features to transform corruption-invariant representations into pseudo-individual source-domain features close to the original source features, enabling supervision with dense representations instead of pseudo-labels; seamlessly integrates into open-vocabulary backbones for OVOD-TTA.
AI.result: Empirical results on corrupted VOC-C, COCO-C, and LVIS-C across three base models show substantial gains in localization precision and category recognition; achieves state-of-the-art performance without access to source-domain data, e.g., +3.92 AP@50 on COCO-C compared to prior methods.
AI.conclusion: PISA effectively converts corruption-invariant CLIP features into dense pseudo-source-domain features through CIFE, FAM, and BAA, enabling robust, source-free OVOD-TTA with strong gains in both localization and recognition under domain shifts; suitable for integration into open-vocabulary backbones.

title: Implementing Computational Law in Wolfram Language for the Governance of Artificial Intelligence
comment: 25 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, 12 code listings. Wolfram Language implementation and verification script (31 assertions) available at https://github.com/Zaffer/research-computational-law
summary: How do we govern AI systems whose reasoning we cannot fully inspect? Governance does not require understanding a system's reasoning. It requires stating what the system is obliged, permitted, and forbidden to do, and checking whether it complied. I present an implementation of Reified Input/Output Logic, the formalism behind the DAPRECO knowledge base, in Wolfram Language: the core I/O axioms, obligations, permissions, constitutive norms, reified eventualities, and temporal operators. I then test whether GPT-4 can translate English legal statements into the formalism, and report the failures: hallucinated functions, omitted temporal scope, deviation from the formalism, and (in the worst cases) code that runs, reads plausibly, but silently encodes the wrong norm. A case study, an AI guard dog operating under a computational contract, shows how formalized rules can extend from a contract directly into the operational code of an embodied agent, producing symbolic, auditable justifications for its behaviour. I argue that computational law can be used as a governance tool and that a desirable goal would be to formalize the law that can and ought to be programmatically executable.

AI.tldr: Proposes implementing Reified Input/Output Logic (R-I/O) for governance of opaque AI systems, tests GPT-4's ability to translate legal English into the formalism, and demonstrates an embodied agent governed by a computational contract; argues computational law can enable auditable governance.
AI.motivation: Govern AI systems with inscrutable reasoning by specifying obligations, permissions, and prohibitions, and verifying compliance rather than fully inspecting internal reasoning; address opacity and risk through formalizable, executable legal rules.
AI.method: Implement core I/O axioms, obligations, permissions, constitutive norms, reified eventualities, and temporal operators of R-I/O in Wolfram Language (DAPRECO framework). Evaluate GPT-4's translation of English legal statements into the formalism, identify failures (hallucinated functions, omitted temporal scope, deviation from formalism). Conduct a case study of an AI guard dog governed by a computational contract, showing how formalized rules extend into operational code to generate auditable justifications.
AI.result: Notable findings include translation failures by GPT-4 (hallucinations, scope omissions, misalignment) and, in worst case, code that runs but encodes an incorrect norm. The case study demonstrates that formalized rules can be embedded in agent code, producing symbolic, auditable justifications for behavior. Overall, computational law can function as a governance tool, but achieving programmatically executable law remains challenging.
AI.conclusion: Computational law has potential as a governance tool by codifying legal norms into executable rules; the authors advocate formalizing laws that can and ought to be programmatically executed. Key challenges include accurate translation from natural language to formalism, verification of compliance, and ensuring normative fidelity in deployed systems.

title: Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning for One-Warehouse Multi-Store Systems with Censored Demand
summary: The one-warehouse multi-store (OWMS) system is a fundamental inventory network in which a nonreplenishable warehouse allocates shared stock across multiple stores over time. Existing OWMS learning policies are built around a fixed target calibrated to the initial average resource rate, but such a fixed-target architecture cannot re-center after realized sales change the remaining resource available per future period. We develop Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning, a new learning framework that tracks the primal-dual resolving path with censored demand as the remaining-resource state evolves. In each period, the current resource rate indexes the target store allocations and dual variable, while censored sales provide gradient estimates for updating both. The analysis combines expected-sales geometry with a moving-target argument to yield logarithmic expected regret, improving on the state-of-the-art square-root-order guarantees of existing OWMS learning policies. The underlying design and analytical ideas may inform other online learning problems with depleting shared resources. Numerical experiments further demonstrate good finite-horizon performance of a practical variant across different horizon lengths and inventory regimes.

AI.tldr: Introduces Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning for an on-warehouse multi-store (OWMS) with nonreplenishable stock, enabling adaptive allocation as remaining resources evolve. The framework tracks a moving primal-dual path using censored demand to update targets and dual variables, achieving logarithmic regret and improving over prior sqrt-regret policies. Validated by finite-horizon numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: Fixed-target OWMS policies anchored to the initial average resource rate cannot re-center when realized sales change the remaining resource for future periods. An adaptive method is needed to track depletion dynamics and re-balance allocations.
AI.method: A resource-adaptive primal-dual learning framework. In each period, the current resource rate selects the target store allocations and the dual variable; censored sales provide gradient estimates for updating both. The analysis combines expected-sales geometry with a moving-target argument to bound regret, yielding a logarithmic regret rate. The approach tracks the primal-dual resolving path as the remaining-resource state evolves.
AI.result: Theoretical: logarithmic expected regret for the OWMS setting under the proposed policy. Empirical: numerical experiments show good finite-horizon performance across different horizon lengths and inventory regimes, demonstrating practical viability.
AI.conclusion: The design and analytical ideas may generalize to other online learning problems with depleting shared resources. Potential extensions include richer demand models, multiple replenishments, and deployment considerations for real-world OWMS settings.

title: Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation
summary: Visual on-policy distillation relies heavily on an informative teacher-student asymmetry, through either a larger, stronger teacher or privileged supervision, such as reference answers or ground-truth regions of interest. This raises a fundamental question: where can informative asymmetry come from when nothing privileged is available? We answer this by inverting where the asymmetry comes from. Rather than adding privileged information to the teacher, we subtract information from the student. This asymmetry creates the same effective learning signal for free as a teacher with access to information unavailable to the student, without ground-truth annotations, rewards, or a separate stronger teacher model. Building on this principle, we introduce Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation (S$^2$VOPD), a simple yet effective method that constructs on-policy learning signals from asymmetric augmented views. S$^2$VOPD distills the teacher's distribution conditioned on the original image on-policy into the student distribution conditioned on a strongly augmented view of the same image. We systematically explore a broad design space of visual augmentations and uncover that (1) asymmetry matters: all four augmentation families improve performance, while symmetric self-distillation degrades it; (2) strength matters: performance peaks at a moderate strength; and (3) the gap must remain task-consistent: augmentations that completely remove the question-relevant evidence can induce large but uninformative discrepancies. Across six fine-grained perception benchmarks, S$^2$VOPD improves Qwen3.5-4B from 70.7% to 77.4%, above all open-source models compared, up to Qwen3-VL at 235B, and surpasses GPT-5.4. While holding training data the same, it recovers 96% of the improvement achieved by methods with privileged information. Website is at https://williamium3000.github.io/s2vopd

AI.tldr: Invert teacher–student asymmetry by subtracting information from the student using strongly augmented views to perform self-supervised on-policy distillation; yields strong gains on fine-grained perception benchmarks, approaching privileged-information methods.
AI.motivation: Visual on-policy distillation relies on informative teacher–student asymmetry. Without privileged information, there is a fundamental need for an equivalent informative signal. The paper addresses this by creating asymmetry from the student side, avoiding extra annotations or separate strong teachers.
AI.method: S^2VOPD constructs on-policy learning signals by distilling the teacher's distribution conditioned on the original image into the student distribution conditioned on a strongly augmented view of the same image. It systematically explores a design space of four augmentation families, analyzes asymmetry strength, and emphasizes task-consistency of augmentations. Evaluations span six fine-grained perception benchmarks, comparing against open-source models and privileged-information methods.
AI.result: S^2VOPD improves Qwen3.5-4B from 70.7% to 77.4% and surpasses open-source models up to Qwen3-VL (235B) and GPT-5.4. With the same training data, it recovers about 96% of the improvement achieved by methods that use privileged information.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric self-distillation via carefully chosen augmentations is an effective mechanism to deliver on-policy learning signals without privileged data. The approach highlights the importance of asymmetry type, augmentation strength (moderate), and task-consistency, offering competitive performance on fine-grained perception tasks.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B on Apple Silicon: Fixing Deployment Bugs and Decreasing Looped Transformer Memory Overhead
summary: Nanbeige4.2-3B is a 3B-parameter agentic model built around a Looped Transformer (LT) that reuses one stack of layers for a second forward pass, adding effective depth without additional parameters. Evaluated on Apple Silicon (MPS), we identify five independent bugs which prevent the released checkpoint from running via Hugging Face transformers out of the box (including a silently-zeroed RoPE buffer and calls to removed transformers cache APIs). Furthermore, we show that fixing these bugs is still not sufficient for agentic tasks, due to the LT's layer-reuse strategy (which effectively doubles peak attention memory) used to achieve parameter efficiency. We thus introduce a chunked-prefill strategy which alleviates the incurred memory-capacity penalty, extending allowable context width by $2.7 \times$ on 32~GiB shared memory. However, even with the reduced memory overhead, we show that patches are required to render Nanbeige4.2-3B usable; resolving both system prompt and MPS-native memory bugs finally allows reliable evaluation on standard MCP and tool-calling benchmarks. On a subset of MCPMark, the debugged model completes up to 30\% of real agentic tasks (up from the original's 0\%), while, on BFCL, it is near-perfect at single tool calls (yet fails the majority of multi-tool tests). We release the patched checkpoint, system prompt optimizer, and evaluation harnesses at https://github.com/johnhalloran321/Nanbeige4.2-3B-mps-fix.

AI.tldr: 3B agentic model Nanbeige4.2-3B uses a Looped Transformer to gain depth without new parameters; requires patches to run on Apple Silicon MPS; memory-penalty due to layer reuse; chunked-prefill mitigates memory; patches enable evaluation on MCPMark and BFCL; partial task success achieved; patched checkpoint released.
AI.motivation: Improve parameter efficiency via layer reuse and validate agentic capabilities on standard benchmarks; identify platform-specific run-time issues and memory constraints; extend context width.
AI.method: Identify five Bugs affecting HuggingFace compatibility and MPS; implement chunked-prefill strategy to reduce peak memory; fix system prompts and MPS memory bugs; evaluate on MCPMark and BFCL; release patched checkpoint and eval harness.
AI.result: Bugs prevented out-of-box usage; memory overhead due to LT; chunked-prefill extends context width by 2.7x on 32GiB; after patches, evaluation becomes reliable; on MCPMark subset, real agentic tasks completed up to 30%; on BFCL single-tool calls near-perfect, multi-tool tests still fail.
AI.conclusion: Patched checkpoint and evaluation harness enable usable agentic evaluation; patches and memory strategies address practical deployment constraints; release to public.

title: Sequence prediction under a lying oracle
summary: We consider the problem of sequential prediction of an $m$-ary sequence, where at each epoch, (i) the environment selects an outcome from an $m$-ary alphabet, (ii) the learner selects a probability distribution over the same alphabet (unaware of the outcome generated by the environment), and finally, (iii) the learner incurs a cost that depends on the probability assigned to the outcome. The cost function we consider captures the complexity of predicting the outcome generated by the environment, in a scenario where the aforementioned prediction is performed via comparative queries to a lying oracle. We consider both stochastic and adversarial environments, propose algorithms for both settings, and establish logarithmic upper bounds on their regret.

AI.tldr: Sequential m-ary prediction with a learner predicting distributions and incurring cost based on the probability assigned to the observed outcome, using comparative queries to a lying oracle; presents algorithms for stochastic and adversarial environments with logarithmic regret bounds.
AI.motivation: Understand the complexity of sequential prediction when feedback comes from a potentially deceptive oracle and predictions are probability distributions over the outcome alphabet.
AI.method: Propose prediction algorithms for both stochastic and adversarial environments, where at each step the environment reveals an outcome, the learner outputs a distribution over m outcomes, and the incurred cost depends on the assigned probability to the actual outcome; analyze using competitive/logarithmic regret notions under a lying oracle model.
AI.result: Establish logarithmic upper bounds on the regret in both stochastic and adversarial settings.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that low-regret sequential prediction is achievable under an unreliable oracle via tailored algorithms; clarifies the interplay between oracle reliability, prediction distributions, and cost-based feedback.

title: CSG-Mamba: A Convolutional Scoring Gating Vision State Space Network for Endoscopic Polyp Segmentation
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, and 5 tables. Accepted by ICONIP 2026
summary: Accurate polyp segmentation is critical for computer-aided colonoscopy, yet endoscopic images often contain low-contrast boundaries, mucosal texture interference, specular highlights, and device-dependent appearance shifts. Vision State Space Models (SSMs) provide efficient long-range modeling with linear complexity, but existing Vision Mamba segmentation models typically convert 2D features into 1D scanning sequences, which may weaken local geometric continuity and over-smooth irregular contours. We propose CSG-Mamba, a convolutional scoring gating Vision State Space network for endoscopic polyp segmentation. Built on a VM-UNet-style asymmetric U-shaped encoder-decoder, CSG-Mamba inserts a Convolutional Scoring Gating (CSG) module at the semantically rich bottleneck. CSG generates a local spatial score map through pointwise and large-kernel depthwise convolutions and recalibrates state-space features by multiplicative gating. Experiments with three random seeds show that CSG-Mamba achieves 0.9220 Dice and 15.87 HD95 on Kvasir-SEG, and 0.7418 Dice and 0.6570 mIoU on CVC-ColonDB, outperforming the baselines on most overlap and recall metrics while maintaining competitive boundary accuracy.

AI.tldr: CSG-Mamba improves endoscopic polyp segmentation by introducing a convolutional scoring gating module within a Vision State Space network, preserving local geometry and improving Dice/HD95 on Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ColonDB compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of 2D-to-1D scanning in Vision Mamba models that can weaken local geometric continuity and smooth irregular polyp contours, while tackling endoscopic image challenges (low-contrast boundaries, texture interference, specular highlights, and device-related appearance shifts).
AI.method: A VM-UNet-style asymmetric U-shaped encoder-decoder with a bottleneck Convolutional Scoring Gating (CSG) module. CSG builds a local spatial score map via pointwise and large-kernel depthwise convolutions and applies multiplicative gating to recalibrate state-space features.
AI.result: With three random seeds, CSG-Mamba achieves 0.9220 Dice and 15.87 HD95 on Kvasir-SEG, and 0.7418 Dice and 0.6570 mIoU on CVC-ColonDB, outperforming baselines on most overlap and recall metrics while maintaining competitive boundary accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CSG-Mamba demonstrates that integrating a local spatial scoring gate into Vision State Space networks enhances polyp segmentation performance, yielding robust cross-dataset improvements without sacrificing boundary quality.

title: Content Depth Matters in Short-Video Recommendation: Rethinking the Attention Economy
summary: Driven by the attention economy, short-video Recommender Systems (RSs) are primarily optimized to maximize user engagement by promoting videos that capture attention within seconds. These systems inherently favor shallow-content videos that are effective at attracting immediate attention. However, growing evidence suggests that prolonged exposure to such content may negatively affect users' cognitive engagement and mental well-being, raising concerns about the long-term societal impact of the short-video platform. To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces a new metric, the \textbf{Content Depth Score (CDS)}, to quantify the content depth of short videos. CDS measures the extent to which a video is expected to stimulate higher-order cognitive processes, using a seven-level scale grounded in established theories of cognitive psychology and learning. As an initial step toward this vision, we present \textbf{SCOPE-Bench}, the first benchmark for content-depth evaluation in short-video recommendation. Built upon a large-scale open-source short-video dataset, SCOPE-Bench provides CDS annotations for 150K videos, enabling systematic evaluation of RSs from a cognitive-content perspective. Leveraging SCOPE-Bench, we evaluate 13 representative RSs and reveal a consistent preference for shallow-content videos. Moreover, we find that these algorithms recommending cognitively deep content are only marginally better than random selection, highlighting a previously overlooked limitation of existing recommendation objectives. Our code and datasets are available at https://liweidengdavid.github.io/SCOPE-Bench/.

AI.tldr: Introduces Content Depth Score (CDS) and SCOPE-Bench, a benchmark with CDS-annotated videos to evaluate short-video recommender systems on cognitive-content depth; finds pervasive bias toward shallow content and that deep-content recommendations offer only marginal gains over random.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between engagement-driven optimization and potential negative cognitive/well-being effects of short-video consumption; establish a measurable, theory-backed metric of content depth to evaluate and guide recommender systems.
AI.method: Define a seven-level Content Depth Score (CDS) grounded in cognitive psychology and learning theories; annotate 150K videos with CDS; construct SCOPE-Bench benchmark; evaluate 13 representative short-video recommender systems.
AI.result: Recommenders show a strong preference for shallow content; algorithms aiming for cognitively deep content perform only marginally better than random; CDS-enabled evaluation reveals a neglected limitation of current objectives.
AI.conclusion: CDS and SCOPE-Bench provide a principled framework to assess and steer short-video RSs toward deeper cognitive engagement, highlighting potential societal impact and offering data/tools (code and datasets) for reproducible research.

title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: When forecasting hourly returns for 1,000 US equities, we observe an unexpected phenomenon: predictions become nearly flat and show poor stock ranking, as measured by cross-sectional correlation. We call this forecast collapse. Surprisingly, the phenomenon largely disappears when forecasting trading volume under the same setting. We investigate forecast collapse across time-series foundation models (TSFMs), twelve deep-learning forecasting models, and 97 public benchmark configurations, and find that it is closely tied to target predictability. We identify two distinct reasons behind it: low predictability limits the amplitude of calibrated point forecasts, while per-series objectives leave cross-series structure unidentified. These findings reveal a calibration-ranking tradeoff: optimizing squared error leads to flat predictions, whereas directly optimizing cross-sectional correlation improves ranking but can inflate forecast amplitude by more than an order of magnitude. To address this tradeoff, we introduce CalibRank, a simple objective that balances calibration and ranking. On Finance1K, CalibRank nearly triples cross-sectional correlation while keeping amplitude close to the target, and improves correlation on all tested models. Our results reveal a blind spot in conventional time-series evaluation: per-series metrics can hide failures in cross-series structure needed by downstream decisions.

AI.tldr: Forecast collapse in hourly returns for 1,000 US equities; misalignment between per-series accuracy and cross-sectional ranking due to limited predictability; CalibRank balances calibration and ranking, yielding large gains in cross-sectional correlation without inflating amplitude.
AI.motivation: Understand why forecast performance degrades in cross-sectional ranking despite low per-series error, and how to design objectives that align forecasts with downstream decision needs.
AI.method: Empirical analysis across time-series foundation models (TSFMs), twelve deep-learning forecasting models, and 97 public benchmark configurations; examination of target predictability; development and evaluation of a new objective (CalibRank) on Finance1K.
AI.result: Identified two drivers of forecast collapse: (1) low predictability constrains forecast amplitude, (2) per-series objectives fail to capture cross-series structure. Demonstrated a calibration-ranking tradeoff: squared-error optimization yields flat forecasts; cross-sectional-correlation optimization improves ranking but inflates amplitude by >10x. CalibRank balances calibration and ranking, nearly triples cross-sectional correlation on Finance1K while keeping amplitude near target; improvements across tested models.
AI.conclusion: Per-series evaluation metrics can mask underperformance in cross-series structure critical for downstream decisions. A simple, joint calibration-ranking objective (CalibRank) mitigates this blind spot and enhances cross-sectional predictive usefulness.

title: SCVIB: Editable State-Conditioned Visual Instance Binding forMulti-Turn Personalized Localization
summary: We introduce editable state-conditioned visual instance binding, a multi-turn localization setting in which several support-defined instances are introduced across turns and protocol-defined state events determine the final target. We instantiate this setting as SCVIB, comprising 1,050 manually verified support--query base pairs and 1,500 episodes spanning five visual domains, three difficulty levels, and four target-state dependency groups. Direct Seq-free inference reaches only 60.13\% Joint@0.5, indicating that resolving the final reference does not ensure effective use of the corresponding visual evidence for query-side localization. We address this gap with TT-VG (Transition-Tree Visual Grounding), which combines a Target-State Transition Tree (TSTT) with Visual Evidence Grounding Adaptation (VEGA). TSTT compiles the visible interaction into protocol-defined events, executes them over versioned target states, and resolves the final-query reference to the corresponding support evidence. Adapted on trajectory-derived same-instance pairs, VEGA performs support-conditioned grounding of the resolved instance using a Visual Evidence Package. TT-VG reaches 70.27\% Joint@0.5; under matched target resolution, VEGA exceeds the strongest comparison method by 16.20 points. Gains over direct inference are largest on Counter-Recency and Rollback, which require routing to non-latest or restored support evidence. Together, these results establish SCVIB as a controlled testbed and highlight the effective use of resolved support evidence for query-side same-instance localization as a central challenge in multi-turn personalized localization.

AI.tldr: A new multi-turn localization framework SCVIB with TT-VG method, combining TSTT and VEGA to improve Joint@0.5 from 60.13 to 70.27. It uses 1,050 support–query pairs and 1,500 episodes across domains. It addresses the gap that direct inference fails to leverage visual evidence; gains are largest on Counter-Recency and Rollback. Establishes SCVIB as a controlled testbed for multi-turn personalized localization.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn visual grounding, resolving the final reference from supporting evidence does not ensure effective use of that evidence for query localization; a structured, state-aware process is needed to route to appropriate support evidence across turns.
AI.method: TT-VG (Transition-Tree Visual Grounding) combines a Target-State Transition Tree (TSTT) that encodes protocol-defined events over versioned target states to resolve the final query reference, with Visual Evidence Grounding Adaptation (VEGA) that grounds the resolved instance using a Visual Evidence Package conditioned on the support. TSTT converts interactions into events and resolves references; VEGA uses trajectory-derived same-instance pairs for support-conditioned grounding.
AI.result: Joint@0.5 improves to 70.27%. VEGA, under matched target resolution, exceeds the strongest comparison method by 16.20 points. Gains are pronounced on Counter-Recency and Rollback tasks.
AI.conclusion: SCVIB provides a controlled testbed to study multi-turn personalized localization; resolving and effectively using support evidence is crucial, and TT-VG with VEGA offers a strong approach to improve query-side localization by leveraging resolved support across turns.

title: Simulation-Driven Vehicular Traffic Data Augmentation: Extending Sensor Coverage Through Virtual Sensing
summary: Urban traffic management relies on sensor networks whose spatial coverage is limited by deployment costs and privacy regulations. Machine learning models trained on such sparse data cannot generalize to unmonitored locations and must be retrained whenever the sensor infrastructure changes. We propose a simulation-based methodology that addresses this problem by generating augmented traffic count datasets in which each physical sensor is replaced by a virtual sensor placed at a surrogate location in the road network. Virtual sensors are selected by a graph-search heuristic that jointly maximises vehicle-flow continuity and traffic-metric similarity between the original and surrogate locations, while enforcing a minimum spatial displacement to ensure diversity of observed traffic conditions. We validate the method on two Belgian cities: Brussels, using a calibrated model, and Namur, using synthetic models. The augmented datasets preserve the bimodal daily demand profile and the dynamics of traffic at the observed locations.

AI.tldr: A simulation-based data augmentation method for urban traffic sensor networks that replaces real sensors with virtual surrogate sensors chosen by a graph-search heuristic to preserve traffic flow and metrics, with diversity via displacement. Validated on Brussels (calibrated) and Namur (synthetic) and able to retain bimodal daily demand and traffic dynamics at observed sites.
AI.motivation: Sensor networks in cities are sparsely deployed due to cost and privacy, causing ML models to underperform on unmonitored locations or after sensor changes. A transferable, simulation-driven data augmentation approach could generate realistic surrogate data to improve generalization without additional field sensors.
AI.method: For each real sensor, generate a virtual sensor at a surrogate node in the road network. Use a graph-search heuristic to jointly maximize (i) vehicle-flow continuity between original and surrogate locations and (ii) similarity of traffic metrics, while enforcing a minimum spatial displacement to ensure diverse traffic conditions. Data are generated via a calibrated model for Brussels and synthetic models for Namur to create augmented datasets that imitate the observed site dynamics.
AI.result: The augmented datasets preserve the bimodal daily demand profile and traffic dynamics at the observed locations, indicating that the surrogate-based augmentation can maintain essential temporal patterns while enabling analysis under alternative sensor configurations.
AI.conclusion: A scalable, simulation-based approach to augment traffic datasets with virtual sensors offers a viable solution to sparse coverage and sensor-change challenges in urban traffic analytics. Validated in real (Brussels) and synthetic (Namur) contexts, it preserves key traffic patterns and supports transferable ML models; further work could extend to additional cities and richer traffic regimes.

title: Learning to Run Power Networks: Effective AlphaZero-inspired Topological Control
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in ACM SIGENERGY Energy Informatics Review, Volume 6, Issue 3, September 2026
summary: As the integration of volatile renewable energy sources increases the strain on modern power grids, the use of Reinforcement Learning (RL) for autonomous topological reconfiguration has emerged as a promising research field to keep strained grids stable and operational. Compared to traditional redispatching measures, topological actions offer a cheaper and more cost-effective way to manage grid congestion. However, their implementation is hindered by a vast combinatorial action space and strict operational constraints. This paper investigates the effectiveness of model-based AlphaZero-inspired approaches that utilize Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for proactive grid management. We systematically evaluate how reward functions, observation density, and search guidance influence an agent's survivability. Our results demonstrate that the optimized AlphaZero approach achieves a peak survivability of 98.43%, significantly outperforming the proximal policy optimization (PPO) variant. We find that conducting the MCTS without guidance from a prior learned policy or value function can enhance training efficiency, and that a straightforward binary survival reward provides more effective search guidance than complex, multi-objective functions. Our findings demonstrate that while AlphaZero is a powerful framework for topological control, pure reinforcement learning is not sufficient; rather, an effective and reliable system requires a 'minimalist' integration of domain-specific heuristics, binary rewards, and a restricted observation space of line loads.

AI.tldr: Model-based AlphaZero with MCTS for proactive grid topology control; minimalist, domain-informed design outperforms PPO, achieving 98.43% survivability.
AI.motivation: Rising penetration of volatile renewables strains modern power grids; topological actions are cheaper than redispatch but suffer from a huge action space and stringent constraints.
AI.method: AlphaZero-inspired framework using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to perform proactive topology control. Systematic ablations on reward functions, observation density, and search guidance. Experiments include MCTS with and without prior policy/value function guidance, and comparison to PPO. Use of binary survival rewards and restricted line-load observation space as guidance.
AI.result: Optimized AlphaZero achieves up to 98.43% survivability, outperforming PPO. MCTS without guidance from a prior policy/value function can improve training efficiency. A simple binary survival reward provides better search guidance than complex multi-objective rewards. Overall, pure RL is insufficient; a minimalist integration of domain heuristics, binary rewards, and restricted observations is essential.
AI.conclusion: AlphaZero is powerful for grid topology control, but effectiveness hinges on combining domain-specific heuristics with binary rewards and a constrained observation space; pure RL must be complemented by minimalist, pragmatic design choices.

title: Concept Guidance: Precise, Training-Free Latent Control for Text-to-Image Generation
comment: Accepted at GCPR 2026 (Oral). 28 pages, includes supplementary material
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models have two major drawbacks that severely limit their practical utility: (1) standard models lack an intrinsic mechanism for continuous, concept-specific guidance (e.g., for precisely controlling how aesthetically pleasing an image looks), and (2) they lack reliability for tasks requiring high local coherence (e.g., generating text or human hands). To tackle these issues, we introduce a novel notion of concept-wise mutual information and find large, concept-dependent differences between individual layers, demonstrating that the generation of specific structures is localized in distinct parts of the network. We exploit this insight by reinforcing the impact of concept-relevant layers in Concept Guidance (CoG), a precise, target-specific guidance method that works for models out-of-the-box without additional training, external models, gradients, or prompt engineering. CoG first quantifies each layer's concept-specific impact and then guides denoising using a weighted combination of predictions generated with concept-relevant layers skipped. We demonstrate performance increases across various targets and popular models like PixArt-alpha, SD3, SD3.5, and FLUX.1-dev. Code is available at https://github.com/CompVis/concept_guidance

AI.tldr: Proposes Concept Guidance (CoG) using concept-wise mutual information to identify layer-specific influence in diffusion models and applies a weighted, skip-based ensemble to reinforce concept-relevant layers during denoising, enabling precise, out-of-the-box concept control without retraining; shows improvements across PixArt-alpha, SD3, SD3.5, and FLUX; code released.
AI.motivation: Address two key drawbacks of text-to-image diffusion models: lack of intrinsic, continuous, concept-specific guidance and unreliable local coherence. The goal is a lightweight, training-free method to achieve target-focused control and better handling of structured elements (e.g., text or hands).
AI.method: Introduce concept-wise mutual information to quantify layer-wise, concept-specific impact. Identify that specific structures localize to distinct layers. Develop Concept Guidance (CoG): compute each layer's concept-specific impact and guide denoising with a weighted combination of predictions where concept-relevant layers are skipped, enabling target-specific guidance without training, external models, gradients, or prompt engineering.
AI.result: Empirical demonstrations show performance gains across multiple targets and models (PixArt-alpha, SD3, SD3.5, FLUX). The method is out-of-the-box and model-agnostic, with code available.
AI.conclusion: CoG provides a precise, target-specific guidance mechanism for diffusion models that enhances concept control and local coherence without additional training or external tools; the analysis of layer-wise, concept-specific influence via concept-wise mutual information underpins its effectiveness.

title: Buy the Rumor, Sell the News: When Is News Priced In?
summary: Two old market sayings hold that news is already priced in by the time it is published, and that the rumor is bought while the news is sold. Both place the price move associated with a piece of news before and at publication rather than after it. Whether the claims hold, for which kinds of news, and by how much are basic questions about how fast markets absorb public information. We test them on 4.57 million financial news articles covering roughly 3,000 US stocks (2023-2026). A large language model teacher, distilled into a compact classifier through active learning, assigns each article one of 17 event tags and five attributes; articles are clustered into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage; and beta-adjusted abnormal returns are measured around the resulting 1.68 million stock-day events, with 364,405 neutral-sentiment events as a placebo group. Three results follow. First, the price move associated with news concentrates before and at publication: pooled across all signed events, the cumulative move in the news direction by the close of publication day is 2.8 times its value 20 days later, and for rumor-flagged events the rumor day captures the entire move while the subsequent confirmation contributes nothing. Second, measured against the placebo of comparable stocks, markets underreact to numbers and overreact to stories: quantified fundamental news (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions) keeps drifting in the direction of the news for weeks, while soft story-driven news (launches, macro commentary, leadership) gives back its move. Third, news carries width as well as direction: publicity raises volatility before the publication day, and volatility declines once the news is out, because publication resolves uncertainty. The study also produces a table of measured drift for each event tag, usable as a prior in news-conditioned forecasting models.

AI.tldr: The paper tests the adage that news moves prices before or at publication using a huge dataset of 4.57M financial news articles about ~3,000 US stocks (2023–2026). It finds that price moves concentrate around publication, that markets underreact to quantitative news but overreact to story-driven news, and that news volatility rises before publication and falls after, with a usable event-tag drift table for forecasting.
AI.motivation: To empirically evaluate classic market-adage claims about information absorption, identify how different types of news (numbers vs. stories) influence price moves and volatility, and quantify the timing of price adjustments surrounding public information.
AI.method: Annotate articles with 17 event tags and 5 attributes using a distilled large-language-model teacher via active learning; cluster articles into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage; measure beta-adjusted abnormal returns around 1.68 million stock-day events; use 364,405 neutral-sentiment events as placebo; analyze timing and drift across event categories.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) price moves concentrate before and at publication; the cumulative move in the news direction by close of publication day is 2.8x its value 20 days later; for rumor-flagged events, the rumor day captures the whole move with no added effect from confirmation. (2) Compared to placebo, markets underreact to numbers (fundamental news) and overreact to stories (soft news), with fundamental news drifting post-publication while soft news reverses. (3) News increases pre-publication volatility and reduces post-publication volatility as publication resolves uncertainty; a tabulated drift per event tag is provided for forecasting models.
AI.conclusion: The study provides quantitative support for traditional sayings about information absorption, delineates how different news types drive distinct price dynamics and volatility patterns, and offers a practical drift table by event tag to inform news-conditioned trading or forecasting models.

title: From Fixed Grids to Moving Particles:A Transferable Latent Operator for Fluid Dynamics
summary: Lagrangian modeling is vital to fluid dynamics, as it characterizes particle transport and complements the Eulerian description.However, Lagrangian trajectories are less commonly available than Eulerian fields, while most neural operators are trained and evaluated primarily in the Eulerian representation. This mismatch motivates a new learning problem: can a model trained solely on Eulerian observations generalize zero-shot from Eulerian field prediction to Lagrangian particle rollout, without Lagrangian supervision or task-specific adaptation? To address this problem, we propose the Transferable Latent Operator (TLO), which learns a unified flow representation shared by Eulerian field prediction and Lagrangian particle rollout. TLO decouples latent flow evolution from coordinate-dependent decoding: querying the evolving latent representation at fixed spatial coordinates yields Eulerian fields, whereas querying velocities at particle positions and recursively updating these positions enables Lagrangian rollout. Across five fluid-dynamics benchmarks, TLO consistently outperforms existing neural operators in both Eulerian field prediction and zero-shot Lagrangian rollout, with further gains from limited Lagrangian fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: A transferable latent operator (TLO) learns a unified latent flow representation from Eulerian data that enables zero-shot Lagrangian particle rollout, by decoupling latent evolution from coordinate-dependent decoding.
AI.motivation: There is a mismatch between available data (Eulerian fields) and tasks of interest (Lagrangian trajectories); existing neural operators struggle to generalize to Lagrangian rollout without supervision.
AI.method: Introduce TLO, which learns a shared latent flow representation; decouples latent evolution from decoding; Eulerian fields obtained by querying latent at fixed coordinates; Lagrangian rollout via querying velocities at particle positions and updating positions; evaluated on five fluid-dynamics benchmarks; shows improvements in both Eulerian predictions and zero-shot Lagrangian rollout, with gains from few Lagrangian fine-tuning.
AI.result: TLO consistently outperforms existing neural operators in Eulerian field prediction and zero-shot Lagrangian rollout across five benchmarks; limited Lagrangian fine-tuning yields additional gains.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of cross-representation transferable latent models for fluid dynamics, enabling unified handling of Eulerian and Lagrangian tasks and suggesting broader applicability to transport phenomena.

title: LightTeaNet: A Weakly Supervised Lightweight CNN for Multi-Label Tea Leaf Disease Detection and Localization
summary: Tea is known as an important crop in many parts of South and Southeast Asia, yet the production of tea is still hampered by the multiple diseases that decrease the quantity and quality. Traditional methods of inspection, which are manual, are not consistent, labor-intensive, and depend on extensive monitoring. This paper introduces a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for weakly supervised multi-label classification and disease localization in tea leaves called LightTeaNet. LightTeaNet learns directly from image-level labels and employs Class Activation Mapping (CAM) to localize disease-affected regions automatically, unlike conventional object detection models such as YOLO, which require extensive bounding box annotations. For Parameter efficiency, the network integrates Depthwise Separable Convolutions, and for enhanced feature discrimination, it integrates Channel Attention. LightTeaNet has achieved a Precision of 0.9615, a Recall of 0.8772, and an F1-score of 0.9179, while it shows mAP@0.50=0.1810 without any manual annotations, which delivers a competitive localization performance in the experimental results. These results validate the model as an interpretable as well as a resource-efficient framework for intelligent disease monitoring in agriculture.

AI.tldr: LightTeaNet is a lightweight, weakly supervised CNN for multi-label tea leaf disease classification with CAM-based localization, using depthwise separable convs and channel attention to achieve competitive precision/recall and low annotation needs.
AI.motivation: Tea cultivation faces disease-induced losses and reliance on manual inspection is labor-intensive and inconsistent. Object detectors require bounding boxes; there is a need for weakly supervised, interpretable, and resource-efficient disease monitoring.
AI.method: A lightweight CNN (LightTeaNet) trained with image-level labels for multi-label disease classification. It incorporates Depthwise Separable Convolutions for efficiency and Channel Attention for discriminative features, and uses Class Activation Mapping (CAM) to localize diseased regions without bounding-box annotations.
AI.result: Precision 0.9615, Recall 0.8772, F1 0.9179; mAP@0.50 = 0.1810 without manual bounding-box annotations; shows competitive localization and interpretable, resource-efficient performance.
AI.conclusion: LightTeaNet offers an interpretable and resource-efficient framework for automatic tea disease monitoring under weak supervision, with CAM-based localization to avoid the need for bounding boxes.

title: Residual Dominance as a Structural Account of Last-Item Reliance in Causal Self-Attention Recommenders
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys'26)
summary: Transformer-based sequential recommenders with causal self-attention often rely heavily on the most recent interaction at inference time, but how this behavior is structurally expressed in the representation used for prediction remains unclear. We combine prediction-time diagnostics with norm-based analysis of the full attention block. First, we show that SASRec-style models exhibit highly localized last-item reliance. We then find that, although self-attention aggregates contextual information, residual addition sharply shifts the full-block representation toward same-position contributions, which we term residual dominance. To probe this interpretation, we use inference-time residual scaling as a controlled diagnostic intervention. Changing the residual strength induces a monotonic trade-off between structural mixing and last-item reliance, while reducing residual strength recovers a subset of final-position misses for which representations at non-final positions already rank the ground-truth item correctly. Our results provide a structural account linking extreme last-item reliance to residual dominance at inference time. The code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: SASRec-style transformers show extreme last-item reliance due to residual dominance in the full attention block; inference-time residual scaling reveals a controllable trade-off between contextual mixing and last-item emphasis.
AI.motivation: Clarify the structural manifestation of last-item reliance in prediction representations for transformer-based sequential recommenders and explain why the most recent interaction dominates at inference.
AI.method: Combine prediction-time diagnostics with norm-based analysis of the full attention block; quantify last-item reliance; analyze how the residual addition bias shifts representations toward same-position contributions; use inference-time residual scaling as a diagnostic intervention.
AI.result: 1) SASRec-style models exhibit highly localized last-item reliance; 2) full-block representations are shifted toward same-position contributions (residual dominance) due to residual addition; 3) increasing/decreasing residual strength modulates a monotonic trade-off between structural mixing and last-item reliance; reducing residual strength recovers some non-final-position misses where the ground-truth item is already ranked at non-final positions;
AI.conclusion: Provides a structural account linking extreme last-item reliance to residual dominance at inference; demonstrates that inference-time residual control can tune the balance between contextual mixing and last-item emphasis; code for the analysis is publicly available.

title: Overcoming Shortcut Learning in Graph Neural Networks through Active Explanation Guidance
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can solve prediction tasks by unintentionally exploiting shortcuts---that is, edges, nodes, and features that correlate with but are not causal for the prediction---which compromise their reliability in out-of-distribution tasks. We introduce XIGL, an architecture-agnostic human-in-the-loop strategy for removing such shortcuts from GNNs. Our key insight is twofold. On the one hand, reliance on shortcuts can be detected by inspecting GNN explanations. On the other hand, once made aware of such shortcuts, sufficiently expert users can provide tailored corrective feedback, which helps deconfound the model. XIGL supports any query strategy; however, since corrective feedback can be expensive to acquire, we develop an active learning strategy for prioritizing explanations that are more likely to display shortcut behavior, lowering annotation and cognitive costs. We showcase the effectiveness of XIGL, including both existing and proposed explanation-based strategies, on several GNN architectures. Our implementation is available online.

AI.tldr: XIGL is an architecture-agnostic, human-in-the-loop framework that uses explanations and expert feedback, aided by active learning, to remove non-causal shortcuts in GNNs and improve robustness.
AI.motivation: GNNs can rely on non-causal shortcuts (edges, nodes, features) that correlate with labels, hurting reliability and out-of-distribution performance.
AI.method: XIGL detects shortcut reliance by inspecting GNN explanations, then uses tailored corrective feedback from domain experts to deconfound the model. It supports any query strategy and employs an active-learning strategy to prioritize explanations likely to reveal shortcut behavior, reducing annotation/cognitive costs.
