AI.result: Empirical demonstrations of effectiveness across multiple GNN architectures; improvements in removing shortcut reliance and robustness; annotation costs lowered via active-learning prioritization; implementation is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: An architecture-agnostic, human-in-the-loop approach can effectively deconfound GNNs from shortcut signals, with active learning making the workflow practical and broadly applicable.

title: RankT2I: A Submodular Framework for Discovering Interpretable and Diverse Semantics in Text-to-Image Models
summary: Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) models have revolutionized the field of image generation and editing. However, identifying semantics that a T2I model can successfully edit in an image continues to be a challenging task. Most existing approaches require users to manually specify semantics to modify a particular image, a time-consuming process that often involves extensive trial and error. In this paper, we present RankT2I, a novel, training-free, and model-agnostic framework that automates the discovery of editable semantics in diffusion and FLUX-based models. Given a visual domain, we first utilize a multimodal vision-language model to gather a broad set of candidate semantics. We then frame semantic discovery as a set selection problem and use a submodular objective to identify semantics that are relevant, editable, and diverse. Our method helps users efficiently identify a wide range of semantics for text-to-image editing models across several domains while outperforming existing methods.

AI.tldr: RankT2I is a training-free, model-agnostic framework that automatically discovers editable semantics for text-to-image editing by selecting a diverse, relevant subset of candidate semantics generated from a vision-language model, applicable to diffusion and FLUX-based models.
AI.motivation: Identifying semantics that a T2I model can edit is hard and currently requires manual specification and trial-and-error; automation is needed to streamline editing workflows across domains.
AI.method: 1) Use a multimodal vision-language model to gather a broad set of candidate semantics in a given visual domain. 2) Frame semantic discovery as a set selection problem. 3) Optimize a submodular objective that enforces relevance, editability, and diversity to select a practical subset of semantics. 4) The framework is training-free and model-agnostic, working with diffusion and FLUX-based models.
AI.result: The method efficiently identifies a wide range of editable semantics and outperforms existing methods across several domains, enabling more effective and diverse text-to-image editing.
AI.conclusion: RankT2I provides a practical, training-free pathway to discover editable semantics for T2I editors, with broad applicability and potential to reduce manual effort; limitations may include dependence on the quality of the vision-language model and the submodular objective's ability to capture true editability.

title: Agent-Orchestration in Autonomous Chip Design
summary:
Recent developments in large language models (LLMs) and tool-using agents encourage people to explore the potential of using agents in chip design. The core question is what kind of AI we really need in such a sophisticated industry.
  To this end, we bring the idea of modeling a chip-design superintelligence as an enormous \textit{AI-organization}.

AI.tldr: Proposes modeling chip-design superintelligence as a large AI-organization, leveraging LLMs and tool-using agents to explore AI-enabled chip design.
AI.motivation: Address the question of what AI is needed for the highly complex field of chip design and how advances in LLMs and agent-enabled workflows can be harnessed.
AI.method: Conceptual framing and analysis. Treats a chip-design superintelligence as an enormous AI-organization and discusses potential roles of AI agents and tools in design workflows.
AI.result: Introduces a conceptual framework for viewing chip-design superintelligence as an AI-organization; outlines the promise and challenges of this approach without presenting empirical results.
AI.conclusion: Framing chip-design superintelligence as an AI-organization is a promising direction for integrating AI capabilities into sophisticated design processes.

title: Smart routes: a system for development and comparison of algorithms for solving vehicle routing problems with realistic constraints
summary: The problem of route optimization with realistic constraints is becoming extremely relevant in the face of global urban population growth. While we are aware of approaches that theoretically provide an exact optimal solution, their application becomes challenging as the problem size increases because of exponential complexity. We investigate the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW) and compare solutions obtaining by exact solver SCIP with heuristic algorithms such as LKH, 2-OPT, 3-OPT, the ORTools framework, and the deep learning model JAMPR. We demonstrate that for problem of size 50 deep learning and classical heuristic solutions became close to SCIP exact solution but requires less time. Additionally for problems with size 100, SCIP exact methods around 13 times slower that neural and classical heuristics with the same route cost and on around 50% worse for the first feasible solution on the same time. To conduct experiments, we developed the Smart Routes platform for solving route optimization problems, which includes exact, heuristic, and deep learning models, and facilitates convenient integration of custom algorithms and datasets.

AI.tldr: DL and classical heuristics perform closely to SCIP on CVRPTW for moderate sizes and scale better than the exact solver; for size 50 they approach optimality with lower time, while for size 100 SCIP slows by ~13x compared to neural/classic heuristics and yields a slower first feasible solution by ~50%. A Smart Routes platform integrates exact, heuristic, and DL methods for experimentation.
AI.motivation: Evaluate the practicality of exact vs heuristic and deep-learning approaches for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows under realistic constraints, and assess scalability with instance size.
AI.method: Empirical comparison on CVRPTW instances of sizes 50 and 100 using an exact solver (SCIP) and heuristic/DL methods (LKH, 2-OPT, 3-OPT, OR-Tools, JAMPR). Development of the Smart Routes platform to facilitate integration of algorithms and datasets.
AI.result: For size 50, deep learning and classical heuristics approach the SCIP optimum with reduced computation time. For size 100, SCIP is about 13 times slower than neural and classical heuristics for the same route cost, and the first feasible solution is about 50% worse within the same time budget. The authors also implemented the Smart Routes platform to support such comparisons and integrations.
AI.conclusion: Neural and classical heuristics provide favorable scalability for CVRPTW relative to exact solvers on larger instances, with deep learning models like JAMPR offering competitive performance; the Smart Routes platform enables streamlined experimentation and integration of diverse methods.

title: AppleScab-LT: A Longitudinal Real-Field Apple Scab Dataset for Temporal Disease Progression Analysis
summary: The development of reliable plant disease monitoring systems is constrained by limited longitudinal datasets capturing disease progression under natural field conditions. Although existing plant disease datasets have advanced image-based recognition, most consist of static images acquired at a single time point, limiting analysis of temporal disease evolution and severity progression. To address this gap, this study presents AppleScab-LT, a longitudinal real-field dataset developed to monitor apple scab progression through repeated observations of individually tracked infected leaves. Guided by a research-question-driven framework, the dataset was systematically developed, validated, and characterized for reliable longitudinal disease analysis. AppleScab-LT was constructed through systematic orchard monitoring under natural environmental conditions, incorporating longitudinal leaf tracking, expert-guided disease verification, polygon-based annotation, leaf isolation, disease severity quantification, and temporal sequence construction. A comprehensive quality assurance framework, including standardized annotation protocols, expert validation, automated integrity checks, sequence-level verification, and temporal consistency analysis, was applied throughout curation. The dataset contains 21 longitudinal leaf sequences, 2,101 high-resolution images, and 264 progressive temporal samples from repeated monitoring of same infected leaves. It captures variability in severity accumulation, progression rates, monitoring duration, and inter-leaf progression. Quantitative disease descriptors based on pixel severity, color-intensity severity, and normalized relative severity provide standardized measurements for temporal disease analysis. AppleScab-LT provides a reliable resource for temporal disease intelligence, disease progression modelling, precision agriculture, and future crop health monitoring

AI.tldr: A longitudinal field dataset (AppleScab-LT) for apple scab progression, with repeated observations of tracked infected leaves, enabling temporal disease analysis in precision agriculture.
AI.motivation: Addresses the scarcity of longitudinal plant disease data under natural field conditions, enabling analysis of disease progression and severity over time rather than static snapshots.
AI.method: Systematic orchard monitoring with longitudinal leaf tracking, expert disease verification, polygon-based annotation, leaf isolation, disease severity quantification, and construction of temporal sequences; a comprehensive QA framework with standardized protocols, expert validation, automated integrity checks, and sequence-level/temporal consistency checks.
AI.result: AppleScab-LT comprises 21 longitudinal leaf sequences, 2,101 high-resolution images, and 264 progressive temporal samples. It captures variability in severity progression and provides quantitative descriptors based on pixel severity, color-intensity severity, and normalized relative severity for temporal analysis.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides a reliable resource for temporal disease intelligence, progression modelling, precision agriculture, and future crop health monitoring, highlighting its value for longitudinal disease analysis in apples.

title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work-Until They Don't
summary: Skills have emerged as a practical and effective approach for enhancing LLM agents at inference time through structured packages of knowledge. However, existing evaluations largely measure whether skills improve aggregated task success, leaving a more fundamental question underexplored: \emph{\textbf{When do skills help, why do they work, and where do they fail?}} Through controlled experiments across various benchmarks, agent harnesses and LLMs, we isolate the effects of representation, outcome annotation, retrieval difficulty, and cross-framework robustness of skills. To further answer this question, we design a contrastive study that combines controlled quantitative experiments with paired trajectory analysis. We normalize 8,135 trial records from controlled experiments and retain 238 valid unique labels from 240 open-coded records. We consolidate these observations into a taxonomy of three high-level categories and twelve skill-use modes: skills work when noisy trajectories become procedural anchors that stabilize execution. Skills improve over Workflow Memory by 6.06 points in matched comparisons. Procedural anchoring accounts for 65.7\% of skill cases, versus 4.5\% for explicit knowledge injection, showing that skills stabilize action rather than inject missing facts. Retrieval is a separate bottleneck: as pools grow from 5 to 100, actual-use precision falls from 29.6\% to 3.3\%. Confusable distractors impair offline identification, yet downstream success remains stable; exact ground-truth invocation is neither sufficient nor necessary. Skills fail under brittle assumptions, incompatible contexts, or insufficient adaptation. These findings move evaluation beyond aggregate success rates and guide reliable self-evolving agents.

AI.tldr: The study analyzes when, why, and where skills help LLM agents and reveals procedural anchoring as the primary mechanism, significant retrieval bottlenecks, and that evaluation should go beyond aggregate success to understand failure modes.
AI.motivation: To move beyond aggregate task-success metrics and understand the conditions, mechanisms, and failure cases of using skills with LLM agents.
AI.method: Controlled experiments across benchmarks with variations in representation, outcome annotation, and retrieval difficulty; a contrastive study of 8,135 trial records, 238 unique labels, 240 open-coded records; taxonomy of 3 categories and 12 skill-use modes; matched comparisons; analysis of retrieval pool sizes (5-100).
AI.result: Skills stabilize execution via procedural anchoring, increasing performance by ~6.06 points over Workflow Memory; procedural anchoring 65.7% of cases vs 4.5% for explicit knowledge injection; retrieval accuracy declines as pool grows (29.6% -> 3.3%); offline identification is confusable but downstream success remains stable; exact ground-truth invocation is neither sufficient nor necessary.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation should focus on reliability and robustness of self-evolving agents; identify when skills help, why, and where they fail; provide guidance for reliable deployment.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning solution for pickup and delivery routing problems with time window and capacity constraints
summary: The task of constructing vehicles optimal routes for pickup and delivery of goods is one of most promising tasks in the context of global urban population growth. Although this kind of problems with small size can be solved by various classical approaches, a fast (or realtime) route optimizer under the constraints of the real world (such as capacity and time windows constraints) for medium-large size problems still remains a highly challenging task. In this work we, for the first time, successfully applied a deep Reinforcing Learning approach (modified JAMPR model) to solve Pickup and Delivery problem with Capacity and Time Window constraints (CPDPTW). We obtained a robust model that gives a fast optimal solution for problems of small and medium size, and gives fast suboptimal solution for problems of larger (> 200) size.

AI.tldr: DRL approach (modified JAMPR) applied to CPDPTW; yields fast optimal solutions for small/medium instances and fast suboptimal for large (>200).
AI.motivation: Address real-world pickup-delivery with capacity and time window constraints; fast real-time routing for medium-large problems is challenging with classical methods.
AI.method: Apply a deep reinforcement learning model (modified JAMPR) to CPDPTW.
AI.result: Robust model achieving fast optimal solutions for small/medium problems; fast suboptimal for large instances (>200).
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates potential of DRL for real-time CPDPTW; effective for smaller instances, scalable suboptimality for larger instances; further work needed for large-scale performance.

title: Zero-Shot Skeleton-Based Action Anticipation
summary: Action anticipation (AA) aims to recognize ongoing human or humanoids actions from partial observations, enabling robots to predict intentions before the actions are completed. Although skeleton-based AA offers efficiency advantages, existing approaches assume that all action classes are seen during training, which limits their deployment in real-world scenarios where novel actions inevitably arise. To address this gap, we study the new task of Zero-Shot Skeleton-Based Action Anticipation (ZS-SkAA). This task requires recognizing unseen action classes using only limited early-stage skeleton sequences, combining the challenges of partial observations, temporal dynamics, and zero-shot generalization. To establish foundational research for ZS-SkAA, we introduce:(1) A baseline model comprising a spatio-temporal feature extractor and a mutual information estimation and maximization module. This baseline model explicitly aligns partial visual features with semantic class embeddings across modalities by estimating and maximizing their mutual information, enhancing generalization to unseen classes.(2) A benchmark protocol using the NTU RGB+D dataset, which is adapted for rigorous ZS-SkAA evaluation. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model as a strong baseline for ZS-SkAA, achieving high zero-shot accuracy on NTU RGB+D. This work establishes ZS-SkAA as a vital research direction for real-world systems requiring generalization to novel actions.

AI.tldr: Introduces Zero-Shot Skeleton-Based Action Anticipation (ZS-SkAA) and a baseline method with cross-modal mutual information maximization, plus a NTU RGB+D-based benchmark; demonstrates strong zero-shot performance for unseen actions.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where action anticipation models assume all classes are seen during training; real-world scenarios require recognizing unseen actions from partial observations with temporal dynamics.
AI.method: A baseline model with a spatio-temporal feature extractor and a mutual information estimation and maximization module that aligns partial skeleton features with semantic class embeddings across modalities to enable zero-shot generalization.
AI.result: Experiments show high zero-shot accuracy on NTU RGB+D, validating the baseline as a strong starting point for ZS-SkAA.
AI.conclusion: ZS-SkAA is a vital research direction for real-world systems needing generalization to novel actions, with the proposed baseline and benchmark establishing foundational capabilities.

title: Benchmarking data-driven material models on the classic Treloar dataset
summary: Machine learning is rapidly reshaping constitutive modeling, offers new ways to learn material behavior directly from experimental data, and challenges long-established modeling paradigms. But with a growing number of machine-learning-based approaches available, how do they compare in practice? In this paper, we use the classic experimental data of Treloar to benchmark popular frameworks for hyperelasticity: (Generalized-Invariant) Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks, Physics-Augmented Neural Networks, (Adaptive) Material Fingerprinting, and Efficient Unsupervised Constitutive Law Identification & Discovery. We compare their fitting performance, computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and ease of implementation. Furthermore, we discuss the trade-offs between predictive accuracy and model complexity. The latter is assessed by quantifying both the number of material parameters in the discovered models and the computational time required to evaluate the constitutive model and its derivatives. The results show that all methods can reproduce the benchmark data remarkably well. Rather than identifying a single winner, we highlight the strengths and limitations of each approach and provide practical guidance for their use. The source code for all six methods, including the training and comparison scripts, as well as all results and data used in this study, is publicly available via https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21915635.

AI.tldr: Benchmark comparison of ML-based hyperelastic models on Treloar data across six methods (GINN, Physics-Augmented NN, Adaptive Material Fingerprinting, EUCLID variants); no clear winner; trade-offs between accuracy, complexity, and compute; code and data openly available.
AI.motivation: The rapid rise of ML in constitutive modeling calls for pragmatic benchmarks to compare competing approaches on a classical, well-characterized dataset; Treloar data provides a standard testbed for hyperelastic laws and derivative computations.
AI.method: Empirical benchmarking of six methods spanning Generalized-Invariant Constitutive ANNs, Physics-Augmented NNs, Adaptive Material Fingerprinting, and Efficient Unsupervised Constitutive Law Identification & Discovery. Assess fitting performance, computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and ease of implementation; quantify model complexity via parameter count and derivative evaluation time; discuss trade-offs between predictive accuracy and model simplicity; provide training and comparison scripts.
AI.result: All methods reproduce the benchmark data remarkably well; no single winner; each approach has distinct strengths and limitations; practitioners are guided by context-dependent trade-offs; full results and data are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The study offers practical guidance for selecting ML-based constitutive models by balancing accuracy and complexity. It emphasizes reproducibility through open-source code and data, and suggests that the optimal choice depends on the application’s priorities (speed, interpretability, or fidelity).

title: Structure-Guided Spatiotemporal Attention Graph Neural Network for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Deep spatiotemporal models integrating graph convolutions and attention mechanisms have demonstrated excellent performance in network-level traffic flow prediction, owing to their exceptional ability to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies. Despite their predictive success, deployment of such models in safety-critical urban systems remains constrained by their inherent lack of transparency. Existing post-hoc diagnostic methods often struggle with spurious correlations and fail to unveil the intrinsic decision-making mechanisms governing traffic dynamics, resulting in suboptimal interpretability and limited operational trustworthiness. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Structure-Guided Spatiotemporal Attention Graph Neural Network (SGSAN). Departing from traditional architectures that rely on unconstrained adaptive graphs, SGSAN explicitly learns a static Directed Dependency Graph (DDG) to identify the invariant macroscopic propagation paths of traffic states. We further introduce an InfoNCE-based soft-coupling mechanism that anchors the model's dynamic spatiotemporal attention to this structural prior, offering a mechanistic account of the model's decision-making process while ensuring robust forecasting by aligning attention-based reasoning with identified macroscopic dependencies and preventing over-reliance on ephemeral local noise. Furthermore, a decoupled two-stage optimization framework is developed to resolve the fundamental conflict between structural discovery and predictive error minimization. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that SGSAN achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy while providing built-in interpretability that organically aligns with the physical logic of traffic networks.

AI.tldr: SGSAN introduces a Structure-Guided Spatiotemporal Attention Graph Neural Network that learns a static Directed Dependency Graph (DDG) and uses an InfoNCE-based soft-coupling to align dynamic attention with macroscopic traffic dependencies, along with a two-stage optimizationhalting conflict between discovery and prediction. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with built-in interpretability aligned to traffic physics.
AI.motivation: Address the limited interpretability and trustworthiness of deep spatiotemporal traffic models by embedding a structural prior (DDG) and coupling attention to it, reducing spurious correlations and revealing mechanistic decision-making.
AI.method: 1) Learn a static Directed Dependency Graph (DDG) representing invariant macroscopic propagation paths. 2) Use an InfoNCE-based soft coupling to tie the model's dynamic spatiotemporal attention to the DDG. 3) Employ a decoupled two-stage optimization framework to separate structure discovery from predictive error minimization.
AI.result: Empirical results on real-world traffic datasets show state-of-the-art predictive accuracy and interpretable outputs that align with the physical logic of traffic networks; robustness against ephemeral local noise due to the structural prior.
AI.conclusion: SGSAN offers a unified framework that couples structural discovery with predictive modeling, delivering both high performance and built-in interpretability grounded in the physics of traffic flow, suitable for deployment in safety-critical urban systems.

title: On the Robustness of Temporal Vision-Language Models for Surgical Endoscopy Videos
summary: Temporal vision-language models (TVLMs) offer a reusable, prompt-based interface for surgical video understanding, yet, their robustness under clinically realistic acquisition artifacts in endoscopy remains insufficiently characterized. In practice, degradations such as defocus, haze, motion blur, noise, cautery smoke, and packet loss introduce structured distribution shifts which may compromise video-text alignment. We study the robustness of temporal VLMs under such shifts caused by corruptions in clip frames. We introduce Endo-C6, a compact corruption benchmark of six endoscopy-realistic perturbations evaluated at a fixed high severity, and apply it to public Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy and laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos. Under a standardized prompt protocol, we benchmark 3 recent surgical TVLM baselines and analyze robustness in both mean and worst-case settings, spanning 294 dataset-level evaluations. Finally, we present RobustEndoCLIP, obtained by few-shot parameter-efficient tuning with VeRA, outperforming existing TVLM baselines. Our findings show that off-the-shelf TVLMs can exhibit severe worst-case collapse under endoscopy-specific corruptions, whereas lightweight few-shot adaptation can substantially improve corrupted performance and robustness without changing the prompt-based interface. We expect Endo-C6 to support standardized robustness reporting and promote more reliable clinical vision-language systems.

AI.tldr: Endo-C6 benchmarks robustness of temporal vision-language models on endoscopy data under six realistic corruptions; shows few-shot tuning (RobustEndoCLIP) improves robustness while preserving prompt-based interface.
AI.motivation: To quantify and standardize robustness of TVLMs to clinically realistic artifacts in endoscopy, addressing structured distribution shifts that degrade video-text alignment.
AI.method: Introduce Endo-C6 with six endoscopy-realistic perturbations at fixed high severity; evaluate three TVLM baselines on GI endoscopy and laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos; analyze mean and worst-case performance across 294 dataset-level runs; apply VeRA-based few-shot parameter-efficient tuning to obtain RobustEndoCLIP.
AI.result: Off-the-shelf TVLMs exhibit severe worst-case collapse under endoscopy corruptions; RobustEndoCLIP achieved superior robustness, outperforming baselines; substantial gains in corrupted performance without changing the prompt interface; 294 evaluations indicate consistent improvement.
AI.conclusion: Endo-C6 enables standardized robustness reporting for clinical VLMs and promotes more reliable systems; lightweight adaptation can substantially improve robustness to endoscopy-specific corruptions while keeping the prompt-based workflow.

title: Scaling Domain Data Repetition in LLM Pretraining
summary: As large language models scale, their training-token budgets must also increase to maintain an appropriate tokens-per-parameter ratio (\(\mathrm{TPP}\)). However, high-quality domain data is much harder to scale than general web data. As model size and the training-token budget increase, its fraction in the training mixture tends to decrease. Repeating the available high-quality data provides an effective way to counteract this dilution, but excessive repetition may lead to overfitting. We study this trade-off under practical LLM scaling, where the training-token budget grows proportionally with model size. For a fixed domain, we first find that, surprisingly at a fixed \(\mathrm{TPP}\), the optimal repetition count mildly increases with model size. Across different domains, we find that the optimal repetition count is strongly negatively correlated with the final validation loss of a domain: domains with lower loss can generally benefit from more repetitions. In contrast, the amount of unique domain data is only weakly related to the optimal repetition count. These findings suggest that repetition counts tuned on smaller proxy models with the same \(\mathrm{TPP}\) can provide a practical estimate for larger models.

AI.tldr: Optimal repetition of high-quality domain data under fixed tokens-per-parameter mildly increases with model size; the repetition count is strongly negatively correlated with a domain's final validation loss; the amount of unique domain data is weakly related; small proxy-model tuning can guide large-model strategies.
AI.motivation: As LLMs scale, training data budgets must scale accordingly, but high-quality domain data is scarce. Repetition of such data can counteract dilution as model size grows, yet excessive repetition risks overfitting. Understanding how repetition interacts with model size and domain quality informs practical data sourcing.
AI.method: Empirical analysis under practical LLM scaling with fixed TPP. Systematically vary repetition counts of domain data across multiple domains and model sizes, measure validation performance, and analyze the relation between repetition, domain loss, and data quantity. Evaluate whether findings on small proxy models generalize to larger models.
AI.result: The optimal repetition count mildly increases with model size at fixed TPP. Across domains, domains with lower final validation loss benefit from more repetitions. The amount of unique domain data is only weakly related to the optimal repetition count. Repetition counts tuned on smaller proxy models with the same TPP can provide a practical estimate for larger models.
AI.conclusion: Repetition tuning on small proxy models with the same TPP offers a practical path to configure data augmentation for large models. Focus repetitions on domains with lower final validation loss; use small-model extrapolation to guide large-model data allocation and avoid unnecessary overfitting.

title: Revisiting Energy-based Tabular Anomaly Detection: Energy and Reconstruction are Complementary
comment: This is the author's version of a paper accepted at the 33rd International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Tabular anomaly detection is dominated by classical density-proxy methods (Isolation Forest, OCSVM, LOF), reconstruction-based detectors (Autoencoders, VAEs), and modern non-parametric scorers (COPOD, ECOD, Deep SVDD), all of which approximate the inlier distribution only indirectly; explicit energy-based models are largely absent. Motivated by the recent revival of EBMs in deep learning (e.g., Energy-Based Transformers, JEPA), we revisit the classical Deep Boltzmann Machine (DBM) for this task and hypothesize that its mean-field energy combines more effectively with a reconstruction-based score than same-lineage pairs do. We evaluate a two-hidden-layer DBM on two tabular benchmarks spanning distinct domains (UCI Bank Marketing and NSL-KDD) against eight classical and modern baselines across twenty random seeds. The DBM mean-field energy matches the strongest baseline (the Autoencoder) on Bank Marketing and statistically beats it on NSL-KDD, while significantly outperforming the remaining seven on both datasets. When fused with the Autoencoder via rank fusion, the DBM energy yields a statistically significant improvement on both datasets (AUROC=+0.014, p<0.01 on Bank Marketing; +0.002, p<0.001 on NSL-KDD); every non-DBM-derived base model instead fails to improve or significantly degrades the AE-paired ensemble. Our position is that classical EBMs, exemplified by the DBM, deserve a place in the tabular anomaly detection toolbox as a non-redundant complementary view to the reconstruction-based scores that dominate current practice.

AI.tldr: A two-hidden-layer Deep Boltzmann Machine (DBM) is revisited for tabular anomaly detection. Its mean-field energy is competitive with reconstruction-based Autoencoders (AE) and, when fused with AE, yields consistent, statistically significant improvements over strong baselines across two tabular benchmarks, suggesting classical energy-based models offer a non-redundant complementary perspective to reconstruction-based methods.
AI.motivation: Tabular anomaly detection is dominated by density-proxy methods, reconstruction-based detectors, and non-parametric scorers, with explicit energy-based models largely absent. The work hypothesizes that a mean-field energy from a DBM could complement reconstruction scores, addressing the gap of explicit energy modeling in tabular data.
AI.method: Evaluate a two-hidden-layer DBM on two tabular benchmarks (UCI Bank Marketing, NSL-KDD) against eight baselines across twenty random seeds. Compare DBM mean-field energy to the Autoencoder (AE). Fuse DBM energy with AE via rank fusion and assess statistical significance (AUROC, p-values).
AI.result: DBM mean-field energy matches the strongest baseline (AE) on Bank Marketing and statistically beats AE on NSL-KDD; it significantly outperforms the other seven baselines on both datasets. Fusion of DBM energy with AE yields a statistically significant improvement on both datasets (AUROC gains: +0.014, p<0.01 on Bank Marketing; +0.002, p<0.001 on NSL-KDD). All non-DBM-derived baselines fail to improve or degrade the AE-paired ensemble.
AI.conclusion: Classical energy-based models (e.g., DBM) provide a non-redundant complementary view to reconstruction-based scores in tabular anomaly detection and deserve a place in the toolbox alongside traditional detectors and modern EBMs.

title: Learning to Forecast Crop Growth from Earth Observation Data
summary: Forecasting crop growth across agricultural landscapes is important for improving the productivity, resilience, and operational management of farming systems. In this work, we investigate whether Earth observation time series and meteorological drivers can be used to predict future canopy development at country scale. We focus on winter wheat and formulate crop growth prediction as forecasting future leaf area index (LAI) trajectories beyond the last available Sentinel-2 observation. We evaluate this task on a multi-year dataset which spans the entire country of Switzerland, containing over 20 million pixel-level Sentinel-2-derived LAI time series paired with meteorological variables. Because cloud cover and revisit gaps leave LAI supervision sparse, models fit the few valid (cloud-free) LAI observations yet oscillate implausibly between them, producing trajectories no real canopy could follow. We introduce a lightweight unimodal shape regulariser which improves trajectory plausibility with negligible loss in accuracy. We compare deep learning sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models with classic machine learning baselines and show that Seq2Seq models generalise well across years, achieving $\mathrm{R}^2$ above 0.8 and consistently outperforming conventional approaches. Together, these results demonstrate that remote sensing and weather-driven sequence modelling can learn crop growth dynamics at landscape scale. S

AI.tldr: Seq2Seq deep learning with a lightweight unimodal regulariser improves country-scale LAI trajectory forecasting from Sentinel-2 and weather data, achieving R^2 > 0.8 and outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Forecast canopy development across landscapes at national scale is valuable for productivity and management, but cloud-induced gaps in LAI data make trajectory forecasting challenging. The work seeks to predict future LAI trajectories beyond the last observation using Earth observation time series and meteorological drivers.
AI.method: Train sequence-to-sequence models on multi-year Swiss data (20M pixel-level Sentinel-2-derived LAI time series) with meteorological variables. Introduce a lightweight unimodal shape regulariser to enforce plausible LAI trajectories between sparse cloud-free observations. Compare Seq2Seq models to classic ML baselines and evaluate cross-year generalization.
AI.result: Seq2Seq models generalize well across years, achieving R^2 > 0.8 and consistently outperforming conventional baselines. The unimodal regulariser improves trajectory plausibility with negligible loss in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Remote sensing and weather-driven sequence modelling can learn crop growth dynamics at landscape (country) scale, enabling more scalable, weather-informed crop forecasting.

title: Mandato: Protocol-Level Enforcement of Digitally Signed Mandates on AI Agent Actions with Cryptographically Chained Audit Trails
summary: AI agents increasingly act on external systems through standardized tool-calling protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), yet no infrastructure layer constrains their actions to what a principal has verifiably authorized: authorization logic lives in application code, is neither signed nor independently auditable, and the resulting logs lack evidentiary value. We present Mandato, a governance proxy that enforces digitally signed mandates on agent actions at the protocol level. A mandate is a machine-readable, cryptographically signed authorization artifact specifying which tools an agent may invoke, under which parameter constraints and contextual conditions, for how long, and on whose behalf; the proxy evaluates every tool call against the applicable mandate chain, blocks non-conforming calls in line, and records every decision -- permit, deny, and the evidence for each -- in an append-only, hash-chained audit log designed for evidentiary use and periodically anchored via qualified timestamps. The mandate is deliberately modeled on the civil-law institution of delegation of authority, making the artifact legible to lawyers and auditors, not only to engineers. We give the mandate model and its decision semantics, the reference architecture as an MCP-transparent proxy with separated decision and enforcement points, and a mapping of the mechanism onto EU AI Act Articles 12 and 14, GDPR accountability, NIS2, and eIDAS 2, including a roadmap to qualified attestation through Qualified Trust Service Providers (QTSPs). We describe the implementation status of the reference system and a quantitative evaluation plan covering enforcement overhead, audit completeness, and tamper-evidence verification cost.

AI.tldr: Mandato presents a governance proxy that enforces digitally signed mandates on AI agent actions at the protocol level, with hash-chained audit logs and evidentiary decision records; it aligns authorization with legal frameworks and outlines reference architecture, implementation status, and evaluation plans.
AI.motivation: To provide verifiable, auditable, and legally legible authorization for AI agents acting on external tools, addressing the lack of a formal, auditable enforcement layer beyond application code and ad-hoc logs.
AI.method: Introduce the Mandato governance proxy and its mandate model: machine-readable, cryptographically signed authorization artifacts specifying allowed tools, parameters, context, duration, and acting party; a protocol-level enforcement proxy with separate decision and enforcement components; an append-only, hash-chained audit log with evidentiary records; mapping to EU AI Act, GDPR accountability, NIS2, eIDAS 2, and a pathway to Qualified Attestation; reference MCP-transparent architecture and status of implementation; evaluation plan for enforcement overhead, audit completeness, and tamper-evidence cost.
AI.result: A concrete governance architecture (Mandato) with signed mandates, protocol-level enforcement, and auditable evidence logs, plus a plan to align with regulatory frameworks and assess performance and security.
AI.conclusion: The approach enhances accountability, audibility, and legal defensibility of AI agent tool usage, with clear next steps for deployment, validation, and regulatory integration.

title: KV Cache Compression Through the Lens of Transform Coding
summary: The key-value (KV) cache stores information from past tokens and is a major memory bottleneck in long-context inference. Existing quantization methods address this bottleneck by representing the KV cache uniformly with lower-precision data types and designing quantization schemes to minimize reconstruction error in the cache itself, without accounting for how that error propagates through attention mechanisms. We prove that, under a white-noise quantization model, the expected attention-aware distortion decomposes into additive key and value contributions that factor across tokens and channels. Building on transform coding and reverse water-filling, which are classical tools from signal processing and rate-distortion theory, we introduce Attention-Aware Transform Coding (AATC), which allocates bits over a calibration set to minimize attention-aware distortion. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, evaluated across LongBench, RULER, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and MATH-500, our method achieves near-lossless accuracy at approximately $5.8\times$ compression, whereas each baseline degrades in at least some settings.

AI.tldr: Attention-aware transform coding (AATC) for KV cache quantization achieves ~5.8x compression with near-lossless accuracy on large LMs; outperforms uniform quantization baselines by accounting for attention distortion.
AI.motivation: KV caches are a major memory bottleneck in long-context inference; existing quantization minimizes reconstruction error of the cache itself but ignores how that error propagates through attention, leading to degraded downstream performance.
AI.method: Under a white-noise quantization model, the expected attention-aware distortion decomposes into additive key and value contributions that factor across tokens and channels. Building on transform coding and reverse water-filling, AATC allocates bits over a calibration set to minimize attention-aware distortion.
AI.result: Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct across LongBench, RULER, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and MATH-500; achieves near-lossless accuracy at approximately 5.8x compression; baselines degrade in at least some settings.
AI.conclusion: Attention-aware transform coding effectively reduces KV cache size with minimal accuracy loss, enabling substantial memory savings for long-context inference and outperforming baseline quantization methods.

title: MAGneT-3D: Monocular and Domain-Generalizable Temporal 3D Detection
comment: To appear at ECCVW 2026 (DriveX workshop; Oral paper). Johannes Meier and Mohamed Kotb - both authors contributed equally. Project page: https://mo-sameh.github.io/MAGneT-3D-Project-Page/
summary: Monocular temporal 3D detection aims to detect objects in 3D, given a monocular video. Query-based 3D detectors unify detection and cross-view association, but their learnable queries fit the spatial distribution of the training data (e.g., field-of-view). We show that this issue is especially severe when these models are applied to monocular video, hindering generalization to unseen datasets and environments. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGneT-3D, the first method for domain-generalized monocular temporal 3D object detection. Instead of relying on static learnable queries, we propose a Domain-Robust Anchor Generator (DRAG) approach that adaptively derives 3D proposals during inference. To further enable domain generalization, we propose a Temporal Refinement and Identity Merging (TRIM) strategy, reducing dependence on specific 3D proposals. To enable comprehensive domain-generalization evaluation, we establish a cross-dataset benchmark spanning nuScenes, Waymo, Lyft, and ONCE. Under zero-shot domain shifts, MAGneT-3D outperforms all baselines, improving NDS from 12.1% to 18.6% while also increasing in-domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: MAGneT-3D introduces domain-robust inference for monocular temporal 3D detection, using DRAG and TRIM to achieve cross-dataset generalization, showing significant NDS gains under zero-shot shifts.
AI.motivation: Cross-domain generalization is poor for query-based monocular temporal 3D detectors due to learnable queries overfitting to training distribution; need domain-robust proposals and temporal identity handling.
AI.method: Domain-Robust Anchor Generator (DRAG) adaptively derives 3D proposals at inference; Temporal Refinement and Identity Merging (TRIM) reduces reliance on specific proposals; comprehensive cross-dataset benchmark across nuScenes, Waymo, Lyft, ONCE.
AI.result: Under zero-shot domain shifts, NDS improves from 12.1% to 18.6%, and in-domain accuracy also increases.
AI.conclusion: MAGneT-3D demonstrates improved domain generalization for monocular temporal 3D detection and provides a new evaluation benchmark; potential to influence robust deployment in diverse environments.

title: A Pathway to General-Purpose Scientific AI: Multimodal Comprehension of Scientific Images
summary: Scientific figures and tables encode essential experimental evidence, yet remain difficult for digital libraries and multimodal AI systems to retrieve and interpret. The ALD/E-ImageMiner benchmark and ICDAR 2026 Competition on Information Extraction from Atomic Layer Deposition/Etching Scientific Figures provide 1,951 figures from 205 publications, expert-annotated for classification, data table extraction, summarization, and visual question answering. In these companion proceedings, we present a forward-looking perspective on how the benchmark can guide future scientific-image challenges. We examine how its tasks probe capabilities from visual and quantitative reading to domain-grounded reasoning and evidential justification, and how Bloom-informed question design can support deeper scientific understanding. We propose "scientific conceptual understanding from images" as a long-term benchmark objective, with future directions including broader domains and figure types, contextual and cross-document synthesis, hypothesis evaluation, provenance, uncertainty, counterfactual grounding, and open-ended multimodal research. This perspective connects the ICDAR 2026 challenge to a broader agenda for machine-actionable scientific visual knowledge and verifiable multimodal scientific AI.

AI.tldr: A forward-looking perspective on ALD/E-ImageMiner and ICDAR 2026, outlining a roadmap for machine-actionable scientific visual knowledge through benchmark tasks and Bloom-inspired question design.
AI.motivation: To address the difficulty of retrieving and interpreting scientific figures/tables and to guide the development of multimodal AI systems and digital libraries via a benchmark that spans classification, data-table extraction, summarization, and visual QA.
AI.method: Companion proceedings present a conceptual analysis of the benchmark tasks, discuss capabilities from visual/quantitative reading to domain-grounded reasoning and evidential justification, and advocate Bloom-informed question design; proposes long-term objective of scientific conceptual understanding from images.
AI.result: Articulates a roadmap and research agenda rather than reporting empirical results, linking the ICDAR challenge to broader goals in machine-actionable scientific visual knowledge and verifiable multidisciplinary AI.
AI.conclusion: Advances toward broader, cross-domain, and interpretable multimodal scientific AI; highlights future directions—contextual and cross-document synthesis, hypothesis evaluation, provenance, uncertainty, counterfactual grounding, and open-ended multimodal research.

title: MINT: A Universal Zero-Shot Predictor for Transaction Data
summary: Banks analyse sequential financial transaction data to perform many tasks, including fraud prevention, credit risk assessment and offer personalization. To improve the predictive accuracy of these tasks, Payments Foundation Models encode transaction sequence data as rich contextual embeddings, which can then be provided to task-specific models as features. However, these Foundation Models are not designed for flexible zero-shot reasoning across novel downstream prediction tasks, limiting their adaptability and utility. Existing LLM-based approaches to zero-shot prediction often fail to fully exploit the predictive signal within transaction data, while relying on costly text serialization or task-specific architectures that scale poorly. To address these limitations, we present the Multimodal Instruction Network for Transactions (MINT), a framework that connects a pretrained transaction sequence encoder to a decoder-only LLM through lightweight embedding injection, transaction-language alignment, and instruction tuning. We find that MINT achieves state-of-the-art predictive question-answering performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution questions, while substantially reducing input tokens, latency, and memory consumption compared to text-serialization baselines. Through comprehensive analyses of representations, alignment strategies, training data, and history length, we establish that compact transaction embeddings are a superior approach to transaction representation than text serialization for multimodal reasoning and zero-shot prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: MINT links a pretrained transaction-sequence encoder with a decoder-only LLM via lightweight embedding injection, alignment, and instruction tuning to enable zero-shot, multimodal reasoning on transaction data, achieving state-of-the-art QA with lower tokens, latency, and memory than text-serialization baselines.
AI.motivation: Banks require flexible zero-shot reasoning across downstream tasks (fraud, credit risk, personalized offers). Foundation models encode transactions as embeddings but lack flexible cross-task zero-shot reasoning; LLM-based approaches either underutilize predictive signals or rely on expensive text serialization. A scalable, cross-task framework is needed.
AI.method: Use a pretrained transaction sequence encoder to produce compact embeddings; connect to a decoder-only LLM using embedding injection. Introduce transaction-language alignment to bridge modalities and instruction tuning to enable task guidance. Evaluate on predictive QA for in- and out-of-distribution questions; compare against text-serialization baselines; analyze representations, alignment strategies, training data, and history length; show that compact embeddings outperform text serialization for multimodal reasoning and zero-shot tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art predictive QA on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution questions; reduced input tokens, latency, and memory versus text-serialization baselines; robust analyses support the superiority of compact embeddings for multimodal reasoning in transactional contexts.
AI.conclusion: Compact transaction embeddings are a superior representation for multimodal reasoning and zero-shot prediction in banking data; MINT advances adaptability and efficiency of foundation-model-based transaction processing; suggests embedding-based bridging as preferred over text serialization for such tasks; room for further exploration in alignment strategies, data, and history length.

title: Seeing Red, Thinking Bad: Color Bias in Vision Language Models
summary:
Vision language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in industrial decision-making systems, such as recruitment support and recommendation. This motivates careful analysis of how VLMs process visual and textual information. In this work, we study how VLMs interpret text rendered as an image, and investigate the influence of visual styling biases. To this end, we introduce Stealth Visual Prompts, which subtly change visual styling of text, such as color and contrast, while preserving semantic content. Using these prompts, we systematically control the visual styling of words in text and measure their impact on the analysis performed by VLMs. We further analyze how such visual perturbations affect the latent representations of the vision encoder. From our experiments, we observed that coloring positive words in green consistently shifts sentiment predictions toward a positive direction. As a result, VLMs often fail to properly account for negative words present in the text. Our analysis suggests that this behavior is correlated with changes in the latent representations of the vision encoder induced by color variations. In addition, we show that reducing text--background contrast increases reliance on visually salient cues and leads to more incorrect Visual Question Answering (VQA) outputs. These results suggest that the visual styling of rendered text can guide VLMs' interpretation in ways that diverge from human semantic understanding.
  Project page: https://github.com/KohsukeIde/color-bias-vlm

AI.tldr: Stealth Visual Prompts reveal that rendering text as images biases VLM interpretation through visual styling cues; green coloring of positive words shifts sentiment positively and low text-background contrast increases reliance on visuals, leading to biased or incorrect outputs and latent-representation shifts in the vision encoder.
AI.motivation: As VLMs integrate vision and language for decision-making, it is critical to understand how text rendered as images and its styling influence model interpretation and downstream tasks.
AI.method: Introduce Stealth Visual Prompts that subtly alter text styling (color, contrast) without changing semantic content; render text as images, systematically vary styling of words; evaluate impact on VLM outputs (sentiment, VQA) and analyze changes in the vision encoder latent representations; examine correlations between styling changes and representation shifts.
AI.result: Coloring positive words green consistently biases sentiment predictions toward positive; negative words are increasingly ignored; reduced text-background contrast increases reliance on visually salient cues and triggers more incorrect VQA outputs; latent representations in the vision encoder vary with color changes, suggesting a mechanistic link between styling and interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Visual styling of rendered text can guide VLM interpretation away from human semantic understanding, highlighting a robustness bias in multimodal models and the need for mitigation or normalization of visual cues in text rendered for VLMs.

title: Regime-Conditional Verification: Correctness Estimation for Adapting and Monitoring Safety Classifiers
summary: Safety classifiers deployed with large language models often fail for two reasons: their decisions reflect the policy learned during training rather than the deployer's desired policy, and their performance degrades as deployment traffic evolves. We present Regime-Conditional Verification (RCV), a lightweight wrapper that adapts an off-the-shelf safety classifier without retraining it. RCV estimates, from the classifier's internal representations, the probability that each prediction disagrees with the deployer's policy, and selectively corrects predictions likely to be wrong. The same correctness estimates also provide a label-free signal for detecting distribution shift, enabling a maintenance loop that updates the correctness estimation layer and resorts to classifier fine-tuning only when necessary. Across three off-the-shelf safety classifiers and two benchmark datasets, RCV improves adherence to the deployer's policy in every classifier-dataset combination, catching up to 0.81 of previously missed unsafe content without modifying the underlying classifier. In a deployment study with ten attack campaigns, each a harm category held out of RCV's training, RCV detects every campaign in a dedicated injection panel; in the maintenance census most drift episodes are repaired without updating the classifier, and the fine-tune is reserved for the residual episodes that repair does not restore.

AI.tldr: RCV: a lightweight wrapper that aligns safety classifiers with deployer policy by estimating per-prediction correctness from internal representations, enabling selective correction and drift detection without retraining.
AI.motivation: Safety classifiers often inherit the training-policy, and their performance degrades as deployment traffic shifts; a non-retraining method is needed to enforce deployer policy and monitor distribution drift.
AI.method: RCV uses internal representations to estimate the probability that a classifier's prediction disagrees with the deployer policy, selectively correcting likely-wrong predictions. It also provides a label-free signal of distribution shift to drive a maintenance loop that updates the correctness estimator and resorts to fine-tuning only when necessary.
AI.result: Across three off-the-shelf safety classifiers and two benchmark datasets, RCV improves adherence to the deployer policy in all classifier-dataset pairs, recovering up to 0.81 of previously missed unsafe content without retraining. In deployment with ten attack campaigns, RCV detects every campaign; maintenance updates repair most drift without retraining, with fine-tuning reserved for residual cases.
AI.conclusion: RCV is an effective, lightweight approach to align safety classifiers with deployer policy and maintain performance under distribution shift, reducing the need for retraining while preserving safety.

title: Adaptive Protection for Evolutionary Feature Construction in Symbolic Regression with Application to Credit Classification
summary: Evolutionary feature construction has shown strong promise in symbolic regression by automatically discovering informative transformations of input features that enhance a simple base learner. However, existing approaches often lack explicit mechanisms to preserve important constructed features discovered during evolution, and valuable genetic material can be lost when genetic operators disrupt effective features. This paper introduces an adaptive protection mechanism that leverages feature importance metrics to selectively preserve constructed features during evolution. The mechanism provides stronger protection for more important constructed features while still allowing less important features to be modified and to incorporate useful building blocks from more important features. We evaluate the approach using multiple feature importance calculation methods and demonstrate its robustness across different base learners. Experimental results on 98 regression benchmark datasets show that the proposed mechanism consistently improves solution quality over baseline approaches, and experiments on two credit classification datasets demonstrate that the method also extends effectively to improve search effectiveness beyond symbolic regression.

AI.tldr: Adaptive feature protection in evolutionary feature construction uses feature-importance to preserve valuable constructed features during evolution, boosting regression benchmarks and extending to credit classification across base learners.
AI.motivation: In symbolic regression, valuable constructed features can be lost due to genetic operators. Protecting important features can preserve useful building blocks and enhance search effectiveness.
AI.method: Compute feature importance for constructed features using multiple metrics; adaptively protect more important features during genetic operations while allowing less-important features to mutate and incorporate building blocks from more important features; robust to different base learners.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 98 regression datasets shows consistent improvement over baselines; two credit classification datasets show the approach also improves search effectiveness beyond symbolic regression and is robust across base learners.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive protection improves solution quality and search effectiveness, generalizing across regression and classification tasks and across different base learners.

title: Conditional Neural Optimal Transport for Predicting Cellular Phenotypes from Molecular Structure
comment: Accepted at the BioImage Computing (BIC) Workshop, ECCV 2026
summary: High-content microscopy enables systematic profiling of cellular responses to chemical perturbations, but the scale of the chemical space makes exhaustive phenotypic characterization experimentally infeasible. This motivates computational models that can predict image-derived phenotypes without acquiring the corresponding treated cells. We formulate molecule-induced phenotype prediction as an inductive conditional transport problem in image representation space. Given a negative-control phenotype and the structure of a molecule, we aim to predict the phenotype induced by the corresponding molecule. We first evaluate classical optimal transport baselines and show that static couplings do not yield useful predictions on large-scale phenotypic image datasets. We then introduce a molecule-conditioned Neural Optimal Transport (NOT) model with a Monge-Gap regularization training objective that learns to transport negative-control unperturbed phenotypes toward perturbed phenotypes using molecular structure as conditioning information. NOT recovers molecule-specific phenotypic effects while reducing microscopy-associated technical variation, thereby facilitating comparisons across experimental batches. On unseen active molecules, the model outperforms baseline approaches, demonstrating that chemically conditioned transport can generalize beyond the molecules observed during training. We identified the molecular encoder as the main limitation to this generalization, while transport in a compressed representation space improves performance and scalability. These results establish NOT as a promising framework for predicting cellular phenotypes from molecular structure and negative-control phenotypes, while highlighting the development of more informative molecular representations as a key direction for improving out-of-distribution performance.

AI.tldr: Molecule-conditioned neural optimal transport (NOT) predicts cell phenotypes from molecular structure by transporting negative-control phenotypes toward molecule-induced perturbed phenotypes, outperforming static OT baselines and generalizing to unseen molecules, with bottlenecks in molecular encoders.
AI.motivation: Scaling of chemical space makes exhaustive image-based phenotyping impractical; need predictive models that infer phenotype from molecular structure using high-content microscopy data.
AI.method: Compare classical optimal transport baselines; propose molecule-conditioned Neural Optimal Transport (NOT) with Monge-Gap regularization to transport negative-control phenotypes toward perturbations, conditioned on molecular structure; evaluate on large-scale phenotypic image datasets; test generalization to unseen active molecules; analyze molecular encoder and representation space.
AI.result: NOT captures molecule-specific phenotypic effects, reduces microscopy-related technical variation, and outperforms baselines on unseen molecules; transport in a compressed representation improves scalability and performance; molecular encoder identified as main generalization bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Molecule-conditioned transport is a promising framework for predicting cellular phenotypes from molecular structure; improving molecular representations is a key direction for enhancing out-of-distribution performance.

title: Retrieval Grounding Latent Reasoning for Dense Retrieval
summary: Reasoning-intensive retrieval requires text representations to capture not only semantic similarity, but also the reasoning needed to determine relevance under a given retrieval instruction. Existing reasoning-enhanced embedding models improve retrieval by incorporating reasoning information into dense representations, yet their supervision is typically dominated by the final retrieval objective. As a result, latent reasoning trajectories may learn shortcut reasoning patterns that preserve retrieval performance without producing meaningful incremental retrieval gains. We propose Retrieval Grounding Latent Reasoning (RGLT), a latent reasoning framework for dense retrieval that explicitly connects intermediate latent transitions with retrieval improvements. RGLT performs non-autoregressive reasoning in hidden space through an instruction-conditioned latent reasoning trajectory constructed from silent tokens. It combines process-supervised explicit-to-implicit distillation with retrieval-grounded supervision, using stage-wise CoT reconstruction to shape intermediate latent states and retrieval-effect credit to optimize incremental retrieval gains across the latent reasoning trajectories. Experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks show that RGLT consistently outperforms strong baselines while preserving efficient embedding inference.

AI.tldr: RGLT introduces a latent, instruction-conditioned reasoning trajectory for dense retrieval, tying intermediate latent states to incremental retrieval gains to reduce shortcut reasoning and improve reasoning-intensive retrieval while preserving fast inference.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning-enhanced embeddings risk learning shortcuts; there is a need for supervision that explicitly ties intermediate latent reasoning steps to actual retrieval improvements.
AI.method: Non-autoregressive latent reasoning in hidden space using silent tokens; explicit-to-implicit distillation; retrieval-grounded supervision; stage-wise CoT reconstruction; retrieval-effect credit to optimize gains across latent steps.
AI.result: Empirically improves reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks over strong baselines while preserving efficient embedding inference.
AI.conclusion: RGLT provides a principled framework that connects latent reasoning trajectories to retrieval performance, mitigating shortcut reasoning while maintaining efficiency.

title: Training Fair Tabular Foundation Models
comment: Spotlight paper at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) have emerged as leading methods for tabular predictive tasks, leveraging in-context learning to predict on new data without task-specific training. Despite the increased use of TFMs in high-stakes decision-making, their fairness properties remain largely unexplored. In this work, we incorporate fairness constraints directly into TFM training, enabling fair predictions in a single forward pass. Our approach addresses two key challenges: limited access to sensitive attributes in training data, and the incompatibility of existing fairness techniques with the in-context learning paradigm. We propose FairTFM, a scalable training strategy based on synthetic fairness tasks and a fairness-aware architecture using a gradient reversal layer, which encourages the model to learn representations invariant to sensitive attributes. Experiments on 132 fairness tasks show consistent improvements in fairness while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: FairTFM enables fair predictions in Tabular Foundation Models by introducing synthetic fairness tasks and a gradient reversal layer, achieving fairness improvements across 132 tasks with competitive accuracy in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Fairness in Tabular Foundation Models with in-context learning is underexplored. Challenges include limited access to sensitive attributes and incompatibility of existing fairness techniques with in-context learning, necessitating a training-time fairness approach that works in one forward pass.
AI.method: A scalable training strategy built on synthetic fairness tasks and a fairness-aware architecture using a gradient reversal layer, designed to encourage representations invariant to sensitive attributes and to integrate fairness into TFM training.
AI.result: Experiments on 132 fairness tasks show consistent improvements in fairness while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FairTFM enables fair predictions in a single forward pass, addressing data access constraints and the in-context learning paradigm.

title: Spatial Message Passing in Language Space for Pathology Image Interpretation
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can generate pathological descriptions from histological images, but gigapixel Whole Slide Images (WSIs) exceed their visual context limits. The standard tiling workaround makes WSIs tractable yet severs the tissue neighborhoods that define tumor-stroma interfaces and morphology. We introduce Spatial Language Message Passing (SLMP), a framework that performs spatial reasoning entirely in language space, human-readable by construction. SLMP represents a WSI region as a spatial text graph: tiles are nodes initialized with MLLM descriptions, and edges encode spatial adjacency. For each tile, an LLM refines its description by integrating language messages from adjacent tiles under a shared aggregation policy that, on the tile grid, acts as an adaptive local kernel operating on text rather than learned embeddings. This policy is an inspectable prompt that can be refined from model-observed tissue phenotypes via textual gradients, enabling automatic semantic optimization from local cellular context to broader tissue morphology without fine-tuning MLLM weights. On representative HER2 and CAMELYON16 regions, SLMP improves tile-level tumor description accuracy in settings spanning general-purpose and pathology-specialized backbones, with gains of +3.3 to +19.6 percentage points. Random-neighbor ablations confirm that these gains stem from spatial context rather than additional text alone, and inspecting the optimized policies reveals interpretable, tissue-specific decision rules. Besides, without any weight updates or fine-tuning the backbone MLLM, SLMP substantially improves general-purpose MLLMs and narrows its gap to pathology-specialized counterparts, offering a transparent and flexible mechanism for incorporating spatial reasoning into MLLM-based pathology analysis.

AI.tldr: Spatial Language Message Passing (SLMP) enables spatial reasoning on gigapixel WSIs entirely in language form, using a text-graph of tiles and an LLM-driven, prompt-based aggregation to refine tile descriptions without MLLM fine-tuning, boosting tile-level tumor description accuracy across HER2 and CAMELYON16.
AI.motivation: WSIs are too large for MLLMs' visual context; tiling breaks tissue neighborhoods; need a method to preserve spatial context and morphology while leveraging LLMs.
AI.method: Construct a spatial text graph: tiles as nodes with initial LLM descriptions; edges encode adjacency; for each tile, LLM refines its description by exchanging language messages from neighbors using a shared aggregation policy that acts as a local kernel on text; policy is an inspectable prompt strengthened by textual gradients; no MLLM weights updated.
AI.result: On HER2 and CAMELYON16 regions, SLMP improves tile-level tumor description accuracy by 3.3 to 19.6 percentage points across backbones; random-neighbor ablations show gains due to spatial context rather than extra text; optimized policies lead to interpretable, tissue-specific decision rules; without weight updates, improves general-purpose MLLMs and narrows gap to pathology-specialized models; transparent mechanism.
AI.conclusion: SLMP provides a transparent, flexible method to inject spatial reasoning into MLLMs for pathology analysis without fine-tuning, boosting performance and interpretability.

title: A Graph-Based Reinforcement Learning Framework for Structured Drift Diagnosis and Recovery in Autonomous LLM Agents
summary: Autonomous LLM agents are increasingly deployed in complex real-world workflows, yet they remain vulnerable to runtime behavioral drift, a silent deviation from the original task that can lead to irreversible side effects on external systems. Existing approaches address drift at the prompt level but lack structured mechanisms for step-level detection, risk assessment, and recovery decision. Because the main task-executing agent is often a large and expensive model that cannot be re-trained on every deployment, this work targets a plug-and-play recovery module instead. It introduces a graph-based framework in which a single small language model is trained via reinforcement learning to specialize at each node of a recovery graph, external to the main agent. Each node has a precise role\,: drift classification, operation detection, risk evaluation, or final decision and the model learns to produce structured XML-formatted reasoning adapted to that role. Training combines rule-based structural rewards with an LLM-as-judge semantic-quality signal, so that the model is graded both on how it answers (schema and length) and on what it says. Experiments on the public AppWorld benchmark show that the method generally exploits information about the suspected drift onset to issue correct recovery decisions using a small language model. In addition, the trained small language model reliably respects the prescribed output schema and produces semantically appropriate content in each field according to its assigned node role.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play recovery module for autonomous LLM agents uses a graph-based framework and a small RL-trained LLM to perform step-level drift detection and recovery decisions, with XML-like structured reasoning, evaluated on AppWorld.
AI.motivation: Runtime drift in autonomous LLM agents can cause irreversible external side effects; main task models are expensive to retrain, so a modular recovery mechanism is desirable.
AI.method: A graph-based recovery architecture with nodes for drift classification, operation detection, risk evaluation, and final decision. A small LLM is trained via reinforcement learning to specialize at each node, producing XML-formatted reasoning. Training uses rule-based structural rewards plus an LLM-as-judge semantic-quality signal.
AI.result: On AppWorld, the approach enables the small LLM to issue correct recovery decisions by leveraging drift onset information, and it adheres to the prescribed output schema with semantically appropriate content for each node role.
AI.conclusion: A modular, low-cost recovery mechanism can effectively detect and respond to runtime drift in autonomous agents, enabling structured, node-specific reasoning without retraining the main model.

title: Connected Subspace Clustering: Hardness, a Scalable Heuristic, and an Application to Sea Level Geodesy
summary: Constrained optimization extends classical optimization by integrating side information, making it widely applicable across scientific and engineering domains. Consider a setting where we measure variables at different physical locations. When grouping these measurements, we often want clusters that are both internally similar and physically coherent. Thus, we have a constrained clustering problem where the constraint models coherence. Motivated by an application in geodesy, where contiguous regions of the sea surface must be identified for principal component analysis, we introduce the Connected Subspace Clustering problem: given high-dimensional points and a connectivity graph, partition them into $k$ connected clusters, minimizing their total squared distance to the clusters' best-fit $m'$-dimensional affine subspaces. We prove that, even for $m' = 0$ and a grid graph with holes, the problem is NP-hard to approximate within $Ω(n^{1/2-\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, where $n$ is the number of measurements. We then introduce an efficient Lloyd-style heuristic that alternates subspace fitting with an iterative merging procedure to enforce connectivity. Our method returns exactly $k$ connected regions by construction, whereas unconstrained methods leave up to $1{,}966$ disconnected fragments at higher cost. In a study of 160 configurations on global sea level time series, our merging-based repair is the strongest of four strategies in $73.75\%$ of cases, and consistently outperforms competitors such as (connected) Ward's method across all tested cluster counts. The resulting regions isolate signals aligning with climate indices such as the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and Indian Ocean Dipole. Although developed for geodesy, the approach applies to other spatially embedded multivariate time series, such as climate fields, remote sensing, neuroimaging, and sensor networks.

AI.tldr: Connected Subspace Clustering with connectivity constraints; NP-hard to approximate; Lloyd-style heuristic enforces exactly k connected clusters; empirical success in geodesy, outperforming connected Ward; broad applicability
AI.motivation: Identify spatially coherent, internally similar clusters for high-dimensional, spatially distributed measurements; motivated by geodesy need to partition sea-surface data into contiguous regions for PCA
AI.method: Formulate Connected Subspace Clustering with a connectivity graph, target k connected clusters, minimize total squared distance to best-fit m'-dimensional subspaces; prove NP-hardness of approximation for m'=0 on grid graphs with holes; propose a Lloyd-style alternating procedure (subspace fitting + iterative merging) that enforces connectivity and yields exactly k regions; include a merging-based repair to enforce global constraint; compare against baselines (including connected Ward) on sea-level time series
AI.result: Hardness: NP-hard to approximate within n^{1/2−ε} for any ε>0 even for m'=0 and grid graphs with holes. Algorithm: Lloyd-style heuristic that alternates subspace fitting with connectivity-enforcing merging; yields exactly k connected regions. Empirical study on 160 configurations of global sea level data: merging-based repair outperforms three other strategies in 73.75% of cases and consistently beats connected Ward; resulting regions align with climate indices (ENSO, IOD).
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a practical method for constrained clustering under connectivity, suitable for geodesy and other spatially embedded multivariate data; despite hardness, efficient heuristics can produce high-quality, physically coherent clusters. Generalizability to climate fields, remote sensing, neuroimaging, and sensor networks is highlighted.

title: Intelligent Detection of Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Metrics Based on 2D Floor Plans
summary: This research developed a neural network-based model to extract various information from 2D floor plans. We detect lighting symbols, identify the appropriate type of light, and extract the associated texts with lights. The study aims to enable efficient floor designing and determining the number and type of lights needed per floor, i.e., allow efficient design and estimate the power requirement of the floor plan. The model was developed using Mask RCNN as the base. The images were annotated and converted into a Coco data format for training the model. The model achieved bbox\_mAP and segm\_mAP values of 0.7596 and 0.7111, respectively. It also performed well at different IoU thresholds, i.e., with bbox\_mAP 50 and segm\_mAP 75 values of 0.9850 and 0.9219, respectively.
