AI.conclusion: Integrating structured domain knowledge into evaluation and optimization yields more reliable and actionable supervision, improving specialized reasoning; APTER offers a practical path to diagnose and repair capability deficiencies in LLMs in professional domains.

title: Boosting Data Augmentation with Stochastic Weight Averaging
summary: The symmetries of a learning task have become an important factor in designing modern deep learning solutions. Data augmentation is a straightforward and effective way of incorporating symmetries into a generic neural network. Recent results show that infinitely large deep ensembles show perfect symmetry when trained on augmented data. However, since training ensembles requires repeating the training process many times, this method is costly. In this work, we study stochastic weight averaging (SWA) as an alternative ensembling technique that does not require repeated training runs. We analyze SWA by approximating the stochastic training trajectory at the end of training with an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process. We show that in the infinite-width limit, SWA on augmented data provides an equiviariance boost that goes beyond what could be expected from the performance increase due to SWA alone. We verify our results with extensive numerical experiments on numerous models spanning computer vision and graph classification with both discrete and continuous symmetries.

AI.tldr: SWA on augmented data delivers an equivariance boost in the infinite-width limit, providing ensemble-like symmetry benefits without retraining; theory via Ornstein–Uhlenbeck approximation corroborated by extensive CV and graph experiments.
AI.motivation: Incorporate task symmetries into learning efficiently. While data augmentation induces symmetry, costly large ensembles achieve it; investigate whether SWA can mimic ensemble benefits when data is augmented, using a stochastic-process view.
AI.method: Model training dynamics as a stochastic process; approximate the end-of-training trajectory with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process; analyze in the infinite-width limit; apply to augmented data; evaluate on computer vision and graph classification with discrete and continuous symmetries.
AI.result: In the infinite-width limit, SWA with augmented data provides an equivariance boost beyond SWA's standalone gains. Extensive experiments across CNN and graph models confirm symmetry gains for both discrete and continuous symmetries.
AI.conclusion: SWA with data augmentation offers a cost-effective alternative to large ensembles for leveraging symmetries, yielding stronger equivariant behavior and generalization, as supported by theoretical OU-process analysis and broad empirical validation.

title: Marionette: Predicting World States, Rendering Geometry, Painting Appearance
summary: Interactive game world models typically autoregress visual observations directly in pixel or latent space, forcing structured properties such as pose, geometry, and occlusion to be implicitly maintained by the same generative sequence. Over long horizons, errors in these latent world properties accumulate, making consistency and controllability fragile. We explicitly model the evolving world state, delegate exact geometric computation to a fixed, zero-parameter renderer, and leave the neural model to synthesize appearance. We instantiate this idea as Marionette, a world model for interactive games with articulated characters. First, a two-stage autoregressive dynamics model predicts an explicit and interpretable 276-dimensional 3D world state comprising multi-entity articulated skeletons, metric root trajectories, and rotations. Second, a zero-parameter graphics bridge converts the predicted state into pose-control videos, computing world-space geometry and occlusion in closed form. Third, a control-conditioned video-diffusion observation model synthesizes photorealistic RGB observations from the resulting structured controls. Our experiments establish two properties of Marionette. First, the predicted world state is directly controllable. Forcing a mismatched action stream changes root-aligned joint error by 31% across 48 held-out segments. Second, long-horizon behaviour is determined in the state, and can be repaired there. Left free, the two generated characters drift to 21.2 m apart (recorded sessions stay near 5 m) and a third of frames show ground penetration. Two rules imposed on the explicit state, a terrain collider and a separation cap, cut penetration by 66% and keep the pair engaged, with no change to the observation model. Routing appearance through the predicted state costs no fidelity we can detect, at an FVD of 831 against 799 for recorded pose.

AI.tldr: Marionette introduces an explicit 3D world-state model for interactive games, paired with a fixed, zero-parameter renderer and a diffusion-based observation model: a 2-stage dynamics predictor (276D state of articulated characters, root trajectories, rotations) followed by a geometry/occlusion bridge and a control-conditioned video diffusion model. It yields direct state controllability and repairable long-horizon behavior, though with some fidelity trade-offs; simple physical constraints further reduce penetration.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive models that predict raw pixels or latent observations accumulate errors over long horizons, making pose, geometry, and occlusion inconsistent and brittle. An explicit world-state representation coupled with a fixed renderer aims to improve controllability, interpretability, and long-horizon stability by decoupling geometry from appearance.
AI.method: 1) Two-stage dynamics predict an explicit 276-dimensional 3D world state including articulated skeletons, root trajectories, and rotations. 2) A zero-parameter graphics bridge computes world-space geometry and occlusion and renders pose-control videos from the predicted state. 3) A control-conditioned video-diffusion observation model synthesizes RGB observations from the structured controls. 4) Physics-like constraints (terrain collider, separation cap) tested to manage penetration and maintain engagement.
AI.result: The predicted state is directly controllable: forcing mismatched action streams increases root-aligned joint error by 31% over 48 held-out segments. Long-horizon behavior is governed by the state and can be repaired there. Without constraints, characters drift (21.2 m apart) and frames show ground penetration; applying terrain collider and separation cap reduces penetration by 66% with no change to the observation model. Perceptual fidelity (FVD) with learned state routing: 831 versus 799 for recorded pose, indicating modest perceptual cost.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state modeling with a fixed geometry bridge yields improved controllability and repairability for long-horizon behavior in interactive scenes. Simple physics-style constraints can substantially reduce artifacts without altering the observation model, though some perceptual fidelity cost remains (FVD).

title: A Generalized Parallelogram Rule for Proportional Analogies on Riemannian Manifolds
summary: Analogies are quaternary relations of the form "a is to b as c is to d", usually denoted a : b :: c : d. This notion is formalized in particular with the notion of proportional analogy, which imposes some constraints on the valid analogies. Whereas proportional analogies have been studied mostly in symbolic domains and in vector spaces, their use is limited in non-Euclidean spaces. In this paper, we introduce a proportional analogy relation in Riemannian domains, extending the parallelogram rule used for arithmetic analogies in Euclidean spaces. We illustrate the introduced analogy on various manifolds, such as the sphere, shape spaces and manifolds of probability distributions.

AI.tldr: Extends proportional analogies to non-Euclidean geometry by defining a Riemannian proportional analogy using a generalized parallelogram rule; illustrates on spheres, shape spaces, and manifolds of probability distributions.
AI.motivation: Proportional analogies are well-studied in symbolic and Euclidean spaces, but lack a principled extension to non-Euclidean (Riemannian) domains where data lies on manifolds. The work aims to enable geometric analogy reasoning for manifold-valued data.
AI.method: Define a proportional analogy relation in Riemannian manifolds by leveraging geodesics and tangent-space transport to generalize the Euclidean parallelogram rule. The construction maps points to tangent spaces via exponential/log maps and enforces a four-point relation akin to a : b :: c : d on the manifold.
AI.result: The approach is illustrated on multiple manifolds, including the sphere, shape spaces, and manifolds of probability distributions, demonstrating the feasibility of analogical reasoning in non-Euclidean settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Riemannian proportional analogy framework broadens the scope of analogy-based reasoning to curved spaces, enabling applications to geometric data analysis and machine learning on manifolds.

title: DeaMoE: Efficient MoE Structure for Fast Small-Batch Decoding
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have been widely adopted in real-time interactive applications such as coding assistants, real-time audio-video interaction systems. To meet the extremely low response latency requirements of these scenarios, practitioners commonly employ small-batch decoding, under which MoE inference becomes memory-bound and is severely bottlenecked by expert weight loading. However, this bottleneck has received limited attention, and existing solutions such as post-training weight compression or fine-grained expert design during pre-training either degrade model accuracy or introduce additional computation and communication overhead. To tackle this issue, we propose DeaMoE, a decoding-efficient MoE architecture, in which the experts are grouped into several departments, and the experts belonging to the same department share most parameters since they come from the same professional field, and additionally each expert contains a few private parameters to reflect its uniqueness. Moreover, we design customized two-stage routing strategy for DeaMoE to avoid redundant loading, under which DeaMoE greatly improves the efficiency during LLM decoding. Compared with vanilla MoE, DeaMoE reduces per-step loaded weights by up to 50.9% and achieves up to 1.33 end-to-end TPOT speedup for the pre-trained 7B model on A40, and up to 2.00x and 1.97x peak speedup for DeepSeek-V3 on A40 and H100 in microbenchmarks.

AI.tldr: DeaMoE introduces a decoding-efficient MoE by grouping experts into departments with shared parameters and adding private per-expert parameters, plus a two-stage routing to minimize loading. It substantially reduces per-step weight loading and yields notable end-to-end speedups during decoding on GPUs.
AI.motivation: Real-time interactive applications require ultra-low latency MoE inference. Small-batch decoding causes the MoE weight loading to become memory-bound, a bottleneck insufficiently addressed by prior compression or pre-training designs, which can hurt accuracy or add overhead.
AI.method: Experts are organized into departments; within a department most parameters are shared, while each expert keeps a small private parameter set to capture uniqueness. A two-stage routing mechanism directs inputs first to a department, then to a specific expert, to avoid redundant loading and reduce memory traffic during decoding.
AI.result: Compared with vanilla MoE, per-step loaded weights are reduced by up to 50.9%. End-to-end TPOT speedups reach up to 1.33x for a pretrained 7B model on A40, and up to 2.00x (A40) / 1.97x (H100) in microbenchmarks on DeepSeek-V3.
AI.conclusion: DeaMoE effectively mitigates the decoding-time memory bottleneck in MoE models by sharing parameters within departments and using a two-stage routing, yielding substantial decoding efficiency gains. Further evaluation on accuracy impact and broader hardware is needed to assess generality.

title: Decoding the Past: An Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Framework for Sex Attribution in Prehistoric Hand Stencils
summary: Determining the biological sex of the individuals who created Upper Paleolithic hand stencils remains a challenging problem due to the absence of ground truth, population differences between contemporary and prehistoric groups, and the uncertainty introduced by image degradation. Traditional morphometric methods suffer from high structural overlap across sexes, poor cross-population generalizability, and subjective feature engineering. This study presents an uncertainty-aware deep learning framework for sex attribution in prehistoric hand stencils that explicitly models, propagates, and aggregates uncertainty throughout the analytical pipeline. The methodology combines dual image processing, dual contour extraction, structured silhouette augmentation, model architectural diversity, and ensemble-based decision aggregation. The pipeline generates twelve plausible silhouette realizations per stencil to capture boundary uncertainties, which are processed by two ensembles of ten deep neural networks each (EfficientNet-B3 and MobileViT-S) trained on 14,036 contemporary hand samples. Furthermore, a triangulated validation scheme integrates ensemble predictions with unsupervised 2D latent-space manifold mapping (UMAP + k-NN) and explainable AI spatial attributions (LayerCAM) to ensure anatomical consistency. On contemporary data, ensemble models achieve strong classification performance, with accuracies exceeding 88% in older age groups. When applied to prehistoric stencils, the framework produces both sex predictions and confidence measures of internal agreement, enabling the distinction between morphologically stable and ambiguous cases. Convergence across ensemble predictions, latent-space structure, and interpretability analyses shows that uncertainty can become a measurable component of archaeological inference, enabling robust and reproducible decoding of ancient rock art.

AI.tldr: Uncertainty-aware deep learning framework for sex attribution in prehistoric hand stencils that models, propagates, and aggregates uncertainty through the full pipeline, achieving high performance on contemporary data and providing confidence measures for prehistoric inference.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of determining biological sex from Upper Paleolithic hand stencils amid ground-truth absence, cross-population differences, and image degradation. Traditional morphometrics suffer from high sex overlap and poor generalizability; propose a probabilistic, uncertainty-aware deep learning approach.
AI.method: Dual image processing and dual contour extraction with structured silhouette augmentation; twelve silhouette realizations per stencil; two ensembles of ten deep nets each (EfficientNet-B3 and MobileViT-S) trained on 14,036 contemporary hand samples; ensemble-based decision aggregation; triangulated validation combining ensemble outputs with unsupervised 2D latent-space (UMAP + k-NN) and LayerCAM explainability for anatomical consistency.
AI.result: On contemporary data, ensemble models exceed 88% accuracy for older ages. Applied to prehistoric stencils, the framework yields sex predictions with internal confidence measures, enabling discrimination between morphologically stable and ambiguous cases. Convergence across ensemble predictions, latent-space structure, and interpretability analyses shows uncertainty is a measurable component of archaeological inference, supporting robust, reproducible decoding of ancient rock art.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty quantification becomes an integral part of archaeological sex attribution, enabling robust, reproducible interpretations of prehistoric hand stencils through a scalable, ensemble-based, uncertainty-aware deep learning framework.

title: MathForm: Scaling Mathematical Autoformalization with Knowledge Retrieval and Verification-Guided Refinement
summary: Autoformalization is commonly framed as translating natural-language mathematical statements into machine-verifiable formal languages such as Lean 4. However, faithful formalization requires more than translation. Models must map mathematical concepts to the complex hierarchy of types and definitions in formal libraries such as Mathlib, while ensuring that generated statements preserve the meaning of the source propositions. Existing approaches struggle because they rely heavily on the model's parametric memory for library-specific knowledge, while common data construction pipelines often resort to filtering single-pass outputs and lack mechanisms for feedback-driven revision. To address these challenges, we introduce MathForm, an autoformalization framework for constructing verified training data through Mathlib knowledge retrieval and verification-guided iterative refinement. Before generation, a retrieval planner gathers relevant definitions and existing formalizations from Mathlib to guide the formalization generator. Generated statements are then revised using compiler diagnostics and semantic-consistency feedback. Using this framework, we construct FormalVerse, a Lean 4 dataset containing approximately 367K verified examples across diverse mathematical domains and sources. We then train MathForm-8B through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Across six benchmarks, MathForm-8B achieves average Pass@8 rates of 88.06% under Syntax Check (SC) and 72.37% under Consistency Check (CC), outperforming multiple specialized 32B autoformalizers. On the challenging FATE-H and FATE-X subsets, it attains CC pass rates of 63% and 37%, exceeding the strongest specialized baselines in both cases.

AI.tldr: Introduces MathForm for autoformalization with retrieval-guided generation and verification-driven refinement; creates FormalVerse (367K verified examples) and achieves strong Pass@8 and CC, outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Faithful formalization requires more than translation; mapping mathematical concepts to Mathlib's type hierarchy; existing methods rely on param memory and lack feedback-driven revision.
AI.method: Retrieval planner gathers relevant Mathlib definitions and formalizations; generation of formal statements; revision using compiler diagnostics and semantic-consistency feedback; supervised fine-tuning of MathForm-8B; reinforcement learning; construction of FormalVerse dataset.
AI.result: FormalVerse ~367K verified examples across diverse domains; six benchmarks with Pass@8 SC 88.06% and CC 72.37%; on FATE-H and FATE-X, CC pass rates 63% and 37%; outperforms specialized 32B autoformalizers.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-guided autoformalization with verification-driven refinement improves faithfulness and scalability, demonstrated by a large verified dataset and strong benchmark performance.

title: CytoBERT: A Foundation Model for Cytometry Data
summary: Cytometry measures the complex characteristics of single cells (e.g., counts and protein expression of immune cells) and is widely used across immunological research and clinical settings. However, cytometry data is highly heterogeneous and unstandardized due to experimental protocols and the choice of measured features. While machine learning methods hold the potential to gain deeper insights into cell biology, these challenges make them difficult to apply and transfer across studies. Recent advances in foundation models can alleviate these issues, but corresponding approaches are still scarce in this field. To address this, we provide CytoBERT, a publicly available, open-source, open-weight foundation model for single-cell cytometry data with variable marker panels. CytoBERT is pretrained in a self-supervised manner on a large-scale cytometry corpus (15 human datasets with heterogeneous marker panels and more than 50 million cells) curated through marker standardization, enabling it to learn transferable inter-marker relationships within cells. Fine-tuning CytoBERT for sample-level classification demonstrates that transfer learning across heterogeneous cytometry datasets is feasible, providing a starting point for scalable, generalizable cytometry analysis. Code is available at GitHub.

AI.tldr: CytoBERT is a public, self-supervised foundation model for single-cell cytometry with heterogeneous marker panels. It is pretrained on a large, diverse cytometry corpus (~50M cells across 15 datasets) to learn inter-marker relationships and enables cross-dataset transfer for sample-level classification; code available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Cytometry data are highly heterogeneous due to experimental protocols and feature choices, hindering transferability of ML models across studies. A foundation-model approach could learn robust, transferable representations across marker panels.
AI.method: Self-supervised pretraining on a large, standardized cytometry corpus with variable marker panels to learn inter-marker relationships within cells; open-weight model; fine-tuning for sample-level classification to demonstrate transfer across heterogeneous datasets.
AI.result: CytoBERT enables transfer learning across heterogeneous cytometry datasets for sample-level classification, indicating improved generalization and a scalable path for cross-study cytometry analysis; model and weights are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: CytoBERT provides a scalable, generalizable framework for cytometry analysis, reducing the burden of data heterogeneity and enabling cross-study transfer; it lays groundwork for broader ML adoption in cytometry and potential expansion to other cytometry tasks.

title: MagnifiQ: Patch-aware Text Guided Progressive Upscaling for High-Resolution Image Restoration
summary: High-resolution image restoration from degraded inputs is challenging because it must preserve global structural consistency while recovering fine-grained local details, especially at 4K resolution where direct diffusion-based restoration is computationally expensive and prone to repeated or inconsistent textures. In this work, we introduce MagnifiQ, an image restoration framework that progressively upscales and restores images across resolutions, e.g., from 1024x1024 to 4096x4096. Our approach leverages a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model such as SDXL and adapts it for more scalable high-resolution inference by replacing its original self-attention layers with convolutional operations whose computational cost grows linearly with image resolution. We further propose a progressive upscaling strategy that iteratively restores images over multiple resolution stages, refining each intermediate output rather than directly hallucinating the final 4K image, thereby improving global coherence and reducing high-resolution artifacts. To enhance local details while controlling content drift, MagnifiQ uses patch-specific text prompts that provide spatially localized semantic guidance during restoration. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world degraded images show that MagnifiQ outperforms prior diffusion-based restoration methods in perceptual quality and human preference, producing sharper textures and more coherent 4K results while offering practical speed--quality trade-offs through its scalable backbone and progressive design.

AI.tldr: A scalable, progressive 4K image restoration framework MagnifiQ that adapts diffusion models for high-resolution inference by replacing self-attention with convolution, progressively upscaling across multiple resolutions, and using patch-level prompts to improve global coherence and local detail at 4K with favorable speed-quality trade-offs.
AI.motivation: High-resolution restoration requires preserving global structure while recovering fine local details; diffusion models incur high computational cost at 4K. A scalable, progressive approach with localized guidance is needed to maintain coherence and reduce artifacts.
AI.method: Replace the diffusion model's self-attention with convolutional layers to achieve linear-cost scaling with image size; progressively restore through multiple resolution stages (e.g., 1024^2 → 4096^2); use patch-specific text prompts to provide spatially localized semantic guidance; perform iterative refinement per stage rather than single-shot 4K synthesis.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and real degraded images shows MagnifiQ outperforms prior diffusion-based restoration methods in perceptual quality and human preference, yielding sharper textures and more coherent 4K outputs, with scalable speed-quality trade-offs due to the backbone design and progressive strategy.
AI.conclusion: MagnifiQ demonstrates that a progressive, resolution-aware diffusion-based restoration with localized prompts can achieve high-quality, globally coherent 4K restoration at reduced computational cost, suggesting broad applicability for scalable high-resolution image restoration.

title: Attributing Preprocessing Invariance in Spectral Foundation Models
summary: Preprocessing invariance is an appealing goal for spectral foundation models: a frozen model should remain useful when laboratories preprocess spectra differently. It is usually measured by training a classifier under one preprocessing pipeline and testing it under another, with preserved accuracy read as evidence of learning. We revisit that reading, using a Raman foundation model as a case study. Such models normalize their inputs before any learned parameter is applied. If that normalization maps two differently preprocessed spectra to the same vector, the encoder receives identical inputs, so the invariance cannot be attributed to learning. For a normalization that uses each spectrum's own statistics, this happens exactly when one spectrum is a positive multiple of the other plus a constant. Several standard preprocessing operations take that form. The encoder should therefore be measured against the normalization alone, which has no learned parameters. On six Raman evaluation datasets, the model does not measurably outperform its own normalization. It improves on raw spectra, but so does the normalization alone. Training does improve the encoder over random initialization, and a controlled experiment shows that it learns to ignore a transformation only when that transformation reaches it. A numerical test settles which transformations a given normalization removes. Across released systems in five modalities, most normalizations already remove transformations of that form, and several of those systems claim that invariance as learned. Replicating the comparison on two of them shows no gain either.

AI.tldr: Normalization, not learning, often drives apparent preprocessing invariance in spectral foundation models; training yields little beyond what the normalization already provides.
AI.motivation: Clarify what “preprocessing invariance” means in spectral foundation models and how to properly evaluate it by separating normalization effects from learned representations, using a Raman foundation model as a case study and extending to multiple modalities.
AI.method: Analyze when a normalization maps two differently preprocessed spectra to the same vector, identify the class of transformations (positive multiples plus constant) that cause this, compare encoder performance to normalization baseline on six Raman datasets, perform controlled experiments to see if the encoder learns to ignore a transformation only when that transformation is removed by normalization, and test which transformations a given normalization eliminates; replicate analysis across five modalities with released systems.
AI.result: The observed invariance largely arises from normalization; the encoder does not outperform the normalization baseline on Raman datasets, only improves over raw spectra, and the normalization alone yields similar gains. Training improves the encoder over random initialization, but only insofar as the transformation is removed by normalization. A numerical test identifies the transformations removed by a normalization. Across five modalities, most normalizations already remove the relevant transformations, and several systems claim invariance as learned; replication on two such systems shows no additional gain beyond normalization.
AI.conclusion: Measures of invariance should be benchmarked against the normalization baseline, not only against raw inputs. Invariance claims in spectral foundation models are often artifacts of the normalization step; genuine learning-based invariance is supported only when the encoder adds value beyond normalization across diverse datasets and transformations.

title: More Correct Mass, Worse Answers: Why Power Sampling Can Fail and How to Fix It
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Haohui Yang and Jiaxing Sun contributed equally. Xiujun Ma is the corresponding author
summary: Power Sampling sharpens a language model's distribution over complete generation trajectories, offering a verifier-free way to improve reasoning at inference time. It also has the potential to serve as a general-purpose front end for a broad range of downstream sampling methods. However, we uncover a striking paradox: Power Sampling can drive more probability mass toward correct trajectories while degrading the downstream inference it is intended to enhance. Using self-consistency as a representative case, we observe accuracy drops of up to 18.5 percentage points across models and reasoning benchmarks. We trace this paradox to two mismatches. Dose mismatch arises because a fixed exponent induces drastically different amounts of distributional change across problems. Coverage mismatch arises because global sharpening concentrates mass on a narrow set of dominant paths: high pass@k, often interpreted as evidence of preserved diversity, can therefore coexist with the loss of broad reasoning-path support required for downstream aggregation, search, and selection. Guided by this diagnosis, we replace uniform trajectory exponentiation with a deformation-controlled, support-preserving Power target that calibrates sharpening across problems while limiting the suppression of moderate-probability paths. In a same-budget instantiation with weighted self-consistency, the repaired sampler reverses the losses caused by global Power and outperforms standard multi-sample inference across reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Power Sampling sharpens trajectory distributions to improve reasoning but can harm downstream inference; two mismatches (dose and coverage) explain the paradox; a deformation-controlled, support-preserving Power target fixes sharpening; with weighted self-consistency, the repaired sampler beats standard multi-sample inference on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address verifier-free inference-time improvements via sampling by understanding why sharpening can reduce downstream performance, and explore remedies.
AI.method: Analyze self-consistency as a case study to diagnose paradoxical effects. Identify dose mismatch (fixed exponent causes variable distributional change) and coverage mismatch (global sharpening narrows mass to dominant paths). Propose a deformation-controlled Power target that preserves support. Evaluate in a same-budget setup using weighted self-consistency and compare to standard multi-sample inference.
AI.result: Original Power Sampling can reduce accuracy by up to 18.5 percentage points. The deformation-controlled, support-preserving Power target reverses these losses and yields better performance than standard multi-sample inference on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Sharpening trajectories must be calibrated across problems to avoid harming downstream aggregation and selection. A deformation-controlled Power target preserves beneficial mass while maintaining moderate-probability paths, enabling improved inference under constrained budgets.

title: CPI-Bench: A Comprehensive,Practical and Intelligent Benchmark for Real-World Image Editing
summary: With the rapid advancement of image editing models and their widespread application across various domains, there is an increasingly urgent need to deploy these model capabilities directly into real-world scenarios. However, existing benchmarks remain confined to simple single-image tasks, suffering from limited coverage dimensions and an inability to effectively differentiate performance among diverse models. Consequently, they fail to reliably evaluate model performance in complex multi-image editing, highly demanding reasoning instructions, and practical deployment settings. To address these limitations, we propose CPI-Bench, a Comprehensive, Practical andIntelligent benchmark for real-world image editing. CPI-Bench comprises three core subsets: CPI-General-Bench, which comprehensively covers diverse editing tasks and pioneers the inclusion of multi-image editing evaluation; CPI-Practical-Bench, which focuses on high-frequency real-user application scenarios; and CPI-Intelligent-Bench, which is dedicated to evaluating capabilities in highly demanding reasoning-based editing. Evaluation results of mainstream image editing models based on CPI-Bench demonstrate that CPI-Bench enhances performance differentiation among models. It provides a comprehensive and reliable quantification of gaps in general editing capabilities, practical deployment efficacy, and advanced reasoning-based editing, offering invaluable guidance for the future optimization of image editing models. Crucially, our ranking analysis reveals that CPI-Bench achieves the highest alignment with the Arena Image Edit Leaderboard, indicating it faithfully captures the preferences and perceptual judgments of human evaluators, serving as a robust proxy for real-world user experience.

AI.tldr: CPI-Bench is a comprehensive benchmark for real-world image editing with three sub-benchmarks (General, Practical, Intelligent) enabling multi-image editing and realistic evaluation; it improves model differentiation and shows high alignment with human judgments as reflected by the Arena Image Edit Leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Existing image-editing benchmarks largely cover simple, single-image tasks and offer limited coverage, hindering reliable evaluation of diverse models, multi-image editing, complex reasoning, and deployment scenarios. This gap motivates a more comprehensive, practical, and intelligent evaluation framework.
AI.method: Introduce CPI-Bench with three core subsets: CPI-General-Bench (diverse editing tasks and multi-image editing), CPI-Practical-Bench (high-frequency real-user scenarios), and CPI-Intelligent-Bench (demanding reasoning-based editing). Evaluate mainstream image editing models and analyze alignment with human judgments (Arena Leaderboard).
AI.result: CPI-Bench enhances differentiation among models, provides a comprehensive quantification of gaps in general editing capabilities, deployment efficacy, and advanced reasoning-based editing, and shows highest alignment with the Arena Image Edit Leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: CPI-Bench offers a robust proxy for real-world user experience in image editing, guiding future model optimization and development by ensuring evaluations reflect practical deployment and human perceptual judgments.

title: Polaris : Multi Agentic System for Conversational Enterprise Analytics
summary: In today's fast-paced environment, the ability to swiftly access, understand, and act on data is no longer optional; it is essential. Yet most organizations remain data-rich but insight-poor, constrained by the complexity of querying, interpreting, and explaining enterprise-scale information. We present Polaris, a supervisor-led multi-agent framework for conversational enterprise analytics that bridges this gap. Polaris introduces Dynamic Task Coordination (DTC), a decision-theoretic orchestration layer that models agent-task assignment as adaptive bipartite matching, enabling real-time coordination, recovery, and optimization across specialized agents for querying, visualization, and reasoning. By coupling DTC with reason-first, ReAct-style agents, Polaris transforms natural-language queries into coherent analytical workflows that not only retrieve and visualize data but also explain the underlying "why." Evaluation on structured enterprise datasets demonstrates high semantic fidelity and answer relevancy, underscoring the potential of multi-agent orchestration to deliver trustworthy, end-to-end business intelligence at scale.

AI.tldr: Polaris is a supervisor-led multi-agent framework for conversational enterprise analytics that introduces Dynamic Task Coordination (DTC), a decision-theoretic orchestration layer that models agent-task assignment as adaptive bipartite matching, enabling real-time coordination across querying, visualization, and reasoning agents. The system uses reason-first, ReAct-style agents to convert natural-language queries into coherent analytical workflows that provide data retrieval, visualization, and explanations of the underlying rationale. Evaluation on structured enterprise datasets reports high semantic fidelity and answer relevancy, highlighting the potential for trustworthy, end-to-end business intelligence at scale.
AI.motivation: Organizations often have abundant data but lack insight due to the complexity of querying, interpreting, and explaining enterprise-scale information. There is a need for an orchestrated, explainable, scalable framework that can transform natural-language queries into coherent analytics workflows across specialized agents.
AI.method: Introduce Polaris, a supervisor-led multi-agent framework. Develop Dynamic Task Coordination (DTC), a decision-theoretic orchestration layer that frames agent-task assignment as adaptive bipartite matching to enable real-time coordination, recovery, and optimization among specialized agents for querying, visualization, and reasoning. Combine DTC with reason-first, ReAct-style agents to convert natural-language queries into cohesive analytical workflows that retrieve data, generate visualizations, and explain the underlying rationale.
AI.result: Evaluation on structured enterprise datasets shows high semantic fidelity and strong answer relevancy.
AI.conclusion: Polaris demonstrates the feasibility and potential of multi-agent orchestration for trustworthy, end-to-end business intelligence at scale, enabling task-coordinated querying, visualization, and reasoning with explainability.

title: Designing Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models: A Unified Path-Space View
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables; work in progress
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training provides a direct way to align diffusion models with human preferences and task-specific rewards. However, current RL algorithms for diffusion models remain fragmented: reverse-trajectory methods rely on discretized likelihood ratios, whereas forward-matching methods train on reward-labeled noising versions of the rollout samples. This paper shows that these seemingly different losses arise from a single path-space principle. Starting from the regularized diffusion-RL objective, we use importance sampling between sampling SDEs to obtain an explicit policy-gradient estimator on trajectory space. The estimator contains the stochastic Itô integral underlying Flow-GRPO-type updates; we derive an equivalent variance-reduced value-gradient form that recovers the forward-matching structure of AWM and DiffusionNFT. This identifies the empirical gap between these method families as a variance-reduction effect rather than a difference in RL principle. The derivation yields a unified design space organized by value-gradient estimation, weight functions, and sampling choices. Within this space, we propose a multi-sample KDE value-gradient estimator that reuses rollout groups, together with scale-bounded weight families that retain stable existing recipes while excluding singular ones. Experiments on SD3.5-M and Qwen-Image models validate the variance-reduction explanation and show that the resulting recipe improves over prior diffusion-RL baselines.

AI.tldr: Unifies RL for diffusion models via a variance-reduced path-space framework that reconciles reverse-trajectory and forward-matching methods, introduces a KDE-based value-gradient estimator with scale-bounded weights, and achieves empirical gains on SD3.5-M and Qwen-Image.
AI.motivation: Current RL approaches for diffusion models are fragmented into reverse-trajectory (likelihood-ratio-based) and forward-matching (reward-labeled noising) families. A unified, principled path-space foundation is needed to understand their connections and improve performance.
AI.method: Begin with a regularized diffusion-RL objective. Use importance sampling between sampling SDEs to derive an explicit policy-gradient estimator on trajectory space. The estimator encompasses a stochastic Itô integral akin to Flow-GRPO updates. Derive an equivalent variance-reduced value-gradient form that recovers forward-matching structures such as AWM and DiffusionNFT. Organize a unified design space around value-gradient estimation, weight functions, and sampling choices. Propose a multi-sample KDE value-gradient estimator that reuses rollout groups and adopt scale-bounded weight families to retain stable existing recipes while avoiding singular ones.
AI.result: The paper supports the variance-reduction interpretation and shows the proposed recipe outperforms prior diffusion-RL baselines on SD3.5-M and Qwen-Image.
AI.conclusion: By linking reverse-trajectory and forward-matching RL through a single path-space principle, the work provides a unified design space for diffusion-RL, introduces a practical KDE-based value-gradient estimator with stable weightings, and demonstrates empirical gains over existing baselines.

title: Grounding Without Corrective Control: Truth-Tracking Profiles for Large Language Models
comment: 24 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. A six-page methodological supplement, reproducible R script, and constructed data are included as ancillary files
summary:
Recent work suggests that some large language model representations have content or reference. Grounding can secure either without supplying live routes for correction. This paper asks what follows from that gap. An output is answerable when discrepancies can affect what a target- and task-specific arrangement produces, accepts, or withdraws. The arrangement has corrective control only when live, sufficiently independent routes can detect and repair fresh discrepancies. A route profile records which routes constrain the arrangement and how they are related. Those profiles support analysis of truth-tracking: patterned support for representational success.
  Language models are the pressure case; text-only arrangements provide a task-relative limiting case. Text-trained models inherit patterns of testimony, coherence, and prior correction. Where target-sensitive correction survives training, these can supply derivative answerability (inherited constraint); live answerability is the relation supplied by a current route for fresh discrepancies. Fluent failures should follow when a task requires independently informative access to the facts. Self-consistency, retrieval, tools, code execution, multimodal input, and feedback should help selectively. Route-by-task interactions test the distinctions. The decomposition's empirical burden is to predict held-out route--task combinations or improve intervention choice without conceptual refitting. Surface improvement and truth-tracking improvement can come apart.

AI.tldr: Proposes a route-based framework to analyze when grounding of LLMs yields answerability and truth-tracking, introducing route profiles to connect constraints with task outcomes and showing that surface fluency and truth-tracking can diverge.
AI.motivation: To formalize how grounding (content/reference in representations) interacts with the availability of live corrective routes, and to provide a framework (route profiles) for predicting when outputs will be truth-tracking and how interventions should be chosen across tasks.
AI.method: Develops a theoretical framework defining output answerability, live vs derivative correction, and route profiles. Argues for testing route–task interactions and evaluating truth-tracking through patterns of support, with attention to self-consistency, retrieval, tools, multimodal inputs, and feedback as selective aids.
AI.result: Conceptual contribution with a formalism for evaluating grounding and answerability in LLMs. No empirical results reported; yields predictions that surface improvements may diverge from truth-tracking improvements and emphasizes route-by-task analyses for intervention choice.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition enables prediction of held-out route–task combinations and informs intervention design, while highlighting that improving surface fluency does not guarantee better truth-tracking; emphasizes the centrality of live, independent routes for correcting fresh discrepancies.

title: Designing Compact Neural Architectures via Neuron Gating and Mixed Activation
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is naturally formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, where the upper-level optimizes the architecture using validation performance and the lower-level trains network parameters using training loss. However, NAS is computationally expensive due to discrete architectural decisions, exponentially growing search spaces, and the high cost of training candidate architectures. This work develops a general bilevel optimization framework for NAS across diverse architectures, including MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers, to identify compact architectures with strong predictive performance. We propose three scalable formulations that replace discrete neuron- and activation-level decisions with continuous relaxations, enabling differentiable optimization over otherwise combinatorial architecture spaces. These formulations give rise to three NAS methods: NAS based on Neuron Gating (NAS-NG), NAS based on Mixed Activation (NAS-MA), and NAS based on Neuron Gating and Mixed Activation (NAS-NGMA). Experiments on MLPs and CNNs using MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that the proposed methods consistently identify compact architectures with competitive or improved predictive performance. On MNIST, NAS-NGMA achieves 98.68% test accuracy with 7.69M MLP parameters, while NAS-NG achieves 99.63% accuracy with only 0.26M CNN parameters. On CIFAR-10, the proposed methods consistently outperform vanilla DARTS. Further experiments demonstrate that NAS-NG can optimize substantially over-parameterized and literature-optimal architectures, improving accuracy while reducing parameters. These results establish relaxed bilevel optimization as a scalable alternative to discrete NAS and provide a general framework for efficient neuron- and activation-level architecture optimization.

AI.tldr: A unified bilevel NAS framework with continuous relaxations (neuron gating, mixed activation, and their combination) to enable differentiable optimization across neuron- and activation-level architecture search, yielding NAS-NG, NAS-MA, and NAS-NGMA. Demonstrates competitive, compact architectures on MNIST and CIFAR-10 and outperforms vanilla DARTS in several settings.
AI.motivation: NAS faces prohibitive computational cost due to discrete architectural decisions and exponentially large search spaces. A scalable, differentiable approach across diverse architectures (MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) is needed to identify compact, high-performing models.
AI.method: Replace discrete neuron- and activation-level decisions with continuous relaxations to enable differentiable bilevel optimization. Propose three formulations: NAS-NG (neuron gating), NAS-MA (mixed activation), and NAS-NGMA (neuron gating + mixed activation). Train architectures in an upper-level validation objective while optimizing network parameters in the lower-level training objective, then evaluate on MNIST and CIFAR-10 across MLPs and CNNs.
AI.result: The methods identify compact architectures with competitive or improved performance. On MNIST, NAS-NGMA achieves 98.68% with 7.69M MLP params, NAS-NG achieves 99.63% with 0.26M CNN params. On CIFAR-10, the proposed methods outperform vanilla DARTS. NAS-NG also improves over-parameterized and literature-optimal baselines, demonstrating scalability and effectiveness of relaxed bilevel NAS.
AI.conclusion: Relaxed bilevel optimization provides a scalable, general framework for neuron- and activation-level NAS across diverse architectures, offering a viable alternative to discrete NAS and enabling efficient architecture optimization.

title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
summary: Time series analysis in high-stakes domains relies on recurring data releases, where new observations can alter the evidence base and the validity of later conclusions. Existing time series QA benchmarks mostly rely on fixed snapshots, leaving temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use unevaluated. We introduce TimeSage-EV, a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis in evolving environments. It tracks 60 real institutional scenarios across 6 domains, comprising 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026 and spanning monthly, weekly, daily, and irregular release cadences. At each period, large language model (LLM) agents receive time series data and source reports, while the withheld target release provides ground truth. TimeSage-EV evaluates state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. Experiments with frontier LLM agents and TimeSage-1.0, a novel self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library, reveal significant performance gaps across model tiers and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation. We release TimeSage-EV as a research resource with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses.

AI.tldr: TimeSage-EV is a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis in evolving environments, designed to evaluate temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use in high-stakes domains. It tracks 60 real institutional scenarios across 6 domains, producing 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs over 2023-2026 with monthly/weekly/daily release cadences, and assesses LLM agents on state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current time-series QA benchmarks rely on fixed snapshots and do not test temporal validity or the ability to reason with evolving evidence and release cutoffs, which are critical in high-stakes decision-making.
AI.method: Construct and publish TimeSage-EV as a live benchmark that monitors 60 real institutional scenarios across 6 domains, generating 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026. At each period, LLM agents receive time-series data and source reports, while the withheld target release provides ground truth. Evaluation focuses on state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. TimeSage-1.0 introduces a self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library; experiments compare frontier LLMs across model tiers.
AI.result: The study reports significant performance gaps across model tiers and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation when dealing with evolving data and release cutoffs.
AI.conclusion: TimeSage-EV provides a living research resource with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses, highlighting the need for improved temporal reasoning and contextual adaptation in evolving time-series QA for high-stakes environments.

title: LP-NAS: Linear Programming-based Neural Architecture Search
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) aims to automate neural network architecture design, reducing reliance on human expertise. Among the various NAS methods, differentiable NAS has gained prominence due to its efficiency and accuracy compared to conventional NAS approaches. Since differentiable NAS relaxes the architecture search space into a continuous domain, it is possible to apply principles from continuous optimization to NAS. In this paper, we propose Linear Programming-based NAS (LP-NAS), a mathematical programming-based framework for differentiable NAS that is applicable to a wide range of continuous search spaces. LP-NAS formulates a linear program (LP) using the validation-loss gradient and the training-loss Hessian to compute an architecture update direction that improves generalization while preserving the optimality of the model parameters. By following this LP-derived descent direction, LP-NAS efficiently navigates the architecture search space, leading to faster and more effective architecture optimization. We introduce two computationally efficient variants of LP-NAS, namely S-LP-NAS and R-LP-NAS. Applying LP-NAS to the Differentiable Architecture Search (DARTS) search space results in two algorithmic variants, S-LP-DARTS and R-LP-DARTS. Both variants achieve faster convergence and significantly higher validation performance during the early search iterations than the standard DARTS algorithm. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show that LP-DARTS outperforms standard DARTS in both the architecture search and evaluation phases. Additionally, we compare our approach with several DARTS variants (P-DARTS, PC-DARTS, and STO-DARTS) on the CIFAR-10 dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness. Furthermore, we validate the transferability of the discovered architectures through experiments on the ImageNet dataset.

AI.tldr: A linear-programming-based differentiable NAS framework (LP-NAS) that uses the validation-loss gradient and training-loss Hessian to compute an architecture update direction, improving generalization and preserving parameter optimality. It yields fast variants (S-LP-NAS, R-LP-NAS) and, when applied to DARTS variants (S-LP-DARTS, R-LP-DARTS), achieves faster convergence and higher early validation performance on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet transferability.
AI.motivation: To address inefficiencies and generalization gaps in differentiable NAS by deriving a principled, optimization-based update direction that leverages a linear-programming formulation, enabling faster and more robust architecture search across continuous NAS spaces.
AI.method: Formulate a linear program using the validation-loss gradient and the training-loss Hessian to obtain a descent direction for architecture updates that improves generalization while preserving model parameter optimality. Develop two efficient variants (S-LP-NAS and R-LP-NAS) and instantiate them in the DARTS search space as S-LP-DARTS and R-LP-DARTS. Evaluate on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet for transferability.
AI.result: LP-NAS variants converge faster and achieve significantly higher validation performance in early search iterations compared to standard DARTS. LP-DARTS outperforms DARTS on both architecture search and evaluation phases on CIFAR-10/100, and shows competitive or superior performance relative to P-DARTS, PC-DARTS, and STO-DARTS on CIFAR-10. architectures discovered transfer well to ImageNet, indicating solid transferability.
AI.conclusion: A principled LP-based framework provides an effective and efficient alternative to gradient-based differentiable NAS, delivering faster convergence, better early performance, and transferable architectures, with practical variants that integrate with existing NAS spaces (e.g., DARTS).

title: Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning
summary: We introduce Mobius-v0, an architecture that comprises a globally shared Memory (FFN) that stores knowledge vectors and multiple Reasoners (Self-Attn) that iteratively achieve compositional reasoning. Using hidden states as cache and carrier, reasoners repeatedly query memory for required knowledge-vectors, while the knowledge is transmitted back to reasoning operators. Through this knowledge-reasoning-separation architecture, Mobius achieves better knowledge compression and reasoning efficiency. Built upon Mobius-v0 architecture: 1) Our 7B model trained-from-scratch achieves similar downstream score as a 7B Transformer baseline with 62.6% of baseline's training data. 2) Our Intern-S2-Mobius, continually-pretrained from Qwen3.5-35B, achieves similar downstream score while delivering nearly 4x end-to-end inference speedup.

AI.tldr: Mobius-v0 uses a globally shared memory (FFN) and multiple iterated Self-Attention Reasoners to perform compositional reasoning with memory-reasoning separation; improves knowledge compression and inference efficiency; 7B-from-scratch matches 7B baseline with 62.6% data; Intern-S2-Mobius pretraining yields ~4x faster inference with similar score.
AI.motivation: Address data- and compute-efficiency gaps in large LMs for compositional reasoning by decoupling knowledge storage from reasoning steps and enabling iterative querying of a shared memory.
AI.method: Architectural design featuring a globally shared memory FFN storing knowledge vectors and multiple Self-Attention Reasoners that query the memory and propagate retrieved vectors back to the reasoning operators. Hidden states act as caches/ carriers for knowledge. Two experimental tracks: (1) a 7B model trained from scratch; (2) Intern-S2-Mobius, continually pretrained from Qwen3.5-35B.
AI.result: Mobius-v0 achieves better knowledge compression and reasoning efficiency. The 7B-from-scratch model attains similar downstream performance as a 7B Transformer baseline but with 62.6% of the baseline's training data. Intern-S2-Mobius delivers nearly 4x end-to-end inference speedup while maintaining comparable downstream scores.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-reasoning separation with a shared memory and iterative reasoners improves data efficiency and inference speed, enabling competitive performance with much less training data and enabling faster continual pretraining deployment.

title: Approximate Muon with low-rank adapters
summary: The Muon optimizer shows clear benefits versus alternatives when pretraining neural networks. However, it is used less frequently for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). One potential reason is that the most common PEFT method, LoRA, does not naturally combine with Muon since it is not mathematically possible to orthogonalize the weight update given by a low-rank parameterization. In this paper, we address this issue by approximating the solution to a relaxed Muon objective in the low-rank setting via linearization and then least-squares. We provide an efficient implementation that uses matmul operations only, as opposed to more complex linear algebra decomposition routines. Our method, sMuon (small Muon), performs favourably across SFT and a ReLoRA pretraining experiment. While results are model- and eval-dependent, we find overall that using Muon for low-rank fine-tuning provides moderate performance improvements.

AI.tldr: sMuon enables Muon-style optimization in low-rank PEFT (e.g., LoRA) by approximating the relaxed Muon objective with linearization and least-squares, yielding an efficient matmul-based implementation and moderate gains in SFT and ReLoRA pretraining.
AI.motivation: To make Muon compatible with parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (like LoRA) by addressing the lack of orthogonalization in low-rank updates and to achieve practical performance gains.
AI.method: Linearize the relaxed Muon objective around the low-rank LoRA parameterization and solve the resulting least-squares problem. Implemented using only matrix-matrix multiplications for efficiency, yielding sMuon (small Muon).
AI.result: sMuon performs favorably across SFT and ReLoRA pretraining experiments. Results are model- and evaluation-dependent, but overall indicate moderate performance improvements when applying Muon in low-rank fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Muon is beneficial for low-rank fine-tuning when combined with efficient approximations like sMuon; the approach offers practical improvements without resorting to complex linear-algebra decompositions.

title: Sensor-Driven Mission Synthesis for UAV/UGV Swarms: A TB-CSPN Coordination Architecture with Hardware-Enforced Safety
summary: This paper presents a coordination architecture for heterogeneous UAV/UGV swarms that synthesises mission actions from uncertain, multi-modal sensor evidence while preserving hardware-enforced safety at the actuation boundary. The approach combines radar, RF, acoustic, and visual observations with Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) orchestration to support incremental mission formation under partial and evolving information. Consultant agents transform sensor outputs into temporally bounded semantic tokens, while supervisor agents provide authorisation and policy-governed release of mission transitions. This separation between interpretation, coordination, and execution yields auditable decision paths, constrains non-determinism within the coordination layer through guards and synchronisation, and enables bounded-time integration of heterogeneous evidence. To improve resilience in contested environments, including cyber compromise, spoofing, jamming, and communication loss, the digital coordination layer is complemented by independent analogue safety envelopes that clamp or veto unsafe actuator commands issued to individual vehicles. A coastal-surveillance case study illustrates how the proposed architecture enables dependable, governed, and physically safe swarm coordination under operational uncertainty.

AI.tldr: A multi-layered coordination architecture for heterogeneous UAV/UGV swarms integrates multi-modal sensor evidence using TB-CSPN orchestration, with separation of interpretation, coordination, and execution, complemented by analogue safety envelopes for safety at the actuation boundary; demonstrated on coastal surveillance for dependable, governed, and physically safe operations under uncertainty and cyber threats.
AI.motivation: To enable dependable, auditable, and safe swarm coordination in uncertain, dynamic environments where heterogeneous sensors provide partial/multi-modal evidence and where cyber and communication risks threaten autonomous actuation.
AI.method: Introduce a two-layer digital coordination framework: consultant agents convert heterogeneous sensor data into temporally bounded semantic tokens; supervisor agents authorize and release mission transitions. A TB-CSPN-based orchestration governs action synthesis and coordination, with guards and synchronization to constrain non-determinism. An independent analogue safety envelope clamps/vetoes unsafe actuator commands. The architecture supports incremental mission formation under partial information and ensures auditable decision paths. A coastal-surveillance case study demonstrates performance.
AI.result: The approach yields auditable, policy-governed, and physically safe swarm coordination under operational uncertainty, with resilience to cyber compromise, spoofing, jamming, and communication loss, demonstrated via a coastal-surveillance scenario.
AI.conclusion: Separating interpretation, coordination, and execution, together with analogue safety envelopes and TB-CSPN orchestration, provides auditable decision paths and bounded non-determinism, enabling dependable swarm coordination in contested environments; the architecture generalizes to other multi-vehicle domains beyond coastal surveillance.

title: Generating Benchmark Health Data Using a Tabular Diffusion Transformer
summary: Cross-Tabular Data Generation (CTDG) seeks to learn a generative model from multiple heterogeneous tables and produce new synthetic tabular datasets. However, existing synthetic tabular data generation methods are largely restricted to single-input-table scenarios and struggle to effectively handle multiple heterogeneous tables with diverse feature sets. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage framework for cross-tabular data generation. In the first stage, each heterogeneous raw table is transformed into a standardized statistical table with the same set of columns across all tables. Each statistical table captures the marginal distributions of the original columns and the pairwise correlations among them. In the second stage, a diffusion transformer model is trained to capture structural patterns across these homogeneous statistical tables and to generate synthetic statistical tables. Synthetic raw tables are subsequently reconstructed from the generated statistical tables via multivariate Gaussian sampling followed by an inverse probability integral transform. This two-stage CTDG framework enables the learning of a unified generative model from multiple heterogeneous tables and supports the generation of an unlimited number of realistic synthetic heterogeneous tables. Experimental results demonstrate high fidelity in the learned statistical representations and a favorable fidelity-diversity trade-off in the generated synthetic data, validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: A two-stage cross-tabular data generation (CTDG) framework that standardizes heterogeneous input tables into identical statistical tables and uses a diffusion transformer to model cross-table structure, then reconstructs synthetic raw tables from generated statistics via multivariate Gaussian sampling and inverse CDF.
AI.motivation: Single-input-table synthetic tabular data methods struggle with multiple heterogeneous tables with diverse feature sets; need a unified generative model across tables.
AI.method: Stage 1: Transform each heterogeneous raw table into a standardized statistical table with a common column set, encoding marginal distributions and pairwise correlations. Stage 2: Train a diffusion transformer on these standardized tables to learn cross-table structure and generate synthetic statistical tables. Reconstruction: Convert generated statistics back to raw tables using multivariate Gaussian sampling followed by inverse probability integral transform (IPIT).
AI.result: Demonstrates high fidelity of the learned statistical representations and a favorable fidelity–diversity trade-off in generated synthetic data; validates effectiveness of the approach across multiple heterogeneous tables.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage CTDG framework enables learning a unified generative model from multiple heterogeneous tables and supports unlimited generation of realistic synthetic heterogeneous tables.

title: AnchorBench: A Multi-Pathway Benchmark for the Anchoring Effect in LLMs
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: The anchoring effect is a cognitive bias in which an initial reference value shifts a later judgment toward itself. This effect is well established in human judgment and decision-making, and recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) exhibit similar behavior. However, existing work on anchoring in LLMs typically evaluates only a narrow set of anchor pathways and rarely distinguishes irrelevant from plausible anchors. We introduce AnchorBench, a benchmark for the anchoring effect in LLMs that evaluates multiple anchor pathways under an explicit anchor relevance axis. Across fourteen models, including ten open-weight models and four frontier API models, and a large set of controlled prompts, we find that (1) anchoring is strongly pathway-dependent, (2) plausible anchors usually induce larger shifts than irrelevant ones when introduced through stronger pathways, (3) anchor influence generally weakens as the anchor moves farther from the evidence-supported answer, most clearly on External and RAG, and (4) high task accuracy on the anchor-free control condition (Acc$_{10}$: answers within 10 points of gold) does not guarantee robustness: even frontier API models above 95% control accuracy remain susceptible to plausible anchors.

AI.tldr: AnchorBench reveals LLM anchoring is highly pathway-dependent; plausible anchors produce larger shifts than irrelevant ones when delivered through stronger pathways; the influence wanes as the anchor diverges from the evidence-backed answer, especially for External and RAG; high anchor-free accuracy does not ensure robustness against plausible anchors.
AI.motivation: Existing anchoring studies in LLMs test few anchor pathways and seldom distinguish anchor relevance, limiting understanding of when and why models get anchored. A comprehensive benchmark with multiple pathways and an explicit relevance axis is needed to assess robustness.
AI.method: Evaluate 14 models (10 open-weight, 4 frontier API) using a large set of controlled prompts across multiple anchor pathways (including plausible and irrelevant anchors) and an explicit anchor relevance axis. Compare anchor-free control (Acc10) with various anchored conditions and analyze shifts toward the anchor.
AI.result: (1) Anchoring is strongly pathway-dependent. (2) Plausible anchors induce larger shifts than irrelevant ones when introduced through stronger pathways. (3) Anchor influence generally weakens as the anchor moves farther from the evidence-supported answer, most clearly on External and RAG. (4) High task accuracy on the anchor-free control (Acc10) does not guarantee robustness: even frontier API models above 95% control accuracy remain susceptible to plausible anchors.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring in LLMs is a robust phenomenon that depends on how anchors are introduced and how relevant they are to the evidence. A comprehensive, relevance-aware benchmark like AnchorBench is essential for evaluating and mitigating anchoring biases, as high anchor-free performance does not generalize to robustness against plausible anchors.

title: Rollplex: Cross-Phase GPU Spatial Sharing for Vision Language Model Post-Training
summary:
Vision-language models (VLMs) enable embodied agents to reason and act from visual observations and language instructions. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training enhances these capabilities using task feedback, but current on-policy RL runtimes execute rollout, reference scoring, and actor training in strict serial phases. While effective for text-only RL, this phase-granular execution is wasteful for VLMs, where processing dense video inputs and prompt prefixes occupies a large fraction of each phase. Because prefix processing is independent of the generated response, it can be run alongside rollout decoding, which leaves GPU compute capacity underutilized, without breaking synchronous on-policy semantics.
  We present Rollplex, a runtime that decomposes the reference and training phase and moves the prefix computation into the rollout decode window. Realizing this schedule requires more than concurrent kernel launches: naive colocation of Qwen2.5-VL-32\,B requires roughly 165\,GiB per GPU, while rollout and training prefer different tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and weight layouts. Rollplex addresses these constraints with two mechanisms. Phase-aware memory management controls HBM residency according to producer--consumer lifetimes. Parallelism-aware weight sharing uses the same physical storage for layout-compatible tensors across distinct TP degrees and reconstructs only incompatible tensors, avoiding a complete second actor copy. On 32 H800 GPUs, Rollplex achieves $1.23\times$--$1.30\times$ speedup over serial colocation and $1.57\times$--$2.24\times$ over disaggregation under the same GPU budget, while preserving the synchronous RL update.

AI.tldr: Rollplex reorganizes on-policy RL for vision-language models by overlapping prefix processing with rollout decoding, enabled by phase-aware memory management and parallelism-aware weight sharing; it yields 1.23–2.24x speedups on 32 H800 GPUs while preserving synchronous RL updates.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy RL pipelines are phase-heavy and sequential, causing underutilization when processing dense video inputs and prompts in vision-language models. Overlapping prefix computation with rollout can improve GPU utilization without violating synchronous RL semantics.
AI.method: Decompose reference and training phases and move the prefix computation into the rollout decode window. Two mechanisms: (1) Phase-aware memory management that keeps tensors resident in high-bandwidth memory based on producer–consumer lifetimes; (2) Parallelism-aware weight sharing that stores layout-compatible tensors in shared physical storage across different tensor-parallel degrees and reconstructs only incompatible tensors, avoiding a full actor copy.
AI.result: Empirical results on 32 H800 GPUs show 1.23×–1.30× speedup over serial colocation and 1.57×–2.24× speedup over disaggregation under the same GPU budget, while preserving synchronous RL updates.
AI.conclusion: Rollplex offers a practical runtime optimization for VLM-based embodiedRL by reconciling phase granularity with compute overlap, achieving substantial speedups without sacrificing RL semantics.

title: Program-space Diffusion for Morphology-to-Transcriptomics Prediction
summary:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables genome-wide gene expression profiling while preserving tissue architecture, but its cost and limited scalability remain major bottlenecks. This has motivated models that predict spatial expression directly from routine histology. Despite promising results, most existing approaches operate at the gene level without leveraging established transcriptomic modeling practices and rely on heterogeneous gene selection strategies, which complicates fair comparison across methods.
  We propose to reformulate morphology-to-transcriptomics prediction as conditional generation in transcriptional program space, thereby exploiting coordinated transcriptional variation instead of predicting genes independently. Using consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF), we extract a low-dimensional set of transcriptional programs capturing coordinated expression variation in the training data, and train a conditional diffusion model to generate program activations from histology. This formulation exploits coordinated transcriptional variation and substantially lowers the dimensionality of the conditional generative task.

AI.tldr: A framework that predicts transcriptional programs from histology by first decomposing gene expression with cNMF and then using a conditional diffusion model to generate program activations, thereby reducing dimensionality and leveraging coordinated transcriptional variation.
AI.motivation: Address the cost and scalability bottlenecks of spatial transcriptomics and improve fair cross-method comparisons by modeling transcriptomics at the program (coordinated) level rather than gene-by-gene.
AI.method: Apply consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to extract a low-dimensional set of transcriptional programs from training data; train a conditional diffusion model to map histology to program activations, exploiting coordinated variation and reducing conditional generation dimensionality.
AI.result: The approach substantially lowers the dimensionality of the generation task by working in program space and leverages coordinated transcriptional variation; quantitative performance metrics are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Modeling morphology-to-transcriptomics in the transcriptional-program space via cNMF and conditional diffusion offers a scalable, interpretable framework and facilitates fairer comparisons across methods by focusing on coordinated transcriptional signals.

title: RecipeNet: A Hierarchical Transformer for Recipe Data
summary: Recipe data arises in domains such as materials synthesis, pharmaceutical formulation, and industrial manufacturing, where procedures are represented as ordered sequences of steps containing heterogeneous structured fields. Existing tabular learning methods typically flatten this structure into fixed-schema representations, limiting their ability to capture hierarchical field interactions and procedural dependencies. We propose RecipeNet, a hierarchical Transformer architecture that encodes field-level interactions within each step and sequential dependencies across steps through stacked Transformer encoders. Experiments on multiple recipe datasets and tasks demonstrate that RecipeNet consistently outperforms existing tabular models, highlighting the value of hierarchical and sequential modeling for recipe representation learning.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical Transformer model, RecipeNet, encodes field-level interactions within each step and sequential dependencies across steps, outperforming tabular models on recipe-like data.
AI.motivation: Tabular methods flatten structured procedural data, losing hierarchical field interactions and procedural dependencies; a model that captures both field-level structure and step-wise order can improve recipe representation learning.
AI.method: Introduce RecipeNet, a hierarchical Transformer that encodes field-level interactions inside each step and stacks Transformer encoders to model cross-step sequential dependencies.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on multiple recipe datasets and tasks shows RecipeNet consistently outperforms existing tabular models, underscoring the value of hierarchical and sequential modeling for recipe representation learning.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical and sequential modeling enhances recipe representation and can generalize to other domains with structured procedural data.

title: Clearing the Fog: Towards Installing and Refining Proactive Exploration Capabilities in LLM Agents
summary: We study proactive exploration in LLM agents, i.e., the ability to explore an environment to acquire information that improves future decision-making. In this regard, we first identify two fundamental bottlenecks that hinder this capability and then propose \ours, a novel method designed to instill and refine proactive exploration. Specifically, \ours\ consists of two components: (1) Exploratory Data Construction, which synthesizes exploration-rich trajectories to mitigate the hindsight bias of standard demonstrations; and (2) RL Optimization with Contrastive Signal Guidance, which leverages contrastive trajectory pairs to distinguish productive exploration from redundant wandering. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of \ours\ and provide insights into the characteristics of proactive exploration. Our code is available at: https://github.com/GuanZhizhao/SAFARI.

AI.tldr: SAFARI introduces proactive exploration for LLM agents by (i) generating exploration-rich trajectories to combat hindsight bias and (ii) using contrastive RL signals to distinguish productive exploration from wandering, yielding improved exploratory behavior and decision-making.
AI.motivation: Proactive exploration is hampered by hindsight bias in demonstrations and ambiguous rewards that fail to incentivize useful exploration. The work aims to enable LLM agents to autonomously seek information that improves future decisions.
AI.method: Two-component framework: (1) Exploratory Data Construction that synthesizes exploration-focused trajectories to mitigate hindsight bias in standard demonstrations; (2) RL Optimization with Contrastive Signal Guidance that uses contrastive trajectory pairs to separate productive exploration from redundant wandering, guiding policy updates with a contrastive objective in addition to standard RL loss.
