AI.result: Extensive experiments validate SAFARI: it improves proactive exploration and provides insights into the nature of productive exploration. Ablation studies highlight the contribution of each component and the benefits of contrastive guidance; code is released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: SAFARI offers a practical and effective framework for fostering proactive exploration in LLM agents by combining curated exploration data with contrastive RL signals, and invites further investigation into the dynamics of productive exploration.

title: ScienceFlow: A long-horizon agent for ML research, scientific discovery and beyond
summary: Enabling LLM agents to sustain productive, stable, and goal-aligned research over extended horizons is a central challenge for autonomous machine learning and scientific discovery, as progress hinges on continuously managing evolving state, exploration decisions, and computational resources. Pioneering autoresearch agents, despite great success, still lack mechanisms for continuity, recovery from dead ends, and value-driven compute allocation, which inherently undermines overall search efficiency, wastes computational resources, and lowers the chance of ultimate success. To bridge this gap, we introduce ScienceFlow, an end-to-end autoresearch agent framework that organizes long-horizon research work into research segments grounded in executable workspaces. It represents research progress as recoverable executable states, enabling efficient exploration, revision, and execution. Transitions between research segments are governed by Executable-State Transition through Re-Anchoring (ESTRA), which selects either the live state or an archived state as the next anchor and determines whether to continue or redirect the research trajectory. An evidence-aware execution controller allocates resources to physical jobs based on resource availability, remaining budget, and validated progress. We evaluate ScienceFlow on tasks spanning machine learning, scientific modeling, and mathematical optimization. Results on diverse long-horizon benchmarks demonstrate its ability to sustain effective research processes, highlighted by a SOTA 70.22 percent Any-Medal score on the full MLE-bench within a 24-hour budget, outperforming prior reported results by 4.92 percentage points. The efficacy of ScienceFlow further demonstrates that efficient state management, adaptive exploration, and objective-aligned execution are critical for scaling autonomous research beyond short-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: ScienceFlow presents an end-to-end autoresearch framework that uses recoverable executable states and ESTRA transitions to maintain long-horizon, goal-aligned research with adaptive resource allocation; achieves SOTA on MLE-bench under a 24h budget.
AI.motivation: To address the core challenge of sustaining productive, stable, goal-aligned autonomous research over long horizons by providing continuity, recovery from dead ends, and efficient compute allocation.
AI.method: The framework partitions research into executable workspaces with recoverable states. Transitions are governed by Executable-State Transition through Re-Anchoring (ESTRA), which can re-anchor to live or archived states and decide continuation or redirection. An evidence-aware controller allocates compute based on resource availability, remaining budget, and validated progress. Evaluation spans machine learning, scientific modeling, and mathematical optimization tasks.
AI.result: Empirical results show sustained long-horizon research progress with a state-management and adaptive-exploration approach, achieving a new SOTA: 70.22% Any-Medal on the full MLE-bench within 24 hours, outperforming prior results by 4.92 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Effective state management, adaptive exploration, and objective-aligned execution are critical for scaling autonomous research beyond short-horizon interactions.

title: Disentangled Shared Representations Improve Morpho-Transcriptomic Integration
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the simultaneous profiling of gene expression and tissue morphology, creating an opportunity to learn multimodal representations capturing shared morpho-transcriptomic structure. However, standard multimodal models often compress modalities into a common latent space without explicitly separating shared and modality-specific sources of variation, which may limit downstream utility. We investigate whether explicit disentanglement of shared and private latent components improves multimodal representation learning for paired Hematoxylin \& Eosin (H\&E) and ST data. We compare VAE-based and contrastive approaches, each in standard and disentangled variants, across two cancer cohorts under matched experimental conditions. Representations are evaluated using cross-modal reconstruction, downstream probing and cross-modal probe transfer. The experiments suggest two main trends. First, contrastive objectives yield higher downstream probing performance than VAE-based models. Second, disentangled variants improve the selected reconstruction and probing metrics, although the gains depend on the model family, task, direction, and disentanglement strength. Overall, our results suggest that explicitly factorizing shared and modality-specific information can improve multimodal representation learning for spatial transcriptomics and provides a useful evaluation framework for future foundation models.

AI.tldr: Explicit disentanglement of shared and private latent components can improve multimodal representation learning for paired H&E and spatial transcriptomics, with contrastive objectives generally outperforming VAE-based models; benefits vary with model family, task, direction, and disentanglement strength.
AI.motivation: To enhance multimodal representation learning by separating shared information from modality-specific variation in paired histology (H&E) and spatial transcriptomics data.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of VAE-based and contrastive methods, each in standard and disentangled variants, evaluated on two cancer cohorts under matched experimental conditions; assessing cross-modal reconstruction, downstream probing, and cross-modal probe transfer.
AI.result: Contrastive objectives yield higher downstream probing performance than VAEs. Disentangled variants improve reconstruction and probing metrics, though gains depend on model family, task, direction, and the level of disentanglement strength.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly factorizing shared and modality-specific information can enhance multimodal representation learning for spatial transcriptomics and provides a useful framework for evaluating future foundation models.

title: Designing Sustainable Federated Learning as a Service using Neural Architecture Search
summary: The sustainability constraints of FLaaS consumers pose significant challenges to maintaining carbon-feasible federated training in FLaaS environments. These constraints often lead to infeasible consumer participation and unstable federated training under hard carbon constraints. We propose a Sustainable Federated Learning as a Service (SFLaaS), a carbon- constrained Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for heteroge- neous sustainable constraints. We introduce a requirement-driven search space that transforms consumer sustainability profiles into a feasible architecture region before federated execution. We develop a consumer-level carbon feasibility estimation mechanism to evaluate candidate architectures under dynamic carbon conditions. We propose a sustainable con- sumer scheduling strategy that adaptively selects feasible consumers and allocates local workloads to preserve consumer participation and statistical data coverage. An evolutionary search strategy jointly optimised for predictive performance, consumer feasibility, and participation coverage under hard carbon constraints. Experiments on real-world datasets and a simulated environment demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Sustainable Federated Learning as a Service (SFLaaS) for carbon-constrained FLaaS: a NAS-based framework that defines a requirement-driven search space, carbon feasibility estimation, sustainable client scheduling, and an evolutionary search optimizing accuracy, feasibility, and participation under hard carbon constraints; validated on real data and simulations.
AI.motivation: Address carbon feasibility challenges in FLaaS where consumer sustainability constraints impede participation and stable federated training under hard carbon budgets.
AI.method: Introduce a carbon-constrained Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework with a requirement-driven search space translating consumer sustainability profiles into a feasible architecture region; develop a consumer-level carbon feasibility estimator for dynamic carbon conditions; propose a sustainable consumer scheduling strategy to select feasible consumers and allocate local workloads; apply an evolutionary search optimized for predictive performance, consumer feasibility, and participation coverage under hard carbon constraints.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world datasets and simulated environments shows the approach achieves feasible, stable federated training under carbon constraints while maintaining predictive performance and broad participation.
AI.conclusion: SFLaaS enables sustainable federated learning under carbon constraints by integrating NAS with feasibility estimation and adaptive client scheduling, balancing performance with sustainability.

title: Wrong but Useful: Trajectory Value Beyond Answer Correctness in Multi-Agent Messages
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Includes an appendix and an ancillary reproducibility artifact
summary: Multi-agent reasoning systems often use agreement, confidence, or automated scores to decide which messages should shape a final answer. Such filtering assumes that a message likely to be correct is also worth keeping. Yet a wrong answer can contain a useful decomposition, constraint, or scientific principle. We test this distinction with Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD), a controlled measurement protocol that caches five independently generated messages and replays the same downstream solver, called the integrator, with each message available or hidden. The replay comparison measures a message's trajectory value: whether making the message available helps or harms subsequent reasoning. Across five mathematics and science benchmarks and two openly available model families, gpt-oss-120b and gemma-4-31B-it, wrong-helpful messages appear in every benchmark-model combination. Among wrong-answer messages that change final correctness, more than four in ten changes are helpful in each model. Controlled repeats show that the number of repeatable message effects is unlikely to arise from replay variation alone (p=0.0002). A focused intervention on repeatable wrong-helpful messages finds that the complete message works best, while retaining its reasoning preserves more success than retaining only its answer; the source of the complete-message advantage remains open. Within the same problem, repeated trajectory-value evidence also identifies a better keep-or-remove choice than answer correctness alone. Answer correctness is therefore informative but does not determine trajectory value. DHD measures this missing property and produces reusable labels for learning when agents should listen.

AI.tldr: Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD) reveals that wrong answers can contribute useful reasoning; trajectory-value-based evaluation, not final correctness, should guide when agents listen; DHD yields reusable labels for learning when to listen.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of agreement-based filtering in multi-agent reasoning by quantifying how a message affects downstream reasoning beyond final answer.
AI.method: Cache five independent messages and replay them to a common integrator with each message available or hidden. Measure trajectory value: whether availability helps or harms downstream reasoning. Test across five math/science benchmarks and two model families (gpt-oss-120b, gemma-4-31B-it). Analyze wrong-answer messages, assess repeatability with controlled repeats, and examine complete vs. partial message retention to understand its effects on final outcomes.
AI.result: Wrong-helpful messages appear across all benchmark-model combinations. Among wrong-answer messages that flip final correctness, more than 40% are helpful in each model. Controlled repeats show effects are unlikely due to replay variation (p=0.0002). Focused intervention indicates the complete message performs best, and retaining its reasoning yields more success than retaining only the final answer; the source of this advantage remains open. Within problems, trajectory-value evidence identifies better keep/remove choices than answer correctness alone. Answer correctness is informative but does not determine trajectory value.
AI.conclusion: DHD provides a measurable property (trajectory value) and reusable labels to learn when agents should listen, enabling learning-based filtering that leverages useful aspects of incorrect messages rather than discarding them solely due to error.

title: AgentRewind: Recoverable Execution for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Many real-world tasks require LLM agents to interact with their environments over long execution horizons. Errors that occur early in execution may propagate through both the agent context and environment state, and their effects may be difficult to reverse through subsequent actions. Existing methods mainly seek to reduce such errors through plan refinement and safety checks but provide little support after errors occur. To enable recovery during long-horizon execution, we present AgentRewind, a runtime recovery framework that records aligned checkpoints of the agent context and controlled environment, allowing agents to return to an earlier state and resume execution with information from previous attempts. We also construct MettleBench, a benchmark for evaluating task completion and partial progress on long-horizon engineering assignments containing a series of related requirements. Experiments across tasks, multiple models, execution strategies, and agent harnesses show that AgentRewind improves task success rate and average checklist progress over the compared baselines.

AI.tldr: Introduces AgentRewind for runtime recovery via checkpoints in long-horizon tasks and MettleBench benchmark; shows improved task success and progress across experiments.
AI.motivation: Errors in long-horizon execution can propagate through agent context and environment states, and are hard to reverse; need recovery mechanisms beyond plan refinement and safety checks.
AI.method: AgentRewind records aligned checkpoints of agent context and controlled environment to rewind and resume execution with information from prior attempts; MettleBench provides a suite of long-horizon engineering tasks with related requirements; extensive experiments across tasks, models, strategies, and agent harnesses.
AI.result: AgentRewind improves task success rate and average checklist progress compared with baselines across multiple tasks and configurations.
AI.conclusion: Runtime recovery via checkpointing is effective for long-horizon LLM agent execution; the proposed benchmark enables robust evaluation and could guide future improvements in recovery mechanisms.

title: Tripwire: Triggering Aligned Refusal via Statistically Certified Safety Neurons
summary: Neuron- and path-level interventions offer the finest-grained route to defending large language models (LLMs) against jailbreak attacks, yet existing methods fall short of this promise, i.e., they often compromise model utility significantly. Specifically, one line of work suppresses toxic neurons to erase harmful semantics, but since such semantics are distributed across the network, blocking every pathway forces a large intervention footprint. An alternative line of research focus on identify safety neurons using external classifiers. While promising, the existing approaches suffer from compromising neurons that are important for the model utility as well. Moreover, both approaches remain always on and thus perturb every benign request even when no attack is present. To address these limitations, we present \ours{}, a training-free defense that first identifies safety-specific neurons through per-neuron hypothesis tests under false-discovery-rate control together with a utility-specificity filter. Based on this identification, a trigger-style clamp holds the selected neurons at their harmful-conditional mean activations, injecting an internal harmful-input signal that triggers the refusal behavior learned during alignment. The clamp is then realized by two provably equivalent deployment modes, namely a detector-gated inference-time intervention and an offline bias-patch weight edit. Extensive experiments across four safety-aligned LLMs and four representative attacks demonstrate that \ours{} reduces the average attack success rate to at most 2.0\% while incurring a utility drop of only 0.5\% to 5.3\% on MT-Bench, the smallest among all defenses. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Tripwire-65C4.

AI.tldr: A training-free, per-neuron safety identification and clamp-based defense against LLM jailbreaks, selectively restricting harmful activations while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Defend LLMs from jailbreak attempts without large utility loss; prior neuron-suppressing methods are costly and external classifier-based approaches often harm utility; both are always-on and perturb benign requests.
AI.method: Identify safety-specific neurons via per-neuron hypothesis tests with false discovery rate control and a utility-specificity filter. Apply a trigger-like clamp to hold those neurons at harmful-conditional mean activations, injecting a harmful-input signal that triggers the model's refusal behavior. Deploy via two equivalent modes: detector-gated inference-time intervention or offline bias-patch weight edit.
AI.result: Empirically evaluated on four safety-aligned LLMs against four attack types; reduces average attack success rate to at most 2.0%; utility drop ranges from 0.5% to 5.3% on MT-Bench, the smallest among defenses.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a training-free, selective defense that maintains model utility while significantly lowering jailbreak success, with two deployment options and publicly available code.

title: LLMs Don't Pay for the Jump
summary: Zahavy [2026] argues that Large Language Models, despite their capabilities in induction and deduction, cannot perform the abductive "Jump" that produced Einstein's equivalence principle, and attributes this limitation to the absence of embodied simulation. Zheng-Xin [2026] and Farmer [2026] question whether embodiment is necessary for abduction, pointing to alternative routes to General Relativity and forms of abduction that require no sensorimotor grounding. Max Planck resolved the blackbody radiation problem in 1900. Planck's move to E = hν required no embodied simulation. It was motivated by a mathematical consequence of classical theory, an infinite predicted energy for a finite measured quantity, that could not be physically accepted. We show that neither induction nor deduction could have produced the postulate and argue that its adoption required a coupling between epistemic error and physical cost. We formalize this distinction through thermodynamic coupling and show that fixed-weight transformer inference lacks such coupling, regardless of model scale. This is consistent with empirical results showing that output entropy remains nearly unchanged across tasks with sharply increasing causal difficulty, even as accuracy falls from 100% to 17%. We therefore argue that the missing ingredient in machine abduction may lie deeper than embodiment: a system must have some physical mechanism through which epistemic error becomes costly enough to force revision.

AI.tldr: The abstract argues that abductive reasoning in AI cannot be achieved by induction/deduction or by embodiment alone; Planck’s blackbody shift to E= hν likely required a thermodynamic coupling between epistemic error and physical cost, which fixed-weight transformer models lack, suggesting that true machine abduction needs a cost-sensitive, physically grounded mechanism beyond mere embodiment.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether embodiment is necessary for abductive reasoning and how fundamental scientific postulates (like Planck’s E= hν) arise in AI, contrasting with claims that LLMs lack embodied grounding.
AI.method: Formalize the distinction using thermodynamic coupling between epistemic error and physical cost; analyze fixed-weight transformer inference for absence of such coupling; provide empirical observation that output entropy remains stable despite rising causal difficulty while accuracy drops, arguing for a need of cost-driven revision.
AI.result: Planck’s postulate cannot be derived from induction or deduction alone; a coupling between epistemic error and physical cost is necessary. Fixed-weight transformers lack this coupling. Empirical results show output entropy remains nearly constant even as causal difficulty sharply increases and accuracy falls, indicating a missing cost-sensitive mechanism in current models.
AI.conclusion: The missing ingredient for machine abduction lies deeper than embodiment: a physical mechanism that makes epistemic error costly enough to force revision is required.

title: The Past and Future of AI Scientists
summary:
We present a survey of the past and future of AI Scientists: machines capable of automating science. AI Scientists can originate hypotheses, deduce their consequences, design and execute experiments, interpret their results, and revise their beliefs. Such systems are integrated scientific agents, connected to the literature, formal knowledge, mathematical models, simulations, data-analysis systems and physical laboratories.
  Adam was the first machine to make novel scientific discoveries through cycles of hypothesis formation and physical experimentation. Eve established the architecture of the modern self-driving laboratory. Foundation models, autonomous agents and laboratory robotics now make it possible to build systems far more general than either Adam or Eve.
  The central problem is no longer whether individual components of science can be automated. They can. The problem is integration. AI Scientists must combine neural learning with logic, probability, mathematics, causal reasoning, simulation, experimental design, robotics and formal scientific records.
  AI Scientists have the potential to transform science: to make science faster, cheaper, more systematic and more reproducible. AI Scientists could investigate systems too complicated for unaided human science, and enable thousands of AI scientists to work together on single problems.
  The Nobel Turing Challenge sets the goal of developing by 2050 AI systems capable of automating Nobel-quality discoveries. Progress is ahead of schedule. When we succeed it will create a new form of science and transform the world.

AI.tldr: Survey of AI Scientists and the push toward integrated autonomous scientific agents, emphasizing the need to combine learning, logic, probability, causality, simulation, robotics, and formal knowledge to automate Nobel-quality science by 2050.
AI.motivation: To understand and map how AI can automate scientific inquiry, from hypothesis to experimentation and theory revision, and to forecast the trajectory and challenges of integrated AI-driven science.
AI.method: Conceptual survey and synthesis of progress: tracing Adam and Eve as historical milestones, analyzing current enablers (foundation models, autonomous agents, lab robotics), and outlining the integration challenges and architectural requirements.
AI.result: Argues that automation succeeds at component levels and now requires system-level integration; notes potential for faster, cheaper, more reproducible science and new forms of collaboration among AI scientists; progress toward Nobel-quality discoveries is ongoing and ahead of schedule.
AI.conclusion: If realized, AI Scientists will transform science and society, with the Nobel Turing Challenge driving a 2050 milestone; the future research is toward general, fully integrated scientific agents.

title: Knowing When to Stop: Bayesian Optimal Stopping for LLM Evaluations
summary: LLM evaluations often use fixed sampling budgets, testing every item the same number of times even after estimates are precise. We introduce optstop, a precision-based adaptive stopping framework that treats evaluation as a sequential measurement problem: keep sampling where uncertainty remains high, and stop where estimates are precise or stable enough. The framework builds on hierarchical Bayesian inference, supports binary, ordinal, and continuous outcomes, and keeps every benchmark item eligible for sampling, without requiring a calibrated item bank. It runs live or retrospectively, and includes a safeguard that samples more cautiously as measured performance approaches zero, where rare successes matter most. In an illustrative 200-item, 10-epoch evaluation, it removes 57%-97% of planned trials across nine validation settings, with overall conclusions equivalent to the full run. These results show that LLM evaluation compute can be allocated by uncertainty rather than by fixed repetition counts, with the magnitude of savings depending on evaluation design.

AI.tldr: Adaptive precision-based stopping for LLM evaluation using hierarchical Bayesian inference to allocate sampling by remaining uncertainty, enabling substantial trial reductions without changing conclusions.
AI.motivation: Fixed sampling budgets waste computational resources when estimates are already precise. A precision-driven, adaptive framework can save compute while accommodating binary, ordinal, and continuous outcomes without requiring a calibrated item bank.
AI.method: Treat evaluation as a sequential measurement problem. The framework adaptively continues sampling where uncertainty is high and stops where estimates are precise or stable. It employs hierarchical Bayesian inference, handles binary/ordinal/continuous outcomes, keeps all items eligible for sampling (no calibrated item bank required), supports live or retrospective runs, and includes safeguards that sample more cautiously as performance approaches zero.
AI.result: In a 200-item, 10-epoch evaluation, optstop removed 57–97% of planned trials across nine validation settings, with overall conclusions equivalent to the full run.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-driven sampling can substantially reduce LLM evaluation compute without altering conclusions; savings depend on evaluation design, and optstop offers a flexible, scalable approach that operates across outcome types and sampling modes.

title: The Dynamics of Intelligence Explosions
summary: AI is increasingly being used to help with AI R&D. Under certain conditions this feedback loop might be able to produce an intelligence explosion, with rapidly escalating AI capabilities. I explore the mathematics of the most explosive possibilities, with an eye to understanding what drives the dynamics. I show that singular growth (towards a vertical asymptote) is harder to achieve than would be expected from recent economics-inspired modelling, and that there is an important but neglected class of growth rates that are faster than exponential but don't lead to a vertical asymptote. I draw out the generation time (the time to go around the feedback loop) as a neglected parameter that plays a pivotal role in determining the behaviour of any intelligence explosion --- one cannot have singular growth unless the generation time rapidly approaches zero.

AI.tldr: Analyzes mathematical dynamics of AI-driven feedback loops; finds singular growth unlikely; identifies a faster-than-exponential regime without a vertical asymptote; generation time is the key parameter governing whether singular growth can occur.
AI.motivation: To understand what drives intelligence explosion dynamics and determine under what conditions explosive growth is feasible, particularly whether singular (vertical-asymptote) growth can occur.
AI.method: Theoretical mathematical analysis of growth models for AI R&D feedback loops; classification of growth regimes (singular vs faster-than-exponential); emphasis on the generation time parameter and its role in the dynamics.
AI.result: Singular growth toward a vertical asymptote is harder to achieve than some models predict; there exists a neglected class of growth rates that are faster than exponential but do not lead to a vertical asymptote; the generation time must approach zero for singular growth to occur; thus, generation time is pivotal in determining the trajectory of an intelligence explosion.
AI.conclusion: Generation time is a critical determinant of growth regime; without generation times approaching zero, singular growth cannot happen—affecting expectations about AI-driven explosions and guiding considerations of policy and research focus.

title: PACE-Bench: Benchmarking Physics Adaptation via Code Evolution in Dynamic Environments
summary: Self-evolving agents improve future behavior from interaction experience, yet existing evaluations typically optimize under fixed execution conditions and do not test recovery after those conditions change. To address this gap, we introduce PACE-Bench (Physics Adaptation via Code Evolution), a simulator-grounded benchmark of 144 source-to-target adaptation pairs across six physics domains. Each pair links a source environment to a mutated target environment with the same goal and interface. A code-driven design that succeeds in the source fails in the target, where agents must iteratively adapt it into a working target design using diagnostic sandbox feedback within a limited attempt budget. We compare ten self-evolving methods from four paradigms. The benchmark remains far from saturated: Reflexion + Qwen3-14B succeeds on only 35.9\% of full-benchmark pairs, while GPT-5.5 solves 66.7\% of the Statics subset under the full budget. Together, these results show that simulator-grounded reflection is more reliable than unverified self-revision, while memory anchors agents to early designs and broad tree search explores without converging. Even revealing exact physical changes does not raise the performance ceiling, pointing to mechanism redesign rather than parameter inference as the central bottleneck. Data and code are available at https://github.com/thunlp/PACE-Bench.

AI.tldr: PACE-Bench provides 144 source-to-target adaptation tasks across six physics domains to test self-evolving agents' adaptation when source-working code fails in the mutated target; current methods show limited success, underscoring the need for mechanism redesign over parameter tuning.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap where evaluations use fixed execution conditions and do not assess recovery after environmental changes; establish a simulator-grounded benchmark to study diagnosis, repair, and adaptation of self-evolving agents across physics domains.
AI.method: Construct 144 source–target pairs with the same goal/interface; require iterative adaptation of a code-driven design that succeeds in the source but not in the target, using diagnostic sandbox feedback within a limited attempt budget; compare ten self-evolving methods across four paradigms; report performance on the full benchmark and subsets; provide data and code publicly.
AI.result: Reflexion + Qwen3-14B solve 35.9% of full-benchmark pairs; GPT-5.5 solves 66.7% of the Statics subset under the full budget. Findings: simulator-grounded reflection outperforms unverified self-revision; memory anchors constrain exploration to early designs; broad tree search explores without convergence; even revealing exact physical changes does not raise the ceiling, indicating the bottleneck is mechanism redesign rather than parameter inference.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals significant gaps in current self-evolving approaches and points to mechanism redesign as the central bottleneck; the work provides a resources for broad evaluation and reports that simulator-grounded reasoning is more reliable than unverified revision. Data and code are available at the authors' GitHub.

title: Wyvern: An Agentic Framework for Generating Grounded Multimodal Reports
summary: In the current artificial intelligence-driven innovation era, the pace of knowledge growth is accelerating, and is hard to keep up with. While generative models are increasingly used to synthesize content, they often lack in information grounding. To address these peculiarities of our time, we propose Wyvern, a multi-agent framework for the automated generation of grounded, multimodal technical reports. Wyvern allows for the generation of multimodal outputs, integrating images, tables, and text with supporting references in a unified report. Additionally, a particular focus is placed on the grounding of the content, with the implementation of a claims auto-revision stage. We conduct a human evaluation study to assess the quality of our proposed framework. The results show that the figures' informativeness is perceived as superior to that of a recent baseline in 87% of cases. Furthermore, Wyvern's reports are rated as more useful than those produced by three alternative methods in 63% to 100% of instances. We also carry out automatic evaluations showing that Wyvern gains up to 2.3$\times$ in citation recall and 1.6$\times$ in citation precision with respect to the baselines.

AI.tldr: Wyvern is a multi-agent framework for grounded, multimodal technical report generation that integrates images, tables, and text with references, featuring a claims auto-revision stage; it achieves higher informativeness and citation performance against baselines.
AI.motivation: Growing pace of knowledge and widespread use of generative models requires content grounding; need for reliable, multimodal reports with verifiable references.
AI.method: Wyvern employs a multi-agent system to generate multimodal outputs (images, tables, text) with supporting references; incorporates a claims auto-revision stage for grounding; evaluates via human studies and automatic metrics on citation recall/precision.
AI.result: Human evaluation shows figures' informativeness surpasses a recent baseline in 87% and Wyvern's reports are more useful than three baselines in 63–100% of cases; automatic evaluation reports up to 2.3x citation recall and 1.6x citation precision vs baselines.
AI.conclusion: Wyvern demonstrates enhanced grounding and usefulness in automated, multimodal technical reporting, driven by systematic reasoning, multimodal integration, and auto-revision, with potential for more reliable AI-generated technical literature.

title: SheetCompass: Hierarchical Relation Graphs for Agentic Spreadsheet Reasoning
summary: Spreadsheets are widely used to organize, analyze, and manipulate semi-structured data, yet automated spreadsheet reasoning remains challenging for large language models (LLMs). Real-world workbooks often contain implicit cross-table associations, fine-grained column dependencies, and complex spatial layouts. Existing methods typically flatten these multidimensional structures into sequential strings, losing important intra-sheet boundaries and inter-sheet semantics. Consequently, LLMs cannot exploit the global spatial context that human experts naturally use when inspecting spreadsheets. We propose SheetCompass, a graph-guided and memory-driven agentic framework for spreadsheet reasoning and automation. SheetCompass explicitly models structural relationships within and across worksheets while maintaining task-relevant information in memory, enabling agents to reason more effectively over complex workbooks.

AI.tldr: SheetCompass uses graph-structured reasoning and memory to improve LLM-based spreadsheet analysis and automation.
AI.motivation: Real-world spreadsheets have implicit cross-table relations and complex spatial layouts that flattening into sequences fails to preserve; enabling global spatial/contextual reasoning is crucial for automated spreadsheet work.
AI.method: A graph-guided, memory-driven agentic framework that explicitly models structural relationships within and across worksheets and retains task-relevant information in memory to support reasoning over complex workbooks.
AI.result: Idea and design proposal; the abstract does not report empirical results or evaluation.
AI.conclusion: A graph-guided, memory-driven approach can enhance spreadsheet reasoning and automation by preserving intra- and inter-sheet structure and context for LLMs.

title: Shift Aware Transfer Learning with Adaptive Dual-Encoder Fusion for PM Forecasting in Data-Limited Environments
summary: Short-horizon forecasting of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) remains difficult when observations from the target domain are limited and the statistical properties of the source and target domains differ. In these settings, models trained only on local data may not capture complex temporal dynamics, while direct transfer learning can result in negative transfer. This study develops a shift-aware dual-encoder transfer framework that combines source-domain knowledge with target-specific representation learning. The source encoder was pretrained using hourly observations from 10 U.S. monitoring locations. The framework was then adapted and evaluated using two years of hourly observations from 77 stations in Taiwan under a chronological train-validation-test protocol. Among the four principal baselines, the frozen-source dual-encoder model achieved the best performance, with MSE = 21.8960, MAE = 3.1597, and R^2 = 0.8725. This corresponds to an MSE reduction of approximately 7.1% relative to TL-v1 and 4.1% relative to TL-v2. The ablation analysis showed that removing the Taiwan-specific branch caused the largest decline in performance. Allowing the source encoder to adapt produced the best overall result, with MSE = 21.6575, MAE = 3.1383, and R^2 = 0.8739. SHAP analysis indicated that predictions were driven mainly by recent PM2.5 observations and meteorological variables related to pollutant transport and dispersion. These results suggest that source-domain knowledge is most effective when target-specific information is preserved and the transferred representation is allowed to adapt under target supervision.

AI.tldr: Shift-aware dual-encoder transfer framework improves short-horizon PM2.5 forecasting under domain shift by combining pretrained source knowledge with target-specific representation learning, showing gains on Taiwan data and identifying recent observations and meteorology as key drivers.
AI.motivation: Forecast PM2.5 with limited target-domain data and distribution shifts between source and target domains; mitigate negative transfer and leverage cross-domain knowledge with target adaptation.
AI.method: Pretrain a source encoder on hourly observations from 10 US stations; adapt to 77 Taiwan stations using a two-branch (dual-encoder) architecture with a Taiwan-specific branch; chronological train-validation-test protocol; compare four baselines including TL variants and a frozen-source model; ablation removing Taiwan branch and enabling source adaptation; SHAP to assess feature influence.
AI.result: Best baseline among four: frozen-source dual-encoder with MSE 21.8960, MAE 3.1597, R^2 0.8725, yielding ~7.1% MSE reduction vs TL-v1 and ~4.1% vs TL-v2. Allowing source encoder adaptation improves to MSE 21.6575, MAE 3.1383, R^2 0.8739. Ablation shows the Taiwan-specific branch is critical; SHAP indicates predictions driven mainly by recent PM2.5 and meteorological factors related to transport/dispersion.
AI.conclusion: Source-domain knowledge is most effective when target-specific information is preserved and the transferred representation is allowed to adapt under target supervision; the approach mitigates negative transfer and exploits cross-domain signals for improved short-horizon PM2.5 forecasting.

title: Twin: Playing an Unknown Game with a Test-Time Digital Twin
comment: Project website with action-by-action replays of all 25 runs: https://arc-agi-3-twin.vercel.app/ Code: https://github.com/Alexyskoutnev/TWIN-ARC-AGI-3
summary: We present a Test-time World-model Inference (Twin) system, in which a frontier coding agent writes an executable world model for completing continual learning tasks, such as ARC-AGI-3 games. Traditional approaches hand-engineer such models, one custom design per task. Each game hides its rules and goal, and our system constructs them from simulation and interaction alone. Its inductive prior over grid games is strong enough to recover the true transitions of the game and the goal on nearly all levels. Replay validation happens in a twin world model. The harness enforces that an action is not made until the program reproduces every previous observed game transition. Each mismatch between a world model prediction and the actual action result becomes a counterexample that is used to repair the world model. Twin clears 179 out of 183 levels (97.8%), and does so more efficiently than humans in 158 out of 179 levels (88.3%). The system infers the goal before any reward on 156 of the levels it clears (87.2%), and in the remaining levels automatically discovers the goal by search. The benchmark scores completion and action efficiency, between 0 and 100, against humans playing each game for the first time. Played directly, the base model scores only 7.8%; an off-the-shelf harness increases it to 61.1%, whereas our twin world model increases the same base model to 93.3%, clearing 23 out of 25 games. Building a usable world model is simpler than anticipated, whereas the harder problem is inferring the right goal.

AI.tldr: Twin: a test-time, frontier-driven world-model inference system where a coding agent generates an executable world model, validated by a twin world-model replay loop. It learns goals from interaction, repairs models via counterexamples, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on ARC-like grid games, often before rewards are observed.
AI.motivation: Automate construction of executable world models without hand-engineered task designs, enabling continual learning across games with hidden rules and goals and reducing reliance on human-crafted priors.
AI.method: A frontier-coding agent writes executable world-models. A twin world model replays observed transitions to validate predictions; mismatches yield counterexamples to repair the model. The harness prevents actions until transitions are reproduced. The system infers goals (often before rewards) and uses search to discover goals when needed. Evaluation on ARC-AGI-3 grid games compares base models, harness-enhanced models, and Twin.
AI.result: Twin clears 179/183 levels (97.8%), outperforming humans in 158/179 levels (88.3%). It infers goals before rewards on 156/179 levels (87.2%), and clears 23/25 games. Baseline scores: 7.8% (no harness), 61.1% (with harness), 93.3% (Twin).
AI.conclusion: The approach shows that building a usable executable world model is feasible with a twin validation loop, while inferring the correct goal remains the harder challenge. The method yields high performance in a suite of grid-world tasks and demonstrates efficient, model-based problem solving with automatic goal discovery.

title: Split the Labor: Separating Evidence Interpretation from Decision Aggregation
summary: Systems that ask a language model to reach a conclusion from many sources usually concatenate them into one prompt. This conflates two operations with different requirements. Interpreting a source rewards capacity and context. Combining interpretations rewards fixed arithmetic, comparability across instances, and the option to return nothing. Once separated, the design problem becomes the interface between them. We propose a four-field evidence tuple (hypothesis, reliability bucket, rationale, provenance) and show that fixing it determines both halves. The separation also reveals a failure mode in how such systems combine, which we call count-scale drift. Thresholding a sum of unnormalized weights is exactly posterior thresholding, but at an operating point that slides with the number of sources consulted. The slide grows with reader reliability. When source reliabilities differ, the vote rule and the posterior order instances differently, and no threshold reconciles them. Pooling calibrated log-likelihood ratios addresses both problems. The fix is arithmetic rather than architectural, and applies to a class of rules beyond language models: score-summing triage engines, diagnostic panels scored by counting positives, and additive multi-signal detectors. We then instantiate the principle twice on one longitudinal corpus, once after outcomes resolve and once before. The same partition helps in both, at different granularities: over reading in the first, over learning capacity in the second. There, a small sequence encoder on an easy auxiliary objective plus a tree ensemble carrying the censored survival loss reaches 0.921 AUPRC against 0.805 for a hand-crafted baseline. We separate what transfers from what must be re-estimated per domain, and state five predictions that would falsify the framework, three negative results, and which comparisons remain confounded.

AI.tldr: Four-field evidence tuple separates interpretation from aggregation in multi-source reasoning; identifies count-scale drift; advocates pooling calibrated log-likelihood ratios; demonstrates arithmetic fix with a longitudinal corpus achieving strong AUPRC gains; outlines falsifiability tests and confounds.
AI.motivation: Clarify the design space for multi-source reasoning by separating two core operations (interpreting sources vs. aggregating interpretations) that are typically conflated when concatenating many sources into a single prompt.
AI.method: Propose an evidence tuple (hypothesis, reliability bucket, rationale, provenance) to fix the interface between interpretation and aggregation. Analyze thresholding of unnormalized weights as a drift-prone posterior rule. Propose calibrated log-likelihood ratio pooling. Instantiate the principle twice on a longitudinal corpus: once after outcomes resolve and once prior to outcomes, using a small sequence encoder on an auxiliary objective plus a tree ensemble trained with censored survival loss; report 0.921 AUPRC vs 0.805 baseline.
AI.result: Separation yields distinct optimization targets for interpretation and aggregation. Calibrated LLR pooling addresses count-scale drift and miscalibration across varying source counts and reliabilities. Empirical gain on a longitudinal corpus (0.921 AUPRC vs 0.805 baseline). Generalizes to other domains (score-summing triage engines, diagnostic panels, additive detectors). Provides a concrete falsifiability plan (five predictions) and notes confounds.
AI.conclusion: The corrective fix is arithmetic rather than architectural, and the approach clarifies what transfers between domains versus what must be re-estimated per domain. The evidence tuple offers a reusable interface for combining sources and identifying where to focus improvements.

title: Participatory Moral AI Is Not Neutral: The Invisible Hand of Developers
summary: As AI systems make more morally loaded decisions across society, one response has been moral preference elicitation. In this approach, researchers poll participants on hypothetical dilemmas and use the aggregated votes to train a policy that an AI model then applies at scale. Before any vote is cast, developers make three key choices in the moral AI elicitation pipeline: feature scoping, voter sampling, and question framing. In other words, they decide which features go to a vote, which voters to include, and how to present the question. These choices are often opaque, undocumented, and treated as technical details rather than normative ones. We examine each of these choices within a common empirical study and show that each can shape the preferences produced by moral AI elicitation. Across two phases (N = 809) in three deployment contexts (i.e., AI kidney allocation, AI agents simulating absent workers, and generative AI depictions of the deceased), we examine the three main stages of the moral AI elicitation pipeline. First, morally relevant features shift across contexts. This suggests that feature schemas should not be assumed to transfer across deployment domains. Second, preferences differ by political ideology for roughly one-third of features, with some differences reversing direction. The ideological composition of the voter pool can therefore affect the resulting aggregated preference profile. Third, the wording of the elicitation question can narrow or widen ideological gaps by up to a full scale point. The framing conditions also change how moral foundations are associated with participants' judgments. Taken together, these findings suggest that voting-based alignment cannot deliver fair or transparent AI by aggregation alone; at minimum, each stage of the moral AI elicitation pipeline should be audited and disclosed.

AI.tldr: Moral AI elicitation choices (feature scoping, voter sampling, framing) shape outcomes; context, ideology, and question wording influence results, so aggregation alone cannot ensure fair alignment—audits of each stage are needed.
AI.motivation: To expose how design choices in moral AI elicitation bias the resulting policy and argue for transparency and auditing of the pipeline.
AI.method: Empirical study (two phases, N=809) across three deployment contexts (AI kidney allocation, AI-deployed absent workers, and depictions of the deceased). Analyzed three pipeline stages: feature schemas, voter composition, and elicitation wording; tested for context shifts, ideological differences, and framing effects on moral judgments and foundations.
AI.result: Findings: feature schemas vary by deployment context; roughly one-third of features show ideological differences in preferences (direction can reverse); voting pool ideology affects aggregated profiles; question framing can narrow or widen ideological gaps by up to one scale point and alters associations with moral foundations.
AI.conclusion: Aggregation-based alignment is insufficient for fairness and transparency. Each stage of the moral AI elicitation pipeline should be audited, documented, and disclosed to ensure responsible deployment.

title: Handover of In-Context Learning State Across Session Boundaries
summary: This study investigates the methodological and theoretical properties of session handover in applications that use large language models. A task may continue in a new session when the context reaches the model's input limit, when the application restarts, or when another agent is asked to finish the task. The application must then decide which information from the earlier session to pass on. We formulate handover as the transfer of a task-relative in-context learning (ICL) state and distinguish exact recovery of earlier material from preservation of the target distribution. Under an exogeneity condition, predictive equivalence characterizes the coarsest deterministic sufficient handover and gives a fixed-length bit requirement. The analysis isolates the effects of the memory constraint, the writer, and the continuation procedure, and quantifies the cost of writing before the realized downstream query is known. We propose a three-part record that stores decisions and constraints exactly, uses task-justified statistics for repeated evidence, and retains original observations whose effect is not preserved by those statistics. Gaussian linear regression gives an exact finite-dimensional handover and finite-bit perturbation bounds, while nonparametric regression gives upper and lower bounds that relate memory to squared prediction error. These results provide a theory and method for deciding what a handover must retain and how its memory requirement depends on the continuation task.

AI.tldr: Formalizes session handover for LLM-based tasks as transferring a task-relative in-context learning state. Defines predictive equivalence under exogeneity, yielding a fixed-length memory budget for the coarsest sufficient handover. Proposes a three-part record, analyzes memory- and writer-continuation roles, and derives exact finite-dimensional results under Gaussian assumptions and bounds under nonparametric settings for memory vs prediction error.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable task continuation across sessions in LLM-driven applications while respecting memory limits, by characterizing what information must be retained to preserve the target distribution of task performance.
AI.method: 1) Model handover as transfer of a task-relative ICL state. 2) Impose exogeneity, derive predictive equivalence, and identify the coarsest deterministic sufficient handover. 3) Introduce a three-part record for decisions, constraints, evidence; analyze effects of memory, writer, and continuation procedure. 4) Provide Gaussian (linear) analysis with exact finite-dimensional handover and perturbation bounds; extend with nonparametric regression to bound memory vs squared prediction error.
AI.result: 1) Existence of a fixed-length, minimum necessary memory budget for the coarsest sufficient handover under the exogeneity condition. 2) A three-part handover framework that exactly preserves decisions/constraints while retaining only task-justified statistics and non-preserved original observations. 3) Exact finite-dimensional handover for Gaussian linear models with finite-bit perturbation bounds; nonparametric results yield upper/lower bounds linking memory to prediction error.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical foundation and practical method for deciding what to retain during handover and how memory requirements scale with the continuation task, enabling principled design of cross-session handover strategies in LLM-based systems.
